What was filed as a first claimed autonomous zero-day chain with unsettled characterization now carries the tool attribution from the victim itself — the chain's autonomy claim still rests on DIVD's account, but the ARTEX link upgrades the entry from unattributed specimen to a named-framework instance, and ties the DIVD incident to the Vapor Panda campaign class (same framework, different operator — ARTEX is now a shared tool, not one actor's signature).

- **Storm-Zero-Nine-Four-Zero and ConnectWise: second ARTEX campaign, supply-chain entry (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, October twenty-first, twenty twenty-six; new to record; material).** A separate China-state-aligned group Microsoft tracks as Storm-Zero-Nine-Four-Zero used ARTEX since as early as September twenty twenty-six and is assessed responsible for the ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain compromise, reaching two thousand two hundred fifty Microsoft three hundred sixty-five tenants; in several observed intrusions Microsoft measured under three hours from initial targeting to privileged cloud access. - **North Korean groups adopt ARTEX (Microsoft, October twenty-ninth, twenty twenty-six; new to record; minor lane datapoint).** Microsoft identified two North Korean groups, Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet, using ARTEX since late October; Microsoft rates North Korean AI adoption as high but assesses their AI-enabled operations remain human-directed, not fully autonomous. Lesson: the diffusion marker — a Chinese-built open-source framework in North Korean hands within weeks of its first public campaign reporting — plus the honest counterweight to the autonomy headline: even the adopters' operations stay human-directed at decision points. ARTEX alone cannot name an attacker — the framework is a tool signature, not an attribution.

- **Slopsquatting: AI-hallucinated package names as a predictable supply-chain surface (USENIX Security twenty twenty-five study, as carried this window; new to record; material).** Researchers analyzed more than five hundred seventy-six thousand Python and JavaScript code samples generated by sixteen language models: nineteen point seven percent of recommended package references did not exist in the target registry (about two hundred five thousand unique non-existent names); commercial models averaged at least five point two percent hallucination, open-source models about twenty-one point seven percent. The exploit-relevant figure: when prompts that produced hallucinated names were rerun, forty-three percent of the fake names reappeared every time — predictable enough for attackers to register in advance and wait for a developer, or an autonomous coding agent, to run the install. The harder variant is already the filed shape: a package that actually exists, looks legitimate, and carries install-script malware — the hallucination is just the cheapest way to pick the name. Lesson: the agent's package choice is an untrusted proposal, not an approved decision — every AI-suggested dependency is treated as untrusted input, and the forty-three percent repeatability figure is the reason an allowlist, not a blocklist, is the control. Pairs with the filed RedC2 import-graph loader as the second npm-lane entry this quarter where the install step itself is the attack.
  - Source: https://medium.com/@ikaruscareer/ai-coding-agents-can-be-steered-into-installing-malicious-open-source-packages-39ba415bc70c
  - [Corroborated — peer-reviewed USENIX Security twenty twenty-five study as carried by a secondary carrier; figures rest on the carrier's summary, study not read first-party this pass]

- **Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant, "ARTEX and Friends": PentAGI and Hexstrike join ARTEX in real incident-response cases (Google Cloud Blog, October 30, 2026; new to record; material).** Since late August 2026, Mandiant incident-response engagements show multiple threat actors abusing open-source agentic penetration-testing frameworks: ARTEX (Go, Next.js console, six specialized sub-agents), PentAGI (VXControl; Kali Linux tools in isolated sandboxes, more than a dozen cloud and local language-model backends), CAIRN, Hexstrike, plus possible custom harnesses — across reconnaissance, cloud permission testing, privilege escalation, lateral movement, database exploitation, and exfiltration preparation. Measurements: ARTEX execution bursts of roughly two to twenty-five seconds; one case generated twenty-seven events in twenty-three seconds during cloud permission checks; a Linux Weaver OA case generated two hundred forty log events during attempts that achieved partial command execution and reconnaissance. An overlapping account from Wiz (October 22): ARTEX-associated activity targeting information-technology and software vendors through identity services (Okta, Entra, Cognito, Microsoft 365 integrations); most attempts described failed; the actor Google tracks as UNC7228 (overlaps Storm-0940) moved from first compromised account to deep system access in about four hours in typical cases and fifteen minutes in one case. Forks and variants: ScopeWeaver (localized), ARTEX PRO (commercial); the creator pulled the original repository on October 8 after more than twelve thousand forks. Lesson: the framework census grows from one named tool to four, and CAIRN's vendor naming corroborates the filed NorForge Cairn campaign from the vendor side; the "fast but noisy" shape (short bursts, large event traces) is the detection handle, and the most-attempts-failed note is the counterweight to the machine-speed headline. Detection must key on framework markers, not actor attribution — the same lesson the filed Storm-0940 entry drew, now with four frameworks on the list. Watch: the Google primary (exact framework-by-case mapping; whether Hexstrike appears in a named intrusion or only in the census) and any second-vendor confirmation of the burst and timing figures.

- **XCPE: manufacturer-built firmware backdoor botnet disrupted at 1.3M+ devices (Google Threat Intelligence Group report, November 2, 2026; new to record; material).** Google assesses with high confidence that Videostrong Technology Co., a Shenzhen Android device maker selling TV boxes under its MECOOL brand and building for other labels, intentionally developed, deployed, and operated the backdoor for financial gain. The implant runs as x.cpe (also seen as com.oemservice), preloaded in device firmware with system-level privileges, in a three-stage architecture that evolved since late 2024. Scale: more than 1.3 million devices enrolled, overwhelmingly Android TV set-top boxes, plus Android-based telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage; TrendAI counted 1,472,554 infected devices across 206 models in more than 170 countries between June and October 2026. The business model was access rental: the maker sold access to criminal affiliates and loaded their malware modules through the backdoor. The takedown used legal action against XCPE's domains and servers plus the command-and-control domains of more than a dozen malware families delivered through the backdoor, with Japan's National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI participating; Google banned Videostrong and any future subsidiaries or affiliates from building certified Android devices, and estimates the affiliate takedowns sever criminal access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices. The caveat that decides the story: the takedown severs control but does not remove the implant — it lives in firmware, cannot be removed by the owner, and can reinstall itself from the manufacturer partition after reboot; Google has published no complete affected-model list. Lesson: the supply chain is not the compromised link here, it is the adversary — and a takedown is a disruption, not a remediation. Firmware provenance is untrusted until proven, and a banned maker's already-shipped fleet stays a live specimen set after the headlines fade. [CORROBORATED — six independent secondary carriers agreeing on the Google report skeleton, the Videostrong attribution, the 1.3M+ scale, the takedown actions, and the firmware-residency caveat; Google primary not read first-party this pass; the 10-million figure is Google's assessment, not an independent count]
