- **AVIF / HEIF: the picture that is a table of contents, or: the index is the picture's shadow, and the payload is somewhere else.** AVIF is an AV1-coded image carried in HEIF, which is the ISO Base Media File Format (ISOBMFF, ISO/IEC 14496-12) under the MIAF profile (ISO/IEC 23000-22) — the same box grammar as MP4, with the video track replaced by an item table. The file opens with `ftyp`: major and compatible brands name the kind — `avif` for a still image, `avis` for an image sequence, `mif1`/`miaf` for the HEIF/MIAF base — and a reader that stops at the brand has read a label, not a picture. The real file is the `meta` box (a FullBox: 4 bytes of version and flags before the children), and `meta` is a table of contents, not content: `hdlr` set to `pict` marks the content as pictures, `pitm` names the primary item the viewer shows by default, `iinf` lists one entry per item with its type (`av01` for a coded AV1 image, `grid` for a tiled derived image, `Exif`, `mime` for XMP), `iloc` gives the byte offsets and lengths — one or more extents per item — pointing into `mdat` (or `idat`, where the payload may ride instead), and `iref` types the links between items: `auxl` (this alpha belongs to that image), `dimg` (these tiles belong to this grid), `thmb` (this thumbnail), `cdsc` (this metadata describes that image). A reader can find the thumbnail, check the dimensions, and read the Exif without decoding a single AV1 byte — which is exactly why the index, not the pixels, is the interrogation surface. [VERIFIED — AVIF specification v1.2.0 (AOM, Oct 2025) box inventory and brand rules; CORROBORATED — the `idat` alternative payload location, per the same specification's note]

- **The item properties are a second index, and the grid is a picture assembled from claims.** Inside `meta`, `iprp` holds `ipco` (the property container) and `ipma` (which item each property attaches to). The properties that decide what the picture *is*: `ispe` (spatial extents — width and height, big-endian, after the version/flags), `pixi` (bits per channel), `av1C` (the AV1 codec configuration, mandatory and essential for every `av01` item, its fields required to match the Sequence Header OBU in the item data), and `colr` (colour information). The grid derivation is the sharpest case: a `grid` item carries row and column counts and output dimensions, and its tiles — ordinary `av01` items — are linked to it by `dimg` references. The viewer never sees a tile; it sees the assembly the grid item claims. An alpha channel is the same shape in a different uniform: an auxiliary image item linked by `auxl`, its role named by the `auxC` property (`urn:mpeg:mpegB:cicp:systems:auxiliary:alpha`). And the metadata items are nested containers in their own right: the Exif item is not bare TIFF — it starts with a 4-byte big-endian offset to the TIFF header, with some writers adding an `Exif\0\0` prefix before it — so the TIFF tree the TIFF entry taught the decoder to distrust rides inside the item table, one offset-skip away from a naive reader. [VERIFIED — AVIF specification: `av1C` mandatory/essential status and Sequence Header match rule, `ispe`/`pixi`/`colr` roles, grid derivation via `dimg`; CORROBORATED — the Exif item's 4-byte TIFF offset prefix and optional `Exif\0\0` prefix, per independent converter writeups]

- **The sanctioned compartments.** Four, and the renderer reads none of them as picture. `free` and `skip` boxes may appear at any level of the hierarchy and readers are expected to ignore them — padding with a license, Matroska's `Void` in box form. Additional boxes in the `meta` hierarchy not listed in the specification may also be present and may be ignored by readers — the unknown-element attic, now inside the table of contents itself. The thumbnail item (`thmb`) is a second, smaller picture the viewer may show instead of the primary — a picture whose pixels need not match the primary's, graded by no rule in the file. And the `Exif`/`mime` items are whole documents (a TIFF tree, an RDF/XML packet) carried as items the image reader is told to carry, not to read — WebP's `EXIF`/`XMP ` chunks in an index's uniform. [VERIFIED — AVIF specification: `free`/`skip` ignore rule, unlisted-`meta`-box ignore rule]

- **Worked miniature (built and walked this pass).** A 294-byte box skeleton — `ftyp` (28 bytes: major `avif`, minor 0, compatible `avif`/`mif1`/`miaf`), `meta` (238 bytes: `hdlr` at 40, `pitm` at 73 naming item 1, `iinf` at 87 with items 1 `av01` and 2 `Exif`, `iloc` at 154, `iprp` at 198 with `ispe` 64×48 and `av1C`), `mdat` (28 bytes: 20 bytes of payload at offset 274). Both walks land exactly: top-level boxes at 0/28/266 ending at 294, `meta` children ending exactly at the `meta` boundary, and the `iloc` extents (274 + 12, 286 + 8) slice back the exact payload bytes. The divergence is the entry, and it needs no malformed box: inflate item 1's extent length from 12 to 10,000 against the 20-byte payload and a naive slicer returns 20 bytes with no error — a short read that grades as a complete item if the reader never checks the length it was promised. The twin divergences cost no bytes at all: an item declared in `iinf` with no `iloc` extent is an orphan the reader can never materialize, and a `pitm` naming a non-image item (the Exif item, say) makes the table of contents point the viewer at metadata and call it the picture. [VERIFIED — the miniature, constructed and walked this pass]

- **Decoder-design note (AVIF → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The item inventory is the intake.** The Gauntlet's container pass on any AVIF/HEIF walks the full box tree and diffs three lists against each other: `iinf` (what the file claims exists), `iloc` (where each item's bytes are claimed to be), and `ipma` (which properties attach to which item). Every orphan item, every extent escaping `mdat`/`idat`, every property attached to an item that does not exist, and every `pitm` pointing at a non-image type is a divergence event — the Matroska `SeekHead` disagreement and the WebP flag-without-chunk disagreement, now between three lists instead of two. (2) **"Renders clean" and "carries only a picture" are different claims.** The renderer is the forgiving reader by spec: it ignores `free`/`skip` and unlisted boxes, shows the primary item, and never opens the metadata items. Grade the file against the inventory — every item named with type and byte budget, every tile and thumbnail and auxiliary accounted for — never against the render. (3) **Nested containers get nested inventories, and short reads suspend.** The Exif item's TIFF tree gets the TIFF entry's treatment, the XMP item's XML gets the XML treatment, and an extent that yields fewer bytes than promised suspends the verdict: UNREAD, never CLEAN — the MacBinary inflated-length lesson in a table of contents' coat. - **JPEG XL: the picture that is two files at once, or: the signature is a fork, and the ancestor rides inside.** JPEG XL (ISO/IEC 18181, 2021–2022) is the only picture format in this section that arrives in two shapes wearing one extension. The bare codestream opens with two bytes, `FF 0A`. The box form opens with a 12-byte signature box — size 12, type `JXL ` (note the trailing space), contents `0D 0A 87 0A` — and then a run of ISOBMFF-style boxes: 4-byte big-endian size (size==1 means a 64-bit largesize follows, size==0 means to end of file, the MP4 entry's escape hatches in a still picture's uniform), then a 4-byte type. A reader that checks only the first two bytes calls the box form a different format; a reader that checks only the box signature misses the bare codestream entirely. The format's own first decision is which file you are holding. [VERIFIED — ISO/IEC 18181-2 box inventory and the two magic numbers, via the standard's table of contents and the format's public specification record]

- **The box inventory, and the ancestor in the attic.** The boxes the standard names: the signature box, the File Type box, the Level box (`jxll`), the JUMBF box, the Exif box (`Exif`, carrying a TIFF tree with a TIFF-header offset, the AVIF entry's nested container in a third uniform), the XML box (`xml`, an XMP packet or any XML document, the WebP entry's `XMP ` chunk in box form), the Brotli-compressed box (a box whose content is another box, compressed — the inventory must decompress before it can list), the Frame Index box (`jxli`), the Codestream box (`jxlc`, the whole codestream in one box), the Partial Codestream box (`jxlp`, the codestream split across boxes, each carrying a 4-byte index), and the JPEG Bitstream Reconstruction Data box (`jbrd`). The last is the sharpest compartment in the whole section: a JPEG transcoded losslessly into JPEG XL can carry, in `jbrd`, the data needed to rebuild the *original JPEG bitstream byte for byte* — the file contains its own ancestor, and the decoder can hand back a JPEG that never passed through a lossy step. A specimen that "is a JXL" may also be, reversibly, a JPEG — and the reconstruction data is itself a second file's worth of bytes riding inside the first. [VERIFIED — ISO/IEC 18181-2 §9 box types: signature, file type, level, JUMBF, Exif, XML, Brotli-compressed, frame index, codestream, partial codestream, JPEG bitstream reconstruction data]

- **The partial codestream is a reassembly claim.** `jxlp` boxes carry an index, and the codestream is the boxes concatenated *in index order*, not in file order. A file that lists index 1 before index 0 is not corrupt — it is a file whose reading order is a claim the walk must test. Worked miniature (built and walked this pass): a 43-byte box-form file — the 12-byte signature box, then a `jxlp` box at offset 12 carrying index 1 (3 bytes `33 44 55`), then a `jxlp` box at offset 27 carrying index 0 (4 bytes `FF 0A 11 22`). Index-order reassembly yields `FF 0A 11 22 33 44 55`, a codestream opening with the bare signature; file-order concatenation yields `33 44 55 FF 0A 11 22`, which opens mid-stream and decodes as nothing. The divergence costs no malformed box at all: the same bytes, read in the file's order instead of the index's order, are a different picture — the fragmented-MP4 entry's reassembly lesson, now inside a single still image. [VERIFIED — the miniature, constructed and walked this pass]

- **The adoption whiplash is the carrier's own history.** JPEG XL shipped in Chrome 91, was removed from Chrome in late 2022 for low ecosystem interest, and — by October 2026 secondary reporting — returned on by default in Chrome 155 and Firefox 158, with Safari carrying still-image support since 2023. A format can be dead in one year's toolchain and live in the next's, which is exactly why the Gauntlet inventories the carrier rather than trusting the ecosystem's current opinion of it: today's "unsupported, therefore unread" is tomorrow's default reader, and a specimen archived as unreadable becomes readable without anyone re-examining it. [CORROBORATED — the Chrome 91 ship / late-2022 removal arc via the format's public history; CLAIMED — the October 2026 Chrome 155 / Firefox 158 return, single secondary roundup, not independently confirmed this pass]

The decoder is `jxl-rs`, described by the Chrome team as a pure Rust implementation. Google claims thirty to fifty percent better compression than JPEG — the claim is Google's, not a benchmark read this pass. This is the format's second arrival in Chrome: behind a flag from version 91 to 109, removed in 110, back after a popular proposal for Interop 2026. The whiplash bullet's CLAIMED on the Chrome 155 return is now CORROBORATED for Chrome; the Firefox 158 half stays CLAIMED (single secondary roundup, not independently confirmed this pass). Decoder significance: a default-on decoder in the world's most-used browser means `.jxl` specimens are now readable on billions of machines without anyone installing anything — the 'unsupported, therefore unread' archive assumption retires for Chrome 155 and up, and the `jbrd` reconstruction box now rides a live default reader.

(1) **The box inventory is the intake, and the fork is the first question.** The Gauntlet's container pass on any `.jxl` first asks which file it holds — bare codestream (`FF 0A`) or box form (`JXL ` signature) — then walks every box: every `jxlp` listed with its index, every `jbrd` named with its byte budget, every `brob` decompressed before listing, every `Exif` TIFF tree and `xml` packet handed to their own entries' treatment. A file whose boxes the walk cannot place is UNREAD, never CLEAN. (2) **"Renders clean" and "carries only a picture" are different claims, and "is a JXL" and "was a JPEG" are different claims too.** The renderer shows the JXL; the `jbrd` box means the file may also *be* a JPEG, reversibly, and the interrogation grades both readings — the polyglot entry's multiple-readings discipline, now sanctioned by the standard itself rather than smuggled past it. (3) **Reassembly order is evidence, not plumbing.** Concatenate `jxlp` by index and diff against file order: a file whose index order disagrees with its file order is announcing which reader it expects, the Matroska `SeekHead` disagreement in a sequence's uniform — and a `jbrd` box whose reconstruction does not reproduce a valid JPEG is a divergence event, not a failed decode. - **GIF: the picture that is a block stream, or: the trailer is a suggestion, and the application extension is a program's attic.** GIF (CompuServe, 1987/1989) is not a picture with metadata attached — it is a stream of blocks, and the picture is only one block kind among several. The file opens with a 6-byte version stamp, `GIF87a` or `GIF89a` (the 89a revision added the extension blocks; an 87a file has no Graphic Control Extension to hide behind, which is itself a dating signal). Then the 7-byte Logical Screen Descriptor: width and height little-endian, a packed byte (Global Color Table flag bit 7, color resolution bits 4–6, sort flag bit 3, GCT size bits 0–2 meaning 2^(N+1) entries), background color index, aspect ratio — followed by the Global Color Table itself when flagged. After that, the grammar is three introducers and nothing else: `0x2C` opens an Image Descriptor (left, top, width, height, its own packed byte with a Local Color Table flag and an interlace flag), `0x21` opens an extension, `0x3B` is the Trailer — and the Trailer is where the spec's story ends, not where the file's bytes do. [VERIFIED — GIF89a specification: header versions, Logical Screen Descriptor layout, block introducers, trailer byte]

- **The extensions are the compartments, and two of them are explicitly for other programs.** An extension is `0x21` plus a label byte, then a run of length-prefixed sub-blocks (each ≤255 bytes) terminated by a `0x00` byte. The labels: `0xF9` Graphic Control (disposal method, delay, transparent index — the animation controls), `0x01` Plain Text (text grid overlaid on the picture), `0xFE` Comment (arbitrary text, rendered by nothing, preserved by convention), and `0xFF` Application — the sanctioned attic with a nameplate. An Application Extension opens with an 11-byte block: the 8-byte application identifier plus a 3-byte authentication code, then sub-blocks of whatever that application wants. The famous tenant is `NETSCAPE2.0` (looping: sub-block `03 01 lo hi`, count 0 meaning forever — the byte that made the animated GIF loop), and the quiet one is XMP: Adobe's XMP packet rides in a GIF as an Application Extension with identifier `XMP Data` and authentication code `XMP`, an RDF/XML document inside the picture's block stream, parsed by metadata engines and ignored by image renderers. A reader that lists only image descriptors has inventoried the picture and missed the programs. [VERIFIED — GIF89a specification: extension labels, sub-block framing, Application Extension nameplate layout, NETSCAPE2.0 looping block; CORROBORATED — XMP-in-GIF application identifier and authentication code, per Adobe's XMP specification]

- **The trailer is a suggestion, and the LZW stream is a second reader's problem.** Everything after `0x3B` is, by every reader's contract, not part of the file — which is exactly why it is the oldest hiding place in the format: decoders stop, the bytes stay, and a file that "is a GIF" can carry an arbitrary tail no GIF tool will ever report. The image data itself is a second compartment in a different uniform: an LZW minimum-code-size byte, then the compressed stream in sub-blocks, then the `0x00` terminator — and LZW's code table is built from the stream, so a decoder that trusts the declared dimensions and never decompresses has not read the picture at all. The format's own polyglot history proves the point from the other side: GIFAR (Black Hat 2008) was a file that was simultaneously a valid GIF and a valid Java Archive, because the server declared GIF and the JVM sniffed JAR — the MIME-sniffing entry's lesson in the format's own uniform, and the reason the Gauntlet re-sniffs every artifact itself. [VERIFIED — GIF89a specification: trailer semantics, LZW sub-block framing; CORROBORATED — GIFAR 2008 GIF/JAR polyglot, per the MIME-sniffing entry's sources]

- **Worked miniature (built and walked this pass).** A 77-byte GIF89a — header (6), Logical Screen Descriptor 1×1 with a 2-entry Global Color Table (13 bytes), Graphic Control Extension at offset 19, Comment Extension (`hello`) at 27, NETSCAPE2.0 Application Extension (loop count 0, forever) at 36, Image Descriptor at 55, LZW minimum code size 2 at 65, image data sub-block, Trailer at offset 70 — and then 6 trailing bytes, `HIDDEN`, at offsets 71–76. The walk lands exactly: every block boundary accounts for every byte up to the Trailer, and the 6 bytes after it are invisible to the format's own grammar. The divergence needs no malformed block at all: a file that renders as a 1×1 looping pixel and carries a 6-byte tail is, to the reader, a complete file — the tail is not an error, it is an attic the spec built and then forgot to lock. Scale the tail and the attic scales: the Comment Extension, the Application Extension, and the post-trailer tail are three compartments with no size limit the format itself enforces. [VERIFIED — the miniature, constructed and walked this pass]

(1) **The block inventory is the intake.** The Gauntlet's container pass on any GIF walks every block — every extension named by label and, for Application Extensions, by identifier and authentication code, every sub-block counted, every Comment and Plain Text block listed with its byte budget — and then keeps walking past the Trailer and reports the tail, byte for byte, as a compartment, never as "trailing garbage." A file whose walk stops at the Trailer is unread past offset 70, not clean. (2) **"Renders clean" and "carries only a picture" are different claims, and "is a GIF" and "is a JAR" are different claims too.** The renderer shows the first frame; the inventory grades the extensions, the tail, and every second reading the sniffers can compute — the polyglot discipline, now against the format that invented the polyglot. (3) **Dimensions are claims the LZW stream must keep.** The Image Descriptor's width and height are graded against the decompressed stream: a descriptor promising pixels the LZW data never delivers, or LZW data delivering pixels the descriptor never promised, is a divergence event — the AVIF extent lesson in a block stream's coat. - **TIFF: the picture that is a filing cabinet, or: the directory is a map, and the map may point anywhere.** TIFF 6.0 (Aldus, 1992; Adobe's stewardship after) is not a picture format with metadata — it is a tag directory that happens to describe a picture. The file opens with an 8-byte header: byte order (`II` little-endian or `MM` big-endian), the magic number 42, and a 4-byte offset to the first Image File Directory — an offset that may point anywhere in the file, not necessarily to byte 8. An IFD is a 2-byte count of entries, then that many 12-byte entries — tag (2 bytes), type (2 bytes), count (4 bytes), value-or-offset (4 bytes) — then a 4-byte offset to the next IFD, or 0 to end the chain. The value field holds the data itself when it fits in 4 bytes and an absolute offset to it when it does not, so every entry is either a fact or a pointer, and the reader cannot tell which without doing the arithmetic. The twelve types run 1 BYTE, 2 ASCII, 3 SHORT, 4 LONG, 5 RATIONAL, 6 SBYTE, 7 UNDEFINED, 8 SSHORT, 9 SLONG, 10 SRATIONAL, 11 FLOAT, 12 DOUBLE — and the tag space is deliberately open: readers are told to ignore tags they do not recognize, and tags 32768 and up are reserved for private use, so the format's own rule is that unknown compartments are to be skipped, not reported. [VERIFIED — TIFF 6.0 specification: header layout, magic 42, IFD structure, 12-byte entry format, twelve types, private-tag range and ignore-unknown rule]

- **The chain is the picture, and the pointers are the compartments.** A TIFF file is a linked list of directories, and each directory may sprout sub-directories by pointer. IFD0's tag 34665 points to the Exif IFD; tag 34853 points to the GPS IFD; inside the Exif IFD, tag 40965 points to the Interoperability IFD; tag 330 (SubIFDs) lists whole further IFD trees. Tag 254 (NewSubfileType) marks a directory as a reduced-resolution image, a single page of a multi-page document, or a transparency mask — the thumbnail is a second picture riding the same chain, graded by no rule in the file. The pixels themselves live wherever the directory says: StripOffsets (273) plus StripByteCounts (279) for strips, TileOffsets (324) for tiles — the raster is not "after the header," it is at the offset the directory claims, which may be before the directory, after it, or interleaved with other directories' data. Around them sit the extension cabinets: GeoTIFF tags for georeferencing, Photoshop tag 34377 for image resources, ICC profile tag 34675 — each a whole document system carried as one tag's value. A reader that follows only the chain to the first raster has inventoried the index card and missed the cabinets. [VERIFIED — TIFF 6.0 / Exif specification tag numbers: 254 NewSubfileType, 273 StripOffsets, 279 StripByteCounts, 324 TileOffsets, 330 SubIFDs, 34377 Photoshop, 34665 ExifIFD, 34675 ICC profile, 34853 GPSInfo, 40965 InteroperabilityIFD]

- **The gaps are the hiding places, and the spec blesses them.** TIFF has no trailer and no end marker: the chain ends when a next-IFD offset reads 0, and every byte after the last directory the chain reaches is unreferenced by the grammar — no reader is obliged to report it, and no reader's contract covers it. The offsets are absolute and unchecked by the grammar itself: an entry may point backward over the header, overlap another entry's value bytes, or point past end-of-file, where a strict reader errors and a forgiving reader short-reads and carries on — the differential-parsing entry's lesson in a directory's uniform. Duplicate tags are the same shape: the spec wants ascending tag order but readers tolerate any order, and two entries carrying the same tag leave first-wins and last-wins readers holding different pictures from the same file. And the dialect fork is quiet: BigTIFF keeps the extension and changes the magic to 43, widens offsets to 8 bytes and entries to 20 bytes, and a classic-TIFF reader handed a BigTIFF file does not fail cleanly — it reads the magic as an unknown version and the first IFD offset as garbage. A file whose magic the reader does not expect is misread, not clean. [VERIFIED — TIFF 6.0: no trailer semantics, next-IFD 0 terminator; BigTIFF magic 43, 8-byte offsets, 20-byte entries; CORROBORATED — duplicate-tag reader variance and short-read tolerance, per independent parser writeups]

- **Worked miniature (built and walked this pass).** A 92-byte little-endian TIFF — header (`II`, 42, first IFD at 8), IFD0 at offset 8 with three entries (ImageWidth 256, LONG, 1; ImageLength 257, LONG, 1; ExifIFD 34665, LONG, pointing to 50), next-IFD offset 68; an Exif IFD at 50 with one entry (ExifVersion 36864, UNDEFINED, count 4, value `0232` stored inline); a thumbnail IFD at 68 with one entry (NewSubfileType 254, LONG, 1 — reduced-resolution image), next-IFD 0, chain ends at 86 — and then 6 trailing bytes, `HIDDEN`, at offsets 86–91. The walk lands exactly: every directory boundary accounts for every byte up to 86, and the 6 bytes after the chain's end are invisible to any reader that follows the chain. Two divergences ride free with no malformed entry at all: IFD0 claims a 1×1 picture but carries no StripOffsets tag, so the dimensions are claims no strip data keeps — a renderer must invent or refuse pixels the directory never located; and the tail is not an error, it is an attic the format built by never defining an end. Scale the tail and the attic scales; orphan an IFD by pointing nothing at it and the attic gains a room no chain walk will ever enter. [VERIFIED — the miniature, constructed and walked this pass]

- **Decoder-design note (TIFF → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The pointer inventory is the intake.** The Gauntlet's container pass on any TIFF walks the header, every IFD in the chain, every sub-IFD pointer (Exif, GPS, Interoperability, SubIFDs), and every value-offset — then lists every byte range claimed and every byte range unclaimed, and reports the unclaimed ranges as compartments, never as "padding." An IFD reachable by no pointer is listed as an orphan directory; a value-offset past end-of-file suspends the verdict: UNREAD, never CLEAN. (2) **"Renders clean" and "carries only a picture" are different claims, and "is a TIFF" and "is a BigTIFF" are different claims too.** The renderer shows the first raster it can find; the inventory grades the chain, the sub-directories, the thumbnail directories, and the tail — the GIF entry's post-trailer discipline, now against a format that never had a trailer to stop at. (3) **Claims are graded against the data they point to.** Dimensions against strip byte counts, the Exif pointer against the IFD actually found there, duplicate tags diffed reader-by-reader — the AVIF extent lesson in a directory's coat. - **DES and the EFF DES cracker ("Deep Crack") — the standard that fell to a budget (1977–1999), or: the key length is the security parameter.** DES, the Data Encryption Standard (FIPS 46, 1977), is a 64-bit-block symmetric cipher with a 56-bit key — 2^56 ≈ 7.2×10^16 possible keys, a keyspace its own critics called too small from the start. In 1977 Diffie and Hellman estimated a machine fast enough to search that keyspace in a day would cost about $20 million — affordable, they argued, to a national intelligence agency. Twenty-one years later the price had collapsed to a civil-liberties budget, and RSA Security's DES Challenges dated the fall in public. The first challenge fell in June 1997 to the DESCHALL Project (Rocke Verser, Loveland, Colorado) after 96 days of distributed volunteer compute; DES Challenge II-1 fell in 39 days (January–February 1998) to distributed.net; then the EFF's purpose-built Deep Crack — 1,856 custom ASIC chips (AWT-4500) testing roughly 90 billion keys per second, designed by Cryptography Research (Paul Kocher), Advanced Wireless Technologies, and the EFF under John Gilmore, built for under $250,000 — solved DES Challenge II-2 in 56 hours in July 1998, after trying about 17.9 quadrillion keys, roughly 25% of the keyspace, winning $10,000. The recovered plaintext was itself the moral: "It's time for those 128-, 192-, and 256-bit keys." Six months later Deep Crack plus distributed.net took DES Challenge III in 22 hours 15 minutes (January 1999). The EFF published the whole machine — block diagrams, schematics, VHDL, emulator — in *Cracking DES* (1998): the cracker as open literature, not a secret weapon. NIST withdrew FIPS 46-3 in 2005; DES survives only inside Triple DES, itself now deprecated. [VERIFIED — EFF DES cracker and DES Challenges records read this pass; the challenge dates, times, costs, chip count, key rate, keys tried, and II-2 plaintext are canonical public record]
- **Decoder-design note (DES → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The key length is the security parameter, and the parameter is priced in dollars, not bits.** 1977: $20M per day of search. 1998: $250k for 56 hours. 1999: a volunteer network plus one box, 22 hours. The SHAttered note's budget ladder and the factoring ladder's rung-pricing are the same discipline stated three ways: a "never broken" claim is a claim about today's rental cost, and the Gauntlet re-prices every run. (2) **A public break beats a secret break.** RSA's challenges and the EFF's open publication turned a break into a migration deadline — the plaintext of II-2 was policy advice, not a secret. The Gauntlet's report cards do the same work: a specimen's weakness, demonstrated in the open with receipts, is what moves a user off it; a whispered break moves nobody. (3) **The contest is the calibration.** DESCHALL's 96 days, distributed.net's 39, Deep Crack's 56 hours, the joint 22h15m — four dated rungs on one keyspace, each with a receipt (a recovered key, a published plaintext). That is what the Gauntlet's battery is: not one probe but a ladder, so a specimen's strength is measured as a slope, not a slogan. [VERIFIED lineage — the challenge dates, times, and costs above; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are doctrine, never run]

- **PNG: the picture that is a chunk list, or: every chunk is a compartment with a checksum on the door.** PNG (W3C, 1996; ISO/IEC 15948) opens with an 8-byte signature — `89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A` — chosen to catch text-mode corruption: the high bit, the letters `PNG`, a CR-LF pair, a control-Z, a lone LF. After it the file is nothing but chunks, each in the same four parts: a 4-byte big-endian length, a 4-byte type of ASCII letters, the data, and a 4-byte CRC-32 (IEEE polynomial, computed over type + data, never over the length). The type's letter case is a flag field in its own right: first letter uppercase means critical, lowercase means ancillary; second letter uppercase means public, lowercase means private; third letter is reserved and must be uppercase; fourth letter uppercase means safe to copy across edits, lowercase means unsafe. A reader that meets an unknown critical chunk must stop; a reader that meets an unknown ancillary chunk must skip it and carry on — the format's own rule is that unknown compartments are to be passed over, not reported. [VERIFIED — PNG specification: signature bytes, chunk layout, CRC scope, case-flag semantics, critical/ancillary handling rule]

- **The critical spine, and the ancillary attic.** Four chunks are critical. `IHDR` must come first and carries 13 bytes: width and height (4 bytes each, big-endian), bit depth (1, 2, 4, 8, or 16), color type (0 grayscale, 2 truecolor RGB, 3 indexed-color, 4 grayscale+alpha, 6 truecolor+alpha), compression method (0, always deflate), filter method (0, always), interlace method (0 none, 1 Adam7). `PLTE` carries the palette for color type 3 and may ride as a suggested palette for types 2 and 6. `IDAT` carries the image data — one zlib stream, split across as many consecutive `IDAT` chunks as the writer likes, concatenated before decompression — and `IEND` closes the file with zero data bytes. Around the spine, the ancillary attic: `tEXt` (keyword, NUL, Latin-1 text), `zTXt` (same, zlib-compressed), `iTXt` (UTF-8, optional compression, optional language tag), `tIME` (last-modification stamp), `gAMA`/`cHRM`/`sRGB`/`iCCP` (color intent — `iCCP` carries a whole ICC profile, compressed, a second interpreter's document inside the picture), `pHYs` (pixel dimensions), `tRNS` (transparency), `sBIT`, `bKGD`, `hIST`. Animation is a second spine grafted onto the first: APNG puts `acTL` (animation control: frame count, loop count) before the first `IDAT`, then each frame gets an `fcTL` (sequence number, size, offset, delay, dispose and blend ops) followed by `fdAT` chunks (sequence number + frame data) — a picture that is also a film, and a still-image reader that stops at the first `IDAT` never sees the frames at all. [VERIFIED — PNG / APNG specification: IHDR field layout, color-type numbers, IDAT concatenation rule, ancillary chunk roles, acTL/fcTL/fdAT structure]

- **The gaps are the hiding places, and the checksum is a suggestion to the forgiving.** PNG has no length in its header and no box table: the chunk walk is the only map, and it ends at `IEND` — every byte after `IEND` is unreferenced by the grammar, and the common readers ignore it, which is the GIF post-trailer attic in a checksum's coat. The CRC is the second gap: the spec says a decoder should reject a chunk whose CRC fails, but the forgiving readers that dominate the ecosystem warn and carry on, or never check at all — so a file with a broken seal and a file with a valid seal render identically in the reader most users have, and the strict reader and the forgiving reader hold different pictures from the same bytes. Duplicate chunks are the third: nothing in the grammar forbids two `tEXt` chunks with the same keyword, two `iCCP` profiles, or two `tIME` stamps, and first-wins versus last-wins readers disagree about which one the file means. The fourth gap is inside the pixels themselves: each decompressed scanline begins with a filter-type byte (0 None, 1 Sub, 2 Up, 3 Average, 4 Paeth) chosen per row by the encoder — a byte the decoder must trust row by row to reconstruct the row — and Adam7 interlacing reorders the whole image into seven passes, so the bytes on disk are never in picture order even before any hiding begins. A length field that escapes end-of-file is the same shape as the MacBinary inflated-length lesson: a strict reader errors, a forgiving reader short-reads, and the interrogation must suspend, never guess. [VERIFIED — PNG specification: IEND semantics, IDAT/zlib framing, filter-type byte per scanline, Adam7 seven passes; CORROBORATED — trailing-data-after-IEND tolerance and forgiving CRC handling, per independent parser writeups]

- **Mach-O: the executable that is a load-command table, or: the loader trusts the table before it verifies anything.** A Mach-O binary opens with a 32-byte `mach_header_64`: magic, cputype, cpusubtype, filetype, ncmds, sizeofcmds, flags, reserved. The 64-bit magic is `0xfeedfacf` (bytes `cf fa ed fe` on a little-endian host); 32-bit is `0xfeedface`; byte-swapped `CIGAM` variants exist for the other endianness. Cputype carries the ABI bit: x86_64 is `0x01000007`, arm64 `0x0100000c`. Filetype names the role: `MH_OBJECT` 1, `MH_EXECUTE` 2, `MH_DYLIB` 6, `MH_BUNDLE` 8. A fat binary instead opens with `0xcafebabe` (big-endian, `FAT_MAGIC`; `0xcafebabf` for 64-bit fat): nfat_arch, then one `fat_arch` per slice — cputype, cpusubtype, offset, size, align (a power of two) — a table of contents pointing at whole binaries inside the file. [VERIFIED — the mach-o header definitions, long-standing public specification]

- **The table is the map, and segments are the only claims on bytes.** After the header come ncmds load commands spanning sizeofcmds bytes. `LC_SEGMENT_64` (`0x19`, 72 bytes with zero sections, plus 80 bytes per `section_64`) names a segment — `__PAGEZERO`, `__TEXT`, `__DATA`, `__LINKEDIT` — with vmaddr, vmsize, fileoff, filesize, maxprot, initprot, nsects, flags. The segment's file extent is fileoff..fileoff+filesize; everything else the table names is metadata about that extent. The other commands worth inventorying: `LC_SYMTAB` (`0x2`) and `LC_DYSYMTAB` (`0xb`) for the symbol tables, `LC_LOAD_DYLIB` (`0xc`) for linked libraries, `LC_UUID` (`0x1b`), `LC_RPATH` (`0x8000001c`) and `LC_MAIN` (`0x80000028`) for the entry point, `LC_CODE_SIGNATURE` (`0x1d`, dataoff/datasize pointing at the superblob in `__LINKEDIT`), and `LC_ENCRYPTION_INFO_64` (`0x2c`, cryptoff/cryptsize/cryptid — a cryptid of 0 means the FairPlay-encrypted slice is already decrypted, nonzero means the on-disk bytes are still ciphertext). [VERIFIED — the mach-o load-command definitions]

- **The gaps are the hiding places, and the table itself is the first one.** First, the header carries no file length: the walk ends at header + sizeofcmds, and a segment's claim ends at fileoff + filesize — bytes beyond the last claimed extent are unreferenced by the grammar, the Mach-O form of the PNG tail and the GIF post-trailer attic. Second, cmdsize is rounded to the 8-byte boundary, so load commands carry padding slack a reader never interprets. Third, segments are page-aligned: vmsize routinely exceeds filesize (the rest is zero-fill at load), and the fileoff gaps between one segment's end and the next segment's start are on-disk bytes no segment claims. Fourth, fat slices are alignment-padded, so slack sits between slices — a whole binary's worth of hiding room inside a file that still parses as a valid fat binary. Fifth, the table is parsed before anything is verified: the loader walks ncmds commands and follows their pointers to build the image, and the code-signature superblob is checked by a different pass than the one that trusts the table's structure. Sixth, `LC_LOAD_DYLIB` and `LC_RPATH` strings are paths the loader follows — `@rpath`, `@loader_path`, `@executable_path` resolve at load time, so a static inventory that lists the strings without resolving them has not finished the job. [VERIFIED — header/segment/fat layout; CORROBORATED — loader parse-before-verify ordering and rpath resolution behavior, per the loader's public documentation]

- **Covert channels: the carrier is the system itself (Lampson 1973,
  Rowland 1997).** Lampson's confinement problem (CACM 16(10), Oct
  1973): a confined service must send information to no program but its
  caller. Channels split three ways — legitimate (declared outputs, like
  the bill), storage (a written variable, file, or socket), and covert
  (mechanisms never meant for transfer: system load, locks, power, and
  above all timing — information in *when*, not *what*). The masking
  principle: the caller must determine all of the confined program's
  inputs to legitimate and covert channels, even at the cost of slowing
  it down; confinement is transitive to untrusted callees. Lipner
  (1975): storage channels close cheaply, covert channels only at a
  steep performance price. [VERIFIED]
- **Rowland's three TCP/IP methods (1996/1997, covert_tcp).** The
  suite's headers are storage channels in plain sight: the 16-bit IP
  Identification field, the 32-bit TCP Initial Sequence Number, and the
  TCP Acknowledgement field bounced off an innocuous host to hide the
  sender. covert_tcp moved a file one byte at a time inside otherwise
  normal packets, past filters and sniffers — nothing in the payload is
  ever abnormal. [CORROBORATED]
- **The header budget (worked example).** 1,000 packets x 16-bit IP ID
  = 2,000 bytes with zero payload bytes to inspect; the 32-bit ISN
  doubles it to 4,000. A payload-only detector sees nothing at all.
  [VERIFIED — arithmetic]
- **Decoder-design note.** The network harness records full headers,
  never payloads alone: non-random ISNs, message-shaped IP ID steps, or
  ACKs bouncing through third hosts announce a channel. Timing gaps are
  measured as signals with a bandwidth estimate, never averaged away as
  jitter. And the container normalizes — rewriting ISNs, randomizing IP
  IDs, pacing timing — because a channel that survives normalization was
  legitimate traffic all along. [DOCTRINE]

- **PE: the executable that is a stub, a signature, and a section table, or: the loader trusts a pointer the file itself supplies.** A PE file opens with a DOS header: the two bytes `MZ` (`0x5A4D`), 64 bytes of header, and at offset `0x3C` the `e_lfanew` field — a 4-byte pointer, supplied by the file, naming where the real header lives. Follow it and find the 4-byte signature `PE\0\0`, then the 20-byte COFF header: Machine, NumberOfSections, TimeDateStamp, PointerToSymbolTable, NumberOfSymbols, SizeOfOptionalHeader, Characteristics. Machine `0x8664` is AMD64, `0x14c` is i386, `0xaa64` is ARM64. Then the Optional Header — magic `0x10b` for PE32, `0x20b` for PE32+ — carrying AddressOfEntryPoint, ImageBase, SectionAlignment, FileAlignment, SizeOfImage, SizeOfHeaders, and finally 16 data directories of 8 bytes each (RVA + size): export 0, import 1, resource 2, exception 3, certificate 4, base relocation 5, debug 6, TLS 9, load config 10, IAT 12, delay import 13. - **WebAssembly: the executable that is a stack machine in sections, or: the attic is sanctioned, and the start function runs before anyone calls anything.** A Wasm module opens with the 4-byte magic `00 61 73 6d` (`\0asm`), then the 4-byte version `01 00 00 00` (version 1). Everything after is sections: a one-byte section id, an unsigned-LEB128 byte count, then that many payload bytes. Section ids: 0 custom, 1 type, 2 import, 3 function, 4 table, 5 memory, 6 global, 7 export, 8 start, 9 element, 10 code, 11 data, 12 data count. Numbered sections appear at most once each and in id order; custom sections (id 0) may appear anywhere, any number of times. The type section declares function types: `0x60`, a param vector, a result vector — value types i32 `0x7F`, i64 `0x7E`, f32 `0x7D`, f64 `0x7C`, v128 `0x7B`, funcref `0x70`, externref `0x6F`. The function section assigns each defined function a type index; the code section carries the bodies — a size, a locals vector, then instructions ending in `0x0B` (end). The import section names what the module needs from its host: module name string, field name string, a kind byte (0 func, 1 table, 2 memory, 3 global), then the type. The export section names what the module offers out, in the same shape. [VERIFIED — WebAssembly core specification, binary format]

- **The gaps are the hiding places, and the first one is the format's own attic.** First, custom sections are ignored by engines: a section id 0 carries a name string and then arbitrary bytes, and validation and execution skip the contents — the sanctioned attic, where tooling conventionally stores the `name` section (function and local names for debuggers) and where anything else rides for free, invisible to every engine that runs the module. Second, the start section (id 8) names a function index that executes automatically at instantiation, before any export is called: a module that "just sits there" still runs code at load — the Wasm form of a constructor, and the reason "it was never invoked" is never a claim about a Wasm specimen. Third, imports are delegation written in the file: the module string and field string name a host capability the engine resolves at instantiation, the Wasm form of the ELF interpreter path, the Mach-O rpath, and the PE import table — listing the strings without resolving them to the host's actual functions has not finished the job. Fourth, data segments come in two kinds: active segments that copy into memory at instantiation, and passive segments that sit unloaded until a `memory.init` instruction runs them — a payload that is present, validated, and inert until the module's own code chooses to arm it. - **tar: the archive with no index, or: the end marker is a suggestion and the metadata is a second file.** A tar archive is a stream of 512-byte blocks, not a file with a table. Each member opens with a 512-byte header: name at 0–99, mode at 100–107, uid at 108–115, gid at 116–123, size at 124–135 (octal ASCII, NUL- or space-terminated), mtime at 136–147, checksum at 148–155, typeflag at 156, linkname at 157–256, magic at 257–262 (`ustar\0` for POSIX ustar, `ustar ` with trailing space for GNU oldgnu), then uname, gname, device numbers, and the ustar prefix at 345–499 for long names. The member's data follows in ceil(size / 512) blocks, zero-padded. The archive ends with two consecutive 512-byte zero blocks. There is no central directory, no box table, no index of any kind — unlike ZIP, a tar reader walks sequentially and trusts each header's size field to find the next member, so the size field is the only map, and a wrong size desyncs every boundary after it. [VERIFIED — POSIX ustar header layout and the two-zero-block end marker, long-standing public standard]
- **The gaps are the hiding places, and the first one is that the format never checks the payload.** The header checksum covers the header only: the sum of all 512 header bytes with the checksum field itself counted as eight spaces — it says nothing about the data blocks, so an altered payload passes every format check tar itself performs; integrity of contents is somebody else's job, and a reader that reports "valid tar" has verified the headers, not the files. Second, the end marker is advisory in practice: readers stop at the two zero blocks and ignore whatever follows, so bytes past the end are an attic with no checksum, no length, and no reader that lists them — the PNG post-IEND tail and the GIF post-trailer attic in a block stream's coat. Third, metadata rides as members: GNU longname entries (typeflag `L` for names, `K` for linknames) carry the real name in the data block of a pseudo-member preceding the member it renames, and POSIX pax extended headers (typeflag `x`) carry arbitrary key-value records — path, size overrides, timestamps, comments — the same way; a reader that does not parse `L`/`x` sees a truncated 100-byte name and the wrong metadata, and a pax comment record is a free-text compartment no name-length limit constrains. Fourth, sparse members (GNU typeflag `S`) declare holes that are not stored at all — the file the reader reconstructs is larger than the bytes on disk, and a hole map is a claim about absent data that no byte in the archive evidences. Fifth, duplicate names are legal: nothing forbids two members with the same path, and first-wins versus last-wins extractors disagree about which one the archive means — the PNG duplicate-chunk lesson, now with whole files at stake. [VERIFIED — ustar/pax/GNU-tar header and typeflag semantics; CORROBORATED — trailing-data-after-end-marker tolerance, per reader behavior verified in the miniature below]

- **ZIP: the archive with an index at the end, or: the directory is the file, and the file is whatever the directory says.** A ZIP archive is two descriptions of the same members, and they need not agree. Each member has a local file header — signature `PK\x03\x04` (0x04034b50), 30 fixed bytes: version needed, general-purpose bit flag, compression method, mod time/date, CRC-32, compressed size, uncompressed size, filename length, extra-field length — followed by its name, its extra field, and its data. Then, at the end, a central directory: one 46-byte record per member — signature `PK\x01\x02` (0x02014b50), version made by, version needed, flag, method, time/date, CRC-32, both sizes, name/extra/comment lengths, disk number, internal and external attributes, and the offset of that member's local header — followed by the end-of-central-directory record (EOCD), signature `PK\x05\x06` (0x06054b50), 22 fixed bytes: disk numbers, entry counts, central-directory size and offset, comment length. There is no pointer to the EOCD: a reader finds it by scanning backwards from the end of the file, because the comment may run up to 65,535 bytes. That search is the first crack. Method 0 is stored, method 8 is deflate; bit 0 of the flag marks encryption, bit 3 marks a data descriptor — CRC and sizes zero in the local header, real values written after the data. Archives past the 32-bit limits use ZIP64 records (EOCD 0x06064b50, locator, and 0xFFFFFFFF sentinels in the 32-bit fields).

- **The gaps are the hiding places, and the first one is that the index outranks the file.** First, central and local names can differ: readers that trust the directory report the central name, and the local name is a second identity the listing never shows — this pass proved two real readers disagree about what to do with it (see miniature). Second, trailing bytes after the EOCD are ignored by design, because the EOCD is found by a backwards scan: anything appended past it is not an error, it is simply not part of the archive. Third, a central entry can point anywhere — at another member's data, at a fabricated local header, at no header at all — and a directory-driven reader follows the offset without checking that the local header it lands on belongs to the entry that sent it. Fourth, extraction trusts the name: a member named `../../evil` or an absolute path escapes the target directory on naive extractors — the Zip-slip class, where the archive's own index is the traversal payload. Fifth, duplicate names: two members with the same name, and first-wins versus last-wins is a reader decision, not a format rule. Sixth, the compression ratio itself is a weapon: a small deflate stream expanding to gigabytes (the zip-bomb class) punishes any reader that decompresses before it budgets. Seventh, the data-descriptor flag lets the local header lie about sizes and CRC until after the data has already been read.

- **Worked miniature (built and walked this pass).** A 126-byte archive, hand-packed field by field: local header at offset 0 for `note.txt`, method 0, data `Hi\n`, CRC-32 0xd5223c9a; central-directory record at offset 41 naming the same member `renamed.txt` — the deliberate disagreement — with local-header offset 0; EOCD at offset 98 declaring 1 entry, central size 57, central offset 41; then 6 trailing bytes `HIDDEN` at offsets 120–125. Three readers, three verdicts, one file: Python's `zipfile` lists `['renamed.txt']` but refuses to read it — `BadZipFile: File name in directory 'renamed.txt' and header b'note.txt' differ`; Info-ZIP `unzip -l` lists `renamed.txt`, extracts it as `Hi\n` under the central name with the warning `mismatching "local" filename (note.txt), continuing with "central" filename version`, and exits 1; both readers ignore the trailing `HIDDEN` bytes entirely. The archive is simultaneously listable, unreadable, and extractable depending on which reader you ask — and none of the three reports the local name `note.txt` as a member.

- **Decoder-design note (ZIP → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The inventory is three walks, diffed.** The Gauntlet's container pass on any ZIP locates the EOCD by backwards scan, walks the central directory, walks the local headers from offset 0, and reports the diff as the finding: names, methods, CRCs, sizes, and offsets that disagree across the two maps are compartments, not errors to reconcile silently. (2) **No byte is treated as the file until both maps agree it is.** A member is graded only when central and local headers agree on name, method, CRC, and sizes, the local offset lands on a matching signature, and the data extent fits inside the file; a data-descriptor member is graded after its descriptor, never from its zeroed local header. (3) **The tail, the duplicates, and the traversal names are graded as claims.** Trailing bytes past the EOCD are reported byte for byte, never as "trailing garbage"; duplicate names are extracted under both first-wins and last-wins and diffed; traversal and absolute names are quarantined before any extraction; decompression is budgeted against the declared uncompressed size before a single byte inflates — the tar lesson carried into an indexed format, where the index itself is the suspect.

- **ELF: the executable with two maps, or: the loader reads segments and the auditor reads sections, and neither sees the whole file.** The Executable and Linkable Format opens with a 64-byte ELF64 header: e_ident[16] (0x7F 'E' 'L' 'F', EI_CLASS 2 = 64-bit, EI_DATA 1 = little-endian / 2 = big-endian, EI_VERSION 1, EI_OSABI), then e_type at 16 (ET_REL 1, ET_EXEC 2, ET_DYN 3, ET_CORE 4), e_machine at 18 (EM_X86_64 62, EM_AARCH64 183, EM_RISCV 243), e_entry at 24, e_phoff at 32, e_shoff at 40, e_ehsize at 52 (64), e_phentsize at 54 (56), e_phnum at 56, e_shentsize at 58 (64), e_shnum at 60, e_shstrndx at 62. Program headers (56 bytes each) carry p_type, p_flags, p_offset, p_vaddr, p_paddr, p_filesz, p_memsz, p_align — PT_LOAD 1, PT_DYNAMIC 2, PT_INTERP 3, PT_NOTE 4, PT_PHDR 6. Section headers (64 bytes each) carry sh_name, sh_type, sh_flags, sh_addr, sh_offset, sh_size, sh_link, sh_info, sh_addralign, sh_entsize — SHT_NULL 0, SHT_PROGBITS 1, SHT_SYMTAB 2, SHT_STRTAB 3, SHT_RELA 4, SHT_DYNAMIC 6, SHT_NOBITS 8, SHT_REL 9, SHT_DYNSYM 11. [VERIFIED — the System V gABI ELF specification; header and program-header layouts confirmed by readelf this pass]

- **The gaps are the hiding places, and the section table is the first one.** First, the two maps can disagree by design: the loader maps program headers and never consults section headers, so a fully stripped binary (e_shoff 0, e_shnum 0) still runs — a reader that walks sections alone sees nothing while the loader sees everything; the DEX map-omission, with the whole second map absent on purpose. Second, extended numbering hides the true counts: when the section count reaches SHN_LORESERVE, e_shnum reads 0 and the real count lives in sh_size of section 0, and e_shstrndx 0xFFFF (SHN_XINDEX) means the real string-table index lives in sh_link of section 0 — a reader that stops at the header fields inventories a truncated file. Third, p_filesz < p_memsz is the BSS rule: the loaded image is larger than the file, zero-filled at load, and NOBITS sections occupy memory with no file bytes at all — the file and the image are different objects, and the difference is a hiding dimension, not an error. Fourth, bytes past the last segment's p_offset + p_filesz are never mapped — the overlay again — and bytes between segments are slack no map accounts for. Fifth, sh_name is an index into the section-header string table — the same indirection discipline as the DEX string_ids — so a corrupt string table renames every section. Sixth, PT_INTERP plus DT_NEEDED name the interpreter path and the needed-library list: the dependency graph is the provenance rung — who loads this specimen and what it pulls in — and .dynsym survives stripping because the runtime needs it, while .symtab does not: the honest inventory survives in the dynamic symbol table. [VERIFIED — gABI layout and extended numbering; the stripped-binary-runs claim executed this pass, see miniature]

- **Worked miniature (built and walked this pass).** A 138-byte ELF64 — header 0–63 (ET_EXEC, EM_X86_64, entry 0x400078, e_phoff 64, e_shoff 0, e_phnum 1, e_shnum 0); one PT_LOAD at 64–119 (R+X, offset 0, vaddr 0x400000, filesz 132, memsz 132, align 0x1000); 12 bytes of code at 120–131 (mov eax, 60; mov edi, 42; syscall); and 6 trailing bytes, HIDDEN, at 132–137. readelf -h and -l parse it cleanly; readelf -S reports no sections; executed, it exits with code 42 — a binary with no section table at all, running on the loader's map alone. The segment claims file [0, 132); the 6 tail bytes are in the file, mapped by nothing, named by nothing. A verifier that checks the headers and a reader that walks the sections both pass this file, and neither one sees the attic — in the format the Gauntlet itself runs on. [VERIFIED — the miniature, constructed, parsed with readelf, and executed this pass]

- **Decoder-design note (ELF → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The segment inventory is the intake.** The Gauntlet's container pass on any ELF walks the program headers first — the loader's truth — then the section headers if present; it reports every byte outside every segment as a compartment, never as slack, and a section table that disagrees with the segments suspends the verdict: UNREAD, never CLEAN. (2) **"Stripped" is not "empty."** .dynsym, .dynamic, PT_INTERP, and the .note.gnu.build-id content hash survive stripping and carry the dependency graph and an auditor's checksum the loader ignores — grade those against the libraries actually present, and treat the build-id as the seal that isn't the file's own claim. (3) **Interrogate the image, not just the file.** p_filesz versus p_memsz means the specimen at runtime is the file plus zero-fill plus interpreter plus needed libraries — the DEX lesson (map versus file) gains a loader clock: the partial-read metric scores the loaded image, and a specimen whose BSS tail or interpreter chain is unexamined is unexamined, not clean. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]

- **cpio: the archive with no index, or: the walk is the file, and the trailer is a suggestion.** A cpio archive is a stream, not a file with a table. In the portable newc format every member opens with a 110-byte header: the 6-byte magic `070701`, then thirteen fields as 8-character ASCII hex — ino, mode, uid, gid, nlink, mtime, filesize, devMajor, devMinor, rdevMajor, rdevMinor, namesize, check. The filename follows (namesize counts the terminating NUL), padded with NULs so header-plus-name lands on a 4-byte boundary; the file data follows, padded the same way to 4. There is no central directory, no member count, no table of contents: the only way to know what is in the archive is to walk it, header by header, until the member named `TRAILER!!!` — itself an ordinary-looking entry with filesize 0. The format's most consequential deployment is the one most readers never see: the Linux kernel unpacks a cpio archive as the initramfs at boot, before any userspace verifier exists to object — the earliest carrier the machine trusts is a stream with no index and no checksum.

- **The gaps are the hiding places, and the first one is that the trailer is a claim, not a wall.** First, a reader that stops at `TRAILER!!!` never sees what follows it: entries after the trailer, and any bytes between the trailer and the end of the block, are invisible to every tool that treats the trailer as the end — the archive's attic is everything past the stop sign, and block padding (archives are conventionally rounded to 512 bytes) gives that attic a legitimate-looking size. Second, there is no header checksum at all in newc — tar at least checksums its headers; cpio checks nothing, and the `check` field is 0 by definition (the `070702` crc variant carries a CRC of the data, which many readers never verify). A lied filesize does not trip any alarm: it simply moves where the next header is read from, so one corrupt or crafted size desynchronizes the whole rest of the walk — a parser that resynchronizes by scanning for the next `070701` magic is guessing, and a parser that does not is lost. Third, names are paths, and the archive is a filesystem the extractor mounts: absolute names and `../` components write outside the target, the cpio form of the zip-slip lesson, and older extraction tools did exactly that. Fourth, content can arrive by reference: a hardlinked member carries nlink > 1, filesize 0, and an ino matching an earlier member — a "file" with no bytes of its own, whose content is whatever the earlier member said it was; an inventory that counts bytes per member undercounts the archive's true payload. Fifth, the alignment padding is unclaimed ground: the NUL pads after each name and each data block, and the block padding at the end, are never checked by any reader — small, scattered, and deniable, the same attic the ELF overlay and the tar block-padding entries already taught.

- **Worked miniature (built and walked this pass).** A 512-byte newc archive: entry @0, `note.txt`, mode 0100644, filesize 3, namesize 9 (8 characters plus NUL), header 110 bytes + 9 name bytes + 1 pad byte, data `Hi\n` + 1 pad byte, entry total 124 bytes; entry @124, `TRAILER!!!`, namesize 11, filesize 0, total 124 bytes, ending @248; trailing bytes 264, of which the only non-zero content is `HIDDEN` at 248–253, the rest zero block padding. The walker stops at the trailer and reports the attic; a reader that trusts the trailer as the end never sees it — in the format the kernel unpacks before anything else runs.

- **Decoder-design note (cpio → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The walk is the intake, and the walk continues past the stop sign.** The Gauntlet's container pass on any cpio walks every header — magic recomputed, ASCII-hex fields re-parsed, never trusted — and keeps walking past `TRAILER!!!` to end-of-file, reporting every post-trailer byte as a compartment, never as padding; an archive whose walk desynchronizes suspends the verdict: UNREAD, never CLEAN. (2) **A size field is a claim about where the next header lives.** Every filesize is checked against the remaining bytes before the next header is read, and a filesize that would land the next header off-alignment or past end-of-file is a framing failure, not a corrupt member to skip — the tar checksum lesson, minus the checksum. (3) **Names are destinations, and references are payload.** Every member name is normalized against the extraction root before any byte is written, and every hardlink reference is resolved to the member that actually carries the bytes — a member with filesize 0 is graded by its reference target, and an unresolvable reference is an unexamined compartment, not an empty file. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]

- **PDF: the document that keeps its drafts, or: the reader shows the newest revision and the file keeps all of them.** A PDF is a body of numbered indirect objects — `N G obj ... endobj` — plus a cross-reference table and a trailer. The file opens with a header line (`%PDF-1.4`), then objects: catalog, pages tree, page, content stream (`stream ... endstream`, with a `/Length` in the object dictionary), font. After the last object comes the xref table — `xref`, then subsections (`first count`) of 20-byte entries, ten-digit byte offset, five-digit generation number, `n` for in-use or `f` for free — then `trailer` with `/Size` (one past the highest object number) and `/Root` (the catalog), then `startxref` giving the xref table's byte offset, then `%%EOF`. The reader finds the file by reading backwards to `startxref`, not by trusting the header. An incremental update appends a whole new revision to the same file: rewritten objects (same numbers, new bytes), a new xref section naming only what changed, and a new trailer carrying `/Prev` — the byte offset of the previous xref table. The old objects are never overwritten and never deleted; the chain of `/Prev` links is the file's revision history, and the newest xref section wins wherever it names an object. [VERIFIED — PDF 1.7 reference (ISO 32000) structure; the backwards `startxref` lookup and `/Prev` chain semantics]

- **The gaps are the hiding places, and the first one is that "edited" is a display property, not a file property.** First, every superseded object survives byte-for-byte: a redaction that paints a black rectangle over text, or an update that rewrites a paragraph, leaves the original bytes in an earlier generation of the same object number — the rendered page shows the newest, the file shows all of them; this is the §(m) incremental-updates bullet with its miniature attached. Second, xref free entries are tombstones, not erasures: an object deleted by an update gets an `f` entry with a next-free-object link, and its bytes sit unreferenced until some later object happens to reuse the space. Third, object streams (PDF 1.5) pack many small objects into one compressed stream object, so a byte scanner looking for `N 0 obj` markers finds nothing — the objects are there, just deflated inside another object. Fourth, the trailer chain is itself a claim: a reader that stops at the newest trailer never walks `/Prev`, and a damaged newest trailer forces the reader into reconstruction heuristics — which generation the heuristics recover is a reader decision, not a format fact. Fifth, the content stream is a program: text is drawn by operators (`BT ... Tj ET`), so the visible text is whatever the newest program draws — and a stream that draws nothing still carries its operands. [VERIFIED — xref/trailer/incremental-update semantics per the specification; CORROBORATED — redaction-survival and object-stream behavior per standard forensic practice]

- **Worked miniature (built and walked this pass).** A 773-byte PDF 1.4: header, five objects — catalog (1), pages (2), page (3, 300×100), content stream (4), Helvetica font (5) — first xref table at offset 404, trailer, `startxref`, `%%EOF`; then the incremental update: object 4 rewritten at offset 587, second xref section at 680 naming only object 4, second trailer with `/Prev 404`, second `startxref`, second `%%EOF`. The two generations of object 4 differ in one operand: the first draws `(DRAFT-VERSION)`, at byte offset 296; the second draws `(FINAL-VERSION)`, at byte offset 642. The walk lands exactly: the xref chain has length 2, newest first — object 4 resolves to 587 in the new section and to 241 in the old — and the real readers agree with the walk: `pdftotext` extracts `FINAL-VERSION` and nothing else, `pdfinfo` reports 1 page, 300×100, PDF 1.4, no complaint — while a raw byte scan still finds `DRAFT-VERSION` at 296. The file is simultaneously a one-page document saying FINAL and a two-revision archive containing DRAFT. Scale the update count and the attic scales: every save is another generation, and no generation is ever collected. [VERIFIED — the miniature, constructed and walked this pass; reader behavior verified with poppler pdftotext/pdfinfo]

- **Decoder-design note (PDF → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The xref chain is the intake.** The Gauntlet's container pass on any PDF reads the last `startxref`, then walks every `/Prev` link to the first trailer, collecting every generation of every object — superseded generations are compartments, never "old versions," and a chain that breaks suspends the verdict: UNREAD, never CLEAN. (2) **"Renders clean" and "contains only the rendered content" are different claims, and "the page shows X" and "the file says only X" are different claims too.** The rendered page is the newest generation's program output; the inventory grades every generation's operands, every free entry's orphaned bytes, and every object stream's deflated members — the SQLite freelist lesson, now with a version chain instead of slack. (3) **Claims are graded against the data they name.** Stream `/Length` values against the bytes between `stream` and `endstream`, xref offsets against the objects they land on, trailer `/Size` against the highest object number seen in any generation, page-tree counts against the pages actually drawn — the AVIF extent lesson in a document's coat. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are doctrine, never run]

- **gzip: the stream that is a list, or: one member is one reading, and the tail is a reader decision.** RFC 1952, the format behind `.gz`, HTTP content-encoding, and half the world's log pipelines. A member opens with a 10-byte header: magic `1f 8b`, compression method `08` (DEFLATE, the only method the spec defines), FLG, MTIME (4 bytes), XFL, OS. FLG bits name the optional compartments: FTEXT `0x01`, FHCRC `0x02` (a CRC16 over the header itself), FEXTRA `0x04` (XLEN plus length-prefixed subfields, each SI1/SI2/LEN/data), FNAME `0x08` (the original filename, NUL-terminated), FCOMMENT `0x10` (free-form comment, NUL-terminated). Then the DEFLATE body, then an 8-byte trailer: CRC32 of the uncompressed data, ISIZE — the uncompressed length modulo 2^32. And the format's most consequential rule is one sentence in the spec: a gzip file may be a concatenation of members, and a reader should decompress them in sequence — so a `.gz` file is a list, and "the" decompressed content is whatever the reader's member walk reaches.

- **The gaps are the hiding places, and the first one is that the member boundary is invisible to a one-member reader.** First, a reader that stops after the first member never sees the rest: a second member is a whole second payload riding behind the first, and the only thing distinguishing "one file" from "two files glued together" is whether the reader keeps walking — the multidex lesson, in a stream. Second, bytes past the last member's trailer are the attic again, but with a twist no earlier entry had: readers disagree about them. GNU gzip decompresses the members and reports "trailing garbage ignored" (exit 2, output still produced); Python's gzip module refuses the entire file with BadGzipFile. The same tail is ignored by one reader and fatal to another — a differential-parsing seam, where the attacker's choice of reader decides whether the attic exists at all. Third, the header's free-text compartments are unchecked unless FHCRC is set: FNAME and FCOMMENT carry arbitrary bytes no reader verifies, and FEXTRA subfields are skipped by any reader that does not recognize their SI — a sanctioned attic inside the header itself, before the compressed body even starts. Fourth, the trailer's claims wrap: ISIZE is modulo 2^32, so a payload over 4 GiB reports a length that is not its length, and CRC32 is a checksum, not a seal — a member whose CRC mismatches is caught only by a reader that actually checks, and a streaming reader that never looks back never does. Fifth, the FLG reserved bits must be zero, and a reader that does not enforce that reads a header the spec says is malformed — the same "forgiving reader" class as the ZIP central-directory tie-break.

- **Worked miniature (built and walked this pass).** A 57-byte gzip file: member 1, 25 bytes — header `1f 8b 08 00 00000000 02 03` (no flags, MTIME 0), DEFLATE body, trailer CRC32 `65252ce7` (verified equal to zlib's CRC32 of `FIRST`) and ISIZE 5 — decompressing to `FIRST`; member 2, 26 bytes, decompressing to `SECOND`; and 6 trailing bytes, `HIDDEN`, at offsets 51–56. The walk lands exactly, three ways. GNU gzip `-dc` outputs `FIRSTSECOND` and warns "trailing garbage ignored" (exit 2) — the tail tolerated, the members both read. Python's `gzip.decompress` on the same file raises BadGzipFile (`Not a gzipped file (b'HI')`) — the tail fatal, nothing returned. And a single-member zlib reader (`decompressobj(31)`) returns `FIRST` alone, with 32 bytes of `unused_data`: the whole second member plus `HIDDEN`, unseen. One file, three readings — and the clean control confirms the seam is the walk, not the bytes: without the tail, Python's gzip returns `FIRSTSECOND` too, while the single-member reader still returns `FIRST` with 26 unused bytes.

- **Decoder-design note (gzip → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The member inventory is the intake.** The Gauntlet's container pass on any gzip parses every member — header flags recomputed, FEXTRA subfields listed by SI and byte budget, FNAME/FCOMMENT captured verbatim, trailer CRC recomputed and ISIZE checked against the actual output length — and reports every byte past the last member's trailer as a compartment, never as garbage to ignore; a member whose CRC mismatches suspends the verdict: UNREAD, never CLEAN. (2) **One member is one reading, and reader disagreement is itself a finding.** The inventory walks all members, and a file whose readers diverge — GNU gzip tolerant, Python gzip fatal, single-member zlib blind past member one — is reported as a divergence event, not resolved by picking the friendliest reader; the verdict names which reader produced it. (3) **Claims are graded against the data they name.** CRC32 against the decompressed bytes, ISIZE against the true length (with the 2^32 wrap stated, not hidden), FHCRC against the header when present and its absence noted when not, FLG reserved bits enforced rather than assumed — the ZIP tie-break lesson and the tar checksum lesson, now on a stream whose whole structure is a list.

- **ar: the archive with no end, or: the walk stops when the bytes do, and nobody checks what is left.** Unix `ar` — the format behind static libraries (`.a`) and, in the same skin, Debian packages (`.deb`) — opens with an 8-byte global magic, `!<arch>\n`, and then is nothing but members. Each member is a 60-byte header — name (16 bytes), modification time (12), owner id (6), group id (6), mode (8), size (10), and the two-byte magic `` `\n `` — followed by the member's bytes, padded with a `\n` when the size is odd so the next header lands on an even offset. There is no member count, no central directory, no end marker, and no total length: the only way to know what is in the archive is to walk it, header by header, until the bytes run out. The format's most consequential deployment is the one its readers never think about: every `.a` static library linked into a binary, and every `.deb` installed by a package manager, is a header walk with no seal — the archive authenticates nothing, and the walk is the whole format.

- **The gaps are the hiding places, and the first one is that there is no end to check.** First, a reader that walks to end-of-file never distinguishes "archive ends here" from "archive ends here plus six more bytes": the tail is not a parse error, it is bytes the walk never reaches — and GNU `ar` lists the members and exits 0 without a word about it, the silent form of the gzip tail (where GNU gzip at least warned). Second, the size field is a claim about where the next header lives: a lied size does not trip any alarm, it simply moves the next header read — one crafted size desynchronizes the whole rest of the walk, the cpio lesson without even cpio's magic to resynchronize on (the next header's only check is its own two-byte magic). Third, names are indirection: GNU long names live in a `//` string-table member, and a member named `/0` means "read my name at offset 0 of that table" — the name is a pointer into another member's bytes, the DEX string-table discipline in an archive's coat, and the table itself is a member any walk can misplace. Fourth, the padding byte and the thin variant are the sanctioned elsewheres: the `\n` pad after every odd-sized member is a byte no reader interprets, and a thin archive (`!<thin>\n`) carries no member bytes at all — only names and paths to files that live outside the archive — so an inventory of the archive is an inventory of pointers, not of payload. Fifth, the BSD dialect changes the hiding rules mid-walk: a name of the form `#1/<len>` means the name bytes ride inline before the data and count toward the size, so the same walk must switch parsers by name prefix — a reader that assumes one dialect misreads the other.

- **Worked miniature (built and walked this pass).** A 224-byte ar archive: global magic at 0–7; `//` string-table member at 8 (header 8–67, table 68–89: `long-member-name.txt/\n`); `note.txt/` at 90 (header 90–149, data 150–152 `Hi\n`, pad 153); `/0` at 154 (header 154–213, data 214–216 `Yo\n`, pad 217) — the long name resolved only through the table; and then 6 trailing bytes, `HIDDEN`, at offsets 218–223. The walk lands exactly: every header's magic verifies, both sizes land their next headers on even offsets, the `/0` reference resolves to the table's first entry — and the tail is fewer than one 60-byte header, so no walk can even begin to parse it. The real readers agree with the walk and then say nothing: GNU `ar t` lists `note.txt` and `long-member-name.txt`, exit 0, identical to the clean control without the tail; `ar p` extracts `Hi\nYo\n` identically; `file` reports "current ar archive" with no complaint. The tail is not an error to any of them. It is an attic the format built by ending its map at end-of-file instead of at an end marker.

- **Decoder-design note (ar → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The walk is the intake, and the walk reports its own remainder.** The Gauntlet's container pass on any ar parses every header — name, size, and magic recomputed, never trusted — resolves every `/N` reference against the string table it actually parsed, and reports every byte past the last member's padded end as a compartment, never as nothing; an archive whose remainder is nonzero is not the archive the members describe. (2) **"Lists clean" and "contains only the listed members" are different claims, and "is an archive" and "is a thin archive" are different claims too.** The lister shows the members; the inventory grades the remainder, the pads, the string table's unreferenced entries, and — for thin archives — the external files the names point at, which are payload the archive does not carry. (3) **Claims are graded against the data they name.** Sizes against the next header's landing offset, string-table offsets against the table's actual bytes, member modes and timestamps against the claim that this archive is what its builder says it is — the ZIP extent lesson and the cpio framing lesson, now on a format with no checksum, no count, and no end.
