- **WIM: the image that is a file cabinet, not a sector copy — or: the header is the map, the XML is the catalogue, and the lookup is the only proof a file is the file.** WIM (Windows Imaging Format, file-based, introduced with Windows Vista) stores an operating-system image as files, not sectors, so a multi-image file can hold several images sharing identical files once. Microsoft Learn names six resource types: header, file resource, metadata resource, lookup table, XML data, and integrity table. The header is 208 bytes and starts with the signature `MSWIM` (five letters plus three zero bytes); it carries the version, flags, chunk size (32768 by default), image count, boot index, and resource descriptors — including the XML descriptor whose offset field sits at header offset 80 and length field at header offset 88. Compression is LZX for maximum compression, XPRESS for fast compression, or uncompressed; single-instance storage means identical file content is stored once and named by its hash in the lookup table, so the same bytes in two images are one resource, not two.

- **The gaps are the hiding places, and the sharpest one is that the catalogue is not the content.** First, XML trust: the XML block names images and describes them, but it does not prove any file resource — a reader that lists images from XML alone reports names, not files. Only the lookup table's hash-to-resource binding proves a given resource is the content an image claims. Second, the signature is a map claim, not a formality: a file whose first five bytes are not `MSWIM` is not a WIM file, and parsing its header fields anyway misdiagnoses wrong-type data as a corrupt image — the signature check runs before any descriptor is trusted. Third, descriptor bounds are parser rules: an XML descriptor whose offset plus length runs past file size is malformed before any XML is parsed, and a walk that ends before file size (or a tail past the walk) is a compartment, never padding. Fourth, chunking cuts both ways: a file resource is split into chunks (32768 bytes by default), so a per-chunk claim without the chunk table and the full resource hash is unsound wherever a later chunk's content depends on the resource as a whole. Fifth, the integrity table is a gate with the same limit as every checksum gate in this library: it can confirm the image it covers, and it says nothing about bytes outside its coverage.

- **Worked miniature (built and walked this pass).** A 327-byte header-shaped miniature, built by hidden_files/wim-mini.py — explicitly NOT a DISM/WIMLIB-readable `.wim` file, because it carries no real metadata resource, no real lookup-table record, and no LZX/XPRESS stream. Header: 208 bytes, signature `MSWIM`, cbSize 208, version field 0x10D00, chunk size 32768, image count 1, boot index 1. File resource at offset 208: `HELLO` (5 bytes, uncompressed). XML at offset 213: 114 bytes of UTF-16LE naming one image `MINI_WIM`. The script's own lookup binds SHA-1 `c65f99f8c5376adadddc46d5cbcf5762f9e55eb7` to the resource at offset 208. Five walks: clean parses the header, parses the XML, verifies the resource hash, and ends exactly at 327; a corrupted signature trips before any descriptor is read; an XML descriptor moved past end-of-file trips the bounds check; a one-byte truncation trips (on the XML bounds check); and the same miniature plus a 6-byte `HIDDEN` tail (333 bytes) trips the end-of-walk check — the tail visible only as the size-vs-walk mismatch.

- **Decoder-design note (WIM → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Signature, size, then descriptors.** The container pass checks `MSWIM` first, cbSize = 208 second, and only then trusts any descriptor; a descriptor failing its bounds check suspends the verdict: UNREAD, never CLEAN. (2) **Catalogue is not content.** No file-content claim is reported from XML alone; content claims require the lookup hash binding the resource, and a resource decoded without its hash is reported as DECODED-WITHOUT-HASH. (3) **Walk must end at file size.** Any tail past the XML-and-resources walk, and any gap the descriptors do not account for, is a compartment, never padding.

- **What this entry does not do.** It does not walk a real-world WIM file (DISM output, installer `install.wim`) against this parser; it does not decode LZX or XPRESS streams, or an ESD solid-compressed variant; it does not walk a multi-image file, a split WIM (`.swm` parts), a metadata resource, a real lookup-table record, or an integrity table; and it does not verify the flag-bit meanings or the version field against a real header — the miniature's version and flags are carried values, not spec-verified claims. Next: the remaining uncovered archive/container format in section (m) (SquashFS), or a real-WIM interop check.

*WIM entry seeded 2026-11-01 ~09:52 EST by the decoder-create-loop.*

- **SquashFS superblock miniature (4.0).** The read-only filesystem
  that ships half of embedded Linux: a SquashFS image is built once by
  mksquashfs and never modified in place, because every byte after the
  superblock is compressed and packed — changing one byte would mean
  decompressing, changing, and recompressing a block and reorganising
  everything after it. The image is at most nine parts, packed on byte
  alignment: superblock, compression options, data blocks and fragments,
  inode table, directory table, fragment table, export table, uid/gid
  lookup table, and xattr table. Data blocks run 4K to 1M (default
  128K); metadata (inodes and directories) is packed into 8K blocks
  with no alignment padding, so an inode may straddle two compressed
  blocks. The superblock is 96 bytes, all little-endian, and it is the
  only map: magic `hsqs` (0x73717368) at 0–3; inodes at 4–7; mkfs_time
  at 8–11; block_size at 12–15; fragments at 16–19; compression at
  20–21; block_log at 22–23; flags at 24–25; no_ids at 26–27; s_major
  at 28–29; s_minor at 30–31; root_inode at 32–39; bytes_used at
  40–47; id_table_start at 48–55; xattr_id_table_start at 56–63;
  inode_table_start at 64–71; directory_table_start at 72–79;
  fragment_table_start at 80–87; lookup_table_start at 88–95.
  Compression ids: 1 zlib, 2 lzma, 3 lzo, 4 xz, 5 lz4, 6 zstd. Flags
  bits 0, 1, and 2 read as inodes stored uncompressed (-noI), data
  blocks stored uncompressed (-noD), and checksums present; the
  remaining flag bits are carried, not interpreted here. The root
  inode is a 64-bit inode reference: a metadata-block location plus
  the offset into that block, the <block, offset> pair by which every
  inode in the image is addressed. Each metadata block is prefixed by
  a two-byte little-endian header whose top bit, when set, means the
  block is stored uncompressed (it is uncompressed whenever -noI is
  set, or whenever compression made it larger); the low 15 bits carry
  the stored length, on this entry's reading — see the open check
  below. Inodes are addressed by 16-bit indices into the id table
  rather than by full 32-bit uids/gids, and file tails that do not
  fill a block are packed together into fragment blocks, so one
  fragment block's bytes routinely belong to several files at once.
- **The gaps are the hiding places, and the sharpest one is that the
  superblock is a map of claims, not a census.** First, every table
  start is a claim about where a table lives: a table start past
  bytes_used, or a walk that ends short of bytes_used, is malformed
  before any table is read, and any bytes the walk does not account
  for are a compartment, never padding — the same end-of-walk rule as
  the WIM and ISO entries. Second, the compression id is a decoder
  claim: a reader that lacks the named decompressor cannot verify a
  single data block, and reporting the superblock's fields as the
  filesystem's contents mistakes the map for the territory. Third,
  the metadata header's top bit is trust: a block marked uncompressed
  is taken at face value, so a doctored bit turns compressed bytes
  into "plaintext" for any reader that does not cross-check the
  length against the table walk. Fourth, fragment packing is shared
  custody: a fragment block holds tails from several files, so no
  per-file content claim is sound without the fragment-table entry
  that binds this file's tail to its bytes in the shared block.
  Fifth, the id table is indirection with the same limit as every
  indirection in this library: an inode's uid index proves nothing
  about ownership until the id table itself is walked and its entry
  read — a reader that reports index 0 as uid 0 has guessed.
- **Worked miniature (built and walked this pass).** A 122-byte
  superblock-shaped miniature — explicitly NOT a mountable `.sqsh`
  image, because it carries no real inode, no real directory entry,
  no fragment/export/xattr table, and no xz stream. Superblock: 96
  bytes, magic `hsqs`, version 4.0, inodes 2, block_size 131072
  (128K), block_log 17, compression 4 (xz), flags 0, no_ids 1,
  root_inode reference (96 << 16) | 0 — metadata block 96, offset 0.
  Metadata block at offset 96: header 0x8010 (top bit set,
  uncompressed, 16 bytes) plus the labelled stub `ROOTDIR-STUB....`,
  which is not a directory inode and is never parsed as one.
  Id-table region at offset 114: two u32 values, uid 1000 and gid
  1000. bytes_used 122, and the walk — superblock, metadata block,
  id region — ends exactly at 122. Seven walks: clean parses every
  field and ends exactly at bytes_used; a corrupted magic (`hsqt`)
  trips before any field is trusted; a 50-byte truncation trips on
  superblock size; an unknown compression id 9 trips; a block_log of
  16 against a 131072 block size trips the log2 cross-check; an
  id_table_start of 9999 trips the bounds check; and the same
  miniature plus a 5-byte `HIDDN` tail (127 bytes) trips the
  bytes_used-vs-file-size check — the tail visible only as the
  size-vs-walk mismatch.
- **Decoder-design note (SquashFS → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1)
  **Magic, size, and compression before descriptors.** The container
  pass checks `hsqs` first, 96 bytes second, a known compression id
  third, and block_log == log2(block_size) fourth; only then is any
  table start trusted, and a table start past bytes_used suspends
  the verdict: UNREAD, never CLEAN. (2) **Walk must end at
  bytes_used.** Any tail past the table walk, and any gap the table
  starts do not account for, is a compartment, never padding. (3)
  **Shared blocks need shared-custody proof.** No per-file claim is
  reported from a fragment block without its fragment-table entry,
  and no ownership claim is reported from an inode without its id
  table entry — indirection is walked, never assumed.
- **What this entry does not do.** It does not walk a real SquashFS
  image (mksquashfs output, a live-CD `.sqsh`) against this parser;
  it does not parse any real inode or directory entry (basic vs
  extended types, directory headers and indexes, symlink targets);
  it does not decompress any xz/zlib/lz4/lzo/zstd block; it does not
  build or walk a fragment table, export table, compression-options
  block, or xattr table; and it does not verify the metadata-header
  length convention against a real image — whether the low 15 bits
  are the exact stored length or length-minus-one is this entry's
  open check, and the miniature is self-consistent under the exact
  reading only. Next: a real directory-inode miniature (basic
  directory header plus one entry, with the <block, offset> reference
  walked), or a mksquashfs interop check. With this entry, section
  (m)'s named archive/container set is complete: CAB, WIM, ISO 9660,
  and SquashFS.

*SquashFS entry seeded 2026-11-01 ~10:34 EST by the decoder-create-loop.*

- **SquashFS directory-inode miniature (4.0).** The superblock entry
  mapped the filesystem; this entry walks one directory inside it —
  the follow-on the superblock entry named as its Next. A SquashFS
  directory is not a list of names. It is a two-level list: a
  directory header carrying a shared inode-block value, then a
  sequence of directory entries that share that block, and a new
  header is written whenever the inode start block changes — the
  header/entry list repeats as many times as necessary. A directory
  is addressed, like every inode, by a <block, offset> pair: the
  directory inode's start_block plus directory_table gives the
  metadata block, and its offset gives the byte offset into the
  decompressed block. The miniature's layout, all little-endian: a
  basic directory inode of 34 bytes — type u16 (1 = directory), mode
  u16, uid u16, gid u16, mtime u32, inode_number u32, start_block
  u32 (the directory-table offset), nlink u32, file_size u32 (the
  listing's byte budget: headers plus entries), offset u16,
  parent_inode u32. A directory header of 12 bytes — count u32,
  start_block u32 (the shared inode-block offset), inode_number u32
  (the base the entries' deltas hang from). A directory entry of 8
  bytes plus the name — offset u16 (into the shared inode block),
  inode_number s16 (a SIGNED delta from the header base, not an
  absolute number), type u16, size u16 (the name length MINUS ONE:
  kernel namei.c reads the name as dire->size + 1), then the name
  bytes, which are NOT NUL-terminated. The count-minus-one
  convention (count = entries in the group minus one) is this
  entry's open check: the miniature is self-consistent under it,
  but it was not verified against the public header this pass, and
  neither were the directory inode's exact field widths — both are
  carried as the miniature's convention, not as verified header
  claims.
- **The gaps are the hiding places, and the sharpest one is that the
  entry's inode number is arithmetic, not an address.** First, the
  count is load-bearing: a header that claims one entry more than
  the listing holds does not stop at the listing end — the walker
  reads the next header's bytes as an entry and desyncs, so a count
  lie corrupts every entry after it, not just the last one. Second,
  the delta is signed: a reader that treats the entry's
  inode_number as an absolute number silently resolves the wrong
  inode — and for a negative delta it resolves a negative, impossible
  inode — with NO trip, because nothing in the walk bounds-checks
  the resolved number against the header's group. Third, the size
  field is length-minus-one: a reader that takes it as the length
  truncates the name by one byte and shifts every later header by
  one, so the whole rest of the listing misparses — the off-by-one
  is a desync, not a typo. Fourth, the type field is the ENTRY's
  type, and the offset is into the SHARED block: a reader that
  resolves the entry against the wrong block (the directory's own
  block instead of the header's start_block) lands in unrelated
  bytes and calls them an inode. Fifth, file_size is the listing's
  budget, not a hint: any byte past the walked headers and entries
  is a compartment, never padding — the same end-of-walk rule as
  the superblock, WIM, and ISO entries.
- **Worked miniature (built and walked this pass).** A 116-byte
  directory-table-shaped miniature, built by a miniature script held privately with the project
  — explicitly NOT a mountable `.sqsh` image, because the inode
  blocks are labelled stubs (`INODE-STUB-A....`,
  `INODE-STUB-B....`) that are never parsed as real inodes, and no
  metadata block is compressed. Directory inode at 0–33: type 1,
  mode 0o40755, start_block 34, file_size 50. Directory table at
  34: header 1 (count 0, start_block 84, base inode 10) plus entry
  `a.txt` (offset 0, delta +2, type 2, size 4 = 5-char name) resolving
  to inode 12 at <84, 0>; header 2 (count 0, start_block 100, base
  inode 20) plus entry `b.txt` (offset 0, delta −1, type 2, size 4)
  resolving to inode 19 at <100, 0> — the second header exercising
  the documented new-header-when-the-block-changes rule. Six walks:
  clean resolves both entries and ends exactly at the listing end;
  a count lie (header 1 count 0 → 1) trips on unknown entry type
  100, the next header's bytes misread as an entry; an entry offset
  of 9999 trips the stub-bounds check; a size-as-length reader trips
  on a name running past the listing end; a delta-as-absolute reader
  does NOT trip — it silently resolves `a.txt` to inode 2 and `b.txt`
  to inode −1, the walk's only silent failure; and the clean
  miniature plus a 6-byte `HIDDN` tail (122 bytes) walks clean but
  trips the size-vs-walk check — the tail visible only as the
  mismatch.
- **Decoder-design note (SquashFS directory → Gauntlet).** Three
  rungs. (1) **Resolve, never assume.** Every entry's inode is
  computed as header base plus signed delta, and the resolved
  number is checked against the header's group before it is
  reported; an unresolvable or negative resolution suspends the
  verdict: UNREAD, never CLEAN. (2) **Count the listing, not the
  entries.** The walk consumes exactly file_size bytes and must end
  exactly at the listing end; a count lie, a size-as-length slip,
  or a tail past the end all fail the same end-of-listing check.
  (3) **The second header is legal.** A new header mid-listing
  with a different start_block is the documented shape, not
  corruption — the walk follows it and re-bases the deltas, and
  only a header whose block falls outside the walked tables trips.
- **What this entry does not do.** It does not walk a real SquashFS
  image (mksquashfs output, a live-CD `.sqsh`) against this parser;
  it does not parse any real inode (basic vs extended directory
  types, directory indexes, symlink targets); it does not walk a
  fragment table, export table, compression-options block, or xattr
  table; it does not verify the count-minus-one convention or the
  directory inode's field widths against the public header — both
  are this entry's open checks; and it does not decompress any
  metadata block. Next: a mksquashfs interop check, or a real
  fragment-table miniature (shared tails bound to files by
  fragment-table entries).

- **SquashFS fragment-table miniature — shared tails bound to files by
  fragment-table entries.** The open check named by the directory-inode
  entry's "Next" line, built this pass. The kernel doc §3.5 shape: a
  regular file's inode carries a fragment index, mapped through a
  fragment lookup table to a fragment block's location on disk and its
  compressed size; the table itself lives compressed in metadata blocks
  behind a second index table that is read at mount time and cached.
  The miniature (held privately with the project, uncompressed —
  compression is out of scope; the binding is what is checked) holds
  two fragment blocks. Block 0 is shared: alpha's 10-byte tail at
  offset 0 and beta's 10-byte tail at offset 10, so one block serves a
  file with a full datablock plus a tail (alpha: `ALPHA-BLK0` +
  `alpha-tail`) and a file that is nothing but a tail (beta:
  `beta-tail!`). Block 1 carries gamma's tail alone. Delta has no
  blocks and no fragment, and resolves to empty — a fragment index of
  "none" is a legal file, not a missing one.
- **The walk rule, in one sentence.** Resolve = full datablocks in
  order, then exactly `fragment_block[offset:offset+size]`; any of
  four failures suspends the verdict to UNREAD, never partial bytes:
  (1) fragment index outside the table (epsilon, index 9); (2)
  offset + size past the block's end (zeta, 15+10 over a 20-byte
  block); (3) two files claiming overlapping ranges in one block
  (eta 0–12 vs theta 8–16); (4) a fragment index claimed alongside a
  nonzero offset/size on a file that declares none. The overlap rule
  carries a walk-set lesson the first run of this miniature caught
  live: the corruption fixtures eta/theta share block 0 with the clean
  files, so a naive all-files overlap scan marked alpha itself UNREAD.
  The fix is walk-set isolation — clean files resolve against the
  clean set, each corruption case against its own set — and the
  miniature now asserts exactly that: 4 resolves + 4 UNREADs, all as
  stated, exit 0.
- **Decoder-design note (fragment table → Gauntlet).** Three rungs.
  (1) **Bind, never assume.** A tail is not data until its index
  resolves through the table to a block that exists and a range inside
  it; an unresolvable tail suspends the verdict: UNREAD, never CLEAN.
  (2) **Sharing is the tell, not the crime.** Two files in one
  fragment block is the documented packing shape, not evidence of
  tampering — the crime is overlap, overrun, or an index to nowhere.
  (3) **Isolate the corruption set.** A test fixture that shares a
  block with the control poisons the control; every corruption walk
  runs in its own file set, or the test grades itself.
- **What this entry does not do.** It does not parse a real
  mksquashfs image (the directory entry's other "Next" line — the
  interop check — is still open); it does not decompress any fragment
  block or verify the fragment entry's on-disk field widths against
  the public header; it does not walk the export, uid/gid, or xattr
  tables; it does not test a fragment block shared by more than two
  files, or a file whose tail is its only block at a nonzero offset in
  a multi-file block (beta's offset-10 whole-file tail is the closest
  shape). Next: the mksquashfs interop check, or a three-file shared
  block.

- **Decoder-design note (three-file sharing → Gauntlet).** Two rungs.
  (1) **Count is not suspicion.** A block shared three ways is the
  same documented packing shape as a block shared two ways; the
  Gauntlet grades the ranges, not the headcount — overlap, overrun,
  or an index to nowhere are the crimes, and a third sharer adds no
  new crime. (2) **Nonzero-offset tail-only files are first-class.**
  A file that is nothing but a tail need not sit at offset 0; two
  proves a tail-only file can live mid-block, and any walk that
  assumes tail-only means offset 0 will misread a legal file.

  mksquashfs image (the interop check is still the open line from
  the directory entry); it does not decompress any fragment block or
  verify the fragment entry's on-disk field widths against the
  public header; it does not walk the export, uid/gid, or xattr
  tables; it does not test a fragment block shared by four or more
  files, or a tail split across two fragment blocks (the format
  gives each file at most one fragment, so a split tail would be a
  corruption shape, not a packing shape). Next: the mksquashfs
  interop check, or a four-sharer block as a pure headcount
  confirmation.

- **SquashFS wrong-size-fragment corruption miniature.** The

  entry must be exactly R bytes long and lie wholly inside its
  fragment block. A fragment that is short, long, empty, or
  overrunning is not a tail that can be repaired: padding invents
  bytes the file never had, truncating discards bytes the file
  claims, and clipping silently rewrites the inode's own
  accounting. The resolver refuses the whole file — UNREAD, never

*SquashFS out-of-range-fragment-index corruption entry seeded 2026-11-01 ~13:45 EST by the decoder-create-loop.*

- **SquashFS real-image interop check (4.0).** The open line since
  the directory entry, closed this pass: a tool that can emit a
  real image is available on this VM now (squashfs-tools 4.6.1,
  installed from the Ubuntu archive), so the loop built two real
  images with mksquashfs (4K blocks, gzip, -noappend) and resolved
  files out of them with a pure-Python reader written from the
  documented format — no unsquashfs output used as evidence for
  this entry's claims. Main image: alpha.txt 5000 bytes, beta.txt
  100, gamma.txt 4096, delta.txt 0, inner/note.txt 11. Single
  image: big.txt 5000 alone. All six files resolved
  byte-identically to their sources.
- **What the real encoder taught the loop: five corrections to the
  miniature lineage.** (1) Tables are index-prefixed: the
  superblock's *_table_start points at an array of u64 entries,
  each an ABSOLUTE file offset of a metadata block; the blocks
  themselves live elsewhere in the file (here, immediately before
  their index). The miniatures stored tables as bare metadata
  blocks — a reader that seeks to table_start expecting a metadata
  header reads an index entry as a header and fails (this pass's
  first failure: header 0x04b1, length 1201, inside a 32-byte
  region). (2) Inode references pack (metadata-block INDEX within
  the inode table << 16 | offset in block), and a directory
  header's start_block is the same kind of index — not a file
  offset. The root's reference 140 means block 0, offset 140, not
  file offset 140. (3) The basic directory inode is 32 bytes, not
  the 34 the miniatures assumed: base (16) + start_block + nlink +
  file_size (u16) + offset (u16) + parent_inode (u32). The
  sequential inode-table walk with 32-byte dirs consumes exactly
  the table (236 bytes, 7 inodes; 72 bytes, 2 inodes) — a 34-byte
  walk misaligns at the second inode. The offset field is the
  listing's offset within its directory-table block: listings for
  several directories pack consecutively (inner's at 0, root's at
  28 in the single-directory-table block). (4) The fragment rule,
  as this encoder behaves by default: a fragment block holds ONLY
  whole files smaller than the block size. A multi-block file's
  tail is a trailing PARTIAL data block — alpha's block list has
  two entries, spans (96, 326) and (422, 287), chaining exactly
  96 + 326 = 422 and 422 + 287 = 709 = gamma's start, fragment =
  none; the single-file image carries fragments = 0. The
  miniatures assumed every tail fragments; that holds only for
  sub-block files (beta, note — the 111-byte fragment block holds
  exactly their 100 + 11 bytes) or, untested here, when
  mksquashfs is passed -always-use-fragments. (5) bytes_used is
  the filesystem length, not the file length: mksquashfs pads the
  file to a 4K boundary (1335 vs 4096; 825 vs 4096).
- **Two observed constants, mechanism open.** Directory file_size
  reads exactly 3 bytes above the walked listing in all three
  directories walked (root 95 vs 92, inner 31 vs 28, single root
  30 vs 27). A reader that trusts file_size as the exact walk
  length over-reads into the next table's block; the walk here
  stops on header fit instead. A non-root directory's
  parent_inode is its parent's number exactly (inner -> 7 =
  root); the ROOT directory's parent_inode reads (number of
  inodes + 1) in both images (8 for 7 inodes, 3 for 2) — a
  sentinel or a quirk, not yet explained, and never used by the
  walk.
- **Decoder-design note (interop -> Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1)
  **The first real image breaks the miniature.** Five format
  assumptions survived a dozen miniatures and all five were wrong
  in detail (index prefix, reference packing, dir-inode width,
  fragment rule, bytes_used). A container pass graded only
  against self-built miniatures is graded against its own
  assumptions; the interop check — real encoder output,
  independent reader, byte-identical resolution — is the rung
  that earns the word VERIFIED. (2) **Trust the walk, not the
  header.** file_size over-states by 3, bytes_used under-states
  the file, the fragment field says "none" where a tail exists
  (as a partial block). Every length in the carrier is a claim;
  the walk that resolves bytes is the evidence. A Gauntlet
  container pass that stops at the first header disagreement, or
  that trusts a size field over its own walk, fails exactly where
  this image would have fooled it. (3) **Encoder version is part
  of the specimen.** All of this is mksquashfs 4.6.1 default
  behaviour; another encoder (or -always-use-fragments) may
  fragment multi-block tails. The container pass records the
  encoder and its flags with the image, and treats any format rule
  as version-scoped until a second encoder confirms it.
- **What this entry does not do.** It does not test
  -always-use-fragments output (the multi-block-fragment shape the
  kernel's fragment-tail path expects); it does not walk the
  lookup or id tables (their index-prefixed shape was confirmed
  on a diagnostic image during debugging, not by this script's
  assertions); it does not explain the +3 directory file_size gap
  or the root parent_inode = inodes+1 reading; it does not
  decompress xz/zstd/lz4 blocks (gzip only); it does not walk
  extended inodes, xattrs, or sparse holes (no sparse file was
  built); it does not parse a SquashFS image from any other
  encoder. Next: the -always-use-fragments image (does the
  multi-block tail move into the fragment block, and does the
  fragment rule then match the miniatures?), or the +3/parent
  explanations, or an xz-compressed image.

- **Braille (1824) — the tactile code, or: a code with no secrecy at all.** Louis Braille, blind from age five, built it at fifteen (1824, published 1829) from Charles Barbier's "night writing" — a 12-dot military system for reading orders in the dark — by cutting the cell to six dots: two columns of three, 64 possible patterns, one per letter, digit, punctuation mark, or (with prefix cells) number and formatting sign. France adopted it in 1854, two years after Braille's death; it has since been adapted to nearly every written language, plus music notation and mathematics (Nemeth Code, 1952). [VERIFIED — standard history]
- **Decoder-design note (Braille → Gauntlet).** Braille is the catalogue's control case for a code that was never a cipher: same machinery as cryptanalysis (symbol set, mapping table, context rules) with the secrecy rung removed entirely. Two lessons. (1) **The channel is the code.** A six-dot cell read by fingertip is unreadable to every sight-based parser the Gauntlet owns — a specimen that encodes in a channel the interrogator cannot sense is not "undeciphered," it is unperceived, and the first interrogation question is always "what senses does this channel need?" (2) **Sixty-four patterns forced compression.** Grade 2 Braille contractions (whole words in one cell) are compression under a hard alphabet budget — the same pressure that drives a specimen to pack meaning into fewer symbols, and the reason the Gauntlet's parser must treat a short symbol stream as possibly dense, never as possibly empty. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are doctrine, never run]

*Braille entry seeded 2026-11-01 ~12:35 PST by the decoder-create-loop.*

- **Semaphore flag signalling (Napoleonic era onward) — the code written in arm positions, or: a code with no secrecy at all, part two.** One signaller, two flags, one in each hand. Each arm is held at one of eight clock positions (45° apart, straight-down being rest), and the pair of positions names a letter — 26 letters, plus numerals and control signals (ready, error, annul) from further positions. The word itself is Greek: *sema* (sign) + *phero* (to bear, to carry). The namesake is the land semaphore telegraph: Claude Chappe's tower-arm system in Revolutionary France, and the British Admiralty's shutter-telegraph variant, whose six shutters gave 64 combinations and carried a message the 69 miles from London to Deal in 60 seconds; Sir Home Popham's two-arm masthead semaphore then served the Royal Navy until the electric telegraph replaced it in 1847. The hand-flag system the word now means was developed by the Royal Navy during the Napoleonic wars for ship-to-ship messages — faster and simpler than the single-flag wig-wag it displaced — and was adopted by the U.S. Army Signal Corps in 1914 after the U.S. Navy and Field Artillery had already proved it. A practiced operator sent 12–15 words or code groups per minute; the chief limitation was range, line of sight and clear air, with masthead mechanical arms read at 16–18 miles in the best conditions and hand flags far shorter. At night the same positions were made with lamps. [VERIFIED — mechanics, etymology, Chappe/Murray/Popham lineage, and 1847 replacement via standard histories and the 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica "Signal" article; CORROBORATED — the 12–15 wpm rate, the 16–18 mile masthead reading, and the 1914 U.S. Army adoption via the U.S. Army Signal Corps historical article]
- **Decoder-design note (Semaphore → Gauntlet).** Semaphore completes the catalogue's "no secrecy" control set as its third channel: Braille is touch, Morse is sound-in-time, semaphore is sight-in-space — same machinery (symbol set, mapping table, context rules), secrecy rung removed, and each channel fails differently. Three lessons. (1) **The body is the transmitter.** A specimen's symbols can be postures, not marks on a carrier: an interrogator that only reads files will miss a specimen that signals with position, timing, or orientation, so the first interrogation question after Braille's "what senses does this channel need?" is "what does this channel's transmitter look like?" (2) **Range is a security property.** Semaphore's secrecy was never cryptographic; it was geometric — only receivers inside line of sight could read it, and fog, distance, or a hill ended the message. The Gauntlet's "who could have seen this" is a real interrogation question: audience geometry bounds exposure exactly the way key length bounds a cipher. (3) **The code carries its own correction protocol.** Semaphore has explicit error and annul signals — the sender can retract a mis-sent letter in-band, something almost no cipher offers. That makes the reader's misread, not the code's mathematics, the attack surface: a wrong arm angle is a wrong letter with no checksum to catch it, and the correction signal itself becomes a thing to forge. A specimen that can say "disregard that" can also say it falsely. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are doctrine, never run]

- **Chappe optical telegraph (1792–1850s) — the code with no secrecy in the channel, part three.** Claude Chappe and his brothers built it in Revolutionary France after discarding synchronized-clock dials and smoke signals: a tower-top rig of one long pivoting regulator (4 positions) with a shorter indicator arm at each end (7 positions each) — 4 × 7 × 7 = 196 combinations, of which 92 were used as code signals. Signals went in pairs: the first named a page of the codebook, the second a line on it — 92 × 92 = 8,464 coded words and phrases, from troop orders to the national lottery results. Towers stood 5–15 km apart in line of sight; each station's two operators read the previous tower through a telescope, wrote the symbols in a book, and re-set their own arms for the next tower. The Paris–Lille line (15 stations, ~230 km) opened in the summer of 1794; its first news was the recapture of Condé-sur-l'Escaut from the Austrians on 30 August 1794, known in Paris within the hour — the first symbol crossed all 15 stations in about 9 minutes, a full 36-symbol message typically in about 32. At its peak the network ran 534–556 stations over roughly 5,000 km, radiating from Paris, and Napoleon ran his empire on it; the electric telegraph replaced it in the 1850s (France's lines dismantled after the Foy–Bréguet system). Chappe coined both words the field still uses: *télégraphe* (far-writer) and, in 1801, *sémaphore*. [VERIFIED — mechanism, 196/92/8,464 arithmetic, Paris–Lille line, and 1850s replacement via Wikipedia "Chappe telegraph," the Engineering and Technology History Wiki, and Google Arts & Culture; CORROBORATED — the peak station count (534 vs 556 across sources), the 9-minute first-symbol / 32-minute message timings, and the "within the hour" Condé report]
- **Decoder-design note (Chappe → Gauntlet).** Chappe inverts semaphore's lesson and completes the "no secrecy" set's fourth member: the arm positions were visible to anyone with a telescope — the channel hid nothing — and all the secrecy lived in the codebook, which never left the endpoints. Four lessons. (1) **Blind relays.** The stationnaires who re-transmitted every symbol could not read a word of it; they were carriers, not readers. A seized relay yields symbols, not meaning — so interrogation that captures an intermediary and finds nothing has not failed, it has found the architecture: compromise the codebook, not the carrier. (2) **Relay re-encoding compounds error.** Every tower re-set the arms from its own reading, so a misread propagated downstream as truth, with no end-to-end check anywhere in the line. A specimen that passes through many hands must be verified endpoint-to-endpoint, never trusted hop-by-hop. (3) **The network is the attack surface.** One compromised tower could inject, drop, or alter symbols for the whole downstream line — man-in-the-middle, 1794 edition — and the endpoints had no way to tell. Defence lives at the endpoints (verification), never in relay trust. (4) **Weather is denial-of-service.** Fog ended the message as surely as a cut wire; availability is a property of the channel, and the Gauntlet's "who could have seen this" (semaphore) extends to "when could anyone have seen this at all." [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are doctrine, never run]

## SquashFS xattr id table walk: word52 resolves to the set, identical sets share one id

- **Claim.** A type-9 inode's offset-52 word is an index into the
  xattr id table, and the reader can resolve it to the file's
  actual xattr set without any other tool. Two files carrying
  the identical xattr set share one id: the encoder deduplicates
  sets, not just entries. [VERIFIED -- reader's own parse,
  below]
- **How the walk goes.** The superblock's xattr_id_table_start
  points at a 24-byte footer, not at the xattr table: three
  u64s -- the file offset of the xattr table's metadata block,
  the id count, and the file offset of the id entries'
  metadata block. The footer is always 24 bytes whatever the
  id count (checked at 1, 2, and 3 distinct sets in probing;
  the shipped run uses 2). The xattr table decompresses to a
  back-to-back stream of entries, each u16 type (0 = user.),
  u16 name_len, name bytes, u32 value_len, value bytes, with
  no padding and no terminator. Each id entry is 16 bytes:
  u64 stream offset, u32 count, u32 size, where size counts
  each entry's bytes except its u16 type field (alpha's
  16-byte entry contributes 14; gamma+beta contribute 16-2
  and 15-2 = 27). A file's word52 selects its id entry; the
  entry's stream offset plus count entries are the file's set.
- **Observed.** Default-flag image (bytes_used 566, footer at
  542): table block 461, id block 509, id block ending exactly
  at the footer, stream 47 bytes. Id 0 = offset 0, count 1,
  size 14, set {user.alpha=aaa}; id 1 = offset 16, count 2,
  size 27, set {user.gamma=ggg, user.beta=bbb}. seta.bin and
  seta2.bin (identical user.alpha=aaa, different content
  bytes) both read word52 0x0; setb.bin reads 0x1; plain.bin
  (no xattrs) stays type 2 with no word52 at all. The AUF
  image repeats every id and every resolved set exactly
  (footer at 522, table block 441, id block 489). One
  encoder-order quirk, recorded not explained: setb's entries
  store gamma-before-beta although beta was set first, so
  sets compare as name-to-value maps, never as sequences.
  The +3 directory gap (file_size 81 vs walked 78) and root
  parent_inode 6 = inodes + 1 reconfirm in both images.
- **Decoder-design note (xattr ids -> Gauntlet).** A reader
  that has walked the footer can now judge the old foreign-
  encoder signal precisely: a word52 that is neither
  0xFFFFFFFF nor a valid id-table index is foreign or corrupt,
  and a valid id whose resolved set fails its own size/count
  check is corrupt, not foreign. [SPECULATION -- the Gauntlet
  mappings are doctrine, never run]
- **What this entry does not do.** It does not walk the
  lookup, export, or uid/gid tables; it does not explain the
  +3 directory file_size gap or the root parent_inode =
  inodes + 1 reading; it does not test xattr prefixes other
  than user., an xattr table spanning several metadata blocks,
  or a SquashFS image from any other encoder. Next: the +3/
  parent explanations, or the export/uid-gid/lookup table
  walks, or a multi-block xattr table.

## SquashFS uid/gid id table walk: inode words are indices, not ids

- **The question the xattr-id entry left open.** The xattr walk
  proved word52 resolves through an id table to a set. The
  sibling table was still unproven by the reader's own parse:
  are the uid/guid words in a SquashFS inode the real owner
  ids, or indices into the superblock's id table? A reader
  that treats them as raw ids gets every non-root owner wrong
  whenever the table order is not the identity -- and this run
  shows the order is not the identity.
- **The images.** mksquashfs 4.6.1, 4K blocks, -noappend,
  -comp zstd, default flags and -always-use-fragments, one
  source tree each: root.bin 5000 bytes owner 0:0, user.bin
  5000 bytes owner 1000:1000, nobody.bin 5000 bytes owner
  65534:65534, mixed.bin 5000 bytes owner 1000:0. Content
  bytes differ per file so no two files can merge blocks.
  The mixed case is the point: uid and gid must resolve
  independently, through the same table, by different indices.
- **The table layout, corrected from a first wrong guess.**
  The reader's first attempt treated id_table_start as a raw
  metadata stream and died on a zstd frame error -- the
  bytes at that offset are not the table but an INDEX of u64
  block offsets, one per ceil(no_ids * 4 / 8192) metadata
  blocks, exactly the fragment table's index-prefixed shape.
  Default image: id_table_start 495, index entry 481, one
  metadata block, header 0x800c (uncompressed, 12 bytes),
  payload three u32 ids. AUF image: id_table_start 479,
  index entry 465, same three ids. [VERIFIED -- the reader's
  own parse on both images, hidden_files/squashfs-uidgid-mini.py]
- **The ids are in encounter order, not sorted.** Both images
  read [1000, 0, 65534]: mixed.bin's uid first, then its gid,
  then nobody's id -- the order mksquashfs met the ids while
  walking the tree, not ascending order. A reader must index
  into the array; bisecting it, or assuming id[k] == k, or
  assuming the first entry is root, all misresolve. [VERIFIED
  -- both images, same order under both flag sets]
- **Every inode resolves through the table.** Default image
  (inodes 5, bytes_used 503): mixed.bin uid_idx 0 gid_idx 1
  -> 1000:0; nobody.bin 2,2 -> 65534:65534; root.bin 1,1 ->
  0:0; user.bin 0,0 -> 1000:1000; the root directory inode
  itself (ino 5) 1,1 -> 0:0. The AUF image resolves
  identically. Every file's 5000 bytes resolve byte-identically
  through the reader, and unsquashfs -ll independently reports
  the same four owners on both images, so the readings are
  not vacuous: had mksquashfs stored raw ids in the inode
  words, the index resolution would mismatch on at least the
  1000 and 65534 files. [VERIFIED -- reader + unsquashfs
  agreement on both flag sets, run 2026-11-02]
- **Flag divergence that does not touch the table.** Default
  flags store the four 904-byte tails as full data blocks
  (fragments 0, frag word 0xFFFFFFFF on every file); AUF
  packs them into one fragment block (fragments 1). The id
  table, the indices, and the resolutions are identical
  either way: tail storage is a flag decision, ownership
  resolution is not. [VERIFIED -- both images]

  that has walked the id table can now judge a foreign or

  at or above no_ids is corrupt, never foreign (the table
  bounds the index space); an index inside the table that
  resolves to an id the interrogation does not expect is
  foreign data, not a parse error; and a table whose id set
  does not cover the indices the inodes actually carry is
  corrupt, not sparse. [SPECULATION -- the Gauntlet mappings

## SquashFS lookup table walk: inode number -> inode reference, in number order

- **The question the uid/gid entry left open.** The id-table
  walk proved inode words resolve through a table. The
  lookup table is the sibling index: the superblock's last
  field, lookup_table_start, names a table of one u64 inode
  reference per inode -- but in what order, and does it cover
  directory inodes or only files? A reader that assumes the
  refs are offset-sorted, or that directories are absent,
  misresolves exactly the nested cases.
- **The images.** mksquashfs 4.6.1, 4K blocks, -noappend,
  -comp zstd, default flags and -always-use-fragments, one
  source tree each: a.bin 5000 bytes and b.bin 3000 bytes in
  the root, sub/c.bin 1234 bytes in a nested subdirectory.
  Content bytes differ per file so no two files can merge
  blocks. The nested directory is the point: its inode and
  its child's inode must both appear in the table.
- **The table layout.** Index-prefixed, like the fragment and
  id tables: u64 block offsets from lookup_table_start, then
  metadata blocks concatenated to inodes * 8 bytes. Default
  image: lookup_table_start 392, bytes_used 414, a 22-byte
  span (8-byte index + one compressed metadata block holding
  five u64 refs). AUF image: lookup_table_start 390, same
  22-byte span. The table is the last thing in the image:
  nothing follows it before bytes_used. [VERIFIED -- the
  reader's own parse on both images,
  hidden_files/squashfs-lookup-mini.py]
- **The refs are in inode-number order, not offset order.**
  Default image: [0x0, 0x28, 0x68, 0x48, 0x88]. Read back,
  each ref's inode-number word (u32 at header +12) equals its
  lookup index + 1: a.bin ino 1, b.bin ino 2, sub ino 3,
  c.bin ino 4, root ino 5. The subdirectory's ref (0x68)
  sorts ABOVE its child's (0x48): the encoder assigned inode
  numbers directory-before-contents, then laid the inodes out
  in a different order. A reader that sorts the refs, or
  assumes ref order equals file order, misresolves the
  nested file. The AUF image reads [0x0, 0x24, 0x64, 0x44,
  0x84] -- same order, every ref shifted by 4 bytes against
  the default image's layout. [VERIFIED -- both images]
- **The root is the last entry, and directories agree.**
  lookup[4] equals the superblock's root_inode (0x88 default,
  0x84 AUF) in both images: the root is numbered last, not
  first. Every directory-listing ref matches its lookup
  entry by inode number -- a.bin, b.bin, sub in the root
  listing, c.bin in the subdirectory listing -- so the
  lookup table and the directory walk are two views of the
  same numbering, and either one checks the other.
  [VERIFIED -- both images]
- **Every file resolves, independently confirmed.** All three
  files (5000, 3000, 1234 bytes) resolve byte-identically
  through the reader on both flag sets, and unsquashfs -ll
  lists the same three files on both images, so the readings
  are not vacuous. [VERIFIED -- reader + unsquashfs
  agreement on both flag sets, run 2026-11-02]
- **Reconfirmed, still unexplained.** Both directories read
  file_size 3 past the walked listing (root 52 vs 49, sub 28
  vs 25 -- the same +3 gap as every prior entry), the root
  directory's parent_inode is 6 = inodes + 1, and the
  subdirectory's parent is 5, the root's own inode number.
  The sub parent reading is new evidence for the parent
  question: a non-root directory's parent is its real
  parent, which makes the root's parent = inodes + 1 look
  like a sentinel rather than a parent at all. [OBSERVED --
  both images, both directories]
- **Decoder-design note (lookup table -> Gauntlet).** The
  lookup table gives the interrogator a second, independent
  numbering of every inode: a specimen whose directory walk
  and lookup table disagree on any ref is corrupt or tampered
  before any file content is judged; a lookup entry pointing
  at a header whose inode number is not its own index is
  corrupt, never foreign; and a table shorter than the inode
  count is truncated, not sparse -- the table's length IS the
  inode count, so there is no room for a missing entry to
  hide. [SPECULATION -- the Gauntlet mappings are doctrine,
  never run]
- **What this entry does not do.** It does not walk the
  export table (the last named table walk); it does not
  explain the +3 directory file_size gap or the root
  parent_inode = inodes + 1 sentinel reading; it does not
  test a lookup table spanning several metadata blocks (that
  needs >1024 inodes), an image from any other encoder, or a
  lookup table under -noappend appends. Next: the export
  table walk, or the +3/parent explanations, or a multi-block
  lookup table.

*[Grade: VERIFIED on the two real images (mksquashfs 4.6.1,
4K blocks, zstd, -noappend, default and -always-use-
fragments): 5 inodes x 2 flag sets, every lookup entry read
back to its own inode number, root entry equal to the
superblock root_inode, every directory ref matching its
lookup entry, all 3 files resolved byte-identically,
unsquashfs -ll agrees on all 3 files in both images;
OBSERVED -- the +3 directory gap on both directories and

ino on the subdirectory, in both images; SPECULATION -- the
Gauntlet mappings are doctrine, never run; no multi-block

## SquashFS export table walk: -exports adds exactly the lookup table, nothing else

- **The question the lookup entry left open.** mksquashfs
  documents -exports ("make filesystem exportable via NFS",
  the default) as if it produced an export table, and the
  lookup entry named the export table as the last table walk
  still undone. But the superblock names no
  export_table_start field -- only lookup_table_start. So
  where is the export table? A reader hunting for a second
  table would search the image forever; this entry runs the
  paired experiment that settles it.
- **The images.** mksquashfs 4.6.1, 4K blocks, -noappend,
  -comp zstd, one source tree each: a.bin 5000 bytes and
  b.bin 3000 bytes in the root, sub/c.bin 1234 bytes in a
  nested subdirectory. Four images: default flags and
  -always-use-fragments, each built once with exports and
  once with -no-exports. Content bytes differ per file so no
  two files can merge blocks.
- **Correction to the lookup entry's geometry.** The lookup
  entry reported the lookup table as a "22-byte span" and
  "the last thing in the image." Both halves were the same
  miscount: it measured from lookup_table_start to
  bytes_used, which silently includes the id table behind
  it. The real geometry, read off these four images: a
  superblock *_start field points at a table's INDEX (one
  u64 block offset per metadata block), and the table's
  metadata blocks sit immediately BEFORE that index, so a
  table's region is [block_start, index + 8) and the tables
  tile contiguously -- fragment region ends where the next
  table's block begins, and the last table ends exactly at
  bytes_used. Default image: fragment block 315..349, index
  349..357; lookup block 357..392, index 392..400 (region
  43 bytes, not 22); id block 400..406, index 406..414 (=
  bytes_used). The reader's read_table works either way
  because it follows the index pointer, which is why the
  miscount survived the lookup entry's own parse.
  [VERIFIED -- all four images]
- **There is no second table.** In the exportable default
  image the bytes tile exactly: fragment region, lookup
  region, id region, bytes_used -- no gap anywhere for an
  export table to hide in, and no region left unaccounted.
  In the -no-exports twin, lookup_table_start is all-ones
  and the id block begins exactly at the fragment region's
  end (357): nothing sits between them. The export table
  and the lookup table are the same structure, not two
  tables. [VERIFIED -- both flag sets]
- **-no-exports deletes exactly that table, and only that
  table.** Within each flag set the two images agree on
  inode_table_start, directory_table_start,
  fragment_table_start and the id entries, and their
  superblock flags differ in exactly one bit, 0x80: set
  iff exportable (0xc0 vs 0x40 default, 0xe0 vs 0x60 AUF).
  bytes_used drops by exactly the lookup region size in
  both pairs: 414 -> 371 default, 412 -> 369 AUF, a 43-byte
  difference both times. The 0x80 bit is reported here
  only as the bit that tracks exportability on these
  images; no wider flag-naming claim is made.
  [VERIFIED -- both pairs]
- **The refs are the lookup entry's refs.** Default
  exportable image: [0x0, 0x28, 0x68, 0x48, 0x88]; AUF:
  [0x0, 0x24, 0x64, 0x44, 0x84] -- identical to the lookup
  entry's readings on the same trees, an independent
  re-parse confirming them. Every ref reads back to its
  own inode number, and the last ref equals the
  superblock's root_inode in both exportable images.
  [VERIFIED -- both exportable images]
- **Every file resolves with or without the table, and
  independently confirmed.** All three files (5000, 3000,
  1234 bytes) resolve byte-identically through the reader
  in ALL FOUR images, and unsquashfs -ll lists the same
  three files in the exportable and the -no-exports image
  alike, so the readings are not vacuous -- and so the
  lookup/export table is an index only: no walk in this
  reader ever needs it, and a missing table loses nothing
  but the shortcut. [VERIFIED -- reader + unsquashfs
  agreement on all four images, run 2026-11-02]
- **Reconfirmed, still unexplained.** Both directories read
  file_size 3 past the walked listing (root 52 vs 49, sub
  28 vs 25), the root directory's parent_inode is 6 =
  inodes + 1, and the subdirectory's parent is 5, the
  root's own inode number -- the same readings as every
  prior entry, on all four images this time. [OBSERVED --
  all four images, both directories]
- **Decoder-design note (export table -> Gauntlet).** The
  exportability bit and the table are one claim made twice:
  a specimen that claims NFS-exportable (bit 0x80 set)
  while lookup_table_start is all-ones is lying about its
  own exportability, and a specimen with a lookup table
  present but the bit clear is inconsistent in the other
  direction. Either mismatch is a tamper-or-corruption
  signal to be raised before any file content is judged --
  the specimen's own header contradicting its own table
  needs no outside reference to catch. [SPECULATION -- the
  Gauntlet mappings are doctrine, never run]
- **What this entry does not do.** It proves the on-disk
  layout only: no kernel NFS export path was run, so the
  claim that the kernel's NFS code reads this same table
  rests on mksquashfs's -exports help text plus the
  layout, not on a kernel run [CLAIMED, not VERIFIED]; it
  does not explain the +3 directory file_size gap or the
  root parent_inode = inodes + 1 sentinel reading; it does
  not test a lookup/export table spanning several metadata
  blocks (that needs >1024 inodes), an image from any
  other encoder, or a table under -noappend appends. Next:
  the +3/parent explanations, or a multi-block
  lookup/export table.

*[Grade: VERIFIED on four real images (mksquashfs 4.6.1, 4K
blocks, zstd, -noappend, default and -always-use-fragments,
each with and without -exports): no second export table in
any image; -no-exports removes exactly the 43-byte lookup
region; flags differ in exactly bit 0x80; every ref reads
back to its own inode number; all 3 files resolve

## SquashFS multi-block lookup table: refs are stream byte offsets, not block indices

The export entry closed the last named table walk and left
"a multi-block lookup/export table" as next. This entry
builds it: mksquashfs 4.6.1, 4K blocks, -comp zstd,
-noappend, default flags and -always-use-fragments, one
flat tree each of 4000 files f00000.bin..f03999.bin, sizes
100 + (i*37 % 4900) bytes, content byte (i*7 % 251)
repeated, so no two files share a size pattern and the
inode refs form an irregular sequence. The lookup table
holds one u64 ref per inode: 4001 inodes, 32008 bytes,
four 8192-byte metadata blocks on both flag sets (32008
= 3 x 8192 + 7432; blocks are filled to 8192 but the
last). Default: lookup_table_start 116275, table region
[111625, 116307), 4682 bytes on disk, stored lens [1141,
1174, 1262, 1065], index 32 bytes. AUF: start 99542,
region [94984, 99574), 4590 bytes, stored lens [1169,
1178, 1137, 1066]. The blocks tile contiguously and the
last ends exactly at lookup_table_start, on both flag
sets -- the export entry's corrected geometry holds at
multi-block scale.

CORRECTION, and it is the point of this entry. A ref's
high word is NOT a block index. It is the BYTE OFFSET of
the metadata block within the table's COMPRESSED stream
(cumulative stored sizes). Default inode blocks start at
[0, 1360, 2771, 4175, 5579, 6958, 8351, 9735, 11129,
12524, 13927, 15324, 16693, 18079, 19491, 20879, 22283];
the refs' high words are exactly those 17 values. AUF:
[0, 1440, 2918, 4433, 5968, 7490, 9013, 10541, 12053,
13572, 15065, 16575, 18109, 19656, 21211, 22747, 24321],
all 17 again -- except that AUF's 17th block holds only
the tail of the straddling root record, so no ref starts
there and only 16 high words appear. Every prior entry
had a single inode metadata block, where index 0 and
offset 0 coincide, so their ref readings stand but their
reader model was wrong: the t9 reader's read_inode (block
index) fails past block 0. The reader here maps each
stored offset to a block index and reads at
block_index * 8192 + (ref & 0xFFFF) in the CONCATENATED
stream -- because inodes STRADDLE block boundaries (14
default, 13 AUF records cross one), so no single-block
read suffices in general. All 4001 refs read back to
their own inode number on both flag sets, and the last
ref equals the superblock root_inode on both.

The root directory of 4000 entries is a type-8 EXTENDED
directory inode (ldir), not a basic dir: 40-byte header
(nlink 2, file_size u32, offset 0, parent u32, i_count
u32, xattr u32 0xFFFFFFFF = none) + i_count index
entries of (header listing-offset u32, header dir-block
byte-offset u32, first-entry name-length-minus-1 u32,
first-entry name). Default: file_size 72303, i_count 8,
index names f00453, f00906, f01359, f01812, f02265,
f02718, f03171, f03624 -- one per internal dir-block
boundary, each pointing at the header spanning it, at
header offsets 8178, 16368, 24558, 32748, 40938, 49128,
57306, 65496 with dir-block byte offsets 0, 1939, 3901,
5903, 7952, 9980, 11988, 14025. Every index entry was
verified against the walked headers (position, first
name, length-minus-1) and the dir-block stored offsets.
AUF: file_size 72291, same 8 names, offsets 0, 2018,
3955, 6005, 8037, 10086, 12106, 14144 (one header
position shifts, f02718 at 49116, because AUF's
different inode stream cuts the headers differently:
24 headers against default's 25, hence the 12-byte
listing difference). The +3 directory gap holds at this
scale on both flag sets (walked 72300 -> 72303; walked
72288 -> 72291), and the root parent sentinel holds
(parent 4002 = inodes + 1 on both). Every directory
entry's (header start_block, entry offset) ref equals
its lookup-table ref, 4000 of 4000 on both flag sets --
so dir-header start_block is the same byte-offset unit,
and the dir table and the lookup table cross-check each
other entry by entry.

Two corrections to earlier geometry fall out of the
walks. First, the dir stream does NOT end at
frag_start: frag_start is the fragment INDEX, and the
blocks before it are the fragment table's blocks. A
naive [dir_start, frag_start) walk decompresses 106316
bytes for a 72300-byte listing; the extra 34016 are
exactly the fragment table (2126 entries x 16 bytes),
not listing data. Second, a reader bug fixed in passing:
an all-zero partial tail stores as hole entry 0, and the
t9 reader emitted a full 4096 zeros for it; it now
emits file_size % BLOCK zeros. Files f00000, f00251,
and every 251st file are all zeros and exercise it.

What it proves, and what it does not do. It proves the
multi-block layout, the byte-offset ref unit, the
straddle rule, the ldir header and index format, and
the +3 gap and parent sentinel at 4001-inode scale; on
default flags it proves all of it end to end, every one
of the 4000 files resolving byte-identically with
unsquashfs -ll agreeing on all 4000 names. It does not
prove AUF file-content resolution: the AUF image passes
every structural check above, but its file-resolution
loop failed in the runs available (one build: a
4765-byte file resolved to 4096, its fragment tail
missing; debug builds: a same-length content mismatch
and a fragment slice that was not a zstd frame). Two
candidate explanations are NOT distinguished: a genuine
AUF fragment-indexing difference the reader mishandles,
or write-flap-corrupted sources (the debug builds ran
while exec writes were intermittently refused with
EPERM, creating empty files -- a build from such
sources fails exactly this way). This entry claims NO
AUF content resolution; the next run must rebuild AUF
from readback-verified sources and re-run. It does not
identify the ldir listing's start_block field: the @16
word reads 2, which fits nlink exactly (a root with no
subdirs), while the listing demonstrably starts at dir
block 0 offset 0; @36 = 0xFFFFFFFF reads as xattr-none
by extended-inode analogy [SPECULATION]. It does not
cover any other encoder, any appended image, or any
kernel read path. Script
hidden_files/squashfs-lookup-multi-mini.py (default:
full pass; AUF: passes through the ldir index check,
stops at file resolution -- the open item above).

*[Grade: VERIFIED on two real images (mksquashfs 4.6.1,
4K blocks, zstd, -noappend, default and
-always-use-fragments): 4-block lookup tables with
contiguous tiling ending at lookup_table_start; ref
high words == inode-block stored offsets (17/17
default, 16/17 AUF with the last-block tail
explained); all 4001 refs resolve via the concatenated
stream; 14/13 straddling inodes; ldir header + 8 index
entries verified against walked headers; +3 gap and
parent 4002 on both flag sets; 4000/4000 dir-entry refs
== lookup refs on both flag sets; OBSERVED -- the
dir-stream end correction (34016 extra bytes ==
2126 x 16 fragment table) and the hole-tail fix;
VERIFIED on default flags only -- all 4000 files

start_block field; CLAIMED -- the kernel reads refs
the same way (layout only, no kernel run);
SPECULATION -- @36 as xattr-none and the Gauntlet
mappings, which are doctrine, never run.]*

## SquashFS AUF + duplicates corruption trigger: the 03:28 open item closes negative

The multi-block entry's OPEN item was AUF file-content
resolution: its reader passed every check on default flags
but stopped at AUF file resolution, and the entry guessed
write-flap-corrupted sources (empty files from refused
exec writes that night). This entry re-runs that leg from
readback-verified sources -- and the failure persists,
with the cause moved from the reader to the encoder: under
-always-use-fragments with duplicate detection on,
mksquashfs 4.6.1 writes a corrupt image for this tree,
and the reference extractor fails on it too. The
corrupted-sources hypothesis is REFUTED for this failure:
sources were verified byte-for-byte before every build
below, and one tree was re-read stable across five passes.

The tree, unchanged from the multi entry: 4000 files
f00000.bin..f03999.bin, sizes 100 + (i*37 % 4900) bytes,
content byte (i*7 % 251) repeated -- single-byte runs, so
files sharing a byte share identical full blocks and
identical tails. Builds: mksquashfs 4.6.1, 4K blocks,
-noappend, -always-use-fragments unless noted, zstd
unless noted, -processors 1 unless noted. Check: full
unsquashfs extraction (single-processor) byte-compared
against the source tree, plus the multi script's reader.

Symptom, in order of discovery. (1) The multi reader,
re-run on a fresh AUF image from verified sources, again
stops at file resolution: "cannot decompress fragment
block (33 bytes): zstd decompress error: Unknown frame
descriptor." (2) The fragment table is NOT misread: an
independent re-parse (fresh index walk, not the reader's
read_table) agrees on all 2213 entries, 0 diffs -- and
the shared entry both parses name (fragment block 1472,
seven files' tails at offsets 0, 732, 1501, 2307, 3150,
4030, 4043 in one build) points at 34 bytes that are not
a zstd frame. (3) The reference tool fails on the same
images: unsquashfs dies mid-extraction, "zstd uncompress
failed with error code 70" in one run and 72 in others,
"FATAL ERROR: writer: failed to read/uncompress file ..."
-- so this is not a reader bug. The reader and
unsquashfs agree the bytes are wrong; they disagree
nowhere.

Discriminators, each a full build + full extraction
check. AUF + zstd + repeated-byte content: corrupt at
4000 files (default threads and -processors 1; /tmp
tmpfs and disk alike -- build location is not the
variable). AUF + gzip + repeated-byte content: corrupt
too, so the compressor is not the variable either.
Default flags (no AUF) + repeated-byte content at 4000:
CLEAN, 4000/4000 -- which also retroactively firms the
multi entry's default-flags leg (its reader pass plus
-ll agreement now joined by a full extraction pass).
AUF + repeated-byte content + -no-duplicates: CLEAN,
4000/4000. AUF + SEEDED RANDOM content at 4000 (same
sizes, bytes from Random(1234 + i)): CLEAN, twice.
Scale, repeated-byte content, AUF: 100, 500, 1000, 1200,
1500, 1800 all clean; 2000 corrupt -- and deterministic
per tree: two separate 2000-file builds both die at the
same file, f01717. The threshold sits between 1800 and
2000 files for this tree and was not bisected further.

What this pins down, and what it does not. Pinned: the
trigger needs all three -- AUF, duplicate detection on,
and highly-duplicative content. Remove any one leg and
the image extracts cleanly. NOT pinned: which dedup
structure misassigns. Note the subtlety that rules out
the naive account: no two files in this tree share a
(byte, size) pair (byte period 251, size period 4900,
coprime, 4000 files), so there are NO whole-file
duplicates for -no-duplicates to suppress -- the
interaction must live at block or fragment level
(identical full blocks across same-byte files, identical
tails across same-byte same-tail-length files), but
that is inference from the discriminator, not a located
fault. The 1800-to-2000 threshold, the exact miswritten
structure, other encoder versions, and the kernel read
path are all OPEN, not claimed.

Gauntlet consequence, stated as doctrine. An AUF
fixture built from duplicative content is untrustworthy
until an extraction check passes: the multi entry's
reader leg alone would have certified structure while
the bytes were corrupt, because the corruption sits in
a fragment block the reader trusts the table to locate.
Fixture rule going forward: AUF fixtures use
-no-duplicates or non-duplicative content, AND every
fixture build ends with a full unsquashfs extraction
byte-compare, not just -ll. The default-flags fixture
family is unaffected. Script
hidden_files/squashfs-lookup-multi-auf-rerun.py (the
re-run), squashfs-auf-frag-locate.py,
squashfs-auf-frag-autopsy2.py,
squashfs-auf-frag-indep.py, squashfs-auf-frag-threads.py,
squashfs-auf-frag-scale.py, squashfs-auf-frag-loc.py,
squashfs-auf-frag-pattern.py, squashfs-auf-frag-nodup.py,
squashfs-auf-frag-default.py,
squashfs-auf-frag-gzip-autopsy.py (autopsy chain).

*[Grade: VERIFIED on mksquashfs 4.6.1 -- the
discriminator matrix above (AUF corrupt, default clean,

## D'Agapeyeff challenge cipher (1939): the specimen whose author lost the key

- **The specimen.** Alexander D'Agapeyeff, a Russian-born British cartographer — not a trained cryptographer — published *Codes and Ciphers* with Oxford University Press in 1939 as an introductory survey for general readers. On page 144, the final page of the first edition, he printed a challenge cipher: digit groups in fives, presented with no hint of method, key, or plaintext language, and invited readers to try it. He later admitted he had forgotten how he encrypted it, and the cipher was dropped from the 1949 second edition and the 1952 third. He died in 1969 without ever publishing a solution, and no notes, worksheets, or key materials have surfaced among his papers. [VERIFIED — the book's publication facts and the author's admission are carried by Wikipedia, Elonka's unsolved-codes list, and the 2026 D'Agapeyeff Research history page, agreeing with each other and with this project's own UNDECIPHERED.md watch-list entry]
- **The shape of the ciphertext.** Read in horizontal pairs, the digits form 196 two-digit cells — a 5×5 Polybius-square shape, the method the book itself teaches (pages 140–143 cover Polybius squares, columnar transposition, and chained substitution-plus-transposition). The independent 2026 research site's structural read: the first digit of each pair comes from {6, 7, 8, 9, 0} and the second from {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, mapping cleanly onto a keyed 5×5 square; and 196 cells form a perfect 14×14 grid, which strongly suggests a columnar-transposition step after the square. [CLAIMED — single independent-researcher site, 2026; the pair-shape and grid arithmetic are checkable from the printed ciphertext, the transposition inference is not] The printed page carries 79 five-digit groups (395 digits), three more than the 196 pairs (392 digits) — the final group's trailing zeros read as padding, not as a 197th cell. That 392-vs-395 discrepancy is recorded here rather than smoothed over: any future facsimile check of page 144 starts by settling it. [SPECULATION — the padding reading; the counts themselves are as printed]
- **The nulls hint, from the author's own book.** On page 111, under *Military Codes and Ciphers*, D'Agapeyeff wrote that a cipher "is of course easily made out, but if every third, fourth, or fifth letter, as may be previously arranged, is a dummy inserted after a message has been put into cipher, it is then extremely difficult to decipher unless you are in the secret." A decoder may therefore not assume every digit counts: some cells may be dummies inserted after encipherment. The flat letter-frequency distribution for a 196-character English message, against a pairs-horizontal index of coincidence of 1.812, is consistent with either a transposition scrambling the pairs or nulls diluting them — the statistics alone cannot choose. [VERIFIED — the page-111 quotation as carried by Wikipedia; the statistical reading is the field's standing observation]
- **The Kerckhoffs reversal (2017).** Nick Pelling found that D'Agapeyeff copied his double-transposition method from Kerckhoffs' 1883 work — with the encryption and decryption steps reversed. A decoder's warning follows: a textbook method copied backwards is not the textbook method, and a solver who implements the book's method faithfully will fail on a specimen built from its mirror image. [CLAIMED — via the 2026 research site's summary of Pelling's finding; Pelling's original note not re-read this pass]
- **The 2026 exclusion result — the honest shape of a null result.** Chase Hendrick's preprint *Excluding Classical Cipher Families for the 1939 D'Agapeyeff Challenge* (October 7, 2026, not peer-reviewed) separates two kinds of evidence, and the separation is the entry's real gift to the Gauntlet. First, counts no key can change: under any one-to-one letter key, with or without any transposition, the fewest single-cell errors needed to turn a text's letter counts into the cells' counts is half the distance between the sorted count vectors (proved in the preprint); among 479,051 windows of 196 letters of English prose, the closest needs 8 such errors. Second, annealing searches whose power is demonstrated on planted held-out texts of the same length, with shuffled cells as control: columnar transposition with a letter key at width 14 recovered 18 of 18 planted texts, yet in every family tested — four-square with standard plain squares, a repeating coordinate shift on a keyed square at every period from 2 to 14, homophonic keys, the book's own dummy rule, 363 transforms from the author's earlier probes, and enciphering errors at the rate of the book's worked example — the D'Agapeyeff cells scored below every recovered planted text, by at least 1.14 nats a letter for English with a one-to-one key. Weaker closures only: 0.45 to 0.97 nats in 5 of 6 Latin rows, 0.48 for Romanian, 0.88 for a capped homophonic key. [CLAIMED — preprint via search-indexed text, not read first-party this pass; no peer review; the "demonstrated power" design is the preprint's own stated method]
- **What this entry does for the Decoder.** Three transferable rules. (1) *A null result closes a family only if the search demonstrably recovers planted texts of the same length.* Unpowered nulls — searches that never showed they could find a planted answer — close nothing, and the Gauntlet's elimination runs must carry a positive control or say so. (2) *A creator-lost-key specimen has no ground truth to appeal to.* Any future claimed solution can be judged only by internal consistency — language statistics, key plausibility, method plausibility against the book's own pages — never by author confirmation, because the author is gone and forgot first. A solution claim without that discipline is a story, not a decryption. (3) *Copy-errors are a cipher family of their own.* A transposition copied backwards, a dummy rule applied after encipherment, a transcription typo in the printed page — each breaks the mathematical relationship between ciphertext and plaintext in ways no key search can repair, and the "botched by its own author" hypothesis stays live until a facsimile check or a consistent reading kills it. [DOCTRINE — design implications drawn from the filed evidence; no Gauntlet run, no verdict]
- **What this entry does not do.** It does not solve the cipher, endorse any 2026 solver claim, or upgrade the Hendrick preprint past CLAIMED. It does not resolve the 392-vs-395 digit count against a facsimile, re-read Pelling's 2017 note first-party, or read the Hendrick preprint first-party. Next: first-party read of the preprint and a facsimile check of page 144; then, if the counts settle at 196 cells, a Gauntlet design (never a run) for a positive-controlled elimination pass over the Latin-row and homophonic closures the preprint left weakest.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — 1939 first-edition challenge cipher, author's forgotten method, removal from later editions, still unsolved; CLAIMED — the 5×5 pair structure, the 14×14 transposition suggestion, Pelling's Kerckhoffs reversal, and the Hendrick preprint's exclusion figures (preprint not read first-party, not peer-reviewed); SPECULATION — the trailing-zero padding reading and the botched-by-author hypothesis, which stays live, not settled.]*

The differing inodes, mapped. The decompressed inode streams
are the same length (65628 bytes) with exactly 32 bytes
differing, and every differing byte sits in a start_block

f01854.bin (inodes 1842-1855) and f01973.bin through
f01986.bin (inodes 1974-1987). For every one, the ONLY field

hidden_files/squashfs-auf-frag-diff-map.py, log

into a shifted fragment layout; the -32 start_block shift is
exactly the data-region deletion tracked, not corruption.
All 28 differing inodes extract byte-identically through
BOTH images' inodes. [VERIFIED -- same script]

The fragment table tells the real story. Of 1106 fragment
entries, 81 differ. Eighty of them shift by exactly -32 with

Exactly ONE does not: index 955, clean start 24378 size 32,

opposite direction, with no size change anywhere in the
table. [VERIFIED -- same script; delta histogram {-32: 80,
+18: 1}]

table. The walked root listing itself (36147 bytes) is

## SquashFS AUF + duplicates lottery: the stale pointer lands exactly on f01842's block, not mid-chunk

The lottery-diff-map entry left exactly one named item:
identify which neighboring chunk lives at corrupt offset
24396 (clean 24428). Against the preserved pair (no
rebuild: the lottery is a per-build draw), the answer is
exact, and it is a chunk boundary, not a mid-chunk drift.

The chunk at the stale pointer is f01842.bin's block 0.
In the clean image it sits at 24428..24446 (inode 1843,
an 18-byte zstd chunk); in the corrupt image it sits at
24396..24414 -- the same chunk, shifted -32 like the
eighty tracked fragment entries and the twenty-eight
tracked inodes, with byte-identical content
(corrupt 24396..24414 == clean 24428..24446, and the
full stale 32-byte read corrupt 24396..24428 ==
clean 24428..24460). [VERIFIED -- script
hidden_files/squashfs-auf-frag-neighbor.py, log
squashfs-auf-frag-neighbor.log]

The corrupt layout around the pointer, in order, is:
fragment 1025 ends at 24378; f01841.bin block 0 runs
24378..24396; f01842.bin block 0 runs 24396..24414;
f01843.bin block 0 runs 24414..24432. The stale
fragment 955 read (24396..24428, size field 32) therefore
overlaps real chunks for its whole length: the first 18
bytes are f01842's complete block frame, and the last 14
bytes are the opening of f01843's block frame. In the
chunk map, two entries claim the same start -- file
block f01842 and fragment 955 -- an overlap, never a gap.
[VERIFIED -- same script]

Why the corruption is silent for a stream reader. The
stale read's first 18 bytes are a complete, valid zstd
frame: they decompress to 4096 bytes of 0x5D (93),
f01842's repeated byte ((1842 x 7) % 251 = 93). A
stream reader decodes that frame and ignores the
trailing 14 bytes, returning 4096 bytes of 93 -- and the
stale 32-byte read decompresses byte-identically to
f01842's block 0 alone. Every one of the six sharers
then slices that block at its own fragment offset, so
every tail reads 93 regardless of offset: f01717
(foff 0, want 222), f01718 (foff 733, want 229), f01719
(foff 1503, want 236), f01720 (foff 2310, want 243),
f01721 (foff 3154, want 250), f01830 (foff 4035,
want 9) -- all got 93. [VERIFIED -- same script]

The clean fragment, by contrast, is a packed tail block,
not a full block: it decompresses to 4049 bytes whose
byte set is exactly the six sharers' bytes
{9, 222, 229, 236, 243, 250}, and 4049 is exactly the
sum of the six tail lengths (733 + 770 + 807 + 844 +
881 + 14). The stale read substitutes a 4096-byte
single-byte block for a 4049-byte six-byte packed block,
and the offset slicing hides the substitution -- the
tails keep their lengths and only their bytes are wrong.
[VERIFIED -- same script]

What this rules in and out. RULED IN: the stale pointer
is an exact-boundary landing, and that boundary is what
makes the corruption silent for a stream reader -- the
first frame is complete, so no error is raised and no
length check trips. The unsquashfs hard error on the
same image is consistent with a reader that demands
exact frame consumption rather than first-frame
tolerance, but that strictness difference is not probed
here and stays SPECULATION. RULED OUT as a description:
"the pointer drifts into the middle of a neighbor" --
it lands exactly on a neighbor's first byte, and the
neighbor it lands on is a file block, not a fragment.
Numerically, +18 is also the size of f01841's block
chunk, which occupies 24378..24396 in the corrupt
image -- the stale pointer sits exactly at its end --
but why the writer computed +18 is still not shown, and
stays SPECULATION, as does any writer-race mechanism.

What this entry does not do. It does not test whether
the lottery, redrawn, produces a stale fragment pointer
again, or whether a redrawn stale pointer again lands
exactly on a chunk start. Next: redraw the lottery (new
build, same tree and flags) and check whether a stale
fragment pointer recurs, and whether it again lands on
a chunk boundary.
