## SquashFS AUF + duplicates lottery redraw: fragment 955 recurs, and a second stale pointer appears at fragment 220

The lottery-neighbor entry left exactly one open question: redraw the
lottery (new build, same tree and flags) and check whether a stale
fragment pointer recurs, and whether it again lands on a chunk
boundary. This entry answers it, and the answer is stronger than the
question: the stale pointer recurs at the SAME index, and a second
stale pointer appears in the same image.

Method. Same tree and flags as every lottery entry: n=2000, sizes
100 + (i*37 % 4900), byte (i*7 % 251) repeated, mksquashfs 4.6.1,
4K blocks, -comp zstd, -noappend, -always-use-fragments,
-processors 1. (The VM replacement had wiped squashfs-tools and
zstandard; both were restored first -- squashfs-tools 4.6.1 via its
Ubuntu noble .deb, zstandard via pip -- so the builder version
matches the earlier entries exactly.) Builds looped until the first
CORRUPT build; CORRUPT = unsquashfs nonzero, fewer than 2000 files,
or any byte mismatch. The corrupt image is preserved as
squashfs-auf-frag-redraw-corrupt.sqsh and analysed standalone with
the diff-map parser: no clean twin is used, because clean builds
themselves differ (determinism entry), so only this image's own

## DTMF — dual-tone multi-frequency: the keypad as a decoder, and the in-band lesson

- **The code.** Every key on a push-button telephone is two simultaneous sine tones: one from the low group (697, 770, 852, 941 Hz) and one from the high group (1209, 1336, 1477, 1633 Hz). Four rows × four columns = sixteen keys; the consumer keypad uses twelve (0–9, *, #); the fourth column (A, B, C, D) survives on military AUTOVON keypads and amateur-radio repeaters. The frequencies were chosen so none is a harmonic of another (Moler notes the ratios run 21/19), so a tone pair survives voice-band noise and the receiver can trust a pair, not a single frequency. [VERIFIED — ITU-T Recommendation Q.23; DTMF keypad frequency table]
- **The date.** Developed by Bell Laboratories / Western Electric; the Touch-Tone trademark was first used in commerce July 5, 1960, and the first push-button telephone was offered to the public November 18, 1963. It replaced rotary pulse dialing and became the standard for landline and mobile keypads. [VERIFIED — Bell System record via DTMF history]
- **The decoder.** Receiving DTMF is a spectral-decision problem, not a secret-breaking one: the classic receiver runs the Goertzel algorithm — a DFT evaluated at exactly the eight candidate frequencies — and accepts a key only when one low and one high tone both clear threshold for a minimum duration (ITU-T Q.24 tolerances: ±1.5% frequency, twist +4 to −8 dB, 40 ms minimum). Twist limits and talk-off guards keep speech from accidentally dialing. [VERIFIED — standard DSP practice; CORROBORATED on the Q.24 numbers via a secondary DTMF reference]
- **The shadow twin: MF trunk signaling and the blue box.** DTMF dialed the local loop, but long-distance trunks were driven by a different in-band system: a steady 2600 Hz tone marked an idle trunk, and multi-frequency digit pairs routed the call — all on the same voice channel the caller could speak into. Joe Engressia found the tone by whistling at age seven (~1957); a Cap'n Crunch cereal-box whistle (one hole covered) produced ~2600 Hz, and John Draper took the "Captain Crunch" handle from it; Ron Rosenbaum's October 1971 Esquire piece "Secrets of the Little Blue Box" took it national; blue boxes generated the MF routing tones, and Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak were among the builders. [CORROBORATED — Wikipedia phreaking / 2600 Hz histories and secondary accounts]
- **The fix, and why it matters to the Gauntlet.** The industry did not patch the tone; it moved the control plane off the channel — AT&T's Common Channel Interoffice Signaling (1976), then SS7 (1980s), carrying call setup on dedicated links the caller cannot reach. DTMF itself survived the fix: it still rides VoIP as RFC 2833/4733 telephone-events — the digit is now data, not audio. [CORROBORATED — phreaking histories; RFC 2833/4733 as the VoIP carriage]
- **Decoder-design note (DTMF → Gauntlet).** Two rungs. (1) **In-band control is a specimen channel.** Any interrogation design that lets specimen-influenced content share a channel with control signals repeats the 2600 Hz error — the Gauntlet's control plane (chamber tokens, probe keys, verdict transport) must never travel a channel the specimen can write to, in any encoding, audio or otherwise. This generalizes the CRIME/BREACH probe-channel rule already on record: separation of control and content is architectural, not a filter setting. (2) **A tone is a fingerprint, not a secret.** DTMF decoding needs no key — the codebook is public — yet it is a real decoder: structure recovery from a noisy signal with thresholds, tolerances, and false-accept guards. The Gauntlet's behavioral probes should be graded the same way: a specimen behavior matching a public signature is a detection, and the false-accept rate (talk-off) is part of the verdict, not an embarrassment to hide. Design only; no run behind this note. [SPECULATION — design, not a run]

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the DTMF frequency matrix, the 1963 public introduction, and the Goertzel receiver shape; CORROBORATED — the Q.24 tolerance numbers, the 2600 Hz / blue-box history, the CCIS/SS7 fix dates, and the RFC 2833/4733 carriage; SPECULATION — the two Gauntlet design rungs, which are proposals, not results.]*

## Noise Protocol Framework — the handshake as a language, and the pattern name as a fingerprint

- **The framework.** Trevor Perrin's Noise Protocol Framework (rev 34, July 2018) is not one protocol but a language for building Diffie-Hellman handshakes. A handshake is a sequence of message patterns built from tokens: `e` (ephemeral key), `s` (static key), `ee` / `es` / `se` / `ss` (DH operations between the two parties' keys), and `psk` (pre-shared-key mix). Processing tokens in order drives MixHash and MixKey; when the handshake completes, Split() yields the transport keys for AEAD traffic. A prologue — arbitrary context data mixed into the handshake hash — binds the session to its setting without encrypting it. The spec grades every handshake payload on authentication and confidentiality. [VERIFIED — Noise spec rev 34]
- **The pattern name.** Two letters name the whole handshake. The first letter says what the initiator does with its static key: N = none, X = transmits it, K = the responder already knows it, I = transmits it immediately, encrypted, in message 1. The second letter asks the same of the responder: N = none, X = transmits it, K = the initiator already knows it. Patterns ending in K let the initiator encrypt the first payload — zero-RTT — because the responder's static key is already in hand. IK completes in two messages, XX in three; the spec calls XX the most generically useful pattern, since it is efficient and supports mutual authentication. [VERIFIED — Noise spec rev 34]
- **The name is the whole construction.** A full protocol name is `Noise_<pattern>_<DH>_<Cipher>_<Hash>`, with `psk0` / `psk1` / `psk2` modifiers marking where a pre-shared key token sits. WireGuard's entire cryptographic identity compresses into 37 characters: `Noise_IKpsk2_25519_ChaChaPoly_BLAKE2s` — Curve25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305, BLAKE2s, one fixed suite, no negotiation, no fallback. One round trip over UDP, four message types, merged into the Linux kernel in 2020. [VERIFIED — Noise spec rev 34; WireGuard whitepaper and protocol page via secondary summaries]
- **A second deployment, same language.** Tox's transport layer runs Noise with a fixed suite (25519, ChaChaPoly, SHA256) and supports exactly two patterns: IK where the friend's key is already known, XX for first contact without prior key knowledge. Same tokens, same state machine, different pattern letters — the pattern choice is the policy. [CORROBORATED — single secondary source on the Tox implementation]
- **Decoder-design note (Noise → Gauntlet).** Two rungs. (1) **Handshake shape is a fingerprint.** Message count, direction, and which message first carries an encrypted static key identify the pattern without breaking any encryption: a two-message IK-shaped exchange and a three-message XX-shaped exchange are distinguishable from the wire. The Gauntlet can classify a specimen's crypto posture from handshake shape alone, before any deeper probe — pattern recognition, not key recovery. (2) **Prologue as a binding channel.** The prologue binds unauthenticated context into an authenticated transcript; a chamber could bind a probe tag the same way — the tag rides inside the transcript hash, not on a side channel the specimen can strip or spoof. Design only; no run behind this note. [SPECULATION — design, not a run]

*[Grade: VERIFIED — Perrin's framework, the token language, the pattern-letter reading, the XX/IK message counts, and WireGuard's Noise_IKpsk2 construction; CORROBORATED — the Tox IK/XX deployment via one secondary source; SPECULATION — the two Gauntlet design rungs, which are proposals, not results.]*

## MLS — Messaging Layer Security (RFC 9420): the Double Ratchet's answer for groups of thousands

- **The problem it solves.** The Signal entry's Double Ratchet is a two-party machine; groups built on it pay O(n) re-keying on every membership change (sender keys) or run pairwise sessions. MLS is the IETF's answer: efficient asynchronous group key establishment with forward secrecy and post-compromise security for groups "ranging from two to thousands," published as RFC 9420 in July 2023 (Barnes/Cisco, Beurdouche/Inria & Mozilla, Robert, Millican/Meta, Omara, Cohn-Gordon/Oxford) — the first IETF-standardised end-to-end encryption protocol for group messaging. [VERIFIED — RFC 9420 abstract and header]
- **The ratchet tree (TreeKEM).** Members sit at the leaves of a left-balanced binary tree; each internal node holds an HPKE key pair known only to the members below it, and the root secret is effectively the group key. When a member updates, it creates fresh secrets for every node on its direct path to the root and encrypts each new path secret to the copath (the sibling subtrees) — so encrypting to all-but-one member costs log(N) ciphertexts instead of N−1, and a 50,000-member group re-keys in roughly 16 ciphertexts. Group history runs as a sequence of epochs: each epoch has its own ratchet tree and epoch secret, and the key schedule derives message keys, membership authentication, an exporter secret (so other protocols can borrow MLS as a generic group key exchange), and a resumption secret (proof of membership for subgroups or successor groups). [VERIFIED — RFC 9420 §§ on ratchet trees, key schedule, exporter and resumption secrets]
- **The membership machine.** Changes flow as Proposals (Add, Remove, Update) bundled into a Commit, and the Commit advances the epoch. A new member joins through a pre-published KeyPackage — so an offline member can be added — plus a Welcome message carrying the epoch secrets. Two trust roles are named and separated: the Delivery Service, explicitly untrusted (it may drop, delay, or reorder messages, but must never read content or forge membership changes), which also decides the winner when two Commits race in one epoch; and the Authentication Service, which binds each leaf's signature key to an identity via a Credential (X.509, key-transparency log, or manual check) — the most trusted component in the architecture, since a compromised AS can vouch an attacker's key into the group as a silent ghost user. [VERIFIED — RFC 9420 architecture; CORROBORATED — the ghost-user framing via secondary MLS architecture coverage]
- **Deployment, paper to production.** Draft MLS was already deployed at scale in Webex (and RingCentral) before the RFC landed, and Cisco's quantum-safe roadmap still lists MLS for Webex end-to-end encrypted meetings. The GSMA's RCS Universal Profile 3.0 (March 2025) adopted MLS as its end-to-end encryption standard, and reporting puts Google Messages and Apple Messages into active MLS E2EE rollout from May 2026 — the first interoperable cross-provider group encryption at that scale. Matrix is integrating MLS via a Linearized MLS variant for federated rooms; open implementations span Rust (OpenMLS, mls-rs), C++ (MLS++), and TypeScript (MLS-TS). At IETF 126 (July 2026) the CURRENT birds-of-a-feather session pushed to charter a working group applying MLS key machinery to general network transport — the ratchet leaving messaging for the wire itself. [CORROBORATED — Cisco roadmap; GSMA/IETF adoption announcements via secondary coverage; IETF 126 CURRENT reporting]
- **Decoder-design note (MLS → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Removal is a re-key, not a door closing.** MLS removes a member by re-keying the path so the removed leaf's subtree can no longer decrypt anything new — the Gauntlet's observer-revocation must do the same: revoking an observer re-seals the chamber's evidence keys, never merely unsubscribes them. (2) **Name the ordering authority.** MLS is honest that a racing Commit needs a decider, and hands that power to the untrusted Delivery Service — the Gauntlet's interrogation log must name its own ordering authority explicitly and log every race resolution, never let the transport silently pick a winner. (3) **The binder is not the chamber.** The AS is the single component whose compromise silently admits a ghost; Gauntlet corollary: whoever binds a specimen's credential must be a different party from whoever runs its chamber — the clean-arbiter bar, restated as protocol architecture. Design only; no run behind this note. [SPECULATION — design, not a run]

*[Grade: VERIFIED — RFC 9420 (July 2023, authors, FS + PCS for groups of two to thousands, ratchet-tree/log(N) update cost, epoch/KeyPackage/Proposal/Commit structure, exporter and resumption secrets, untrusted Delivery Service and Authentication Service roles); CORROBORATED — Webex production deployment, GSMA RCS Universal Profile 3.0 adoption (March 2025), the May 2026 Messages rollout, Matrix Linearized MLS, the OpenMLS/MLS++/mls-rs/MLS-TS implementations, and the IETF 126 CURRENT session; SPECULATION — the three Gauntlet design rungs, which are proposals, not results.]*

## minisign — the dead-simple signer, and the trusted comment as a second signature

- **The tool.** minisign, by Frank Denis (author of libsodium), is a deliberately minimal file-signing tool: portable, lightweight, one job — sign files and verify signatures with Ed25519. Key generation, signing, and verification are the whole interface; there is no keyring, no web of trust, no expiry machinery. A public key file is two lines: an untrusted comment naming the key id, and a base64 blob carrying the algorithm tag plus an 8-byte key id and the 32-byte Ed25519 public key. [VERIFIED — minisign man page, jedisct1.github.io/minisign]
- **The signature file is four lines, and two of them are the design.** Line 1 is an untrusted comment — free text anyone may rewrite after signing, never verified. Line 2 is base64 of the algorithm tag (`Ed` for legacy, `ED` for the prehashed form), the 8-byte key id matching the public key, and the Ed25519 signature itself. Line 3 is the trusted comment, and line 4 is base64 of a second signature — the global signature — computed over the first signature concatenated with the trusted comment. Nothing in line 3 can change without the secret key, because line 4 binds it. [VERIFIED — minisign signature-format documentation]
- **Legacy vs prehashed.** In legacy mode the signature covers the file bytes directly, which forces the signer to hold the whole file. In prehashed mode (`ED`) the signature covers Blake2b-512 of the file, so a signer can stream arbitrarily large files with constant memory. New implementations must use the hashed format; legacy support is optional and off by default. [VERIFIED — minisign format docs; CORROBORATED — go-minisign streaming note]
- **The trusted comment is the anti-downgrade channel.** The docs name the use outright: trusted comments carry application metadata — intended file name, timestamps, resource identifiers, version numbers — precisely to prevent downgrade attacks, where an attacker replays a valid old signature against a newer context. The default trusted comment, when none is given, is `timestamp:<unix>` plus `file:<basename>` (with `hashed` appended for prehashed signatures). Verification prints the trusted comment, so a verifier sees the signer's own claim about what this signature is for, not just that some bytes check out. [CORROBORATED — minisign docs and go-minisign default-comment behaviour]
- **Signify kinship, one-way.** OpenBSD's `signify(1)` is conceptually the same tool, and minisign can verify signify signatures — but signify cannot verify minisign's, because minisign requires the trusted-comment section to be present. The asymmetry is the point: minisign's format refuses to be a bare "yes, these bytes were signed" and insists on a signed statement of context. [VERIFIED — minisign documentation]
- **Deployment shape.** Because the whole trust story is one public-key file plus one four-line signature file, minisign shows up wherever a release pipeline wants verifiable artifacts without infrastructure: nightly-build ISO signing (e.g. VyOS publishes a `minisign.pub` at the repo root and signs each build), package and firmware distribution, and small-project release signing. No server, no timestamp authority, no certificate chain — the key id in the signature must match the published public key, and that match is the entire verification. [CORROBORATED — VyOS nightly-build signing docs via secondary coverage]
- **Decoder-design note (minisign → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Sign the context, not just the bytes.** A Gauntlet evidence receipt that signs only a hash proves the bytes existed; it does not prove which specimen, which chamber, or which run they belong to. Every receipt must carry a trusted-comment analogue — specimen id, chamber id, epoch, and the interrogation step — inside the signed payload, so a receipt replayed against a different specimen fails verification by construction. (2) **The untrusted comment is a trap to name, not a flaw to fix.** Line 1 exists precisely so that display text can be tampered with harmlessly; the Gauntlet's evidence viewer must show the trusted comment and the untrusted comment in visibly different registers, never merge them into one "comment" field a specimen could spoof. (3) **Small trust surfaces are auditable trust surfaces.** minisign's whole format fits in four lines and one key file, and that smallness is why a reviewer can hold the entire verification in their head. The Gauntlet's receipt format should aspire to the same property: if the verification story needs a manual, it is too big to trust. Design only; no run behind this note. [SPECULATION — design, not a run]

## Diffie–Hellman key exchange (1976) — the handshake that needs no courier, or: the secret that is never sent

- **The problem it killed.** Before 1976, exchanging an enciphered message required a previously exchanged key, and exchanging the key required a secure channel — in practice, a courier. Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman's "New Directions in Cryptography" (IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 22(6), 644–654, November 1976) broke the circle: two parties who have never met, talking over a channel the enemy reads in full, can still agree on a secret. It was the first full description of a working public-key cryptosystem in the open literature, and it made the rest of the field — RSA a year later, TLS, Signal, the whole catalogue — thinkable. [VERIFIED — the 1976 paper citation and the courier-circle framing via standard textbook and encyclopaedia coverage read this pass]
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Alice and Bob publicly agree on a large prime p and a generator g. Alice picks a secret a and sends A = g^a mod p; Bob picks a secret b and sends B = g^b mod p. Alice computes B^a mod p, Bob computes A^b mod p, and both arrive at g^ab mod p — the shared secret, which neither ever transmitted. An eavesdropper sees p, g, A, and B, and still cannot feasibly recover the secret, because doing so requires solving the discrete logarithm problem (recover a from g^a mod p) or the Diffie–Hellman problem directly (compute g^ab from g^a and g^b) — and no feasible algorithm for either is known for well-chosen groups. The same paper's idea had already been built in secret: the catalogue's GCHQ entry records Malcolm Williamson's 1974 key-exchange protocol, classified until December 1997 — Diffie and Hellman re-derived it in the open, and the open version is the one the world built on. [VERIFIED — the construction and both hardness problems via textbook coverage read this pass; the Williamson predecessor via this file's own GCHQ entry]
- **The honest hole: no authentication.** Diffie–Hellman alone is secure against a passive eavesdropper and helpless against an active one: a man in the middle can run the exchange with each side separately and relay, reading everything, while both parties believe they share a secret. Every real deployment therefore pairs the exchange with authentication — TLS pairs ephemeral DH with certificates, the Noise framework's patterns add static-key (`s`) tokens exactly where authentication is wanted, and Signal's X3DH signs the prekey that starts the ratchet. The exchange negotiates the secret; something else must prove who is on the other end. [VERIFIED — the man-in-the-middle vulnerability is stated in standard textbook coverage read this pass; the deployment pairings via this file's Noise and Signal entries]
- **The parameter fall: Logjam (May 2015).** The mathematics held; the deployment did not. Adrian et al.'s "Imperfect Forward Secrecy: How Diffie–Hellman Fails in Practice" (CCS '15) showed that 1990s US export restrictions had left DHE_EXPORT ciphersuites — 512-bit primes — alive in TLS, and a man in the middle could force a downgrade to export-grade DH on any server that still offered them: 8.4% of the top one million HTTPS domains were initially vulnerable, 3.4% of browser-trusted sites. Worse, the number-field sieve's expensive precomputation depends only on the prime, not the session — so a single widely shared prime is a single target: breaking the most common 1024-bit prime would allow passive eavesdropping on connections to 18% of the top million HTTPS domains, and a second prime would cover 66% of VPN servers and 26% of SSH servers. The prescribed remedy was blunt and correct: disable export suites, generate a unique 2048-bit group per deployment. The lesson generalises past DH: a shared parameter is a shared fate. [VERIFIED — weakdh.org, the Logjam research site, and contemporaneous reporting read this pass]
- **Decoder-design note (Diffie–Hellman → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Negotiate keys, never transport them.** DH's whole point is that the secret is computed at both ends and sent nowhere; the Gauntlet's evidence channel should work the same way — session keys derived inside the chamber and at the recorder, never carried in a message a specimen could intercept or a transcript could leak. (2) **Parameters are the security, and shared parameters are shared fate.** Logjam's primes were public, standard, and reused by millions — and that reuse is what made the precomputation pay. Gauntlet corollary: per-chamber, per-run parameters, generated fresh, never a global constant the whole fleet shares; a parameter file that ships in the repo is a parameter the adversary already owns. (3) **An unauthenticated agreement is an agreement with anyone.** DH without a signature is a handshake with a stranger who answers. Gauntlet corollary: no interrogation session opens until the specimen's credential is bound to the session key — the binding happens before the first question, never after the answers are in, or the transcript may belong to a stand-in. Design only; no run behind this note. [SPECULATION — design, not a run]

## ElGamal encryption (1985) — Diffie–Hellman turned into a mailbox, or: the cipher that multiplies

- **The paper that did two jobs at once.** Taher Elgamal's "A Public Key Cryptosystem and a Signature Scheme Based on Discrete Logarithms" (IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 31(4), 469–472, July 1985; conference version at CRYPTO '84) delivered both an encryption system and a signature scheme from the same discrete-logarithm hardness the catalogue's Diffie–Hellman entry rests on. The two must not be confused: ElGamal encryption and the ElGamal signature scheme are siblings, not the same algorithm, and the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) is a variant of the signature sibling, not of the encryption. [VERIFIED — the 1985 paper citation and the encryption/signature distinction via encyclopaedia coverage read this pass]
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Public parameters are a large prime p and a generator g. The receiver picks a private key x and publishes y = g^x mod p. To encrypt a message m, the sender picks a fresh random k and sends a pair: c1 = g^k mod p, and c2 = m · y^k mod p. The receiver, who knows x, computes c1^x = g^(kx) = y^k, divides it out of c2, and recovers m. The encryption is literally one Diffie–Hellman exchange per message: the sender's ephemeral k plays Alice's role, the receiver's long-term x plays Bob's, and the shared secret y^k masks the message instead of becoming a session key. An eavesdropper sees p, g, y, c1, and c2, and recovering m still requires the discrete logarithm or the Diffie–Hellman problem — the same wall as the 1976 exchange. [VERIFIED — the construction via textbook and encyclopaedia coverage read this pass]
- **Two prices, both honest.** First, ciphertext expansion: every plaintext block becomes two group elements, so an ElGamal ciphertext is twice the plaintext size — the reason real deployments use it as a hybrid, encrypting a symmetric session key (or a short value) with ElGamal and the bulk message with that key, rather than encrypting long messages directly. Second, the encryption is probabilistic by design: the fresh random k means the same plaintext encrypts to a different ciphertext every time, so an attacker cannot even test a guessed plaintext by re-encrypting it. That randomness is load-bearing, not decorative — reuse it across messages and the masking secret repeats, and the scheme's semantic security (indistinguishability under chosen-plaintext attack, under the decisional Diffie–Hellman assumption) fails with it. The signature sibling has the sharper version of the same discipline: reusing its per-signature random value leaks the private key outright, the failure DSA inherited and made famous. [VERIFIED — the 1:2 expansion and the probabilistic property via encyclopaedia coverage read this pass; CORROBORATED — the signature-nonce-leak framing via standard textbook coverage]
- **The property that made it a voting machine: homomorphism.** Multiply two ElGamal ciphertexts componentwise and you get an encryption of the product of the two plaintexts: E(m1) · E(m2) = E(m1 · m2), with the randomnesses multiplying too. Nothing is decrypted in between. Encode a vote as an exponent instead — encrypt g^m rather than m — and the same multiplication now adds the exponents: the product of encrypted ballots is an encryption of the sum of the votes. That exponential variant is the engine of Helios, Ben Adida's web-based open-audit voting system: ballots stay encrypted from browser to tally, the homomorphic product yields an encryption of the total, and only that total is ever decrypted, with zero-knowledge proofs (Chaum–Pedersen style) attesting that each ballot encrypts a valid choice without revealing it. The IACR itself has used Helios to elect its directors. [VERIFIED — the multiplicative homomorphism via standard coverage read this pass; CORROBORATED — the Helios exponential-ElGamal tally, the zero-knowledge ballot-validity proofs, and the IACR use via secondary coverage read this pass]
- **Deployment shape, and the malleability caveat.** ElGamal encryption ships in the free GNU Privacy Guard and in recent PGP versions as an encryption option, and it is defined over any cyclic group, not just integers mod p — elliptic-curve ElGamal is the same construction with the group changed. But textbook ElGamal is malleable by construction: anyone can multiply a ciphertext by an encryption of a chosen factor and produce a valid encryption of a related plaintext, without knowing the original. That is why the raw scheme is not chosen-ciphertext secure and must be modified or padded (Cramer–Shoup, DHAES, or an authenticated hybrid wrapper) before it faces an active attacker — the same lesson as the Diffie–Hellman entry's man-in-the-middle hole, restated for encryption: a passive-eavesdropper proof is not an active-attacker proof. [VERIFIED — the GnuPG/PGP deployment and the any-cyclic-group generality via encyclopaedia coverage read this pass; CORROBORATED — the Cramer–Shoup and DHAES chosen-ciphertext remedies via secondary coverage read this pass]
- **Decoder-design note (ElGamal → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Randomness is a secret, not a seasoning.** ElGamal's security collapses when k repeats, so a Gauntlet chamber must treat its per-run randomness the way it treats its keys: generated fresh inside the chamber, logged only as a commitment, never reused across specimens or runs, and a run whose randomness source is suspect is graded UNGRADED, not merely downgraded. (2) **Compute on the sealed evidence.** Homomorphic tallying counts votes without opening a single ballot; the Gauntlet's evidence pipeline should aspire to the same shape — aggregate statistics over sealed transcripts (counts, rates, distributions) computed without unsealing any individual transcript, so the aggregate can be published while the specimens stay sealed. (3) **Malleability is a verdict, not a footnote.** A specimen whose ciphertexts can be related-transformed without detection is not "mostly secure"; the Gauntlet's report card must name malleability as its own failure mode, distinct from key recovery, because a system can keep its keys perfectly and still let an attacker rewrite its messages. Design only; no run behind this note. [SPECULATION — design, not a run]

## RSA (1977) — the trapdoor permutation, or: the lock whose key is a factorization

- **The paper that made public key do both jobs.** Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir, and Leonard Adleman's "A Method for Obtaining Digital Signatures and Public-Key Cryptosystems" (Communications of the ACM, 21(2), 120–126, February 1978; circulated 1977) was the first published system to do encryption and digital signatures with one mechanism — the catalogue's Diffie–Hellman entry (1976) gave the world key agreement, and RSA, a year later, gave it a mailbox and a seal. The same system had been built in secret first: Clifford Cocks at GCHQ described an equivalent scheme in 1973, classified until December 1997 — the catalogue's GCHQ entry records the pattern, and the open version is again the one the world built on. [VERIFIED — the 1978 paper citation and the dual encryption/signature claim via standard textbook and encyclopaedia coverage; CORROBORATED — the Cocks 1973 predecessor via the declassification record]
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Pick two large primes p and q and publish their product n = pq. Let φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1). Choose a public exponent e coprime to φ(n), and compute the private exponent d as the inverse of e modulo φ(n). The public key is (n, e); the private key is (n, d). To encrypt a message m, compute c = m^e mod n; to decrypt, compute c^d mod n, which returns m because ed ≡ 1 (mod φ(n)) and Euler's theorem carries the exponent back around. The trapdoor is the factorization: anyone holding (n, e) can lock the box, but computing d from (n, e) requires φ(n), and φ(n) falls out of p and q — so the whole system rests on factoring n being hard while multiplying p and q is trivial. The honest caveat, stated in the RSA-129 record itself: it is not known whether breaking RSA is mathematically equivalent to factoring — factoring is simply the only publicly known method of breaking it directly. [VERIFIED — the construction and Euler's-theorem correctness via textbook coverage; the non-equivalence caveat via the RSA-129 record]
- **Signatures for free, and that is why RSA owns the certificate world.** The permutation runs both ways: encrypt with the public key and only the private key opens it; "encrypt" with the private key and anyone with the public key can verify it came from the key holder. That second direction is a digital signature — sign a hash of the document with d, verify with (n, e) — and it made RSA the default for the trust infrastructure the catalogue keeps meeting: TLS certificates, code signing, PGP. Diffie–Hellman negotiates a secret between two parties who are already talking; RSA lets a stranger verify a claim from someone who is not in the room. [VERIFIED — the signature direction and the certificate deployment via standard coverage]
- **The factoring ladder is the security parameter, and this entry prices it.** The 1977 challenge that launched the ladder: Martin Gardner's August 1977 Scientific American column published an RSA-129 ciphertext (129 digits, 426 bits, public exponent 9007) with a $100 prize. Ron Rivest estimated in 1977 that factoring it would take 40 quadrillion years at one modular multiplication per nanosecond. It fell in April 1994 to Derek Atkins, Michael Graff, Arjen K. Lenstra, and Paul Leyland — about 1,600 machines from ~600 volunteers over eight months, roughly 5,000 MIPS-years, using the multiple polynomial quadratic sieve — and the decrypted message was "The Magic Words are Squeamish Ossifrage"; the $100 prize was donated to the Free Software Foundation. By 2015 the same number re-factored in about a day on a commercial cloud service for about $30 with CADO-NFS. The ladder kept climbing: RSA-768 (232 digits, 768 bits) fell on December 12, 2009, to Kleinjung et al. by the number field sieve — half a year of polynomial selection on 80 processors, nearly two years of sieving on hundreds of machines, over 1,700 single-core years — with the authors noting a 1024-bit modulus would be about a thousand times harder. The catalogue's own ladder entry carries the later rungs: RSA-250 (2020, 2,700 core-years) and the September 2026 pair, RSA-260 and RSA-896. The reading is the same at every rung: the ladder prices key sizes, never the algorithm's name — production RSA-2048 is untouched by these rungs, and 1024-bit keys are deprecated by NIST guidance (SP 800-131A). [VERIFIED — the RSA-129 challenge, the 1994 team, machine and volunteer counts, the eight-month run, the MIPS-year figure, the plaintext, the prize donation, the 2015 re-factor, and the RSA-768 date, team, and single-core-year cost, via search results read this pass; the later rungs via this file's factoring-ladder entry; CORROBORATED — the NIST 1024-bit deprecation]
- **The implementation graveyard: the mathematics survived, the deployments kept dying at the padding layer.** Textbook RSA — raw m^e mod n — is deterministic (the same plaintext always encrypts to the same ciphertext, so guesses are testable) and malleable (the ElGamal entry's multiplicative homomorphism, restated: E(m1)·E(m2) = E(m1·m2)). Small public exponents without padding invite cube-root attacks on small messages. The deployed fix, PKCS#1 v1.5 padding, fell in turn to Daniel Bleichenbacher's 1998 chosen-ciphertext oracle against SSL — the "million-message attack," which used a server's padding-error responses to decrypt without the key. The modern answer is OAEP (Bellare–Rogaway, 1994), an all-or-nothing padding transform that makes the scheme chosen-ciphertext secure under the RSA assumption in the random-oracle model. The pattern generalises past RSA and restates the Diffie–Hellman entry's lesson: every break in this catalogue's RSA story hit the wrapper, never the trapdoor. [VERIFIED — the determinism, malleability, and OAEP lineage via textbook coverage; CORROBORATED — the Bleichenbacher 1998 oracle and the million-message framing via standard coverage]
- **The quantum shadow, stated once and cross-referenced.** Shor's algorithm (1994) factors in polynomial time on a large fault-tolerant quantum computer; no such machine exists in 2026, and the catalogue's Shor-threat entry carries the harvest-now-decrypt-later consequence. RSA's retirement plan is therefore a migration schedule, not a break announcement — and the ladder above is the clock it runs against. [VERIFIED (cross-reference) — via this file's Shor-threat entry]
- **Decoder-design note (RSA → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The public half must be checkable without the private half.** RSA's whole design is that verification needs no secret; the Gauntlet's evidence receipts inherit the property — any third party holding the public receipt must be able to verify the claim without access to the chamber's private state, or the receipt is a story, not evidence. (2) **Price the parameter, not the name.** "RSA is safe" was true at 129 digits in 1977, false at 129 digits in 1994, and true again at 2048 digits in 2026 — the name never changed, only the rung. The Gauntlet re-prices every run against the current ladder, and a report card that names an algorithm without its parameter is an incomplete verdict. (3) **Attack the wrapper before the mathematics.** Every RSA break in this entry hit padding, error oracles, or key discipline — never the trapdoor itself. Interrogation order for a foreign specimen: error messages, padding behaviour, and parameter choices first; the core algorithm last, because that is where the adversary's cheapest door has always been. Design only; no run behind this note. [SPECULATION — design, not a run]

## DSA — the Digital Signature Algorithm (1991/1994): the government's signature-only child of ElGamal, or: the seal that cannot lock a box

- **The standard, and the deliberate limitation.** DSA is the United States Federal Government standard for digital signatures: NIST proposed it in August 1991 for the Digital Signature Standard (DSS), and FIPS 186 was published in May 1994 — designed by the NSA, selected by NIST through a process that was not public. The DSS is the standard; DSA is the algorithm. The limitation is the point: unlike the catalogue's RSA entry, which encrypts and signs with one mechanism, DSA does only one job — it signs. It cannot encrypt a message, and it was never meant to. A government that wanted a signature standard without handing out a general-purpose encryption algorithm got exactly that. [VERIFIED — FIPS 186 history via NIST's own FIPS 186 retrospective; the signature-only scope via standard coverage read this pass]
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Domain parameters, shareable across users: an N-bit prime q, an L-bit prime p such that q divides p−1, and g, an element of order q modulo p (built as h^((p−1)/q) mod p for some h). Each signer picks a private x with 0 < x < q and publishes y = g^x mod p. To sign a message m: pick a fresh random k with 0 < k < q, compute r = (g^k mod p) mod q, then s = k^−1(H(m) + xr) mod q, where H(m) is the hash of the message; the signature is the pair (r, s). To verify: compute w = s^−1 mod q, u1 = H(m)·w mod q, u2 = r·w mod q, and v = (g^u1 · y^u2 mod p) mod q — accept if and only if v = r. The original sizes were L a multiple of 64 between 512 and 1024 with q fixed at 160 bits and H fixed as SHA-1; FIPS 186-3 widened the approved (L, N) pairs to (1024, 160), (2048, 224), (2048, 256), and (3072, 256), with SHA-2 hashes approved alongside. [VERIFIED — the parameter, signing, and verification equations via standard coverage read this pass; the FIPS 186-3 size pairs via the Federal Register approval notice]
- **The lineage fight, stated plainly.** DSA is a variant of the ElGamal signature scheme — the catalogue's ElGamal entry, narrowed to signatures and re-parameterised around a prime-order subgroup. Two patent claims collided over it: DSA itself is covered by U.S. Patent 5,231,668, filed July 26, 1991, attributed to David W. Kravitz, a former NSA employee; Claus P. Schnorr claimed his U.S. Patent 4,995,082 covered DSA, a claim that was disputed. The dispute matters for the decoder's history, not its mathematics: the algorithm survived the fight and shipped anyway. [CORROBORATED — patent numbers, filing date, and the disputed Schnorr claim via standard coverage read this pass]
- **The nonce is the whole security story.** The mathematics is sound; the per-signature random value k is where every real DSA-family break has lived. If k leaks, the private key falls out by elementary algebra: x = (sk − H(m))·r^−1 mod q. If k is ever reused across two different messages, the two signatures share the same r, and k itself falls out of the difference of the s values — then x follows. In the wild, the same equation family paid out repeatedly: about 1% of SSH DSA host keys were compromised by poor random-number generation in 2012, and Sony's PlayStation 3 code-signing key was extracted in 2010–2011 from a fixed nonce in ECDSA, DSA's elliptic-curve sibling. The modern answer is to stop trusting the RNG for k at all: derive k deterministically from the message and the private key (or hedge it with fresh randomness on top), so two signatures can never silently share a nonce. [VERIFIED — the leak and reuse algebra via lecture coverage read this pass; CORROBORATED — the SSH 2012 figure and the Sony PS3 extraction via the same coverage]
- **The retirement, stated without nostalgia.** NIST's FIPS 186-5 outline records that DSA signatures are no longer approved for signature generation — the algorithm that defined government signatures for three decades has been retired from new signing, with ECDSA, EdDSA, RSA, and the post-quantum signatures carrying the standard forward. Old DSA signatures remain verifiable history; no new ones should be created. The catalogue's lesson is the same one the RSA ladder taught: a standard is a schedule, not a monument. [CORROBORATED — NIST FIPS 186-5 outline slide deck]
- **Decoder-design note (DSA → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **A signature-only primitive is an evidence primitive.** A Gauntlet receipt does not need to encrypt — it needs to bind a claim to a chamber and a run, verifiably, by anyone, without secrets. DSA's deliberate limitation is the receipt's shape: prove origin, reveal nothing else. (2) **Audit the randomness, never assume it.** The interrogation checklist for any discrete-log signature specimen starts with nonce discipline: two signatures sharing an r value are not a curiosity, they are a key recovery already in progress — the specimen's RNG is the finding. (3) **Shared parameters are shared fate, restated.** DSA's (p, q, g) may be shared across users by design, which is efficient and which concentrates risk exactly the way the Diffie–Hellman entry's shared-prime warning did: validate the parameters before trusting any signature under them, because a poisoned group poisons every signer in it. Design only; no run behind this note. [SPECULATION — design, not a run]

## ECDSA — the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (1992/1998): DSA moved onto a curve, or: the same seal, a tenth of the key

- **The proposal, and the standardisation trail.** ECDSA is the elliptic-curve analogue of the catalogue's DSA entry: Scott Vanstone proposed it in 1992 in response to NIST's request for comments on its initial Digital Signature Standard proposal. It was accepted as ANSI X9.62 in 1998 (the Johnson–Menezes–Vanstone paper records acceptance in 1999 as an ANSI standard and in 2000 as IEEE 1363-2000 and FIPS 186-2, with ISO acceptance in 1998), and it remains a FIPS-approved signature algorithm through FIPS 186-4 into the FIPS 186-5 outline — the same outline that retires DSA generation while carrying ECDSA forward. The two lines that meet in it are both 1985: ElGamal's discrete-logarithm signature, sharpened by Schnorr and taken up by NIST as DSA, and elliptic-curve cryptography, proposed independently by Victor Miller and Neal Koblitz. [VERIFIED — the Vanstone 1992 proposal, the ANSI X9.62 1998 acceptance, and the IEEE/FIPS/ISO trail via the Johnson–Menezes–Vanstone paper and standard coverage read this pass; CORROBORATED — the FIPS 186-5 carry-forward via the outline cited in the DSA entry]
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Domain parameters: a curve E over a finite field, a base point G of prime order n, and the field size. Each signer picks a private integer d with 0 < d < n and publishes Q = dG. To sign a message m: pick a fresh secret k with 0 < k < n, compute R = kG = (x_R, y_R), set r = x_R mod n, then s = k^−1(H(m) + r·d) mod n, where H(m) is the hash of the message truncated to the bit-length of n; the signature is the pair (r, s). To verify: compute w = s^−1 mod n, u1 = H(m)·w mod n, u2 = r·w mod n, and R' = u1·G + u2·Q — accept if and only if the x-coordinate of R', mod n, equals r. It works because R' = s^−1(H(m) + r·d)G = kG = R. The DSA entry's equations are visible inside it, point-for-point, with scalar multiplication replacing modular exponentiation. [VERIFIED — the signing and verification equations via standard coverage read this pass]
- **Why the curve buys so much key-size.** The security of DSA rests on the discrete logarithm in a prime-order subgroup of Z_p^*, where index-calculus methods force multi-thousand-bit moduli; the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm has no known subexponential analogue, so the best-known attacks against a well-chosen curve are generic algorithms needing roughly √n group operations. A 256-bit curve therefore buys roughly 128 bits of security — the strength a 3072-bit DSA/RSA modulus buys. That is the whole deployment story: the same seal as DSA, at a tenth of the key, which is why ECDSA, not DSA, is what ships in TLS (the NIST P-256 curve, secp256r1), in code signing, and in blockchains — Bitcoin adopted secp256k1 in 2009, and Ethereum and most later chains inherited it. [VERIFIED — the no-subexponential-analogue claim and the √n generic bound via the Johnson–Menezes–Vanstone paper; CORROBORATED — the P-256/secp256k1 deployment split via SEC 2 coverage read this pass]
- **The nonce, again — and this time it actually paid out.** The DSA entry warned that nonce reuse is a key recovery already in progress; ECDSA is where the warning became history. Sony's PlayStation 3 code signing used a fixed k — not a weak generator, a constant — so anyone holding two signed firmware updates could solve the two signing equations for k and then for the private key; fail0verflow demonstrated the extraction in 2010, and the console's master signing key fell. The same class of mistake drained Bitcoin wallets in 2013, when an Android random-number-generator defect produced predictable k values. The fix that stuck is to stop trusting the RNG for k: RFC 6979 (Thomas Pornin, August 2013) derives k deterministically from the private key and the message hash via HMAC, so the same (key, message) pair always yields the same k and different messages never silently share one; Ed25519, the catalogue's next signature entry, makes determinism a hard requirement rather than an option. A biased k is not safe either — a few bits of bias across enough signatures suffice for lattice recovery — so "random" is a claim the interrogator tests, never assumes. [VERIFIED — the reuse algebra and the RFC 6979 HMAC derivation via coverage read this pass; CORROBORATED — the fail0verflow 2010 extraction, the 2013 Android wallet thefts, and the lattice-from-bias result via secondary coverage read this pass]
- **The two malleabilities the verifier must refuse.** First, signature malleability: (r, s) and (r, −s mod n) are both valid signatures of the same message under the same key, so a verifier that accepts both lets a third party rewrite a signature already in flight — Bitcoin's transaction-malleability era ran on exactly this, and the deployed answer is the low-s rule (reject s > n/2). Second, the invalid-curve attack: a verifier that does not check that Q lies on the stated curve can be handed a point on a weak twist curve, where the discrete logarithm is easy, and tricked into leaking key material through the verification equation — parameter validation is not hygiene, it is the signature. Both are verifier failures, not signer failures, and both are why the Gauntlet grades the verifier separately from the signer. [CORROBORATED — the (r, −s) malleability and low-s rule via standard coverage; CLAIMED — the invalid-curve framing as a verifier-side key leak, stated from the standard attack description, not a run]
- **Decoder-design note (ECDSA → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Grade the verifier as its own specimen.** ECDSA's two malleabilities live entirely on the verifying side; a Gauntlet run that only exercises the signer has tested half the algorithm. Every signature specimen gets a verifier battery: high-s acceptance, off-curve public keys, and wrong-curve parameters, each graded as its own verdict. (2) **A repeated r is a verdict, not a data point.** Two valid signatures sharing r under one key are a key recovery in progress — the run stops, the key is treated as compromised, and the finding is the RNG, not the signatures. (3) **Determinism is evidence-grade.** RFC 6979 makes signing reproducible: the same (key, message) must reproduce the same signature, which turns a nonce audit into a replay check — re-sign a captured message in the chamber and compare. A specimen that cannot reproduce its own signatures has no nonce discipline to audit. Design only; no run behind this note. [SPECULATION — design, not a run]

## EdDSA — the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (2011/2017): DSA's Schnorr cousin, or: the seal whose nonce cannot be reused because it is never random

- **The proposal, and the standardisation trail.** EdDSA was proposed by Daniel J. Bernstein, Niels Duif, Tanja Lange, Peter Schwabe, and Bo-Yin Yang in "High-speed high-security signatures" (2011), and standardised as RFC 8032 (October 2017, Simon Josefsson and Ilari Liusvaara), which specifies Ed25519 and Ed448; FIPS 186-5 carries EdDSA forward as an approved signature algorithm alongside ECDSA and RSA. The lineage matters: EdDSA is a Schnorr signature, not a DSA descendant — the catalogue's DSA/ECDSA line ends here and a Schnorr line begins, which is why the nonce story flips.
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Ed25519 works on the twisted Edwards curve −x² + y² = 1 + dx²y² over p = 2²⁵⁵ − 19, with d = −121665/121666, birationally equivalent to Curve25519. A 32-byte seed is hashed with SHA-512; the first half is clamped into the secret scalar a, the second half kept as a nonce prefix; the public key is A = aB, 32 bytes. To sign, the nonce is derived, never drawn: r = SHA-512(prefix ‖ message), R = rB, then S = (r + SHA-512(R ‖ A ‖ message)·a) mod ℓ, where ℓ is the prime order of the base point; the signature is (R, S), 64 bytes. Verification checks SB = R + H(R, A, M)A. Note what the challenge binds: the signer's public key is inside the hash, so a signature cannot be transplanted onto another key — the transcript-binding lesson the ECDSA entry's malleability section wanted.
- **The nonce, solved by construction.** ECDSA's disasters — Sony's fixed k, Android's broken RNG — were failures of a random number the signer had to invent per message; RFC 6979 patched ECDSA by deriving k deterministically. EdDSA never had the hole: the nonce is a deterministic function of secret material and the message, so the same message re-signs identically and different messages never silently share a nonce. The residual risk moves, it does not vanish: determinism makes a signature a pure function of (key, message), so a fault-injection or side-channel leak during signing is replayable — which is why some implementations mix optional randomness into the nonce, trading reproducibility for fault resistance.
- **Ed448, and the variants the RFC actually names.** Ed448 runs the same scheme on a 448-bit Edwards curve with SHAKE256: 57-byte public keys, 114-byte signatures, roughly 224-bit classical security. RFC 8032 also names three modes: PureEdDSA (Ed25519 proper), Ed25519ctx (a context string bound into the hash, so a signature for one protocol cannot be replayed into another), and HashEdDSA/Ed25519ph (the message is prehashed, for signers that cannot hold the whole message — the same streaming problem minisign's prehashed mode solves).
- **The verifier divergences the Gauntlet must grade.** Ed25519's curve has cofactor 8, and implementations disagree at the edges: whether small-order public keys are rejected, whether S must be canonically less than ℓ, and whether verification is cofactored or cofactorless. The documented result is that a signature valid under one verifier can fail under another — the mirror image of ECDSA's malleability problem, relocated from the signer to the verifier zoo. A specimen's "Ed25519" label is therefore not a verdict; the verifier is the specimen.
- **Decoder-design note (EdDSA → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Replay the signer.** Determinism turns signing into a replay check: re-sign a captured message in the chamber and compare byte-for-byte; any deviation is a defect, not noise. (2) **Grade the verifier battery, not the algorithm.** Run the small-order-key, non-canonical-S, and cofactor-variant cases as separate verdicts, and record which verifier accepted what. (3) **Bind the context.** A specimen that signs without a context string is signing for every protocol at once; the Gauntlet's context test asks whether a captured signature verifies under a different context string, and fails the specimen if it does.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the RFC 8032 Ed25519 construction (twisted Edwards equation, p = 2²⁵⁵ − 19, SHA-512 seed expansion with clamping, deterministic nonce r = SHA-512(prefix ‖ message), S = (r + H(R ‖ A ‖ message)·a) mod ℓ, 32-byte keys, 64-byte signatures, verification equation) and the Ed448 sizes (57/114 bytes, SHAKE256); CORROBORATED — the 2011 Bernstein et al. proposal, the October 2017 RFC 8032 authorship, the FIPS 186-5 carry-forward, the Pure/ctx/prehash variant set, the cofactor-8 verifier divergences and small-order-key acceptance differences, and the optional-randomness fault-resistance trade; SPECULATION — the three Gauntlet design rungs, which are proposals, not results.]*

## Schnorr — the signature that adds, or: the seal whose linearity is the feature

- **The proposal, and why it waited thirty years.** Claus-Peter Schnorr published "Efficient signature generation by smart cards" (Journal of Cryptology, 1991; conference version 1989). The scheme came with a security proof in the random-oracle model, reducing forgery to the discrete-logarithm problem — the cleanest proof any deployed signature scheme had. It did not deploy: Schnorr held a US patent (granted 1991, expired February 2008), and the US government, needing a standard it could use freely, standardised DSA instead — a Schnorr variant deliberately reshaped to dodge the patent. The EdDSA entry's lineage note completes here: EdDSA is Schnorr on an Edwards curve, and the catalogue's DSA/ECDSA line was always a detour around a patent, not a technical preference.
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Over a group of prime order q with generator g: private key x, public key X = gˣ. To sign, pick a nonce k, commit R = gᵏ, compute the challenge e = H(R ‖ M) — the Fiat–Shamir transform, turning an interactive proof of knowledge of x into a signature — and answer s = k + e·x mod q. The signature is (R, s); verification checks gˢ = R · Xᵉ. Modern variants bind the public key into the challenge, e = H(R ‖ X ‖ M), closing the transplant hole the EdDSA entry noted. Note the shape: the equation is linear in (k, x), and that linearity is the whole story of the next two bullets.
- **Linearity as a feature: aggregation.** Because s-values add, n signers can produce one joint signature: each contributes Rᵢ, the aggregate R = ∏Rᵢ, a shared challenge e = H(R ‖ X_agg ‖ M), each answers sᵢ = kᵢ + e·xᵢ, and the sum s = ∑sᵢ verifies against the aggregate key. One signature, one verification, no matter how many signers — the property DSA/ECDSA cannot offer, since their equations are not linear in this way. The naive version is broken by the rogue-key attack (an attacker picks X_attacker = gᵃ · X_victim⁻¹ so the aggregate key is one they alone control), so real aggregation needs either proofs of possession or per-signer coefficients: MuSig2 (Nick, Ruffing, Seurin, 2021) uses two rounds and coefficient-weighted keys and is the deployed standard; FROST (RFC 9591, 2024) extends the same linearity to threshold signing, where any t-of-n signers can jointly sign without ever reconstructing the key.
- **Linearity as a hazard: nonce reuse, again.** Schnorr's nonce story is DSA's story with the same ending: two signatures sharing k give s₁ − s₂ = (e₁ − e₂)·x, and the key falls out. Schnorr's defence, like EdDSA's, is determinism done carefully: BIP 340 (the Bitcoin Schnorr standard, Pieter Wuille et al., 2020) derives the nonce as a tagged hash of the secret key, the public key, auxiliary randomness, and the message, so the same message never silently reuses a nonce and a fault during signing does not deterministically repeat. The residual risk is the mirror of EdDSA's: a nonce derived from secret material means a side-channel leak during signing is a key leak, and auxiliary randomness exists precisely to blunt that.
- **BIP 340, and the deployment that proved it.** BIP 340 specifies Schnorr over secp256k1: 64-byte signatures (the 32-byte x-coordinate of R plus 32-byte s), an even-y convention that drops R's sign bit, and tagged hashes (domain-separated, so a hash meant for one purpose cannot be replayed into another). It activated on Bitcoin with Taproot in November 2021 — the first Schnorr deployment at planetary scale, and the reason multisignature wallets and script trees now verify as one key. The catalogue's lesson: a thirty-year patent delay bought the world DSA; when the patent died, the better scheme arrived within a decade and the detour ended.
- **Decoder-design note (Schnorr → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Grade the aggregation, not the signature.** A specimen claiming multisignature support gets the rogue-key probe first: submit a malicious aggregate key and see whether the verifier accepts a solo signature for a group it never joined. (2) **Replay the nonce.** Re-sign a captured message in the chamber under a fault-injected clock and compare: a deterministic signer repeats; a random signer must never repeat k, and any repeated R across distinct messages is a key-recovery verdict, not a defect note. (3) **Batch-verify, then bisect.** Batch verification (verifying ∑s at once) is Schnorr's speed gift, but one bad signature fails the whole batch; the Gauntlet's batch test inserts a single invalid signature into a valid batch and requires the specimen to bisect to the culprit rather than rejecting the batch wholesale.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the Schnorr 1991 publication and Fiat–Shamir construction (s = k + e·x, verification gˢ = R·Xᵉ), the US patent expiry in February 2008, the DSA-as-patent-workaround history, the BIP 340 64-byte format with even-y convention and tagged hashes, and the November 2021 Taproot activation; CORROBORATED — the random-oracle security reduction, the MuSig2 two-round design (2021), and FROST as RFC 9591 (2024); SPECULATION — the three Gauntlet design rungs, which are proposals, not results.]*

## BLS — the Boneh–Lynn–Shacham signature (2001): the seal that adds without asking, or: one signature for a whole committee

- **The proposal, and the shortest signature of its era.** Dan Boneh, Ben Lynn, and Hovav Shacham published "Short Signatures from the Weil Pairing" (Asiacrypt 2001). The headline then was length: a BLS signature was a single group element — about half the size of a DSA signature at comparable security in the original parameters. The headline now is aggregation: the scheme turned out to be the one signature that compresses a committee into a constant.
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Take two prime-order groups G1, G2 and a bilinear pairing e into GT. Secret key x; public key X = x·G2 (the Ethereum orientation — the G1/G2 roles are swappable, and the catalogue grades the orientation as part of the specimen). Hash the message to a curve point H(m) in G1. Signature σ = x·H(m), one hash-to-curve plus one scalar multiplication. Verification is the pairing equation e(σ, G2) = e(H(m), X): bilinearity makes both sides e(H(m), G2)ˣ. Note the inverted cost profile against ECDSA: signing is cheap, verification pays for pairings, the expensive operation — a specimen's speed claim must say which side it measured.
- **Aggregation is non-interactive — that is the whole point.** Anyone holding σᵢ = xᵢ·H(mᵢ) can add them: σ = Σσᵢ verifies against the signers' public keys via the product of pairings ∏e(H(mᵢ), Xᵢ). No round of interaction, no coordination among the signers — unlike MuSig2's two rounds in the Schnorr entry. Same-message aggregation is the committee case: n validators sign the same block, and one aggregate proves the whole committee at constant size.
- **The rogue-key attack, again — and the two defences.** Naive aggregation is broken the same way Schnorr's was: an attacker who chooses their public key as a function of the victims' keys can make the aggregate key one they alone control, then forge aggregate signatures for a group they never joined. The two defences are proofs of possession at key registration (each signer proves knowledge of x before their key counts) or requiring distinct messages (the attack needs a shared message). Ethereum's validator registration carries a proof-of-possession signature in the deposit; the IETF CFRG BLS signature specification carries both mechanisms.
- **BLS12-381, and the deployment that proved it.** The pairing-friendly curve BLS12-381 (Barreto–Lynn–Scott family): in Ethereum's orientation, 48-byte compressed public keys (G1) and 96-byte compressed signatures (G2), at a 128-bit security target. Ethereum's proof-of-stake consensus aggregates thousands of validator signatures per block into one 96-byte aggregate — the scaling property the Schnorr entry's aggregation section wanted but could not deliver non-interactively. Threshold variant: share x among n parties, each produces a partial signature, and any t partials aggregate into a valid signature without ever reconstructing x.
- **Decoder-design note (BLS → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Grade the aggregation, not the signature.** Rogue-key probe first: submit a crafted aggregate key set and see whether the verifier accepts a solo signature as a committee's. (2) **Grade the hash-to-curve.** A specimen that hashes messages to points with a shortcut (try-and-increment without the full hash-to-curve suite, or a hash without domain separation) fails before any signature is checked — the hash is the scheme. (3) **Grade the pairing zoo.** G1/G2 orientation, compressed versus uncompressed points, and subgroup-membership checks are separate verdicts: a verifier that skips subgroup checks accepts points outside the prime-order group, and the Gauntlet's invalid-point battery must catch it.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the 2001 Boneh–Lynn–Shacham paper and authorship, the pairing construction (σ = x·H(m), verification e(σ, G2) = e(H(m), X)), non-interactive aggregation by addition, and the BLS12-381 sizes in Ethereum's orientation (48-byte public keys, 96-byte signatures) with Ethereum proof-of-stake aggregate use; CORROBORATED — the IETF CFRG BLS specification's proof-of-possession and distinct-message defences, the deposit-as-proof-of-possession reading, the threshold-BLS shape, and the subgroup-check verifier divergences; SPECULATION — the three Gauntlet design rungs, which are proposals, not results.]*

## SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) — the hash-based signature, or: the seal that needs no lattice

- **The proposal, and the backup that outlived its rivals.** SPHINCS+ was published by Daniel J. Bernstein, Andreas Hülsing, Stefan Kölbl, Ruben Niederhagen, Joost Rijneveld, and Peter Schwabe in 2015 — a stateless hash-based signature built to answer the oldest objection to hash-based signing: state. Earlier hash-based schemes (XMSS, LMS) were stateful — reuse a one-time key and the security collapses — which made them unusable wherever a key might be copied, backed up, or restored. SPHINCS+ removed the state entirely: a signature never depends on what the signer signed before. NIST selected it on July 5, 2022, alongside ML-DSA, explicitly as the backup on a different foundation — if lattices fall, the hash-based leg still stands — and standardized it as SLH-DSA in FIPS 205, published August 13, 2024, the same day as FIPS 204.
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** A hypertree of Merkle trees, with one-time signatures at the leaves and a few-time signature at the root of the path. The leaves are WOTS+ one-time signatures (a Winternitz chain: hash a secret forward n times, reveal partway down the chain as the signature, so each leaf signs exactly once). The tree layers are XMSS Merkle trees that authenticate the leaf keys up to a single root, which is the public key. The twist that buys statelessness is FORS (Forest of Random Subsets): instead of picking a leaf by a counter, the signer derives a pseudorandom leaf index and a FORS key pair from the message and a randomizer, signs the message digest with FORS, then authenticates that FORS key through one XMSS path. Nothing is remembered between signatures; the same message signed twice yields different signatures, and no counter can be rewound, cloned, or desynchronised. The price is size: signatures run roughly 7–49 KB depending on parameter set, against ML-DSA's ~2–5 KB, and signing is slower — the scheme trades bandwidth for an assumption set that contains exactly one thing: the hash function.
- **The parameter sets, and the s/f fork.** Twelve sets: two hash functions (SHA-2, SHAKE) × three security categories (128, 192, 256-bit, named -128, -192, -256) × two tunings — "s" (small: shorter signatures, slower signing) and "f" (fast: larger signatures, faster signing). Public keys are 32, 48, or 64 bytes by category; private keys 64, 96, or 128 bytes. The naming carries the tuning openly — SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s versus -128f — so a specimen's parameter string already discloses which side of the size/speed fork it chose, and a deployment that picks "f" for a bandwidth-starved channel, or "s" for a latency-starved one, has misread its own label.
- **Decoder-design note (SLH-DSA → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Grade the assumption, not the size.** A specimen claiming post-quantum signatures gets the foundation probe first: is its security claim resting on one assumption (hash) or a lattice family? The Gauntlet's migration-ledger rule follows NIST's own pairing: a receipt chain stamped only with ML-DSA is one surprise from unsigned, and the ledger's backup stamp is SLH-DSA, not a second lattice scheme. (2) **Grade the randomizer.** Statelessness dies if the FORS randomness is predictable or reused: feed the specimen a captured signature, re-sign the same message, and require a different signature with a different FORS path — an identical second signature is a state leak, not an optimisation. (3) **Grade the parameter string.** Parse the specimen's claimed set and check it against the twelve: an unlisted combination (a SHAKE-192s with ML-DSA-sized signatures, a 128-category key at 64 bytes) is a forgery of the label, and the Gauntlet rejects the specimen before any signature is verified.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the SPHINCS+ 2015 authorship and stateless design, the July 5, 2022 NIST selection as the hash-based backup, the FIPS 205 publication on August 13, 2024, the hypertree/WOTS+/XMSS/FORS construction shape, and the twelve parameter sets with s/f tuning; CORROBORATED — the signature-size range (~7–49 KB) and the public/private key sizes by category; SPECULATION — the three Gauntlet design rungs, which are proposals, not results.]*

## XMSS/LMS — the stateful hash-based signatures (RFC 8391 / RFC 8554, SP 800-208): the seal that counts, or: the counter that must never rewind

- **The pair, and the standardisation trail.** Two schemes, one idea, standardised a year apart: XMSS (eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme), RFC 8391, May 2018; LMS (Leighton–Micali Signature), RFC 8554, April 2019. NIST's SP 800-208, *Recommendation for Stateful Hash-Based Signature Schemes* (October 2020), approves both — plus their multi-tree variants, XMSS^MT and HSS — as a supplement to FIPS 186. The approval is narrow on purpose: only a subset of the RFC parameter sets (SHA-256 or SHAKE256, 192- or 256-bit outputs), and key and signature generation inside hardware cryptographic modules that do not allow secret keying material to be exported. NIST's own warning travels with the approval: these schemes are secure against quantum computers but "not suitable for general use because their security depends on careful state management." The SLH-DSA entry's prehistory completes here: XMSS and LMS are the stateful schemes SPHINCS+ was built to escape.
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** A one-time signature signs exactly one message — WOTS+ Winternitz chains in XMSS, LM-OTS in LMS — and a Merkle tree authenticates 2^h one-time keys under a single root, which is the public key. A signature carries the one-time signature plus the authentication path up to the root. The multi-tree variants stack trees so the top tree signs the roots of the trees below, and key generation only has to build one tree per layer up front instead of all 2^h leaves at once. The height h is the budget: h = 20 buys about one million signatures per key, and then the key is spent — there is no refill, no rekey-in-place, only a new key and a new root to distribute.
- **The state, and why it is the whole scheme.** Each signature consumes the next leaf, and the signer must persist a counter that never rewinds: never sign twice with the same leaf, never restore a backup taken before the last signature, never clone the key onto two signers. A reused one-time key leaks enough chain values to forge — the same catastrophe as DSA nonce reuse, relocated from randomness to operations. The SLH-DSA entry's answer to this was to remove the state entirely (FORS picks a pseudorandom leaf per message); the XMSS/LMS answer is to guard the state with hardware and procedure. The Gauntlet distinction follows: SLH-DSA's failure mode is a bad randomizer, XMSS/LMS's is a bad backup policy, and a backup policy is a human procedure wearing a cryptographic costume.
- **The deployment shape, and the export fight.** SP 800-208's no-export rule is the point, not a footnote: a private key that can be copied can be rewound, and a rewound counter is a forgery factory. NIST has since received feedback on the export restriction and is working on a revision of SP 800-208 that would enable key export with mitigations — which is itself a decoder signal: the standard's hardest rule is also its most contested, and any specimen claiming the revision's relief before it exists is claiming a future standard. Until a revision lands, a specimen that exports its XMSS/LMS private key for "convenience" has already failed the standard it claims.
- **Decoder-design note (XMSS/LMS → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Count the leaves.** Parse the specimen's parameter set, compute signatures remaining (2^h minus the counter), and fail any specimen that cannot report its own remaining budget — a signer that does not know how spent it is cannot be trusted near the end of its life. (2) **Rewind the chamber.** Restore a pre-signature backup into the chamber and demand refusal or a state-mismatch alarm; a second signature issued from the rewound state is a forgery factory, not a recovery feature. (3) **Grade the parameter string.** Reject any claimed set outside SP 800-208's approved subset before verifying a single signature — an unapproved hash function or output length is a forgery of the label, and the Gauntlet rejects the specimen before any signature is verified.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the XMSS RFC 8391 (May 2018) and LMS RFC 8554 (April 2019) dates, the SP 800-208 October 2020 approval of XMSS/LMS plus XMSS^MT/HSS, the approved-subset restriction (SHA-256/SHAKE256, 192/256-bit outputs), the hardware-module no-export requirement, and NIST's "not suitable for general use" warning, all via NIST sources read this pass; CORROBORATED — the h = 20 ≈ one-million-signature budget framing, the few-kilobyte signature sizes against Ed25519's 64 bytes, and the pending SP 800-208 export revision; SPECULATION — the three Gauntlet design rungs, which are proposals, not results.]*

## ML-KEM (FIPS 203) — the module-lattice key-encapsulation mechanism, or: the seal that agrees on a secret without ever sending it

- **The standardisation trail.** ML-KEM is the key-exchange half of NIST's first post-quantum trio, published as FIPS 203, *Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard*, on 13 August 2024, alongside FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA). It is the standardised form of CRYSTALS-Kyber, the lattice submission that emerged from NIST's post-quantum competition as the chosen KEM. The name change matters for the decoder: Kyber drafts and FIPS 203 ML-KEM are not bit-compatible — standardisation changed the key-generation domain separator, the encapsulation pre-hash, and the rejection-key derivation — so a specimen labelled "Kyber" that verifies against FIPS 203 test vectors, or vice versa, is mislabelled until proven otherwise.
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** ML-KEM's hardness rests on Module Learning With Errors (Module-LWE): solving noisy linear equations over a module of polynomials of degree less than 256 with coefficients modulo the prime 3329. Key generation produces an encapsulation key (the public key) and a decapsulation key; encapsulation takes the public key and outputs a ciphertext plus a 32-byte shared secret; decapsulation takes the ciphertext and the private key and recovers the same 32 bytes. The secret is never transmitted — both ends derive it independently — and the scheme is IND-CCA2 secure, meaning an adversary who can ask for decapsulations of chosen ciphertexts still cannot distinguish the real shared secret from random. That last property is the whole point of a KEM: it replaces the key-transport half of RSA and the key-agreement half of Diffie–Hellman/ECDH, and the derived secret then feeds an ordinary symmetric cipher.
- **The parameter sets, and what they cost.** Three sets, one module rank each, mapping onto NIST's odd-numbered security categories: ML-KEM-512 (category 1, ~AES-128), ML-KEM-768 (category 3, ~AES-192), ML-KEM-1024 (category 5, ~AES-256). Encapsulation keys run 800 / 1,184 / 1,568 bytes, ciphertexts 768 / 1,088 / 1,568 bytes, decapsulation keys 1,632 / 2,400 / 3,168 bytes, and the shared secret is always 32 bytes. The decoder's size intuition: these are kilobytes where X25519 is 32 bytes a side, so a specimen claiming ML-KEM with a 32-byte public key is not ML-KEM at all, and a specimen claiming ML-KEM-512 with a 1,568-byte key has the wrong set's label on the right scheme. ML-KEM-768 is the working default — the set paired with X25519 in hybrid TLS key exchange, where breaking the tunnel requires breaking both the lattice scheme and the classical curve.
- **Decoder-design note (ML-KEM → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Grade the label before the math.** Parse the claimed parameter set and check every size against the FIPS 203 table before running a single encapsulation — a wrong-size key is a mislabelled specimen, not a failed test. (2) **Decapsulation-oracle discipline.** Run the IND-CCA2 intuition as a chamber rule: feed the specimen malformed and replayed ciphertexts and demand either the correct shared secret or a clean failure, never a leaked intermediate — a KEM that answers sloppily under chosen-ciphertext pressure is a key-transport hole wearing a post-quantum label. (3) **Hybrid honesty.** Where a specimen claims a hybrid (X25519 + ML-KEM), verify both halves independently and fail the hybrid if either half is stubbed — a hybrid whose classical half is a constant is classical security with a lattice sticker, and a hybrid whose lattice half is Kyber-draft code is a draft wearing a standard's name.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the FIPS 203 publication date (13 August 2024), the CRYSTALS-Kyber lineage, the Module-LWE basis, the three parameter sets with their categories (512/1, 768/3, 1024/5), and the encapsulation-key / ciphertext / decapsulation-key sizes (800/768/1,632; 1,184/1,088/2,400; 1,568/1,568/3,168) and the 32-byte shared secret, all via sources read this pass; CORROBORATED — the Kyber-to-ML-KEM non-bit-compatibility (domain separator, pre-hash, rejection key), the IND-CCA2 characterisation, and the X25519+ML-KEM-768 hybrid-TLS deployment shape; SPECULATION — the three Gauntlet design rungs, which are proposals, not results.]*
