## CROSS — the code-based signature that restricts its errors, or: the seal that signs with a short alphabet

- **The family gap this entry closes.** The code-based shelf so far signs by decoding (Classic McEliece, BIKE, HQC) or by equivalence (MEDS, LESS). CROSS signs by restricted decoding: it takes the classical Syndrome Decoding Problem (SDP) and adds one constraint — every entry of the secret error vector must lie in a fixed restricted set of the field, in the base case the cyclic subgroup generated by an element g of F_p^*. That problem, Restricted Syndrome Decoding (R-SDP), is the entry. A specimen that says "code-based signature" and stops there is hiding which of three different hardness bets it is making: plain decoding, equivalence, or restricted decoding — and CROSS is the restricted one.
- **The mechanism, in one line.** CROSS (Codes and Restricted Objects Signature Scheme) builds a zero-knowledge identification protocol on R-SDP — the signer proves knowledge of a restricted error vector matching a public syndrome, without revealing it — and turns that protocol into a signature with the Fiat-Shamir transform, the same pattern the whole post-quantum shelf uses. The restriction is the feature, not a footnote: restricted vectors admit a compact representation (only the restricted alphabet needs encoding, not the full field), and the scheme's Round 2 update stresses compact representations and efficient arithmetic, including efficient hardware performance. The cost of the restriction is novelty: R-SDP is a younger problem than SDP, and NIST's interest in CROSS comes with an explicit appetite for further analysis of it.
- **Two families, two hardness bets — never quote one as the other.** CROSS ships in two families. Instances based on plain R-SDP have slightly larger signatures but are the more conservative choice, because the problem is analogous to SDP. Instances based on R-SDP(G) — the specialized variant with the subgroup — offer more compact signatures, but rest on a somewhat less standard problem. A decoder must demand which family a specimen runs: a signature size quoted from the R-SDP(G) corner beside a security story told from the R-SDP corner is a mismatch, and the mismatch is the tell. This entry makes no point-size claim: sizes trade against performance across parameter sets, and no single size number was verified this pass.
- **Why it still grades specimens.** CROSS is the control for any claim that "code-based" means "settled." Two findings from its Round 2 season cut against that reading. First, a horizontal side-channel attack targets the syndrome computation itself — recovering the map and then the secret error from a single power trace — with masking or shuffling named as the prevention; an implementation claim with no masking/shuffling posture is therefore incomplete, whatever its mathematical parameters. Second, cross-paradigm work reduces Restricted Syndrome Decoding to both code-based problems (regular syndrome decoding) and lattice-based problems (closest-vector and short-vector variants), evaluated on reduced parameters — which widens, not narrows, the attack surface a decoder must watch. Separately, investigated BUFF security properties (S-CEO, S-DEO, MBS, wNR) are reported as achieved by CROSS; that is a secondary report recorded here, not a property measured this pass.
- **Decoder-design note (three checks for a CROSS specimen).** First, the restriction test: demand the restricted set named in full — which field, which subgroup generator, whether R-SDP or R-SDP(G) — because an unnamed restriction is an unnamed hardness assumption. Second, the family-size pair: demand the signature size beside the family label, and check the size belongs to that family's corner, not the other family's. Third, the implementation posture test: demand the masking/shuffling answer to the single-trace horizontal attack before crediting any "runs on a microcontroller" claim — the Round 2 update's microcontroller note and the single-trace attack are the same story, told from opposite ends.

## LESS — the linear-code equivalence signature, or: the seal that walks a code by isometry

- **The family gap this entry closes.** The equivalence shelf so far has two members and a missing middle. MEDS signs by matrix-code equivalence — invertible matrices acting on a subspace of matrices. CROSS, named in the same breath as LESS, signs by restricted decoding, not by equivalence at all. LESS is the plain equivalence member: linear-code equivalence, the Linear Equivalence Problem (LEP). Two linear codes are equivalent when an isometry carries one to the other — in the Hamming metric, a monomial map, a permutation of coordinates combined with a rescaling of each coordinate — and the signer's secret is exactly that map. A specimen that says "code-equivalence signature" without naming which equivalence — matrix-code or linear-code — is hiding which problem its security rests on, and LESS is the name that forces the question.

- **The mechanism, in one line.** LESS builds a zero-knowledge identification protocol on code equivalence alone — the signer proves knowledge of the isometry between a public code and its hidden equivalent, without revealing it — and turns that protocol into a signature with the Fiat-Shamir transform, repeated t times to drive the soundness error down, the same pattern the whole post-quantum shelf uses. The public key is a code in reduced row-echelon form; the private key is the isometry to a code the signer chose; the efficiency tweaks are the standard shelf toolkit, named here because a specimen may claim any of them: multiple public keys, fixed-weight challenges, and a seed tree for the commitments. None of those tweaks changes the hardness assumption — they change the size and speed corners, and a specimen quoting a size without naming its tweaks is quoting a corner, not the scheme.

- **The Round 2 shape of the scheme.** LESS advanced to the second round of NIST's additional-digital-signatures call, and its Round 2 specification differs from its Round 1 one in exactly one disciplined way. The Round 1 specification halved signature sizes by committing to an information set (Asiacrypt 2023); the Round 2 specification compacts the representation further with canonical forms (DCC 2025). The direction is consistent — every round buys size with representation, not with a new problem — and that is what a decoder checks: a Round 2 size claim must come with its canonical-form story, and a Round 1 size quoted as current is stale by a full round. This entry makes no point-size claim: the Round 2 tables were not verified to a single number this pass, and the scheme's own history says sizes move between rounds.

- **Why it still grades specimens.** LESS is the control for any claim that imports a group-action trick into a code setting without paying the transfer cost — the mirror image of the MEDS note, from the other side. Its own designers' seminar frames code equivalence as a group action "although without commutativity," which is precisely the sentence a careless import skips: the isometry group is not abelian, so a mechanism that leans on commutativity (a SeaSign-style walk, a CSIDH-style exchange) does not port by renaming. And the implementation season cuts the other way: fault-attack work on LESS version 1 (Asiacrypt 2024) found exploitable surfaces, and follow-up work on version 2 reports forgery paths from interrupted execution that need only one faulted signature for most parameter sets to recover secret-related information. A mathematical parameter set with no fault posture is therefore an incomplete specimen, whatever its round — the same implementation-posture rule CROSS taught with its single-trace attack, now in the fault domain.

- **Decoder-design note (three checks for a LESS specimen).** First, the equivalence test: demand the equivalence named in full — which codes, which isometry, monomial or otherwise — because "equivalence-based" without the equivalence is a label, not a problem. Second, the round test: demand the specification round beside any size or speed number, since Round 1 and Round 2 sizes differ by representation changes, and a Round 1 number sold as current is stale. Third, the fault-posture test: demand the interrupted-execution answer — what a single faulted signature leaks, and what stops it — before crediting any "runs on a device" claim, because the version-2 fault work says one faulted signature is the unit of exposure.

## FAEST — the symmetric-primitive signature, or: the seal that trusts AES and nothing else

- **The family gap this entry closes.** The post-quantum signature shelf now signs by lattice (ML-DSA, FN-DSA), by hash (SLH-DSA, XMSS/LMS), by multivariate equation (UOV, MAYO, SNOVA, QR-UOV), by isogeny walk (SQIsign, SeaSign, CSI-FiSh), and by code equivalence or restricted decoding (MEDS, CROSS, LESS). None of them signs by a symmetric primitive alone. FAEST is that member: its hardness is the one-wayness of AES itself — recover the key from a plaintext/ciphertext pair — not a new structured problem invented for the signature. It also opens the VOLE-in-the-Head shelf, and the shelf's first naming trap comes with it: NIST's round tables file FAEST under "MPC-in-the-Head," but the construction is deliberately not MPC-in-the-Head (the Picnic/Banquet lineage). VOLEitH is a different proof system, and a specimen that calls FAEST "MPCitH" is using the table's label, not the construction's name.
- **The mechanism, in one line.** A FAEST key pair is pk = (x, y) and sk = k such that E_k(x) = y, where E is AES and k is an AES key; a signature is a non-interactive argument of knowledge of k, in the Fiat-Shamir pattern the whole shelf uses. The proof system is QuickSilver, a VOLE-based zero-knowledge system: the prover homomorphically commits to its witness through VOLE correlations, and VOLE-in-the-Head generates those correlations from a public-coin protocol (SoftSpokenVOLE with its base oblivious transfers replaced by hash-based commitments), so no designated verifier or interactive setup is needed — the verifier's share is revealed only after the proof messages are sent, which is what keeps the proof sound. The efficiency hinge is a property of AES itself: the only non-linear operation in the cipher is the S-box, an inversion over a small field, so the AES computation is cheap to prove in zero knowledge. Everything else in the scheme is symmetric-key plumbing — AES and SHA-3, primitives with decades of cryptanalysis behind them — which is the whole pitch: no new math to break, only AES.
- **The Round 3 shape of the scheme.** FAEST was one of the 14 candidates advanced to Round 2 of NIST's additional-digital-signatures call in October 2024, and one of the nine advanced to Round 3 in May 2026, per NIST IR 8610 (the Round 2 status report). Its security levels track AES key sizes directly: AES-128, AES-192, AES-256 map to NIST Categories 1, 3, and 5. Parameter sets come in small (s) and fast (f) corners, and in plain and EM variants — twelve sets in v2. One v2-era size datapoint, reported in secondary literature: FAEST-128s signatures around 4,506 bytes, against 7,856 bytes for SPHINCS+-128s, roughly a 42% reduction — but that is a v2 number, and the v3 specification is dated September 1, 2026. A v3 size quoted from v2 tables, or a v2 size sold as current, is stale by a full version; this entry verifies no v3 size this pass. The s/f trade is the familiar one: the small corner buys size with computation, dominated by GGM-tree seed expansion, so "small signature" and "fast signing" are different corners, never one claim.
- **Why it still grades specimens.** FAEST is the control for any claim that a signature needs a new hardness assumption. A specimen that runs an AES-key proof while telling a lattice, code, or multivariate security story is misdescribing its own assumption — the assumption is AES, and AES is the part that has survived. Second, the physical-attack season has now reached VOLEitH: the first side-channel and fault analysis of VOLEitH schemes reports four practical attacks against a masked FAEST implementation on ARM Cortex-M4, recovering the full secret key with probability above 0.87 from a single signature, exploiting components specific to VOLEitH and FAEST — the all-but-one vector commitments, VOLE generation, and AES proof generation — with countermeasures proposed. That is the same implementation-posture rule CROSS taught with its single-trace attack and LESS with its fault work, now in the VOLEitH domain: a mathematical parameter set with no physical posture is an incomplete specimen. Third, the plain/EM confusion is a live mismatch risk: FAEST-EM uses AES in Even-Mansour mode, with the AES key revealed as part of the public key, so the key expansion need not be proven in zero knowledge — and for 192- and 256-bit security it uses Rijndael-192 and Rijndael-256, block sizes AES itself never standardized. A specimen quoting EM sizes beside a plain-construction story, or a 256-bit EM claim built on AES-256's 128-bit block, is mismatched on its face.
- **Decoder-design note (three checks for a FAEST specimen).** First, the one-way-function test: demand the pair (x, y) and the cipher named in full — which AES size, which block size — because "AES-based" without the pair is a label, not a key. Second, the variant test: demand plain or EM, s or f, and the specification version beside any size or speed number, since v2 and v3 numbers differ and EM changes what the public key even contains. Third, the physical-posture test: demand the answer to the single-signature VOLEitH attacks — what hardens the all-but-one commitments, the VOLE generation, and the AES proof generation — before crediting any "runs on a microcontroller" claim, because the Cortex-M4 work says one signature is the unit of exposure.

## X25519 — the Diffie–Hellman exchange on Curve25519, or: the handshake that never signs anything

- **The family gap this entry closes.** The catalogue already carries Ed25519, the signature that lives on the Edwards form of Curve25519, and ML-KEM, the post-quantum key agreement that is replacing classical exchange — but it has no entry for the classical exchange itself. X25519 is that member: the Diffie–Hellman key agreement over the Montgomery form of the same curve, and the exchange underneath modern TLS, SSH, WireGuard, and the Signal protocol. A decoder that can read an Ed25519 signature but cannot name the handshake that set up the session is missing half the curve.
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** X25519 works over the prime field p = 2²⁵⁵ − 19, on the Montgomery curve y² = x³ + 486662x² + x, with base point u = 9. Each party holds a 32-byte secret scalar, clamped before use — the lowest three bits cleared, the highest bit cleared, bit 254 set — and publishes the 32-byte u-coordinate of the scalar multiple of the base point. Each party then multiplies the peer's u-coordinate by its own scalar, using the Montgomery ladder, which needs only the u-coordinate and therefore never reconstructs a y. Both sides land on the same 32-byte shared secret, which is fed into a key-derivation function; the raw shared secret itself is never used as a session key. X448 is the same construction on a 448-bit Montgomery curve (p = 2⁴⁴⁸ − 2²²⁴ − 1), with 56-byte keys.
- **What X25519 is not.** It is not a signature: it authenticates nothing on its own, and an unauthenticated X25519 handshake is open to a man in the middle — the authentication must come from elsewhere (a signature, a pre-shared key, a certificate). It is not post-quantum: Shor's algorithm breaks the discrete-logarithm problem it rests on, which is exactly why current deployments pair it with ML-KEM in a hybrid handshake, so that breaking either leg alone does not break the session. And it is not Ed25519 under another name: the two share a field and a birationally equivalent curve, but Ed25519 signs with a twisted-Edwards equation, a hashed deterministic nonce, and a full point, while X25519 exchanges with a Montgomery ladder, a clamped scalar, and a u-coordinate alone. A specimen labelled with one must never be graded as the other.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The Montgomery ladder accepts any 32-byte peer value, including low-order points, and a peer that sends one can force a shared secret from a tiny set — the classic small-subgroup trap, relocated from DSA's parameter zoo to a single curve. The defence is contributory behaviour: reject an all-zero shared secret, which is what a low-order peer forces. The ladder also runs in constant time by design, so a timing probe that distinguishes scalar bits on a naive implementation is probing the implementation, not the curve. A specimen's "X25519" label is therefore, as with Ed25519, not a verdict: the scalar clamping, the all-zero check, and the KDF after the ladder are the specimen.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the Curve25519 field p = 2²⁵⁵ − 19, the Montgomery curve equation and base point u = 9, the 32-byte key and shared-secret sizes, the clamping rules, the u-coordinate-only Montgomery ladder, the RFC 7748 (October 2016) standardisation of X25519 and X448, and the X448 field and 56-byte key size; CORROBORATED — the 2006 Bernstein Curve25519 proposal, the TLS/SSH/WireGuard/Signal deployment footprint, the unauthenticated-exchange man-in-the-middle exposure, the Shor vulnerability and the ML-KEM hybrid rationale, and the all-zero shared-secret rejection practice; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet grading rungs implied by the edge cases, which are proposals, not results.]*

## ChaCha20-Poly1305 — the AEAD that needs no AES hardware, or: the seal that encrypts and authenticates in one pass

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue's Noise and WireGuard entries name `ChaChaPoly` as their fixed cipher suite, and the X25519 entry hands off a shared secret — but no entry until now says what happens to that secret next. ChaCha20-Poly1305 is the answer in those deployments: an authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) construction that encrypts the message and attaches a tag proving neither the ciphertext nor its unencrypted headers were touched. It is a symmetric seal, not a key exchange and not a signature: it needs a key from elsewhere (X25519, ML-KEM, or a pre-shared key) and gives back confidentiality plus integrity in one pass.
- **The two halves, both Bernstein's.** ChaCha20 is a stream cipher descended from Salsa20, built only from addition, rotation, and XOR (ARX) — no lookup tables, no AES hardware required, constant-time by construction and fast on CPUs without AES-NI. Its state is sixteen 32-bit words: four constants, eight key words (256-bit key), a block counter, and a nonce; twenty rounds of quarter-rounds scramble the state into 64-byte keystream blocks. Poly1305 is a one-time authenticator: it evaluates a polynomial modulo the prime 2^130 − 5 under a one-time key and emits a 128-bit tag. The one-time property is the whole discipline of the construction — a Poly1305 key used twice is a forgery waiting to happen, which is why the AEAD wiring derives a fresh one per message.
- **The AEAD wiring (RFC 8439).** The IETF variant takes a 32-byte key, a 96-bit nonce, and a 32-bit block counter. Block counter 0 generates the Poly1305 one-time key (the first 32 bytes of that keystream block); encryption proper starts at counter 1, XORing plaintext with the keystream. The tag is Poly1305 over the padded additional authenticated data (AAD), the padded ciphertext, and the two lengths as 8-byte little-endian values — so headers bound as AAD are authenticated without being encrypted, and any change to ciphertext, AAD, or lengths trips the tag. RFC 8439 (June 2018) superseded RFC 7539 (2015); the IETF variant's 96-bit nonce plus 32-bit counter differs from Bernstein's original 64-bit nonce plus 64-bit counter, and the two variants are not interchangeable. A specimen's "ChaCha20-Poly1305" label must therefore name its variant, or it names nothing.
- **XChaCha20-Poly1305, the extended-nonce sibling.** Where the 96-bit nonce makes random nonces under one long-lived key a collision risk, XChaCha20 stretches the nonce to 192 bits: HChaCha20 derives a subkey from the key and the first 128 nonce bits, then ordinary ChaCha20-Poly1305 runs under that subkey with the remaining 64 bits. It is the libsodium/draft-standard answer for random-nonce deployments, not part of RFC 8439, and a decoder must not grade an XChaCha specimen against the RFC 8439 test vectors or vice versa.
- **The failure modes the Gauntlet must grade.** Nonce reuse under one key is catastrophic twice over: the keystream repeats, so two ciphertexts XOR to the XOR of their plaintexts, and the Poly1305 one-time key repeats, so the tag scheme can be forged. Decryption must verify before release — plaintext from a failed tag must never reach the caller, since a partial release turns a tamper detector into an oracle. The 32-bit block counter caps each (key, nonce) pair at 2^32 blocks, about 256 GiB; a specimen that silently wraps the counter is reusing keystream by another name. And the quantum footnote belongs in the same breath as the deployment list: as a symmetric construction it degrades under Grover, not Shor — 256-bit keys keep roughly 128 bits of post-quantum strength — so the AEAD survives the transition its X25519 key exchange does not, provided the key exchange itself is hybridised.
- **Where it lives.** TLS 1.3 cipher suite TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, WireGuard's data cipher, SSH, and QUIC — the software-friendly AEAD wherever AES hardware cannot be assumed, and the fixed suite that makes the Noise/WireGuard "no negotiation" policy possible. A specimen labelled "ChaCha20-Poly1305" is therefore, as with X25519, not a verdict: the variant, the nonce discipline, the verify-before-release rule, and the counter limit are the specimen.

*[Grade: CORROBORATED — the RFC 8439 construction (32-byte key, 96-bit nonce, 32-bit counter, counter-0 Poly1305 key derivation, counter-1 encryption start, padded AAD and ciphertext with 8-byte lengths, 16-byte tag), the June 2018 RFC 8439 supersession of RFC 7539, the original-vs-IETF nonce/counter difference, the XChaCha20 192-bit nonce via HChaCha20, the TLS 1.3 suite name and the WireGuard/SSH/QUIC deployment footprint, and the nonce-reuse and counter-wrap failure modes, all via multiple independent secondary sources read this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet grading rungs implied by the failure modes, which are proposals, not results.]*

## AES-GCM — the AEAD that trades software speed for a nonce discipline, or: the seal whose hardware does the work

- **The gap this entry closes.** The ChaCha20-Poly1305 entry is the software-friendly AEAD, the one that runs fast where AES hardware cannot be assumed — but TLS 1.3 ships two AEADs, not one, and the other is the default wherever AES hardware exists. AES-GCM (Galois/Counter Mode, NIST SP 800-38D, 2007) is that second AEAD: the hardware-accelerated seal behind most TLS connections, and the counterpart that makes the catalogue's AEAD pair complete. A decoder that grades only ChaChaPoly reads half of TLS 1.3, and grades the half that is rarer on servers with AES-NI.
- **The two halves.** AES in counter mode supplies secrecy; GHASH, a polynomial hash over GF(2^128), supplies the tag. The hash key is H = AES_K(0^128) — the block cipher encrypting the all-zero block under the message key. GHASH runs over the padded additional authenticated data (AAD), the padded ciphertext, and a final lengths block carrying the AAD and ciphertext lengths in bits as two 64-bit values. The tag is that GHASH output masked with AES_K(J0), where J0 is the initial counter block derived from the nonce; encryption proper starts at inc32(J0). For the recommended 96-bit nonce, J0 is simply the nonce followed by thirty-one zero bits and a final 1; for any other nonce length, J0 is GHASH over the padded nonce plus its length — which is why non-96-bit nonces cost a GHASH pass and are discouraged, not just unusual.
- **The nonce discipline is the whole construction.** One rule, no exceptions: a (key, nonce) pair must never be used for two different messages. GCM does not detect a repeat, and nothing downstream repairs one. SP 800-38D offers two honest ways to keep the promise: a deterministic construction (a fixed field plus an invocation counter, so uniqueness is a counter's job) or a random 96-bit nonce drawn per message, capped at 2^32 invocations per key so the birthday collision probability stays below 2^-32. TLS 1.3 shows the deterministic pattern done well: each record's nonce is the per-direction static IV derived in the handshake XORed with the 64-bit record sequence number, so no nonce is ever transmitted and none can repeat within a connection — and RFC 8446 still bounds AES-GCM to about 2^24.5 full-size records per key before a KeyUpdate, keeping the AE safety margin near 2^-57.
- **The failure modes the Gauntlet must grade.** Nonce reuse under one key is catastrophic twice over, in the mirror image of ChaCha20-Poly1305's reuse: the counter-mode keystream repeats, so two ciphertexts XOR to the XOR of their plaintexts — and the GHASH key H is exposed, so the authentication itself can be forged for that key. A specimen that reuses a nonce has not made a small error; it has handed over both halves of the seal. Tag truncation is the quieter failure: 128 bits is the standard tag, and shorter tags (SP 800-38D permits down to 32 bits in constrained settings) buy bandwidth with forgery probability, so a specimen using a short tag owes a justification, not just a length. Decryption must verify before release, as with every AEAD — plaintext from a failed tag must never reach the caller. And the implementation posture matters as much as the construction: a table-driven GHASH invites cache-timing leakage of H, so a "fast GCM" claim without a constant-time or hardware-GHASH answer is an ungraded claim. Where nonce uniqueness cannot be guaranteed at all, the answer is not GCM with crossed fingers — it is AES-GCM-SIV (RFC 8452), the misuse-resistant variant that survives a repeated nonce with only plaintext-equality leakage, at the cost of a two-pass construction GCM deliberately avoided.
- **Where it lives.** TLS 1.3 cipher suites TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384; the TLS 1.2 ECDHE + AES-GCM suites that preceded them; SSH, IPsec, disk and database encryption, and cloud KMS envelopes — anywhere AES hardware is present and the nonce discipline can be enforced by the protocol, which is exactly why TLS 1.3 could adopt it as a default. A specimen labelled "AES-GCM" is therefore, as with ChaCha20-Poly1305, not a verdict: the nonce construction, the tag length, the verify-before-release rule, and the GHASH implementation are the specimen — and a ChaChaPoly specimen and a GCM specimen must never be graded against each other's failure modes, because their reuse catastrophes, though equally total, arrive by different halves of the construction.

*[Grade: CORROBORATED — the SP 800-38D construction (counter-mode AES plus GHASH over GF(2^128), H = AES_K(0^128), the padded AAD/ciphertext/lengths-block tag input, the J0 derivation for 96-bit and other-length nonces, the deterministic and random nonce constructions with the 2^32 random-invocation cap), the TLS 1.3 suite names and the static-IV XOR sequence-number nonce construction with the ~2^24.5-record KeyUpdate bound, the nonce-reuse consequences (keystream repeat plus H exposure and forgery), the tag-length range, and AES-GCM-SIV (RFC 8452) as the misuse-resistant variant, all via standard secondary sources and the search pass this run; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet grading rungs implied by the failure modes, which are proposals, not results.]*

## HKDF — the HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (RFC 5869), or: the bridge from a shared secret to a set of keys

- **The gap this entry closes.** The X25519 and ML-KEM entries both end with the same handoff — a raw shared secret — and both warn that it must never be used directly as a session key, while the ChaCha20-Poly1305 and AES-GCM entries both begin with a key already in hand. Nothing until now names the bridge between those two sentences, and a single secret is rarely enough anyway: a session needs an encryption key, a traffic key, an IV, a resumption secret, each distinct. HKDF is that bridge: the HMAC-based key derivation function (Krawczyk and Eronen, RFC 5869, May 2010) that turns one input secret into one pseudorandom key, then into as many purpose-separated output keys as the protocol needs.
- **Extract, then expand — and the role swap is the point.** HKDF-Extract takes a salt and the input keying material (IKM) and returns a pseudorandom key, PRK = HMAC-Hash(salt, IKM), of HashLen bytes; if no salt is supplied, it is a string of HashLen zero bytes, so a missing salt is a defined default, not an error. Here the salt is the HMAC key and the secret is the message. HKDF-Expand then reverses the roles: the PRK becomes the HMAC key, and T(1) = HMAC(PRK, info || 0x01), T(i) = HMAC(PRK, T(i−1) || info || i), concatenating blocks until the requested length L is reached and truncating to exactly L. The counter is a single byte, so L ≤ 255 × HashLen — 8,160 bytes for SHA-256, 16,320 for SHA-512 — and asking for more must fail, never wrap. The two steps answer two different questions: Extract concentrates unevenly distributed input entropy into a uniform PRK, and Expand stretches that PRK under a PRF into independent-looking outputs.
- **Info is the key-separation mechanism, not decoration.** Two Expand calls from the same PRK with different info strings yield keys that are independent for practical purposes, so one master secret can safely yield an encryption key, a MAC key, and a nonce prefix — provided every info string binds protocol, version, and purpose. A specimen that expands with empty or constant info for every purpose has collapsed the separation HKDF exists to provide, and two protocols sharing a PRK with the same info have, in effect, shared a key. Expand-only use is legitimate only where the input is already pseudorandom at PRK strength; feeding a raw Diffie–Hellman output straight into Expand skips the concentration step and asks the PRF to do Extract's job. A decoder must therefore check which step a specimen actually ran, not just that it says "HKDF".
- **What HKDF is not.** It is not a password stretcher: it runs fast, with no work factor and no memory cost, so an IKM that is a human password falls to dictionary search no matter how cleanly HKDF is applied — passwords go through Argon2, scrypt, or PBKDF2 first, and HKDF may then expand the stretched output. It is not a cipher, a signature, or an authenticator: its output keys prove nothing about a peer, and a leaked PRK leaks every key expanded from it. And it creates no entropy: if the IKM is weak, predictable, or already exposed, the outputs inherit exactly that weakness, polished into uniform-looking bytes. Salt, for the same reason, is not a secret — it is a non-secret randomiser that helps Extract concentrate entropy — and treating it as a second password mistakes the model in both directions.
- **Where it lives.** TLS 1.3 builds its entire key schedule from HKDF: Extract folds the pre-shared key and the (EC)DHE secret into handshake and master secrets, and HKDF-Expand-Label derives each traffic secret with labels prefixed "tls13 " and the transcript hash as context, so every key is bound to the handshake that produced it. HPKE and the Messaging Layer Security (RFC 9420) key schedule use the same extract-and-expand shape. A specimen labelled "HKDF" is therefore, as with the AEADs, not a verdict: the hash, the salt handling, the info binding, the output length against the 255-block cap, and whether Extract actually ran are the specimen — and a password fed straight to HKDF is a specimen for Argon2's entry, not this one.

*[Grade: CORROBORATED — the RFC 5869 construction (PRK = HMAC-Hash(salt, IKM), HashLen-zero default salt, T(i) = HMAC(PRK, T(i−1) || info || i), L ≤ 255 × HashLen, the 8,160-byte SHA-256 and 16,320-byte SHA-512 caps), the May 2010 Krawczyk and Eronen authorship, the TLS 1.3 HKDF key schedule with "tls13 " Expand-Label prefixes, and the password-stretching distinction, all via the RFC text and multiple independent secondary sources read this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet grading rungs implied by the failure modes, which are proposals, not results.]*

## Argon2 — the memory-hard password hash (RFC 9106), or: the stretcher that makes guessing expensive

- **The gap this entry closes.** The HKDF entry ends with a warning it does not itself answer: HKDF is fast by design, so a human password fed straight to it falls to dictionary search no matter how clean the expansion. Passwords need the opposite property — a function deliberately slow and deliberately hungry for memory, so that each guess costs the attacker real RAM as well as real time, and so that cheap parallel hardware gains little. Argon2 is that function: the memory-hard password-hashing and key-derivation function designed by Alex Biryukov, Daniel Dinu, and Dmitry Khovratovich, selected as the winner of the Password Hashing Competition in 2015 and standardised as RFC 9106 in September 2021. It is the answer HKDF points to, and the specimen a decoder meets whenever a stored credential is supposed to survive a database leak.
- **Three variants, one choice for passwords.** Argon2d accesses its memory array in a password-dependent order, which maximises resistance to GPU cracking and time–memory trade-offs but leaks timing information through that dependence. Argon2i accesses memory in a password-independent order, which resists side channels but gives up some GPU resistance. Argon2id is the hybrid RFC 9106 recommends when the threat model is uncertain or side channels are plausible: it follows the Argon2i approach for the first half pass over memory and the Argon2d approach for subsequent passes. For password storage, the default answer is therefore Argon2id, not a coin flip between the other two — and a specimen stored as Argon2d on a shared or observable host, or as Argon2i where GPU cracking is the live threat, has chosen the wrong half of the trade.
- **Three knobs, and memory is the point.** Every Argon2 call is tuned by memory cost m in kibibytes, time cost t in iterations (passes over the memory), and parallelism p in lanes (threads), plus a salt (16 bytes recommended for password hashing), an output length, a version — v=19, i.e. 0x13, is current — and optional secret-key and associated-data inputs. The memory array is made of 1 KiB blocks, filled from a Blake2b-based compression function, and the cost that crushes GPU and ASIC attackers is m above all: a card with 16 GiB of RAM can only run a few hundred guesses in parallel when each guess demands tens of mebibytes, where a memory-light hash would let it run millions. OWASP's baseline for interactive logins is Argon2id at m=19,456 KiB (19 MiB), t=2, p=1, with higher-memory sets (64 MiB at t=3, and beyond) trading CPU time for memory as headroom allows; the right set is the largest the login path can afford without timing out, re-tuned as hardware moves, never a value copied once and frozen. A specimen with a small m, a t of 1 on Argon2i, or parameters that verify in a few milliseconds has kept the name and surrendered the property.
- **The stored string carries everything verification needs — except secrecy it must not claim.** Argon2 hashes are stored in the PHC string format, for example `$argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=1$<base64 salt>$<base64 hash>`, which encodes variant, version, all three parameters, salt, and output in one field, so parameters can be raised over time and each stored hash still verifies under the parameters it was made with. Verification re-hashes the presented password with the stored salt and parameters and compares in constant time. The salt is not a secret: it must be unique per password so identical passwords hash differently and rainbow tables die, but it may sit beside the hash in the same field. What must stay secret, when it is used at all, is the optional pepper — the secret-key input K — which turns a leaked database alone into an insufficient prize; a design that calls its salt a pepper, or that stores a pepper in the same row as the hash, has misunderstood which input does which job.
- **What Argon2 is not.** It is not encryption and it is not reversible: there is no decryption step, only re-hash and compare, so a "decrypted password" from an Argon2 specimen is a fabrication, not a finding. It is not a general-purpose key stretcher for high-entropy secrets: feeding an already-strong Diffie–Hellman output or a random master key through Argon2 wastes the memory-hardness on an input that needs HKDF's fast, purpose-separated expansion instead. And it is not a substitute for a strong password or for rate limiting: it multiplies the cost of each guess, it does not make a password from a breach list unguessable, and an online endpoint without throttling hands the attacker free guesses regardless of m. A specimen labelled "Argon2" is therefore, as with HKDF and the AEADs, not a verdict: variant, version, m, t, p, salt uniqueness, and whether a pepper is genuinely held apart are the specimen — and a fast, low-memory, or salt-reused Argon2 is a specimen for the HKDF entry's warning, not this entry's promise.

*[Grade: CORROBORATED — the 2015 Password Hashing Competition win, the Biryukov/Dinu/Khovratovich authorship, the RFC 9106 September 2021 standardisation, the three variants and their data-dependent / data-independent / hybrid memory-access orders with the Argon2id default recommendation, the m/t/p parameter meanings, the 1 KiB block memory array, the 16-byte recommended salt, version v=19 (0x13), and the PHC string format, all via the RFC text and multiple independent secondary sources read this pass; the OWASP baseline (Argon2id m=19,456 KiB, t=2, p=1, with higher-memory sets) via OWASP-derived secondary sources read this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet grading rungs implied by the failure modes, which are proposals, not results.]*

## scrypt — the memory-hard password derivation (RFC 7914), or: the stretcher that made memory the price

- **The gap this entry closes.** The Argon2 entry names scrypt as one of the functions a password should go through before HKDF, but nothing until now says what scrypt is — and a decoder meets scrypt specimens everywhere Argon2 has not yet arrived: older password stores, backup systems, and standard libraries. scrypt is the predecessor that made memory-hardness practical: designed by Colin Percival in his 2009 paper "Stronger Key Derivation via Sequential Memory-Hard Functions," then standardised as RFC 7914 in August 2016 (Percival and Simon Josefsson). Note its status honestly: RFC 7914 is informational, not an Internet Standards Track specification — a widely implemented description, not a standards-track mandate.
- **The sandwich construction.** scrypt(P, S, N, r, p, dkLen) runs in three steps, and the cost lives in the middle one. First, B = PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256(P, S, 1, p × 128 × r), split into p blocks of 128 × r bytes each. Second, each block goes through scryptROMix, which fills an array V of N blocks of 128 × r bytes using scryptBlockMix — whose core is the Salsa20/8 stream-cipher core — and then mixes again, reading V back in an order derived from the data itself. Third, DK = PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256(P, the concatenated mixed blocks, 1, dkLen). PBKDF2 runs exactly once at each end: its job is mixing, not slowness. ROMix is the memory-hard core, and it is sequential: the second phase cannot be shortcut without holding V, which is what prices out the GPU and ASIC attacker that a merely CPU-hard function invites.
- **Three knobs, and N binds time to memory.** N is the CPU/memory cost parameter: it must be larger than 1, a power of 2, and less than 2^(128 × r / 8). r is the block size; p is the parallelisation parameter, a positive integer bounded by ((2^32 − 1) × 32) / (128 × r), giving each lane its own independent ROMix instance. Memory is roughly 128 × N × r × p bytes, so Percival's original suggested set — N = 2^20, r = 8, p = 1 — demands about 1 GiB and took under five seconds on a 2009-era Core 2 Duo. The RFC's contemporary note was that r = 8 and p = 1 appeared to yield good results. The tuning rough edge, and the reason Argon2 later split the knobs, is that raising N doubles both time and memory at once: there is no independent time dial. An OWASP-derived starting point cited in a secondary source read this pass is N of at least 2^17 with r = 8 and p = 1 — a floor, not a target, to be re-tuned against the login path's latency budget and verified in wall-clock time on the deploying hardware. A specimen with a small N, or with p raised as if lanes were free security, has kept the name and surrendered the property.
- **Salt, output, and the missing string format.** The salt is normally uniquely and randomly generated, and it is not a secret: it must be stored alongside the parameters and the output, or verification is impossible — a bare output with no N, r, p, or salt is unverifiable, not merely weak. dkLen is a positive integer bounded by (2^32 − 1) × 32. Unlike Argon2, RFC 7914 standardises the function and an ASN.1 schema, not a single PHC-style password-hash string format, so a specimen's encoding must be read on its own terms: the decoder checks that the parameters travel with the hash in whatever encoding the implementation chose, rather than assuming a canonical string.
- **What scrypt is not.** It is not side-channel silent: ROMix's second phase indexes V by data derived from the password, so on a shared or observable host it carries the same class of timing and cache leakage the Argon2 entry names for Argon2d — one reason the Argon2id hybrid exists for uncertain threat models. It is not a general-purpose key stretcher for high-entropy secrets: a Diffie–Hellman output or a random master key goes through HKDF's fast, purpose-separated expansion, not through a memory-hard password function. And it is not a substitute for a strong password or for rate limiting: it multiplies the cost of each guess, it does not make a breach-list password unguessable, and a proof-of-work-tuned low N reused for passwords is a category error, not a setting. A specimen labelled "scrypt" is therefore, as with Argon2, not a verdict: N, r, p, salt uniqueness, the encoding that carries them, and whether the host is observable are the specimen.

*[Grade: CORROBORATED — the August 2016 RFC 7914 standardisation, the Percival and Josefsson authorship, the informational (non-Standards-Track) status, the 2009 "Stronger Key Derivation via Sequential Memory-Hard Functions" origin, the sandwich construction (PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 once at each end, ROMix over an N-block V, Salsa20/8 BlockMix), the parameter constraints (N a power of 2 greater than 1 and less than 2^(128 × r / 8); the p and dkLen bounds), the r = 8 and p = 1 contemporary note, the roughly 128 × N × r × p memory figure, and Percival's original N = 2^20, r = 8, p = 1 set at about 1 GiB, all via the RFC text and OpenSSL documentation read this pass; the OWASP-derived N of at least 2^17 with r = 8 and p = 1 starting point via a secondary source read this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet grading rungs implied by the failure modes, which are proposals, not results.]*

## Vigenère — the polyalphabetic cipher, or: the cipher that hid the frequency profile for three centuries

- **The gap this entry closes.** The Beaufort entry already treats Vigenère as the baseline it subtracts from, the M-209 entry runs a Beaufort wheel, and the Kasiski name recurs across the classical entries — but nothing until now states the cipher itself. Vigenère is the polyalphabetic cipher: not one substitution alphabet but a key-length cycle of Caesar shifts, so the same plaintext letter encrypts differently at different positions and the frequency profile that breaks every monoalphabetic cipher dissolves into the key cycle. Every later polyalphabetic system — Beaufort, Gronsfeld, the running key, the autokey, the M-209's wheels — is a variation on this one idea, and a decoder that cannot name it cannot grade any of them.
- **The mechanism, in one line.** Choose a keyword; repeat it to the length of the message; add each plaintext letter to the corresponding key letter modulo 26: C = P + K. The tabula recta — 26 Caesar alphabets stacked, each row shifted one further — is the whole machine in one table: the row is the key letter, the column is the plaintext letter, the cell is the ciphertext. Worked miniature, hand-checked this pass: ATTACKATDAWN under key LEMON (repeated LEMONLEMONLE) gives LXFOPVEFRNHR — A+L=L, T+E=X, T+M=F, A+O=O, C+N=P, K+L=V, A+E=E, T+M=F, D+O=R, A+N=N, W+L=H, N+E=R. Note what the miniature already shows: the repeated plaintext T encrypts as X, then F, then F again only where the key cycle coincides — repetition in the ciphertext tracks the key, not the message, which is exactly the thread the break pulls.
- **The history, and the misattribution inside the name.** The cipher is not Vigenère's invention. Giovan Battista Bellaso published the polyalphabetic method first, in *La cifra del Sig. Giovan Battista Bellaso* (1553), with a reciprocal table and a keyword. Blaise de Vigenère's *Traicté des chiffres* (1586) popularised the form and added the autokey variant, in which the key stream after the primer is the plaintext itself — a key that never repeats and therefore never leaks a period. The name stuck to Vigenère anyway, and the cipher carried the nickname *le chiffrage indéchiffrable* — "the indecipherable cipher" — for roughly three hundred years, through its use by the Confederacy in the American Civil War and into the nineteenth century. The reputation outlived the cipher by a century: the break had already been found before anyone published it.
- **How it falls: two rungs, and the period is everything.** First, recover the key length. Charles Babbage broke Vigenère around 1854 but never published; Friedrich Kasiski published the method in 1863 in *Die Geheimschriften und die Dechiffrirkunst*. Kasiski's examination: a repeated plaintext trigram encrypts identically only when it falls at the same position in the key cycle, so the distances between repeated ciphertext trigrams are multiples of the key length, and their greatest common divisor exposes the period. Second, once the period is known, each column is a single Caesar shift and falls to frequency analysis — William Friedman's index of coincidence (1920s) automates the period hunt by measuring, for each candidate period, how far each column's letter distribution departs from flat. The autokey variant resists Kasiski because the key stream is the message, but it pays for that resistance with a different leak: a guessed plaintext fragment (a crib) propagates through the key stream and unlocks the rest. A short key, a stereotyped keyword (a name, a dictionary word), or a message much longer than the key all shorten the hunt; a key as long as the message, used once, is not Vigenère at all — it is the one-time pad, and the pad's entry states the price.
- **Decoder-design note (the period-first rung; the key-cycle signature).** Two Gauntlet rungs. (1) **Find the period before touching the key.** A specimen that looks polyalphabetic is graded first on period evidence — repeated-trigram distances, index of coincidence across candidate periods — and only then on key recovery, because a period claim without that evidence is a guess wearing a method's clothes. (2) **The key cycle is the specimen's fingerprint.** Two specimens with the same keyword length but different keywords are the same cipher with different keys and must be graded as one family; a specimen whose "key" is a running text, a plaintext-derived stream, or a wheel cycle is a different family (running-key, autokey, M-209-class) and must never be graded against Vigenère's failure modes, because its period, if it has one, is not the keyword. Where a specimen's ciphertext shows no repeated trigrams at all over a long message, the decoder's first hypothesis is not "unbreakable" — it is "key longer than the message, or autokey" — and the interrogation shifts to crib propagation, not period hunting.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the C = P + K mechanism, the tabula recta description, and the ATTACKATDAWN → LXFOPVEFRNHR miniature under LEMON, all re-derivable by hand this pass; CORROBORATED — the Bellaso 1553 priority, Vigenère's 1586 Traicté and autokey addition, the "le chiffrage indéchiffrable" nickname, Babbage's unpublished ~1854 break, Kasiski's 1863 publication and trigram-distance method, and Friedman's index of coincidence, all via standard secondary sources, no primary text consulted this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet period-first and key-cycle-signature rungs, which are proposals, never run.]*

## PBKDF2 — the time-only password stretcher (RFC 2898 / RFC 8018), or: the dial with one knob

- **The gap this entry closes.** Three entries already name PBKDF2 without ever stating it: the HKDF entry lists it as what a password goes through first, the Argon2 entry names it beside scrypt, and the scrypt entry runs it twice — once at each end of its sandwich — while the RAR5 entry uses PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 for file encryption and WPA2 derives its keys from it. PBKDF2 is the elder of the password stretchers, the one every later design measures itself against, and the one a decoder meets most often in the wild precisely because it predates memory-hardness. It deserves its own entry before the cluster is called complete.
- **The function, in one line.** DK = PBKDF2(PRF, Password, Salt, c, dkLen). The output is built in hLen-sized blocks, one per index i, and each block Ti is the XOR of c chained applications of the pseudorandom function: U1 = PRF(Password, Salt || INT32_BE(i)), then U2 = PRF(Password, U1), U3 = PRF(Password, U2), and so on, with Ti = U1 ^ U2 ^ ... ^ Uc, and the blocks concatenated to dkLen. The PRF is normally an HMAC — HMAC-SHA256 or HMAC-SHA512 in current use, HMAC-SHA1 in legacy specimens — and the password is the PRF key at every step, never the data. Worked miniature, recomputed locally this pass against the published RFC 6070 test vectors: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1 with password "password", salt "salt", c = 1, dkLen = 20 gives 0c60c80f961f0e71f3a9b524af6012062fe037a6, and c = 2 gives ea6c014dc72d6f8ccd1ed92ace1d41f0d8de8957 — both matching the published vectors byte for byte, so the chaining rule above is not a paraphrase but a checked mechanism.
- **The lineage, honestly dated.** PBKDF2 is RSA Laboratories' PKCS #5 v2.0, published as RFC 2898 in 2000, superseding PBKDF1 (which could only produce derived keys up to 160 bits). RFC 8018 (PKCS #5 v2.1), published in 2017, still recommends PBKDF2 for password hashing, and it is approved by NIST in SP 800-132 with FIPS-140 validated implementations — which is why it survives alongside Argon2 and scrypt: where FIPS compliance is required, OWASP's order of preference puts PBKDF2 first, not because it is strongest but because it is the validated one. Its age shows in the iteration history: the recommended minimum was 1,000 when the standard was written in 2000, a 2005 Kerberos standard recommended 4,096, and the count has climbed ever since as hardware cheapened — the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet figures read this pass are 600,000 iterations for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 and 210,000 for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512, minimums to benchmark upward against the login path's latency budget, never values to copy once and freeze.
- **Three knobs, and only one of them is a cost.** c, the iteration count, is the whole price: raising it multiplies time per guess and nothing else. The salt is a non-secret randomiser — the standard recommends at least 64 bits, NIST at least 128 bits — unique per password so identical passwords hash differently and rainbow tables die; it must be stored alongside the parameters and the output, or verification is impossible. dkLen is the desired output length, arbitrary in principle, but output beyond one hash block costs full blocks: asking SHA-256 for 16 bytes costs the same work as asking for 32, truncated. Unlike Argon2, RFC 8018 standardises the function, not a single PHC-style password-hash string, so a specimen's encoding must be read on its own terms — PHC-style `$pbkdf2-sha256$<iterations>$<salt>$<hash>`, framework-native formats, or raw stored fields — and graded on whether the parameters travel with the hash, not on which string it wears.
- **What PBKDF2 is not.** It is not memory-hard: c buys time only, so a GPU farm runs many guesses in parallel where Argon2's memory cost would price it out — the exact weakness the Argon2 and scrypt entries were built to close, and the reason OWASP ranks Argon2id first and scrypt second for new systems. It is not encryption: its output is a key (or a stored verifier), not ciphertext, and there is no decryption step — a "decrypted password" from a PBKDF2 specimen is a fabrication. It is not a substitute for a strong password or for rate limiting: it multiplies the cost of each guess, it does not make a breach-list password unguessable, and an online endpoint without throttling hands the attacker free guesses regardless of c. A specimen labelled "PBKDF2" is therefore, as with Argon2 and scrypt, not a verdict: PRF, c against the current OWASP floor, salt uniqueness and length, the encoding that carries the parameters, and whether the job actually needed memory-hardness are the specimen — and a PBKDF2 doing a memory-hard job, or a PBKDF2 at a 2000-era iteration count, has kept the name and surrendered the property.
- **Decoder-design note (the one-knob audit; the FIPS fork).** Two Gauntlet rungs. (1) **Audit the single knob against the floor, then ask what the knob cannot buy.** A specimen's c is compared to the OWASP floor for its PRF, and a passing c still fails the memory-hardness question: if the threat model includes GPU cracking, PBKDF2 at any c is the wrong family, and the grading must say so rather than pass a big number. (2) **The FIPS fork is a routing decision, not a quality verdict.** A specimen that chose PBKDF2 where FIPS-140 validation is required is compliant-by-design; the same specimen where Argon2id was available and no validation constraint applied chose the weaker family, and the report must name the fork, not just the function.

*[Grade: CORROBORATED — the PKCS #5 v2.0 / RFC 2898 (2000) origin, the PBKDF1 160-bit supersession, the RFC 8018 (2017) v2.1 recommendation, the five-parameter form and the chained-XOR block construction, the salt-length recommendations (64-bit standard, 128-bit NIST), the iteration history (1,000 at writing, 4,096 Kerberos 2005), the OWASP floors (600,000 HMAC-SHA256, 210,000 HMAC-SHA512), and the NIST SP 800-132 / FIPS-140 standing, all via the RFC-derived and OWASP-derived secondary sources read this pass; VERIFIED — the two RFC 6070 test vectors (c = 1 and c = 2, HMAC-SHA1, "password"/"salt") recomputed locally with Python hashlib this pass, matching byte for byte; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet one-knob-audit and FIPS-fork rungs, which are proposals, never run.]*

## bcrypt — the Blowfish password hash (1999), or: the stretcher that predates memory-hardness but still earns its keep

- **The gap this entry closes.** The PBKDF2 entry states OWASP's order of preference — Argon2id first, scrypt second, PBKDF2 where FIPS-140 validation is required — and the OWASP ladder behind that sentence has a fourth rung the catalogue has never stated: bcrypt, the legacy-systems answer. Every other rung now has its own entry, but a decoder meeting a `$2b$` string in the wild has had no entry to read it against. bcrypt is the elder of the adaptive password hashes, the one that taught the field that the cost of a password function should be a dial turned up over time, and it remains defensible where it already lives — which is not the same as recommended where nothing lives yet.
- **The lineage, and the expensive key schedule.** bcrypt was designed by Niels Provos and David Mazières and presented at USENIX in 1999, built on Bruce Schneier's Blowfish block cipher and adopted as OpenBSD's default password hash. Its core is EksBlowfish — "expensive key schedule Blowfish": the Blowfish key schedule is run with the salt and the password alternating as keys, deliberately made slow, and then the resulting state encrypts the fixed 24-byte string "OrpheanBeholderScryDoubt" (three Blowfish blocks) 64 times in ECB mode; the final byte of the ciphertext is dropped, leaving a 23-byte output. The slowness is the point, and it lives entirely in the key setup: the cipher itself is ordinary Blowfish, the schedule is the weapon.
- **One knob, exponential.** The cost parameter runs from 4 to 31 and sets the key-expansion iteration count to 2^cost, so every increment doubles the work: cost 10 means 1,024 rounds, cost 12 means 4,096. OWASP's Password Storage Cheat Sheet gives bcrypt to legacy systems only — where Argon2id and scrypt are unavailable — at a work factor of 10 or more, as large as verification-server performance will allow, targeting a hash time in the low hundreds of milliseconds on the serving hardware. Because the cost travels inside the stored string, it can be raised over time without a migration: a login that verifies an old-cost hash can re-hash at the new cost, so the store upgrades itself one login at a time. A specimen at cost 4, or at a cost frozen since the hardware it was tuned on retired, has kept the name and surrendered the property.
- **The string carries everything verification needs.** A bcrypt hash is 60 characters in modular crypt format: `$2b$12$` + 22 characters of salt + 31 characters of hash. The salt is 16 random bytes, unique per password, encoded in the crypt base-64 alphabet (`./A-Za-z0-9`, not standard base-64 — a parser that decodes it with a standard decoder misreads the salt). The 31 characters carry the 23-byte output (184 bits). The version prefix matters: `$2b$` is the current standard, `$2a$` is the legacy form whose handling of certain inputs was buggy in older implementations, and `$2y$` marks the fixed crypt_blowfish variant — a specimen's prefix is part of its identity, not decoration. Verification re-runs the function with the stored salt and cost and compares in constant time; the salt is not a secret and sits beside the hash by design, which is what kills rainbow tables without any separate salt column to lose.
- **The 72-byte ceiling, and the pre-hash answer.** bcrypt uses at most the first 72 bytes of the password; anything beyond that is silently truncated. Two passphrases that differ only after byte 72 therefore hash identically, and a user who believes a 100-character passphrase bought extra security bought nothing past the ceiling. OWASP's rule is to enforce a maximum password length of 72 bytes (or less, if the implementation in use has a smaller limit). The common mitigation — hash the password first, then bcrypt the digest, as `bcrypt(H(password))` — removes the ceiling but changes the scheme: it must be applied consistently at verification and at every migration, or the store holds two incompatible kinds of verifier under one name. A specimen that accepts arbitrarily long passwords into raw bcrypt without enforcing or documenting the ceiling is misdescribing its own security margin.
- **What bcrypt is not.** It is not memory-hard: the Blowfish state is a few kibibytes, small enough to fit in cache, so a GPU farm runs many guesses in parallel where Argon2's tens of mebibytes would price it out — the exact weakness the Argon2 and scrypt entries were built to close, and the reason OWASP ranks bcrypt as a legacy answer rather than a new-system choice. It is not encryption and it is not reversible: there is no decryption step, only re-hash and compare, so a "decrypted password" from a bcrypt specimen is a fabrication. It is not a general-purpose key stretcher for high-entropy secrets: a Diffie–Hellman output or a random master key goes through HKDF's fast, purpose-separated expansion, not through a password function. And it is not a substitute for a strong password or for rate limiting: it multiplies the cost of each guess, it does not make a breach-list password unguessable, and an online endpoint without throttling hands the attacker free guesses regardless of cost. A specimen labelled "bcrypt" is therefore, as with Argon2, scrypt, and PBKDF2, not a verdict: version prefix, cost against the OWASP floor, salt uniqueness, the 72-byte handling, and whether the job actually needed memory-hardness are the specimen.
- **Decoder-design note (the cost-and-ceiling audit; the version-and-alphabet rung).** Two Gauntlet rungs. (1) **Audit the single knob and the ceiling together.** A specimen's cost is compared to the OWASP floor for legacy bcrypt, and its password-length handling is checked in the same pass — a cost-12 hash that silently truncates a 90-byte passphrase has passed the cost audit and failed the ceiling audit, and the report must say both. (2) **Read the prefix and the alphabet before decoding anything.** A `$2a$` specimen, a `$2y$` specimen, and a `$2b$` specimen are not interchangeable encodings of one hash, and a decoder that treats the 22+31 characters as standard base-64 has already misread the salt it claims to have verified.

*[Grade: CORROBORATED — the 1999 Provos/Mazières USENIX origin, the Blowfish basis, the EksBlowfish expensive-key-schedule construction, the OpenBSD default adoption, the cost range 4–31 with 2^cost iterations, the 16-byte salt, the 22-character salt and 31-character hash encodings in the crypt base-64 alphabet, the "OrpheanBeholderScryDoubt" 64-times-ECB step with the final byte dropped to 23 bytes, the 72-byte password ceiling, the $2a$/$2b$/$2y$ version prefixes, and the OWASP legacy-systems standing with a work factor of 10 or more and a 72-byte password limit, all via secondary sources and the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet read this pass; VERIFIED — the 60-character string anatomy (7 + 22 + 31) and the 2^10 = 1,024 / 2^12 = 4,096 iteration counts, checked by arithmetic locally this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet cost-and-ceiling and version-and-alphabet rungs, which are proposals, never run.]*

## X448 — the Diffie–Hellman exchange on Curve448, or: the handshake that buys 224 bits for 56 bytes

- **The gap this entry closes.** The X25519 entry names X448 in a single sentence, and the EdDSA entry carries Ed448, the signature on the Edwards form of the same curve — but no entry until now says how the Montgomery form of Curve448 exchanges keys. X448 is that member: the Diffie–Hellman key agreement over Curve448 (the Ed448-Goldilocks curve), standardised alongside X25519 in RFC 7748 (October 2016), for designs that want a classical-security margin above the 128-bit level without leaving the Montgomery-ladder family.
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** X448 is the same construction as X25519, scaled up: a Montgomery ladder that needs only the u-coordinate, over the prime field p = 2⁴⁴⁸ − 2²²⁴ − 1. Each party holds a 56-byte secret scalar, clamped (pruned) before use under RFC 7748 §5, and publishes the 56-byte u-coordinate of the scalar multiple of the base point; each side then multiplies the peer's u-coordinate by its own scalar and lands on the same 56-byte shared secret. The security level is roughly 224 bits, against X25519's roughly 128 — the extra 24 bytes of key buy roughly 96 bits of classical margin. As with X25519, the raw shared secret is never a session key: it is fed into a key-derivation function, which is also what destroys any structure the ladder output carries.
- **What X448 is not.** It is not a signature: Ed448 signs, with 57-byte public keys and 114-byte signatures, and the two key forms are not interchangeable — a 57-byte value labelled X448 is an Ed448 key wearing the wrong name. It is not post-quantum: Shor's algorithm breaks the discrete-logarithm problem it rests on exactly as it breaks X25519, which is why the hybrid-with-ML-KEM rationale from the X25519 entry applies unchanged. And it is not a drop-in upgrade for X25519: 56 bytes is not 32, the SSH method names differ (curve448-sha512 against curve25519-sha256), and a decoder that grades a 56-byte specimen against X25519 test vectors — or vice versa — has misread the specimen before it starts.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** Size discipline is the first screen: 32 bytes means X25519, 56 bytes means X448, 57 bytes means Ed448, and any other length under an X448 label is a mislabel or a truncation. The low-order trap from the X25519 entry carries over in form — the ladder accepts any 56-byte peer value — so the contributory check belongs here too: a shared secret of all zeros is not a secret, and a specimen that accepts one has failed the same rung X25519 specimens fail. The deployment footprint is narrower than X25519's — SSH and IKEv2 (RFC 8031) name Curve448 methods, and the TLS 1.3 named-group registry carries it — so an X448 specimen found in the wild deserves a second look at why the deployment paid the larger key, rather than an assumption that it is the default. A specimen labelled "X448" is therefore, as with X25519, not a verdict: the size, the clamping, the all-zero check, and the KDF after the ladder are the specimen.

## Ed448 — the Edwards-curve signature on Curve448, or: the seal that buys 224 bits for 57 bytes

- **The gap this entry closes.** The EdDSA entry carries Ed448 in a single paragraph, and the X448 entry uses it only as a contrast — 57-byte keys against 56-byte exchange keys — but no entry until now says how the Edwards form of Curve448 signs. Ed448 is that member: EdDSA instantiated on edwards448 (the Goldilocks curve), standardised alongside Ed25519 in RFC 8032 (January 2017), for designs that want a classical-security margin above the 128-bit level without leaving the EdDSA family.
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Ed448 is the same Schnorr-shaped scheme as Ed25519, scaled up: the signer expands a 57-byte seed with SHAKE256 (where Ed25519 uses SHA-512), derives a deterministic nonce from a prefix of that expansion plus the message — so no random nonce ever exists to be reused or leaked — and emits a 114-byte signature, the 57-byte encoded point R followed by the 57-byte scalar S. The public key is a 57-byte encoding of a 455-bit y-coordinate plus a sign bit for x, over the field p = 2⁴⁴⁸ − 2²²⁴ − 1 shared with X448. The security level is roughly 224 bits, against Ed25519's roughly 128 — the extra 25 bytes of key buy roughly 96 bits of classical margin. Verification checks the cofactor-scaled group equation and rejects out-of-range S; a signature that verifies under the Ed25519 equation, or against a 32-byte key, has been graded against the wrong curve before it starts.
- **What Ed448 is not.** It is not an exchange: X448 agrees on keys with 56-byte u-coordinates, Ed448 signs with 57-byte Edwards keys, and the two key forms are derived differently and are not interchangeable — a 56-byte value labelled Ed448 is an X448 key wearing the wrong name, and vice versa. It is not post-quantum: Shor's algorithm breaks the discrete-logarithm problem it rests on exactly as it breaks Ed25519, which is why the hybrid-with-ML-DSA rationale from the EdDSA entry applies unchanged. And it is not a drop-in upgrade for Ed25519: 57 bytes is not 32, 114 is not 64, the hash is SHAKE256 not SHA-512, and the SSH method name differs (ssh-ed448, RFC 8709, against ssh-ed25519) — a decoder that grades a 114-byte specimen against Ed25519 test vectors has misread the specimen before it starts. The prehash variant Ed448ph exists for signers that cannot hold the whole message, exactly as Ed25519ph does for Ed25519, and the context-string variant binds a signature to one protocol so it cannot be replayed into another.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** Size discipline is the first screen: 32 bytes means Ed25519, 57 bytes means Ed448, 56 bytes means X448, and any other length under an Ed448 label is a mislabel or a truncation. The deterministic nonce is the second: Ed448 has no random-nonce failure mode to hunt, so a specimen whose signatures vary across identical re-signings of the same message under the same key is either using the optional-randomness variant or is not Ed448 at all. The deployment footprint is narrower than Ed25519's — SSH names ssh-ed448, but the library and hardware support is thinner — so an Ed448 specimen found in the wild deserves a second look at why the deployment paid the larger key and signature, rather than an assumption that it is the default. A specimen labelled "Ed448" is therefore, as with X448, not a verdict: the size, the hash, the nonce determinism, and the verification equation are the specimen.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the RFC 8032 (January 2017) standardisation of Ed25519 and Ed448, the edwards448 field p = 2⁴⁴⁸ − 2²²⁴ − 1, the 57-byte public-key and 114-byte signature sizes, the 455-bit little-endian encoding, the SHAKE256 hash with 114-byte output, and the ssh-ed448 method name with 57-octet keys and 114-octet signatures per RFC 8709, all via the RFC texts read this pass; CORROBORATED — the roughly 224-bit security level, the Goldilocks curve name, the deterministic-nonce construction, the cofactor-scaled verification equation with out-of-range-S rejection, the Ed448ph prehash and context-string variants, and the X448 56-byte non-interchangeability contrast; CLAIMED — the narrower-than-Ed25519 deployment footprint, a qualitative reading of the method lists rather than a measured census; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet size-discipline, nonce-determinism, and verification rungs, which are proposals, never run.]*

## Camellia — the AES-interface block cipher from Japan, or: the seal that answers AES with a Feistel

- **The gap this entry closes.** The AES entries carry the 128-bit-block, 128/192/256-bit-key interface as if AES owned it, and the catalogue's symmetric bench has no second member at that interface at all — Twofish, Serpent, and Camellia are all absent. Camellia is that missing second member: a 128-bit block cipher with 128-, 192-, and 256-bit keys, jointly developed by Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation and Mitsubishi Electric Corporation in 2000 and described in RFC 3713 (April 2004), designed to the same interface as AES so it can slot into the same protocols.
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Camellia is a balanced Feistel cipher: the 128-bit plaintext splits into two 64-bit halves, pre-whitened with kw1 and kw2, then run through 18 Feistel rounds for a 128-bit key or 24 rounds for a 192- or 256-bit key, with post-whitening by kw3 and kw4 and a final half-swap on output. Each round's F-function is a byte-oriented SP network — the round key XORed in, then an S-layer of 8 S-boxes in parallel, then a P-layer of linear diffusion — and every six rounds an additional word-oriented layer is inserted, the FL-function on one side and its inverse FLINV on the other (after rounds 6 and 12 in the 18-round form, after 6, 12, and 18 in the 24-round form). The key schedule derives the round subkeys with the same Feistel transform plus word rotations, and decryption is the same procedure with the subkeys in reverse order — the Feistel dividend, shared with every Feistel entry in this catalogue.
- **What Camellia is not.** It is not AES: AES is a substitution–permutation network, Camellia is a Feistel network with FL layers, and their test vectors, S-boxes, and round counts are not interchangeable — a specimen that verifies against AES vectors is not Camellia, and a Camellia specimen graded against AES vectors has been misread before it starts. It is not an AEAD and not a mode: raw Camellia encrypts one 128-bit block, so a specimen showing multi-block traffic without a mode (CBC, CTR, or a TLS ciphersuite wrapping it) is either a single-block test or an incomplete capture. And it is not post-quantum: it is a classical block cipher, so the standard quantum-search argument halves its effective key strength in theory, which is why the 256-bit key size — not the 128-bit one — is the long-horizon choice, exactly as with AES-256.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** Round count is the first screen: 18 rounds means a 128-bit key, 24 rounds means 192 or 256 — the round count alone cannot separate 192 from 256, and any entry claiming otherwise is guessing. The FL/FLINV layers are the fingerprint: a generic Feistel specimen without them is not Camellia, and a specimen with them at the wrong positions (anything but every six rounds) is a variant or a corruption. The block-size bound is shared with AES: at 128-bit blocks, the birthday bound sits near 2⁶⁴ blocks under one key, so a Camellia specimen encrypting enormous volumes under a single key in a mode without rekeying deserves the same scrutiny an AES specimen would get. A specimen labelled "Camellia" is therefore, as with every entry here, not a verdict: the block size, the key size, the round count, the FL positions, and the subkey-reversal decryption are the specimen.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the RFC 3713 (April 2004) description: 128-bit block size, 128/192/256-bit keys, the NTT and Mitsubishi Electric 2000 origin, the 18-round (128-bit key) and 24-round (192/256-bit key) Feistel structures, FL/FLINV insertion every 6 rounds, pre- and post-whitening with kw1–kw4, and decryption by reversing the subkey order, all via the RFC text read this pass; CORROBORATED — the ISO/IEC 18033-3 standardisation, the NESSIE and CRYPTREC approvals, the TLS ciphersuites via RFC 5932/6367, the F-function's 8-S-box S-layer plus P-layer structure, and the key schedule's reuse of the Feistel transform with rotations; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet round-count, FL-fingerprint, and volume-under-one-key rungs, which are proposals, never run.]*

## MQOM — the multivariate MPC-in-the-Head signature, or: the seal that proves it knows a solution without showing one

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue's MPC-in-the-Head shelf holds one member, FAEST — and FAEST is deliberately not MPC-in-the-Head at all, but VOLE-in-the-Head, filed under NIST's round tables by the table's label rather than the construction's name. The shelf's genuine MPCitH members were all absent, and so was the performance story of the round: MQOM earned its third-round place by having the best performance numbers among the six MPCitH candidates in round 2, with the smallest combined public-key-plus-signature sizes in the MPCitH category at all three NIST security levels. MQOM is that member: the multivariate-quadratic signature that signs by simulating a multiparty computation in its own head.
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** MQOM's name expands to "MQ on my Mind": its hardness is the MQ problem, solving a random system of multivariate quadratic equations over a finite field — a problem with decades of study behind it, and a different assumption from FAEST's AES one-wayness and from SDitH's syndrome decoding. The signing pattern is the MPC-in-the-Head template the whole shelf shares: the prover splits its secret witness among simulated parties, runs the multiparty computation that checks the witness against the public MQ system, commits to every party's view, and lets the verifier open a subset of those views — the Fiat-Shamir transform making the interaction non-interactive. MQOM's variant of the template is Threshold Computation in the Head (TCitH): the computation is arranged so that the verifier's opened subset reveals nothing about the witness, while a cheating prover that does not know a solution is caught with overwhelming probability. The public key is the MQ system itself (plus its evaluation at the secret), the signature is the committed views plus the opened subset, and verification re-runs the opened parties and checks the commitments — no lattice, no code, no isogeny anywhere in the assumption.
- **What MQOM is not.** It is not FAEST with a different name: FAEST proves knowledge of an AES key through VOLE correlations, MQOM proves knowledge of an MQ solution through simulated parties — same proof-shape family, different mathematics, different assumption, different failure modes. It is not a multivariate signature in the UOV sense either: UOV, MAYO, SNOVA, and QR-UOV sign by inverting a trapdoor (oil-and-vinegar structure hidden in the public map), while MQOM signs by proving knowledge of a solution to a random system with no trapdoor at all — a specimen that describes MQOM as a trapdoor scheme has confused the two multivariate branches. And it is not a standard: round-3 candidacy in NIST IR 8610 (May 2026) is a longer evaluation, not a verdict, and NIST flagged the caveat explicitly — MQOM's security proofs in both the Random Oracle Model and the Quantum Random Oracle Model need further maturation. A specimen labelled "FIPS MQOM" is mislabelled, full stop, exactly as "FIPS SQIsign" is.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The assumption test is the first screen: demand the MQ system named in full — field, number of variables, number of equations — because "multivariate" without the system is a label, not a key, and because the MQ branch split above (trapdoor UOV versus trapdoor-free MQOM) is exactly the confusion a mislabelled specimen exploits. The proof-maturity test is the second: any MQOM claim that quotes its round-2 performance (smallest combined sizes in the MPCitH category, competitive signing and verification speeds) as if it were a security argument has mistaken the reason it advanced for a proof — NIST advanced it on performance while explicitly noting the proofs were immature, and the third round exists to close that gap. The parameter discipline is the third: MQOM's sizes and speeds are quoted per security level (Categories 1, 3, 5), and this entry verifies no byte-size figure this pass — a size quoted without its category, or a round-2 size sold as a round-3 figure, is stale or unanchored until checked against the current specification. A specimen labelled "MQOM" is therefore, as with every entry here, not a verdict: the MQ system, the TCitH proof shape, the category beside any size, and the proof-maturity caveat are the specimen.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — nothing in this entry is claimed as first-party verified this pass; CORROBORATED — the MQOM expansion "MQ on my Mind," the MQ-problem hardness basis, the TCitH (Threshold Computation in the Head) construction, the MPCitH category membership alongside FAEST and SDitH, the round-3 advance in NIST IR 8610 (May 14, 2026) among nine candidates, the best-performance-among-six-MPCitH-candidates and smallest-combined-public-key-plus-signature-sizes-in-category characterisation, and NIST's explicit caveat that the ROM and QROM security proofs need further maturation, all via the round-3 coverage read this pass; CLAIMED — the Fiat-Shamir non-interactive framing, the commit-and-open-subset verification sketch, and the Categories 1/3/5 level mapping, which rest on the general MPCitH template and secondary summaries rather than the MQOM specification read this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet assumption, proof-maturity, and parameter-discipline checks, which are proposals, never run.]*
