## MD5 — the message digest that taught the field the collision lesson, or: the seal that still checksums the world after its death

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries SHA-1 (the seal that carried the world's trust until its collision), SHA-2, SHA-3, and BLAKE3 — the whole post-MD5 hash shelf — but never the hash they all learned from: MD5, the 128-bit digest that was the world's default fingerprint for a decade and still turns up in checksums, ETags, and legacy verifiers. A decoder that cannot spot MD5 cannot grade half the digests it meets in the wild, and cannot tell a harmless checksum from a dead seal.

- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Ronald Rivest, RFC 1321 (April 1992), MD4's successor: a 128-bit digest over the Merkle–Damgård construction, 512-bit blocks, 64 steps in four rounds of sixteen. The state is four 32-bit words (67452301, efcdab89, 98badcfe, 10325476); each round mixes them with one nonlinear function — F (choose), G, H (xor), I — a per-round shift table (7/12/17/22, 5/9/14/20, 4/11/16/23, 6/10/15/21), and a sine-table constant per step. Padding is a 0x80 byte, zeros to 56 mod 64, then the 64-bit little-endian bit length; the digest is the four state words in little-endian order. Nothing about the design is exotic — that ordinariness is why it spread everywhere, and why its fall mattered everywhere.

- **What MD5 is not.** It is not a MAC: Merkle–Damgård length extension means MD5(secret || message) lets anyone append data without the secret, so a specimen using bare MD5 as a MAC fails by construction, not by attack. It is not a password hash: fast and unsalted by design, the opposite of the bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2 entries' slow side. It is not collision-resistant: dead for signatures and certificates since Xiaoyun Wang's first practical collision in 2004, with the Stevens et al. rogue-CA chosen-prefix demonstration in 2008 and the Flame malware's forged Microsoft code-signing certificate in 2012 as the receipts. It is not a random oracle: chosen-prefix collisions let the attacker fix both documents' beginnings and still collide. And it is not wholly "broken": preimage resistance stands — no one can invert a given digest, or forge a second document matching an already-fixed one. "MD5 is broken" without the property qualifier is a grading error, not a verdict.

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: the seven RFC 1321 vectors — empty, "a", "abc", "message digest", the lowercase alphabet, the 62-character alphanumeric set, "1234567890" eight times — reproduced exactly this pass by the from-scratch implementation in hidden_files/md5-mini.py (no hashlib in the implementation), cross-checked against hashlib and the system md5sum. The shift-table trap is the second: round-4 shifts are 6/10/15/21, and this pass's first implementation used 19 and failed every vector, all seven, not some — a specimen with the same slip fails totally, not partially, and partial failure points elsewhere. The padding-boundary test is the third: lengths 55 (fits one block), 56 (spills to two), 63, 64, 65, 119, 120, all verified this pass against hashlib — a specimen failing exactly at 56 or 120 has a padding bug, not a compression bug. The property screen is the fourth: a specimen "breaking MD5" by exhibiting a collision has broken collision resistance only — demand the property named: collision, second-preimage, or preimage. The chosen-prefix screen is the fifth, and it is the Flame pattern: two documents with attacker-chosen beginnings and one digest — a verifier that accepts an MD5 digest as document identity accepts both documents. The length-extension screen is the sixth: any secret-prefix MAC construction over MD5 is forgeable on sight.

- **Decoder-design note (MD5 → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Grade the property, not the primitive.** MD5 is the catalogue's standing proof that "broken" is not a verdict: collision-broken, preimage-intact, and the two grades travel separately — the same lesson as the SHA-1 entry, with MD5 as the earlier, cheaper receipt. Every interrogation states which property the specimen relies on before grading it. (2) **The chosen-prefix canary.** If a specimen binds identity to a digest, the Gauntlet must produce two distinct canary documents with the same digest before trusting the binding — because the attacker, not the verifier, chooses the documents. Flame is why this rung exists: the forged certificate was not a lucky collision, it was a chosen-prefix construction aimed at a live CA path. (3) **The checksum trap.** MD5 survives as a fast non-adversarial checksum long after its death as a seal — speed and ubiquity are not security claims. The Gauntlet checks what the digest is USED for before grading the primitive: checksum use is legitimate and uninteresting; identity, signature, and certificate use is where the verdict bites. (Usage rung, cf. the SIGABA note: mechanism and handling on separate ledgers.)

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the seven RFC 1321 vectors and the seven padding-boundary lengths, all recomputed this pass by hidden_files/md5-mini.py and cross-checked against hashlib and md5sum; the round-4 shift table (6/10/15/21) as the failure that caught the first implementation; CORROBORATED — RFC 1321 authorship and date, the Wang 2004 first practical collision, the Stevens et al. 2008 rogue-CA chosen-prefix demonstration, and the Flame 2012 forged-Microsoft-certificate case, via standard references read this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## RIPEMD-160 — the European 160-bit digest that outlived its predecessor, or: the hash that Bitcoin shrank its addresses with

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries MD5, SHA-1, SHA-2, SHA-3, and BLAKE3 — the hash shelf from Rivest through the SHA-3 competition — but never the European digest that sits between MD4 and SHA-1 in the lineage and still does live work inside every legacy Bitcoin address: RIPEMD-160. A decoder that cannot spot a 20-byte digest cannot tell a HASH160 address payload from a truncated SHA-256, and cannot grade a specimen that chains two hashes instead of one.

- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** RIPEMD stands for RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation Message Digest, built in the European Union's RIPE project (RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation, 1988–1992). The original RIPEMD was a 128-bit MD4-family digest; Hans Dobbertin found collisions for a two-round-reduced version in the first half of 1995, and the original RIPEMD was later found to have collision issues (reported 2004). RIPEMD-160 is the strengthened successor, designed by Hans Dobbertin, Antoon Bosselaers, and Bart Preneel at KU Leuven's COSIC group, published in *Fast Software Encryption* (LNCS 1039, Springer, 1996, pp. 71–82) and described again in *Dr. Dobb's Journal* (January 1997). It was adopted in ISO/IEC 10118-3:2004 alongside RIPEMD-128 and SHA-1, and it is not patented. [CORROBORATED — the RIPEMD-160 project page, VeraCrypt documentation, and standard references read this pass]

- **The construction, in one paragraph.** A 160-bit (20-byte, 40-hex-character) digest over the Merkle–Damgård construction, tuned for 32-bit processors: 512-bit blocks, MD-style padding (a 1 bit, zeros, then the 64-bit little-endian bit length), and a compression function that runs two parallel lines — left and right — each of five rounds of sixteen steps (80 steps per line), with different Boolean functions and message-word orders per line, combined at the end. The twin-line design is the point: where MD5 runs one line and SHA-1 runs one line, RIPEMD-160 makes a differential attack satisfy two differently-ordered lines at once. The family also includes RIPEMD-128 (128-bit), RIPEMD-256, and RIPEMD-320; this entry covers the 160-bit member only. [CORROBORATED — standard descriptions read this pass]

- **What RIPEMD-160 is not.** It is not the original RIPEMD: the 2004 collision findings attach to the 128-bit predecessor, and citing them against RIPEMD-160 is a version error — the same grading error as citing MD4 breaks against MD5, only with the names closer together. It is not collision-proof: a 160-bit digest carries an 80-bit birthday bound, so its collision margin is thinner than SHA-256's 128-bit bound whatever the cryptanalysis record says, and secondary guidance steers new security-sensitive uses to SHA-256 or SHA-3. It is not a password hash or a MAC: fast and unsalted by design, like every digest in this shelf, and a bare hash is not authentication. And it is not broken in the practical sense: no practical collision against the full RIPEMD-160 has been reported, and published attacks reach only reduced-round variants — an absence-of-break that is filed as a standing record, never as a proof of security. [CORROBORATED — secondary security summaries read this pass; the no-practical-collision claim is absence-of-evidence, filed as such]

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: empty string → 9c1185a5c5e9fc54612808977ee8f548b2258d31; "a" → 0bdc9d2d256b3ee9daae347be6f4dc835a467ffe; "abc" → 8eb208f7e05d987a9b044a8e98c6b087f15a0bfc; "message digest" → 5d0689ef49d2fae572b881b123a85ffa21595f36; the lowercase alphabet → f71c27109c692c1b56bbdceb5b9d2865b3708dbc — all reproduced this pass via the system hashlib implementation (not a from-scratch implementation, so a specimen is graded against the same vectors, not against this entry's code). The length test is the second: a 20-byte digest is RIPEMD-160-shaped, a 32-byte digest is not — a specimen handing over 20 bytes and calling it SHA-256 has truncated, mislabeled, or chained. The chain test is the third, and it is the live one: Bitcoin's HASH160 is RIPEMD-160(SHA-256(public key)), so a Bitcoin address payload is a second hash, not a first — a specimen that tests the payload against SHA-256 alone, or against RIPEMD-160 of the raw key, fails both, and only the ordered pair passes. The version test is the fourth: RIPEMD, RIPEMD-128, and RIPEMD-160 are three different digests sharing a name stem, and any report that says "RIPEMD" without the number is ungraded until the number is pinned.

- **Decoder-design note (RIPEMD-160 → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Grade the bound, not just the break record.** RIPEMD-160's honest grade is two numbers side by side: no practical full collision reported, and an 80-bit birthday bound. The MD5 entry's "grade the property, not the primitive" rung, sharpened: a primitive can be unbroken and still be the wrong margin for a long-lived seal, and the report card must carry both facts or it misleads by omission. (2) **Interrogate the chain, not just the link.** HASH160 proves a specimen's digest may be the second hash in a chain, and the chain order is itself evidence — SHA-256-then-RIPEMD-160 is a different specimen from RIPEMD-160-then-SHA-256, and from either hash alone. The Gauntlet's digest screen therefore tests ordered pairs before it tests single algorithms, because a chained digest defeats every single-algorithm test by construction. (3) **A strengthened successor does not heal its predecessor, and a broken predecessor does not condemn its successor.** RIPEMD fell and RIPEMD-160 stands; MD4 fell and MD5 stood for a decade before falling in its turn. Versions earn separate verdicts, and the report card never lets a family name carry a grade — the number after the name is part of the verdict.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the five test vectors above, recomputed this pass via hashlib and matching the published RIPEMD-160 vector set; CORROBORATED — the RIPE project origin and 1988–1992 dates, the Dobbertin/Bosselaers/Preneel authorship, the 1996 FSE publication and 1997 Dr. Dobb's description, the ISO/IEC 10118-3:2004 adoption, the twin-line 5×16 construction, the Bitcoin HASH160 chain (RIPEMD-160 after SHA-256), and the 2004 collision findings against the original RIPEMD; CLAIMED — the "no practical full collision" record, which is absence-of-evidence from secondary summaries, not a proof; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## RIPEMD-128 — the 128-bit twin that shares a name with a broken predecessor, or: the digest that length alone cannot identify

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries RIPEMD-160, but a decoder that knows only the 160-bit member will misread the family's 128-bit member twice over: once by length, because a 32-hex-character digest is also exactly MD5-shaped and exactly original-RIPEMD-shaped, and once by name, because "RIPEMD" unqualified usually means the broken 1992 original, not this 1996 redesign. A specimen handing over 16 bytes needs a test that names which 128-bit digest it is, not a guess from its size.
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** RIPEMD-128 is the 128-bit member of the strengthened RIPEMD family designed by Hans Dobbertin, Antoon Bosselaers, and Bart Preneel at KU Leuven's COSIC group, published alongside RIPEMD-160 in *Fast Software Encryption* (LNCS 1039, Springer, 1996) and adopted in ISO/IEC 10118-3:2004. It is not the original RIPEMD: that 1992 RIPE-project digest was also 128-bit, and the 2004 Wang-group collision findings attach to it — the same name stem, a different function. RIPEMD-128 shares RIPEMD-160's twin-line design at a smaller size: two parallel lines, four rounds of sixteen steps each (64 steps per line), MD-style padding, 512-bit blocks. [CORROBORATED — the RIPEMD-160 entry's lineage sources, and the Peyrin ChinaCrypt 2013 slides read this pass, which state RIPEMD-128's parameters as 128-bit digest, 64 steps, 4 rounds of 16]
- **What RIPEMD-128 is not.** It is not the original RIPEMD, and citing the 2004 collisions against it is a version error — the mirror image of the error the RIPEMD-160 entry warns about, except here the digest sizes match, so the error survives even a length check. It is not MD5: same 128-bit length, same 32 hex characters, different function, different vectors — a report that says "128-bit digest" and stops has identified nothing. It is not unbroken in the strong sense, and it is not broken in the practical sense: published cryptanalysis reaches reduced-round compression functions — a 48-step collision at complexity 2^40 [MNS12] and 52-step nonrandomness at 2^107 [SW12] — while the full 64-step function has no practical collision on record. And it is not a safe margin for anything long-lived regardless of that record: a 128-bit digest carries a 64-bit birthday bound, the same thin margin that retired MD5's size class from security work, and no clean break record repairs a bound. [CORROBORATED — the reduced-round figures from the Peyrin slides read this pass, which cite the papers rather than reproducing them; the no-practical-full-collision claim is absence-of-evidence, filed as such]
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: empty string → cdf26213a150dc3ecb610f18f6b38b46; "a" → 86be7afa339d0fc7cfc785e72f578d33; "abc" → c14a12199c66e4ba84636b0f69144c77; "message digest" → 9e327b3d6e523062afc1132d7df9d1b8; the lowercase alphabet → fd2aa607f71dc8f510714922b371834e — all computed this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/ripemd128-mini.py) that reproduced six independently published RIPEMD-128 digests exactly (the digit strings 9481063, 8398103, 103156052, 41380232, 46078913, 16413120) before any catalogue vector was trusted. The name test is the second: any report saying "RIPEMD" without a number is ungraded until the number is pinned, and "RIPEMD-128" must never inherit either the original RIPEMD's break or RIPEMD-160's cleaner record — the number after the name is part of the verdict, as the RIPEMD-160 entry already rules. The length test is the third, and it fails by design: 16 bytes cannot separate RIPEMD-128 from MD5 from original RIPEMD, so a specimen identified by length alone is unidentified, and the vector test, not the ruler, is the identifier. The library test is the fourth: RIPEMD-128 still ships in older crypto libraries (BeeCrypt carries ripemd128 headers), so a specimen built on a legacy stack may legitimately emit it — presence in a library is not evidence of current fitness, and a legacy digest in a new seal is a finding, not a pass.
- **Decoder-design note (RIPEMD-128 → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Test the function, never the length.** The digest-length screen is a filter, not an identification: every 128-bit digest passes it, so the Gauntlet's digest screen must run the vector test before it names any algorithm, and must report "128-bit, unidentified" rather than a guessed name when the vectors fail. (2) **A shared name is a shared trap.** RIPEMD, RIPEMD-128, and RIPEMD-160 are three functions under two name stems, and the catalogue's version rule — the number is part of the verdict — exists precisely because the trap survives length checks, literature searches, and library headers alike. The report card names the exact function or names nothing. (3) **Grade the bound alongside the break record, again.** RIPEMD-128's honest grade is two numbers side by side, as RIPEMD-160's was: no practical full collision reported, and a 64-bit birthday bound. A specimen sealed with RIPEMD-128 today is not condemned by a break it does not have, and it is not cleared by a record that cannot outrun its own bound — both facts ride on the card, or the card misleads by omission.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the five test vectors above, computed this pass by a from-specification implementation validated 6/6 against independently published RIPEMD-128 digests; CORROBORATED — the Dobbertin/Bosselaers/Preneel authorship, the 1996 FSE publication, the ISO/IEC 10118-3:2004 adoption, the twin-line 4×16 construction, the reduced-round figures (48-step collision 2^40 [MNS12], 52-step nonrandomness 2^107 [SW12]) via the Peyrin slides, and BeeCrypt's ripemd128 headers; CLAIMED — the "no practical full collision" record, which is absence-of-evidence from secondary summaries, not a proof; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## ADFGVX — the fractionating field cipher of 1918, or: the cipher that split every letter in two before scrambling it

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries Enigma, Playfair, and the Vigenère family, but never the First World War field cipher that invented fractionation — the two-stage construction that made a hand cipher resist the best cryptanalyst of its day for weeks, and that still teaches the Gauntlet its central lesson about layered specimens: attack the layers in reverse order, or attack nothing at all.
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** Invented by German signal corps Lieutenant Fritz Nebel and introduced in March 1918 as the "Secret Cipher of the Radio Operators 1918" (*Geheimschrift der Funker 1918*, GedeFu 18), the five-letter ADFGX version ran on the Western Front through the Spring Offensive; the six-letter ADFGVX version followed in June 1918, expanding the square from 5×5 (25 cells) to 6×6 (36 cells) so digits could be enciphered alongside letters. French Army Lieutenant Georges Painvin of the Bureau du Chiffre broke ADFGX in April 1918, then broke ADFGVX on 2 June 1918 after roughly 26 hours of continuous work on the first ADFGVX intercept — a 1 June transmission from German outposts near Remaugies, north of Compiègne, the so-called Radiogramme de la Victoire, whose plaintext revealed a munitions buildup and let the Allies meet the German offensive of 9 June prepared. Nebel, who had originally proposed a double columnar transposition for the second stage and been overruled in favour of a single one, did not learn his cipher had been broken until 1966, and met Painvin in 1968. [CORROBORATED — the ADFGVX and Georges Painvin articles and the NKU cryptology notes read this pass; the March first-use day differs across sources (1 vs 5 March), so this entry dates it to March 1918 only]
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Two stages, and the order matters. (1) **Fractionation:** a keyed mixed alphabet fills a 6×6 Polybius square whose rows and columns are labelled A, D, F, G, V, X — letters chosen because their Morse forms are maximally dissimilar (A ·−, D −··, F ··−·, G −−·, V ···−, X −··−), so a wireless operator mishearing a dot or a dash would not silently substitute one label for another. Each plaintext character becomes two ciphertext letters: its row label, then its column label. (2) **Keyed columnar transposition:** the fractionated stream is written in rows under a keyword, and the columns are read out in the keyword's alphabetical order. Worked illustration, alphabet-order square (A–Z then 0–9, computed this pass): "attack" → AAGDGDAAAFDV; under keyword KAISER the transposition then reads AAGDGAAADVDF. The ADFGX predecessor is the same machine with a 5×5 square and no V label.
- **What ADFGVX is not.** It is not a substitution cipher: frequency analysis run on the raw ciphertext fails, because the transposition scatters the two halves of each digraph into different columns, so no ciphertext letter-pair corresponds to a plaintext letter. It is not unbroken: Painvin broke each version within days to weeks of its debut, and modern hill-climbing breaks it routinely — its reputation as "the most famous field cipher" is about its design, not its survival. It is not the same cipher as ADFGX: the 5×5 and 6×6 squares differ in alphabet size, and a break of one is not a break of the other. And its six-letter alphabet is not a keyspace: six letters is a transmission feature (Morse-robust labels), while the real secret is the keyed square plus the keyword.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The alphabet test is the first screen: any ciphertext character outside A, D, F, G, V, X is not ADFGVX, or is corrupted in transit — and a V anywhere proves the 6×6 version, never the 5×5. The length test is the second: fractionation doubles length, so a genuine ADFGVX ciphertext is even-length before and after transposition. The digit test is the third: digits in the recovered plaintext prove the 6×6 square, since ADFGX had no room for them. The ragged-column test is the fourth, and it is Painvin's lever: when the message length is not a multiple of the keyword length, the final row is incomplete, so columns come out uneven — and that unevenness leaks the keyword length to anyone counting. The repeated-beginning test is the fifth: messages sharing a plaintext beginning or ending under the same day key ("messages en tête") let the analyst line the columns up against each other, which is exactly how Painvin entered the 1 June intercept.
- **Decoder-design note (ADFGVX → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Strip the layers in reverse order.** A layered specimen must be interrogated layer by layer, last-applied first: recover the transposition, then solve the substitution. Any Gauntlet screen that attacks the composite ciphertext with a single method — frequency counts on fractionated text, say — is testing its own method, not the specimen. (2) **Usage flaws beat mathematics, again.** Painvin's break came from repeated beginnings and ragged columns, the same family as Enigma's operator errors and JN-25's additive reuse: the Gauntlet hunts usage flaws before it hunts mathematical ones, because history keeps breaking ciphers at the operator, not the algorithm. (3) **A rejected stronger design is a finding, not a footnote.** Nebel's double transposition would have cost Painvin far more than 26 hours; the single transposition that shipped was an organisational decision, not a design limit. A report card that grades only the shipped specimen without noting the stronger design that was refused understates what the specimen's authors knew — and what the next specimen from the same shop might ship.

## RIPEMD-256 — the 256-bit digest that is only 128 bits strong, or: the length that lies twice

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries RIPEMD-128 and RIPEMD-160, but a decoder that knows only those two will misread the family's 256-bit member twice over: once by length, because a 64-hex-character digest is exactly SHA-256-shaped and exactly SHA3-256-shaped, and once by name, because "256" sounds like double the RIPEMD-128 strength. Both readings are wrong. RIPEMD-256 is RIPEMD-128's construction stretched to twice the output, not a 256-bit design — and a specimen handing over 32 bytes needs a test that names which 256-bit digest it is, not a guess from its size.
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** RIPEMD-256 is the double-length extension proposed by Hans Dobbertin, Antoon Bosselaers, and Bart Preneel in the same 1996 paper as RIPEMD-128/160 (*Fast Software Encryption*, LNCS 1039, section 3.3, "Optional Extensions to 256 and 320 bit Hash-Results"). The construction needs no second instance: RIPEMD-128 already has two parallel lines, so the extension omits the combination of the two lines at the end of every compression-function application, and introduces interaction between the lines by swapping registers across them — after round 1 the contents of A and A', after round 2 B and B', after round 3 C and C', after round 4 D and D'. The chaining variable grows to eight words (67452301, EFCDAB89, 98BADCFE, 10325476, 76543210, FEDCBA98, 89ABCDEF, 01234567); each line's final state is added back to its own half of the chaining variable (feed-forward), since the RIPEMD-128 combination step is the thing omitted. Padding is MD-style, blocks are 512 bits. [CORROBORATED — the 1996 paper, section 3.3, read this pass; the swap schedule, eight-word state, and feed-forward form are also the exact form of the implementation validated 4/4 below]
- **What RIPEMD-256 is not.** It is not SHA-256 and it is not SHA3-256: same 32-byte length, different function, different vectors — a report that says "256-bit digest" and stops has identified nothing, and a report that credits SHA-256-class strength on length alone has graded nothing. It is not twice RIPEMD-128's strength: secondary summaries state plainly that it carries only RIPEMD-128-class collision resistance, because it is built from RIPEMD-128's rounds, not from a 256-bit design — the longer digest does not deliver 256-bit security. It is not two RIPEMD-128 digests concatenated: the cross-line swaps mix the halves, so neither half of a RIPEMD-256 digest equals the RIPEMD-128 digest of the same input (checked this pass: RIPEMD-128("abc") is c14a12199c66e4ba84636b0f69144c77, while RIPEMD-256("abc") begins afbd6e228b9d8cbbcef5ca2d03e6dba1 and ends 0ac0bc7dcbe4680e1e42d2e975459b65 — neither half matches). And it is not a drop-in modern seal: no local implementation existed this pass (Python hashlib, OpenSSL, and Node crypto all lack RIPEMD-256, offering only RIPEMD-160), so a specimen emitting it is running a legacy or dedicated stack, and must name its library.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: empty string → 02ba4c4e5f8ecd1877fc52d64d30e37a2d9774fb1e5d026380ae0168e3c5522d; "a" → f9333e45d857f5d90a91bab70a1eba0cfb1be4b0783c9acfcd883a9134692925; "abc" → afbd6e228b9d8cbbcef5ca2d03e6dba10ac0bc7dcbe4680e1e42d2e975459b65; "message digest" → 87e971759a1ce47a514d5c914c392c9018c7c46bc14465554afcdf54a5070c0e; the lowercase alphabet → 649d3034751ea216776bf9a18acc81bc7896118a5197968782dd1fd97d8d5133 — all computed this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/ripemd256-mini.py) that reproduced four independently published RIPEMD-256 digests exactly (the digit strings 103156052, 8042576, 9481063, 8398103) before any catalogue vector was trusted. The length test is the second, and it fails by design: 32 bytes cannot separate RIPEMD-256 from SHA-256 from SHA3-256, so a specimen identified by length alone is unidentified, and the vector test, not the ruler, is the identifier. The halves test is the third: neither half of a claimed RIPEMD-256 digest may be graded as RIPEMD-128 — the swaps forbid it, and a report that splits the digest and grades the halves has invented two specimens. The library test is the fourth: RIPEMD-256's absence from the standard libraries above means a specimen claiming native support without naming its implementation is ungraded until the implementation is pinned.
- **Decoder-design note (RIPEMD-256 → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Length is not a security grade.** A 64-hex-character digest earns no SHA-256-class credit: the Gauntlet grades the construction, not the size, and a 256-bit output built from 128-bit rounds carries its parent's margin on the card, not its own length's. (2) **Test the function, never the length — now in the 256-bit class.** The RIPEMD-128 entry's rung extends upward: every 256-bit digest passes the length screen, so the digest screen must run the vector test before it names any algorithm, and must report "256-bit, unidentified" rather than a guessed name when the vectors fail. (3) **A doubled digest is not a doubled margin.** Extensions inherit their parent's margin: RIPEMD-256 inherits RIPEMD-128's, as RIPEMD-320 will inherit RIPEMD-160's. The report card names the construction lineage alongside the digest size, or a longer digest quietly launders a shorter design's weakness into a stronger-looking grade.

## RIPEMD-320 — the 320-bit digest that is only 160 bits strong, or: the widest member of the family

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries RIPEMD-128, RIPEMD-160, and RIPEMD-256, but not the family's widest member — and a decoder that knows only those three will misread a 40-byte digest twice over: once by width, because an 80-hex-character digest looks like a stronger grade than any 160-bit design, and once by name, because "320" sounds like double the RIPEMD-160 strength. Both readings are wrong. RIPEMD-320 is RIPEMD-160's construction stretched to twice the output, not a 320-bit design — and with this entry the 1996 family's shelf is complete: 128, 160, 256, 320, each with its own vectors, its own construction, and its own margin.
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** RIPEMD-320 is the double-length extension proposed by Hans Dobbertin, Antoon Bosselaers, and Bart Preneel in the same 1996 paper as RIPEMD-128/160 (*Fast Software Encryption*, LNCS 1039, section 3.3, "Optional Extensions to 256 and 320 bit Hash-Results"). The construction needs no second instance: RIPEMD-160 already has two parallel lines, so the extension omits the combination of the two lines at the end of every compression-function application, and introduces interaction between the lines by swapping registers across them — but NOT in the order a reader of the RIPEMD-256 entry would predict. The RIPEMD-320 swap schedule is permuted: after round 1 swap B and B', after round 2 swap D and D', after round 3 swap A and A', after round 4 swap C and C', after round 5 swap E and E'. The chaining variable grows to ten words (67452301, EFCDAB89, 98BADCFE, 10325476, C3D2E1F0, 76543210, FEDCBA98, 89ABCDEF, 01234567, 3C2D1E0F); each line's final state is added back to its own half of the chaining variable (feed-forward), since the RIPEMD-160 combination step is the thing omitted. Padding is MD-style, blocks are 512 bits. [CORROBORATED — the 1996 paper, section 3.3, for the extension itself; the permuted B/D/A/C/E swap schedule was NOT read from the paper this pass — it was found by brute-force search over all 6^5 per-round swap choices x 4 candidate second-half IVs x 3 final combinations (93,312 constructions), of which exactly one matched the independently published empty-string digest, and that construction then matched the full 8-vector set below]
- **What RIPEMD-320 is not.** It is not twice RIPEMD-160's strength: secondary summaries state plainly that it carries only RIPEMD-160-class collision resistance, because it is built from RIPEMD-160's rounds, not from a 320-bit design — the longer digest buys a wider fingerprint, not a deeper margin, and its birthday bound is still its parent's 80-bit bound. It is not two RIPEMD-160 digests concatenated: the cross-line swaps mix the halves, so neither half of a RIPEMD-320 digest equals the RIPEMD-160 digest of the same input (checked this pass: RIPEMD-160("abc") is 8eb208f7e05d987a9b044a8e98c6b087f15a0bfc, while RIPEMD-320("abc") begins de4c01b3054f8930a79d09ae738e92301e5a17 and ends 085beffdc1b8d116713e74f82fa942d64cdbc4682d — neither half matches). It is not a truncated SHA-512 or a SHA-384 variant: 40 bytes matches no SHA-2 output length, and a report that calls an 80-hex digest "SHA-family" on length alone has identified nothing. And it is not a drop-in modern seal: no local implementation existed this pass (Python hashlib, OpenSSL, and Node crypto all lack RIPEMD-320, offering only RIPEMD-160), so a specimen emitting it is running a legacy or dedicated stack, and must name its library.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: empty string → 22d65d5661536cdc75c1fdf5c6de7b41b9f27325ebc61e8557177d705a0ec880151c3a32a00899b8; "a" → ce78850638f92658a5a585097579926dda667a5716562cfcf6fbe77f63542f99b04705d6970dff5d; "abc" → de4c01b3054f8930a79d09ae738e92301e5a17085beffdc1b8d116713e74f82fa942d64cdbc4682d; "message digest" → 3a8e28502ed45d422f68844f9dd316e7b98533fa3f2a91d29f84d425c88d6b4eff727df66a7c0197; the lowercase alphabet → cabdb1810b92470a2093aa6bce05952c28348cf43ff60841975166bb40ed234004b8824463e6b009 — all computed this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/ripemd320-mini.py) that matched the Linux kernel tcrypt RIPEMD-320 vector set 8/8, including the 62-character, 80-digit, and 56-character multi-block vectors, before any catalogue vector was trusted. The halves test is the second: neither half of a claimed RIPEMD-320 digest may be graded as RIPEMD-160 — the swaps forbid it, and a report that splits the digest and grades the halves has invented two specimens. The schedule test is the third, and it is the live one: a from-specification reimplementation that assumes the RIPEMD-256 sequential swap order (A, B, C, D, E) fails every vector — an earlier draft of this entry's own implementation did exactly that, and matched nothing until its round-5 tables were corrected against the KU Leuven pseudo-code and its swap schedule was search-derived. Any implementation claiming RIPEMD-320 must be run against the vectors, not trusted on its construction story. The library test is the fourth: RIPEMD-320's absence from the standard libraries above means a specimen claiming native support without naming its implementation is ungraded until the implementation is pinned.
- **Decoder-design note (RIPEMD-320 → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Never extrapolate a construction across family members.** The sequential swap order that RIPEMD-256 validated does not extend to RIPEMD-320 — the permuted B/D/A/C/E schedule was found only because 93,311 other constructions were tried and rejected. A decoder that reasons "the 256 pattern, plus one round" builds a function that matches no published vector and then blames the specimen. Constructions are verified per member, never inherited by analogy. (2) **A repaired implementation is evidence, not embarrassment.** This entry's implementation failed twice in public ways — wrong round-5 tables, wrong swap order — and each failure named its own fix: the tables against the KU Leuven pseudo-code, the schedule against the vector set. The Gauntlet keeps the failed drafts on record (hidden_files/ripemd320-mini.py carries the repair history in its docstring) because a repair trail is what lets the next reader trust the passing vectors. (3) **The shelf is now complete, and the shelf is the lesson.** Four members, one lineage, four different margins — 128-class, 160-class, 128-class again, 160-class again — and the digest length in every case is the wrong number to grade. The report card names the construction lineage alongside the digest size, or a longer digest quietly launders a shorter design's weakness into a stronger-looking grade. RIPEMD-320 closes the family; the next gap is a family the catalogue does not carry at all.

## Trivium — the eSTREAM stream cipher that fits in 3,488 gates, or: the cipher whose whole state is three shift registers and one AND per register

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries Grain and SNOW, but not the eSTREAM hardware portfolio's simplest member — and a decoder that knows only block ciphers and hashes will misread a Trivium specimen twice over: once by size, because an 80-bit key looks like a toy next to AES-256, and once by shape, because a stream cipher has no rounds, no S-box, and no block to test. Trivium's whole design is three shift registers, three taps, and one AND gate per register. With this entry the catalogue's stream-cipher shelf gains the design that proves how little machinery a serious cipher needs — and how thin the margin gets when the machinery is that small.
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** Trivium was designed by Christophe De Cannière and Bart Preneel, submitted to Profile II (hardware) of the eSTREAM competition, and selected for the eSTREAM portfolio for low-area hardware ciphers. It is not patented and is specified as an International Standard under ISO/IEC 29192-3. It takes an 80-bit key and an 80-bit IV and generates up to 2^64 bits of keystream from a 288-bit internal state: three shift registers of 93, 84, and 111 bits. To initialize, the key is written into the first register, the IV into the second, and the third register's last three bits are set to 1,1,1 with the rest zero; the cipher is then clocked 1,152 times (4 × 288) with no output, so that every state bit depends on every key and IV bit in a complex nonlinear way, before keystream begins. Each round computes three intermediate values — t1 from the first register's taps at bits 66 and 93, t2 from the second's at 162 and 177, t3 from the third's at 243 and 288 — outputs their XOR, then feeds each register a new bit that XORs its intermediate value with one AND of two neighbouring bits and one tap from another register (s91·s92 with s171; s175·s176 with s264; s286·s287 with s69). No tap falls on the first 65 bits of any register, so a newly generated bit is not used for at least 65 rounds — the property that lets 64 bits be generated in parallel in hardware (5,504 gates) and that gives software implementations around 4 cycles per byte. A straightforward hardware implementation needs 3,488 gates and produces one bit per clock cycle. [VERIFIED — the multi-source consensus: the register sizes, tap positions, 1,152-round warm-up, gate counts, and 4 cycles/byte figure agree across the sources read this pass]
- **What Trivium is not.** It is not a 128-bit cipher wearing an 80-bit key: the key is 80 bits, the brute-force bound is 2^80, and a report that grades it alongside AES-256 has graded the wrong number. It is not broken — as of 2025 no published attack beats brute force on the full cipher — but it is not comfortable either: the best published practical cube attacks recover the key of reduced-round Trivium with up to 832 of its 1,152 initialization rounds, at a reported time complexity not exceeding 2^50, which is why secondary summaries call the security margin "rather slim." It is not Bivium: Bivium is Trivium's weakened two-register cousin, and Bivium falls to algebraic IV-differential attack outright — a specimen calling itself "Trivium-like" with two registers is a different, broken cipher, not a variant. And it is not safe under IV reuse: Trivium is a synchronous stream cipher, so the same key with the same IV produces the same keystream, and two plaintexts under one keystream XOR to each other — the break that needs no cryptanalysis at all.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen, and it must name its bit order before it names any result: key and IV hex are read LSb-first within each byte, and keystream bits are packed back into bytes the same way (byte = Σ 2^j · bit_j), the mapping the specification itself states for stream-to-byte conversion. Under that mapping, first 16 keystream bytes: key 00000000000000000000, IV 00000000000000000000 → fbe0bf265859051b517a2e4e239fc97f; key 00000000000000000001, IV 00000000000000000000 → 38eb86ff730d7a9caf8df13a4420540d; key FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, IV 00000000000000000000 → dda5be0d7acf12398c4c0823c793a06b; key 00000000000000000000, IV FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF → 14cec428681646ee598fda312e8bcb36; key 80000000000000000000, IV 80000000000000000000 → 02aaeb59c5a4109d38d70125f7613457 — all computed this pass by a from-specification implementation in two independent formulations (shift-register pseudocode and recursive-equation form) agreeing 5/5 over 128 bits each, with an encrypt/decrypt roundtrip on "attack at dawn" (ciphertext 599ff29e10665afddbad955b334e under key 00000000000000000001, IV zero) returning the plaintext exactly. The ordering test is the second, and it is the live one: the two published formulations agree ONLY when the recursive form's pre-history segments carry the key/IV bits reversed relative to the shift form's loading — the formulations differ in the direction key bits are read into the pre-history, not in the cipher — so an implementation that reads key bits the other way produces a different stream from the same hex and fails every vector above. Any implementation claiming Trivium must be run against the vectors under a stated mapping, not trusted on its construction story. The warm-up test is the third: output taken before 1,152 rounds is not Trivium keystream, and a specimen streaming from round zero is ungraded, not broken. The IV test is the fourth: a specimen reusing an IV under one key is graded on the reuse, not on the cipher — two ciphertexts under one keystream are one finding, whatever the cipher's margin.
- **Decoder-design note (Trivium → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Name the bit order before grading any stream.** A stream cipher's vectors are meaningless without their byte mapping: the Gauntlet's stream screen states key, IV, mapping, and warm-up count on the card, and a vector that fails under one mapping is re-tested under the other before any verdict, because this entry's own two formulations disagreed until the mapping was pinned. (2) **Test IV discipline before mathematics.** Reuse breaks a synchronous stream cipher with no attack at all, the same family as Enigma's operator errors and the ADFGVX repeated beginnings: the Gauntlet hunts usage flaws before it hunts mathematical ones, and a reused IV is a finding about the operator, graded before the cipher. (3) **A thin margin is graded as thin.** A cipher with published attacks at 832 of 1,152 rounds does not earn a clean bill because the full cipher still stands: the report card carries the round count of the best attack beside the full round count, so a reader can see how much margin is left instead of reading "unbroken" as "comfortable."

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the De Cannière/Preneel authorship, eSTREAM Profile II submission and low-area portfolio selection, unpatented status, ISO/IEC 29192-3 standardization, 80-bit key and IV, 288-bit state in 93/84/111 registers, 1,152-round warm-up, 3,488-gate (5,504 parallel) figures, and 4 cycles/byte software figure, from the multi-source consensus read this pass; CORROBORATED — the five keystream vectors above, computed this pass by a from-specification implementation in two independent formulations agreeing 5/5 over 128 bits each, plus an exact encrypt/decrypt roundtrip, under the stated LSb-first mapping; no published eSTREAM vector set was matched this pass, so the published-vector match remains an open watch item and the vectors are not graded VERIFIED; CLAIMED — the "no attack better than brute force as of 2025" status and the 832-round cube-attack figure with 2^50 complexity, from secondary summaries, not from an attack record graded in this entry; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## SM3 — the Chinese national hash that wears SHA-256's shape, or: the 256-bit digest that is not SHA-256

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue's 256-bit class runs SHA-256, SHA3-256, RIPEMD-256, and BLAKE2s, but not the member a Chinese commercial-cryptography stack actually emits — and a specimen arriving with an SM2 signature or a GM/TLS handshake that hands over a 64-hex-character digest will be misread as SHA-256 by any decoder that grades the 256-bit class by length. SM3 is the first catalogue member from a national standards family outside the NIST/ISO Western lineage, and its presence in OpenSSL and Python's hashlib means a specimen emitting it may be mainstream, not legacy.
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** SM3 (ShangMi 3) is China's commercial-cryptography hash, published by the State Cryptography Administration on December 17, 2010 as GM/T 0004-2012, standardized nationally as GB/T 32905-2016, and admitted to ISO/IEC 10118-3:2018 — the same ISO part that carries RIPEMD-160 and SHA-256. It was designed by Wang Xiaoyun's group, and the design is a deliberate SHA-256 cousin, not a copy: Merkle–Damgård over 512-bit blocks, 64 rounds, 256-bit output, MD-style padding with a 64-bit big-endian length. The differences are where the decoder must look: the initial value is 7380166f 4914b2b9 172442d7 da8a0600 a96f30bc 163138aa e38dee4d b0fb0e4e; the Boolean functions switch at round 16 (FF is XOR below 16, majority at and above; GG is XOR below 16, the (X AND Y) OR (X AND Z) OR (Y AND Z) form at and above); the permutations are P0(x) = x XOR rotl(x,9) XOR rotl(x,17) and P1(x) = x XOR rotl(x,15) XOR rotl(x,23); the round constants are 79cc4519 below round 16 and 7a879d8a at and above, each rotated left by (j mod 32); and the message expansion is the widest in the catalogue — 68 words W plus 64 derived words W'[j] = W[j] XOR W[j+4], 132 words against SHA-256's 64. [CORROBORATED — multi-source consensus read this pass: publication date and GM/T number, GB/T 32905-2016, ISO/IEC 10118-3:2018, Wang et al. design, 512-bit blocks, 64 rounds, 256-bit output]
- **What SM3 is not.** It is not SHA-256: same output length, same block size, same round count, unrelated digests — a report that says "256-bit digest" and stops has identified nothing, and a report that credits SHA-256's analysis record to an SM3 digest has graded the wrong function. It is not a SHA-256 variant in the compatible sense: the "improved on the basis of SHA-256" phrasing in IETF drafts describes design lineage, not shared vectors — no SHA-256 vector validates an SM3 implementation, and this entry's implementation was validated against SM3 vectors only. It is not broken in the practical sense, and it is not unattacked: published cryptanalysis reaches step-reduced versions — preimage attacks on 29- and 30-step SM3 and pseudo-preimage attacks on 31- and 32-step SM3 out of 64 (Wang/Shen, 2012) — while the full 64-round function has no practical attack on record, filed as absence-of-evidence. And it is not an obscure national curiosity a decoder may skip: it is the hash of the SM2 signature suite and of GM TLS cipher suites, so any specimen speaking Chinese commercial cryptography speaks SM3 by default.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: empty string → 1ab21d8355cfa17f8e61194831e81a8f22bec8c728fefb747ed035eb5082aa2b; "abc" → 66c7f0f462eeedd9d1f2d46bdc10e4e24167c4875cf2f7a2297da02b8f4ba8e0; "message digest" → c522a942e89bd80d97dd666e7a5531b36188c9817149e9b258dfe51ece98ed77; the lowercase alphabet → b80fe97a4da24afc277564f66a359ef440462ad28dcc6d63adb24d5c20a61595; "abcd" repeated 16 times (exactly one block before padding) → debe9ff92275b8a138604889c18e5a4d6fdb70e5387e5765293dcba39c0c5732 — all computed this pass by a from-specification implementation matching OpenSSL's sm3 7/7, including two multi-block inputs ("a" × 200 and bytes 0–255), and the empty and "abc" vectors matching the standard's published example vectors. The suite test is the second: SM3 travels with SM2 signatures and the SM4 cipher — a specimen naming SM2 but hashing with SHA-256 has mixed suites, and a specimen naming SHA-256 inside a GM/TLS handshake has done the same in reverse; the hash is graded against the suite it arrived with, not the suite the reader expected. The library test is the third: SM3 ships in OpenSSL 3 and Python's hashlib, but standard OpenJDK has no SM3 MessageDigest (Bouncy Castle's SM3Digest is the route) — a Java specimen claiming native SM3 without naming Bouncy Castle is ungraded until the implementation is pinned. The shape test is the fourth, and it fails by design: 32 bytes cannot separate SM3 from SHA-256 from SHA3-256 from RIPEMD-256 from BLAKE2s, so a specimen identified by length alone is unidentified, and the vector test, not the ruler, is the identifier.
- **Decoder-design note (SM3 → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Same shape, different standards family.** The RIPEMD-256 rung extends beyond one family: the 256-bit class now has a national-standard member, so a report card must name the standard body (NIST, ISO, GB/T) alongside the digest size, or a Chinese-stack specimen gets graded against an American record. (2) **Suite coherence before mathematics.** Check the hash against the signature and cipher it arrived with before attacking any of them — a mixed suite is a finding about the operator, graded before the functions, in the same family as the Trivium IV-reuse rung. (3) **Grade step-reduced attacks by rounds remaining, not by the headline.** "Attacked" without a round count is ungraded: 32 of 64 steps attacked leaves half the rounds standing, which is margin, not a break — the report card carries the attacked step count beside the full round count, as the Trivium entry carries 832 of 1,152.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the seven vectors above, computed this pass by a from-specification implementation matching OpenSSL's sm3 7/7 including multi-block inputs, with the empty-string and "abc" vectors matching the standard's published example vectors, which also verifies the IV, the round-16 Boolean switch, the P0/P1 permutations, the rotating T_j constants, and the 132-word expansion as implemented; CORROBORATED — the December 17, 2010 SCA publication, GM/T 0004-2012, GB/T 32905-2016, ISO/IEC 10118-3:2018, Wang et al. design, the SM2/SM4 suite pairing, and the OpenSSL/Python availability with the standard-JDK absence, from the multi-source consensus read this pass; CLAIMED — the "no practical full-round attack" status, from the step-reduced record plus absence of a full-round claim, not from a graded attack survey; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## CBOR — Concise Binary Object Representation (RFC 8949), or: the grammar that fits a whole JSON in a handful of bytes

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries ASN.1/DER — the grammar every certificate speaks — but no CBOR, the grammar every COSE signature, CWT token, and WebAuthn attestation speaks. A specimen arriving as a COSE_Sign1 object or a CTAP2 attestation would be misread as opaque binary by any decoder that only knows DER, JSON, and the catalogue's ciphers. CBOR is the first catalogue member whose whole design is a serialization format for structured data rather than a cipher or a hash, and its presence closes the gap between "we can decode the message" and "we can decode the envelope the message arrived in."
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** CBOR was designed by Carsten Bormann and Paul Hoffman, published as RFC 7049 in 2013 and obsoleted — without any wire-format change — by RFC 8949 in December 2020 (STD 94). Its data model is JSON extended with byte strings: eight major types carried in the top three bits of the first byte (0 unsigned, 1 negative, 2 byte string, 3 text string, 4 array, 5 map, 6 tag, 7 float/simple), an additional-information field that holds values 0–23 inline and lengths of 1, 2, 4, or 8 bytes for larger ones (additional-information values 24–27), indefinite lengths for byte strings, text strings, arrays, and maps closed by the break byte 0xff, and tags (major type 6) that extend the model — tag 0 a standard date/time string, tag 1 an epoch-based date/time, tags 2 and 3 bignums, tags 4 and 5 decimal fractions and bigfloats, and tag 55799 self-described CBOR (encoded 0xd9d9f7), a deliberate magic number so a sniffer can name the format from three bytes. Deterministic encoding (RFC 8949 §4.2) is preferred serialization — the shortest form of every value — plus length-first map key ordering, the rule that makes a CBOR byte string a signable object. The media type is application/cbor, and the format carries COSE (RFC 9052), CWT (RFC 8392), and the WebAuthn/CTAP2 attestation objects. [VERIFIED — the format facts above, from RFC 8949 read first-party this pass: authors, RFC 7049 → 8949 lineage with no wire change, STD 94, the eight major types, the additional-information scheme, indefinite lengths with break 0xff, the tag numbers named, tag 55799, the §4.2 deterministic rules, and the application/cbor media type]
- **What CBOR is not.** It is not JSON: binary, byte strings native, no schema required but self-describing, and a CBOR text string is UTF-8 by definition where JSON is text by definition. It is not ASN.1 DER: DER needs a schema to mean anything and encodes tag-length-value with explicit lengths throughout, while CBOR's major type rides in the first byte and a generic decoder can walk any CBOR item blind. It is not MessagePack: the two share a JSON-plus-binary shape, but CBOR's tag extension model and indefinite lengths are its own, and MessagePack's type families do not map one-to-one onto CBOR's major types — a decoder that reads CBOR as MessagePack misreads every tag and every indefinite-length item. It is not canonical by default: the same value has many well-formed encodings (0 as 0x00, 0x1800, 0x190000, 0x1a00000000, or 0x1b0000000000000000), so byte equality is not value equality unless deterministic encoding was used. And it is not self-validating: RFC 8949's own hierarchy is well-formed (processable at all), valid (checked by a validity-checking generic decoder), and expected (checked by the application) — three different bars, and a report that calls a well-formed item "valid" has graded one rung up from what it checked.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: 47 RFC 8949 Appendix A examples matched this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/cbor-mini.py), encode and decode both ways — 0 → 00, 24 → 1818, 1000 → 1903e8, 2^64−1 → 1bffffffffffffffff, 2^64 → c249010000000000000000 (tag 2 bignum), −1 → 20, −1000 → 3903e7, 1.5 → f93e00, h'01020304' → 4401020304, "IETF" → 6449455446, [1,2,3] → 83010203, {"a":1,"b":[2,3]} → a26161016162820203, tag 0 date → c074323031332d30332d32315432303a30343a30305a, tag 24 content → d818456449455446. The non-preferred test is the second: 0x1800 and 0x190000 both decode to 0 and are both well-formed, but neither is preferred serialization — a decoder that compares bytes will call two encodings of the same value different, so the Gauntlet compares decoded values, never raw bytes. The indefinite-length test is the third: (_ h'0102', h'030405') → 5f42010243030405ff decodes to h'0102030405' and (_ "strea", "ming") → 7f657374726561646d696e67ff decodes to "streaming" — a decoder that stops at the first chunk, or treats 0xff as data, fails both. The bignum test is the fourth: a decoder without tag 2/3 support reads c249010000000000000000 as a 9-byte string, not the number 18446744073709551616. The self-description test is the fifth: d9d9f700 is tag 55799 wrapping 0, and any specimen whose first three bytes are d9d9f7 announces itself as CBOR before a single item is parsed. The deterministic test is the sixth: {"bb":2,"a":1} encodes deterministically as a261610162626202 — "a" first, because its encoded key is shorter — and {"b":2,"a":1} as a2616101616202, "a" before "b" by encoded bytes; a specimen whose map keys arrive in any other order is not deterministically encoded, whatever else it claims.
- **Decoder-design note (CBOR → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Decode to value, compare values, never bytes.** Non-preferred encodings are well-formed, so byte comparison is a false difference: the Gauntlet's CBOR screen decodes first and compares the decoded structure, in the same family as the Trivium bit-order rung — the mapping is pinned before any verdict. (2) **Deterministic encoding is the seal.** A specimen claiming a signature over CBOR must be checked against the deterministic form — re-encode with preferred serialization and length-first key order and compare — because a signature over non-deterministic bytes verifies against bytes the signer never canonicalized, and a report that verifies the signature without checking the encoding has verified the wrong object. (3) **Tags are the extension surface, not an error.** An unknown tag must not fail the decode — the format is designed for decades of extension, and a generic decoder carries the tag through — so the Gauntlet grades tag handling as CARRY vs REJECT, and a specimen that rejects an unknown tag has failed the format's own evolution rule, in the same family as the ASN.1/DER screen that grades unknown OIDs.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the 47 Appendix A vectors above, matched this pass by a from-specification implementation in both directions, plus the non-preferred, indefinite-length, bignum, self-described-tag, and deterministic-ordering checks, all run this pass; the RFC 8949 facts (authors, RFC 7049 → 8949 lineage with no wire change, STD 94, eight major types, additional-information scheme, indefinite lengths with break 0xff, the tag numbers named, tag 55799, §4.2 deterministic rules, application/cbor media type, the well-formed/valid/expected hierarchy) from RFC 8949 read first-party this pass; CORROBORATED — COSE (RFC 9052), CWT (RFC 8392), and WebAuthn/CTAP2 attestation usage, from the standards record, not from a fresh read this pass; CLAIMED — the MessagePack non-mapping, from the RFC's own Appendix E comparison, not graded in this entry; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## MessagePack — the JSON-shaped binary wire format, or: the grammar that fits a whole JSON in one byte per value

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries CBOR — the grammar every COSE signature speaks — but not its older, leaner sibling, and a specimen arriving as a Fluentd event stream or an RPC payload in MessagePack would be misread as opaque binary by any decoder that only knows CBOR, JSON, and DER. MessagePack is the first catalogue member whose whole design is "JSON, but binary and smaller" — no tags, no indefinite lengths, no schema — and its presence closes the gap between "we can decode the envelope" (CBOR) and "we can decode the wire format the log pipeline actually speaks."
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** MessagePack was designed by Sadayuki Furuhashi; the specification (msgpack/msgpack spec.md, last modified 2017-08-09) defines two concepts — a type system (Integer, Nil, Boolean, Float as IEEE 754 double, Raw split into String and Binary, Array, Map, Extension, Timestamp) and formats, one byte at a time. Integers run −(2^63) to (2^64)−1; binary, string, array, and map sizes cap at (2^32)−1. The format table is a single byte: positive fixint 0x00–0x7f, fixmap 0x80–0x8f, fixarray 0x90–0x9f, fixstr 0xa0–0xbf, nil 0xc0, 0xc1 never used, false 0xc2, true 0xc3, bin 8/16/32 0xc4–0xc6, ext 8/16/32 0xc7–0xc9, float 32/64 0xca–0xcb, uint 8/16/32/64 0xcc–0xcf, int 8/16/32/64 0xd0–0xd3, fixext 1/2/4/8/16 0xd4–0xd8, str 8/16/32 0xd9–0xdb, array 16/32 0xdc–0xdd, map 16/32 0xde–0xdf, negative fixint 0xe0–0xff. All multi-byte integers are big-endian. Extension types run 0–127 for applications and −128 to −1 reserved; the only predefined extension is Timestamp, type −1, in three forms: 32-bit (fixext 4, seconds as uint32, [1970-01-01, 2106-02-07 06:28:16)), 64-bit (fixext 8, 30-bit nanoseconds packed above 34-bit seconds, to 2514-05-30 01:53:04), and 96-bit (ext 8, 12 bytes: nanoseconds uint32 then seconds int64, −292277022657-01-27 to 292277026596-12-04), with nanoseconds never above 999,999,999. The spec's one normative encoder rule is a SHOULD: when several formats fit, use the smallest number of bytes. The old raw 16/32 formats became str 16/32 when the bin family split strings from bytes, and the spec's own "Profile" idea — restrict semantics, sort map keys — is how applications make the bytes deterministic enough to hash. [VERIFIED — the format facts above, from the specification read first-party this pass]
- **What MessagePack is not.** It is not JSON: binary, byte strings native, extension types, no schema — and a JSON parser handed MessagePack sees control bytes, not text. It is not CBOR: the two share a JSON-plus-binary shape, but MessagePack has no tags, no indefinite lengths, and no deterministic-encoding rule — only a SHOULD for the smallest form — so a decoder that reads MessagePack as CBOR misreads every ext and every fixext, and one that reads CBOR as MessagePack chokes on every tag. It is not protobuf: protobuf needs a schema to mean anything and can canonicalize away wire anomalies; MessagePack is self-describing, so a blob with no schema is still a complete document. It is not canonical by default: the same value has many well-formed encodings (0 as 0x00, 0xcc00, 0xcd0000, 0xce00000000, or 0xcf0000000000000000), so byte equality is not value equality unless the producer followed the smallest-form SHOULD and sorted its map keys — and the spec leaves key order unspecified, so two encoders of the same map may legitimately disagree on bytes.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: 28 smallest-form vectors matched this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/msgpack-mini.py), encode and decode both ways — 0 → 00, 127 → 7f, 128 → cc80, 255 → ccff, 256 → cd0100, 65535 → cdffff, 65536 → ce00010000, 2^32−1 → ceffffffff, 2^64−1 → cfffffffffffffffff, −1 → ff, −32 → e0, −33 → d0df, −128 → d080, −129 → d1ff7f, −32768 → d18000, −2^63 → d38000000000000000, nil → c0, false → c2, true → c3, "" → a0, "a" → a161, "hello" → a568656c6c6f, b"\x01\x02\x03" → c403010203, [] → 90, [1,2,3] → 93010203, {} → 80, {"a":1} → 81a16101, {"compact":true,"schema":0} → 82a7636f6d70616374c3a6736368656d6100. The float test is the second: 1.5 as float 32 is ca3fc00000 and as float 64 is cb3ff8000000000000 — same value, different bytes, and a decoder that compares bytes calls them different numbers. The non-canonical test is the third: cc00 and d1007f both decode — to 0 and 127 — and both are well-formed, but neither is the smallest form, so a decoder that rejects them has rejected legal MessagePack, and a decoder that hashes bytes has hashed two encodings of one value. The never-used test is the fourth: 0xc1 is the spec's one reserved byte, and a decoder that accepts it has accepted a format the spec says does not exist — the single hard rejection in the whole format table, and the tripwire a fuzzer aims at. The timestamp test is the fifth: 2026-11-05 00:00:00 UTC (1,793,836,800 s) encodes as d6ff6aebc700 in the 32-bit form, as d7ff773594006aebc700 with 500,000,000 ns in the 64-bit form (30-bit nanoseconds packed above 34-bit seconds), and (−1 s, 999,999,999 ns) as c70cff3b9ac9ffffffffffffffffff in the 96-bit form — and a decoder that reads the 64-bit form's packed word as plain seconds is off by a factor of 2^34. The str/bin test is the sixth: "a" is a161 (fixstr) while b"a" is c40161 (bin 8) — same payload byte, different family — and a decoder that conflates str and bin has merged the type system's one deliberate split, the split the whole raw-to-bin migration was made for.
- **Decoder-design note (MessagePack → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Decode to value, compare values, never bytes.** Non-canonical encodings are well-formed, so byte comparison is a false difference: the Gauntlet's MessagePack screen decodes first and compares the decoded structure, in the same family as the CBOR screen — the mapping is pinned before any verdict. (2) **The smallest-form SHOULD is a producer fingerprint, not a validity rule.** A specimen that encodes 0 as cc00 is legal, but it is not the encoder the spec recommends — and a stream full of padded integers betrays a non-standard producer, in the same family as the protobuf anomaly taxonomy: the padding is evidence, not noise. (3) **0xc1 is the tripwire, and the ext family is the extension surface.** A decoder that accepts 0xc1 has accepted a non-format, and an unknown ext type must be carried as opaque data, never rejected — the spec says so explicitly — so the Gauntlet grades ext handling as CARRY vs REJECT, and a specimen that rejects an unknown ext has failed the format's own evolution rule, in the same family as the CBOR tag rung.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the 28 smallest-form vectors above, the float 32/64 pair, the non-canonical cc00/d1007f decodes, the 0xc1 rejection, the ext roundtrip, and the three timestamp forms, all matched this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/msgpack-mini.py) run twice; the spec facts (author, type system, limits, the full format table, big-endian integers, the ext-type ranges, the three timestamp forms and ranges, the 999,999,999 ns cap, the smallest-form SHOULD, the raw→str/bin split, the Profile idea) from the specification read first-party this pass; CORROBORATED — Fluentd's MessagePack-native event stream, from the ecosystem record, not from a fresh read this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## BSON — Binary JSON, or: the grammar that length-prefixes everything and reads little-endian

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries CBOR and MessagePack — the two self-describing binary JSONs — but not the third member of the family, the one the database actually speaks. A specimen arriving as a MongoDB wire-protocol payload, a dump file, or an oplog entry is BSON, and a decoder that only knows CBOR and MessagePack misreads it twice over: BSON is little-endian where both siblings are big-endian, and every document carries its total length up front, so a CBOR reader sees a length where it expects a type byte. BSON is the first catalogue member whose design is "JSON, but traversable without parsing" — the length prefix lets a reader skip any element wholesale — and its presence closes the gap between "we can decode the envelope" (CBOR) and "we can decode the database's own wire format."

- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** BSON was designed at 10gen (now MongoDB) for the MongoDB wire protocol, first released 2009; the specification (bsonspec.org) defines one rule that governs everything: all integers are little-endian. A document is int32 total length + element list + 0x00 terminator. An element is a type byte + cstring key + value. The type table: 0x01 double (IEEE 754), 0x02 string, 0x03 embedded document, 0x04 array, 0x05 binary, 0x06 undefined (deprecated), 0x07 ObjectId (12 bytes), 0x08 boolean (0x00/0x01), 0x09 UTC datetime (int64 milliseconds since the Unix epoch), 0x0A null, 0x0B regular expression (pattern cstring + options cstring), 0x0C DBPointer (deprecated), 0x0D JavaScript code, 0x0E symbol (deprecated), 0x0F code with scope (deprecated), 0x10 int32, 0x11 timestamp (uint64: increment in the low 4 bytes, seconds in the high 4), 0x12 int64, 0x13 decimal128, 0xFF min key, 0x7F max key. A string is int32 length (bytes plus one for the trailing null) + UTF-8 bytes + 0x00; a cstring is bytes + 0x00 and must not contain 0x00 — modified UTF-8, not full UTF-8. Binary is int32 length + subtype + bytes; subtypes run 0 generic, 1 function, 2 binary-old (deprecated), 3 UUID-old (deprecated), 4 UUID, 5 MD5, 6 encrypted, 7 compressed column, 8 sensitive, 9 vector, 128–255 user-defined. Arrays are documents whose keys are "0", "1", "2", ... — there is no separate array wire form. [VERIFIED — the format facts above, from the specification read first-party this pass]

- **What BSON is not.** It is not JSON: binary, length-prefixed, typed, no schema — and a JSON parser handed BSON sees a length prefix, not text. It is not CBOR: CBOR is big-endian and tag-driven with indefinite lengths; BSON is little-endian, has no tags and no indefinite lengths, and every document announces its total size — a decoder that reads BSON as CBOR misreads the length as a type byte and everything after it as garbage. It is not MessagePack: MessagePack packs a type into a single byte and carries no document length at all; BSON spends four bytes on the length so a reader can skip, and splits its integers into int32 and int64 where MessagePack has one integer family — and BSON has no unsigned integer type at all. It is not canonical by default: key order is significant (it is the document's order, and MongoDB compares documents in key order), and a decoder that sorts keys has reordered the document it was asked to preserve. And it is not self-validating: the length prefix is a claim, not a proof — a document whose stated length disagrees with its actual bytes is malformed, and the check is the first thing a decoder runs, before any element is trusted.

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: 15 vectors matched this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/bson-mini.py), encode and decode both ways — {} → 0500000000, {"a":1} → 0c0000001061000100000000, {"a":"hello"} → 120000000261000600000068656c6c6f0000, {"a":true} → 090000000861000100, {"a":1.5} → 10000000016100000000000000f83f00, {"a":null} → 080000000a610000, {"a":[1,2]} → 1b0000000461001300000010300001000000103100020000000000, {"a":ObjectId(507f1f77bcf86cd799439011)} → 14000000076100507f1f77bcf86cd79943901100, {"a":b"\x01\x02\x03"} → 10000000056100030000000001020300, {"a":MinKey} → 08000000ff610000, {"a":MaxKey} → 080000007f610000, {"a":2^40} → 10000000126100000000000001000000, {"a":/ab*c/i} → 0f0000000b610061622a6300690000, {"a":Timestamp(1, 1793836800)} → 100000001161000100000000c7eb6a00, {"a":{"b":1}} → 140000000361000c000000106200010000000000. The datetime test is the second: 2026-11-05 00:00:00 UTC is 1,793,836,800,000 ms since the epoch, and a decoder that reads the int64 as seconds is off by a factor of a thousand — the same trap as the MessagePack timestamp test, one family over. The traversal test is the third: a document's length prefix lets a reader skip a 100-byte string element wholesale and land exactly on the next element — the property that makes BSON traversable without a full parse, and the property a decoder must verify by checking the stated length against the actual bytes before trusting the skip. The int32/int64 split is the fourth: 2^40 needs int64, and a decoder that reads it as int32 has read four bytes of an eight-byte value and silently truncated the specimen. The deprecated-types test is the fifth: undefined, DBPointer, symbol, code-with-scope, and the old binary/UUID subtypes are deprecated, not absent — a decoder that rejects them has rejected legal BSON from an old producer, and the Gauntlet grades them as CARRY vs REJECT. The cstring test is the sixth: a key containing 0x00 is not a long key, it is a malformed document, and a decoder that accepts it has accepted a document whose keys cannot be read back.

- **Decoder-design note (BSON → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Verify the length before trusting anything.** The int32 total length is the first check: a document whose stated length disagrees with its bytes is malformed, and every element read after a bad length is evidence built on sand — in the same family as the CBOR well-formed/valid/expected hierarchy, the length check is the well-formed rung. (2) **Little-endian is the tripwire, and the int32/int64 split is the truncation trap.** A decoder that reads BSON big-endian misreads every length and every number; a decoder that reads int64 as int32 truncates silently — the Gauntlet's BSON screen checks both by construction, in the same family as the MessagePack smallest-form screen. (3) **Key order is data, and deprecated types are carried, never rejected.** BSON documents compare in key order, so a decoder that sorts keys has altered the specimen; and the deprecated types are part of the format's history, so the Gauntlet grades their handling as CARRY vs REJECT, in the same family as the MessagePack ext rung.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the 15 vectors above, the datetime check, the length-prefix traversal check, and the mixed-document roundtrip, all matched this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/bson-mini.py) run twice; the spec facts (little-endian rule, document grammar, the full type table, string/cstring/binary grammars, the subtype table, code_w_s, array-as-document) from the specification read first-party this pass; CORROBORATED — the MongoDB/10gen origin and 2009 first release, the ObjectId 12-byte layout (4-byte timestamp, 5-byte random, 3-byte counter), and Decimal128 as IEEE 754-2008 BID, from the ecosystem record, not from a fresh read this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*
