## Scritchmus — the chain that named the fast wheel, or: the rod the Banburist read the rotor by

- **The problem it solved.** Banburismus proper ranked the wheels — it said which wheels were probably in the machine, middle and right, and let the bombe do the rest. But ranking is not naming, and a bombe run still had to try every wheel order the ranking left open: 336 possible orders for three wheels chosen from eight, and a bombe that could test the 17,576 ring settings for one wheel order in 15 minutes — 60 runs in 24 hours, nearly five and a half days for all 336. Scritchmus was the part of the Banburismus procedure that could *identify* the right-hand (fast) wheel outright, by reading the distances between the day's indicator letters off the wiring of the wheel itself. [CORROBORATED — Banburismus record; The Turing Guide, Hosgood ch. 37]
- **The evidence — pairs that differ in one letter only.** Take two messages whose indicators differ only in the third letter. Their first two indicator letters were enciphered at the same rotor positions, so the two messages stand in depth up to the third letter — and the Banbury-sheet scoring says how far apart the two third letters stood on the right-hand wheel: bookings like "X = Q−2", "H = X−4", "B = G+3". Each booking is evidence that two key letters stood a given distance apart, though not which letters they were. The Banburist searched the deciban sheets for all distances with odds of better than 1:1 — scores of +34 or more — and kept only those. [CORROBORATED — Wikipedia, Banburismus, Scritchmus section; The Turing Guide]
- **The chain.** Where bookings share a letter they join, and the joined letters lie along a rod in their true order round the right wheel, each at its true distance from the others. From the three bookings above the Banburist could build a chain like `G--B-H---X-Q` — dashes for the unknown letters between, the known letters pinned at their measured gaps. One booking is weak evidence; a chain of them, each constraining the next, is a rod that only fits one rotor. [CORROBORATED — Wikipedia, Banburismus, Scritchmus section; garden.neap.art Banburismus explainer]
- **The test — lay the rod against the rotor.** The chain is compared at progressive offsets with the known letter-sequence of an Enigma rotor, and quite a few possibilities are discounted at once. And every booked pair tells one thing more: between the two messages' starts, the right wheel cannot have passed its notch — the place where it kicks the middle wheel on — because had it, the middle wheel would have moved for one message and not the other, and the two would never have lined up in depth at all. So each pair rules a stretch of the rod out, and what is left is where the wheel turns over. The wheels turned over at different letters, so that narrowed which of them could be on the right. Three of the eight navy wheels — VI, VII and VIII — turned over twice a turn, at Z and at M: with one of those on the right, a pair had half the room to stay in depth, fewer pairs lined up at all, and the rods came harder. [CORROBORATED — Wikipedia, Banburismus, Scritchmus section; garden.neap.art Banburismus explainer]
- **The payoff — 336 orders down to 18.** The Turing Guide's worked example: if Banburismus had precisely identified the middle wheel and established that the right-hand wheel was one of the three special navy wheels, then for each of the three possibilities for the right-hand wheel there were six of the eight wheels remaining for the left-hand wheel — 18 possible combinations, 18 bombe tests instead of the original potential of 336. Scritchmus did not break the day; it made the breaking affordable, the same way Banburismus did — by spending statistics before spending machine time. [CORROBORATED — The Turing Guide, Hosgood ch. 37]
- **The people.** Turing devised Banburismus; Hugh Alexander was regarded as the best of the Banburists; I. J. Good worked the theory alongside Turing; and Joan Clarke — a senior Hut 8 cryptanalyst, one of its longest-serving — became particularly associated with Scritchmus. The method's name, like Banburismus, wears the mock-Latin -ismus; the histories record the name and the method, and no settled etymology for "scritch" is given in the sources consulted this pass — it is filed as recorded, not explained. [CORROBORATED — the Alexander/Good/Clarke associations, Banburismus record as filed in this catalogue's Banburismus entry]
- **The sixth on the shelf.** With Scritchmus filed, the Bletchley shelf in this catalogue is six deep: Banburismus weighed the traffic, Herivelismus watched the operators, Cillies named the clerk's choices, Parkerismus filed the clerk's paperwork, Yoxallismus read the officer's second setting — and Scritchmus read the fast wheel off its own wiring. Five of the six wear the -ismus; Cillies is the one that never took the Latin. [VERIFIED — the six entries as filed in this catalogue; the framing is this entry's own reading]
- **Decoder-design note (Scritchmus → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Relative is enough.** Scritchmus never learned a single absolute letter — only distances between letters — and distances were enough to name the wheel. The Gauntlet's first structural probe asks for relations, not values: how far apart do two outputs stand, in what order, under what step — because a specimen that hides its values usually still leaks their geometry. (2) **A chain beats a point.** One booked distance is weak evidence; a chain of them, each constraining the next, is a rod that only fits one rotor. Probes should be designed to join: each answer should constrain the next question, and the register should keep the chain, not just the verdicts. (3) **The machine's own asymmetry is the tell.** The notch — a security complication the designers added — is what let Bletchley tell the wheels apart, and the double-notched wheels were harder precisely because they had less room to stay in depth. A specimen's hardest feature is usually its most identifying: the Gauntlet probes the asymmetry the designers were proudest of first, because that is where the fingerprint lives. Where Banburismus weighed and Yoxallismus counted the commonest letter, Scritchmus *measured the gaps*. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]

## The Clock Method — Różycki's clock, or: the wheel the indicator betrayed

- **The problem it solved.** Rejewski's grill method could already determine the right-hand rotor, but at a price: trying each possible rotor permutation at each of its 26 starting rotations, with the plugboard settings complicating every test. Jerzy Różycki's clock, devised at the Polish Cipher Bureau during 1933–1935, answered the same question with simple tests that the plugboard could not touch — and for the Poles, learning the rightmost rotor cut the rotor-order search space by a factor of three. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Clock (cryptography)]
- **The flaw it exploited — the doubled key.** The Germans did not send the message key in the clear, but they did something nearly as generous: they enciphered the three-letter message key twice. A key of ABL became ABLABL and was enciphered as a six-letter indicator, say PKPJXI — the doubled key, not the encrypted key sent twice. With about 60 messages on the same daily key, Rejewski's method of characteristics recovered the day's message keys outright (one carrier puts the figure at about 70), and weak clerk-chosen keys (CCC, WER) made the recovery easier still. The clock method started where that recovery ended: it knew the message keys and the ciphertext, and almost nothing else — not the plugboard, not the ring settings, not the rotor order, not the starting position. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Clock (cryptography); CORROBORATED — the ~70-message figure and the weak-key detail, Alchetron mirror of the same article]
- **The method — pairs that start the same.** In a day's traffic there might be about a dozen message pairs whose message keys start with the same two letters. Take such a pair and try both alignments of their ciphertexts: one alignment will use an identical polyalphabetic substitution, and from that alignment the cryptanalyst can read off a window of letters inside which the right-hand rotor's turnover must have fallen. A single pair bounds the turnover to a range; it does not name the rotor. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Clock (cryptography)]
- **The clock — turnovers as a dial.** The rotors turned over at different letters: rotor I at R, rotor II at F, rotor III at W, rotor IV at K, and every later rotor at A — the British mnemonic was "Royal Flags Wave Kings Above". Each pair's window admits only the rotors whose turnover letter falls inside it, and the windows intersect. One pair might say the turnover fell between B and U, leaving rotors I (R), II (F) and IV (K) viable; a second pair might say between M and C, leaving I (R), III (W) and V-onwards (A). Only rotor I satisfies both — so rotor I is the right-hand rotor. With a little luck, and a dozen pairs a day, the clock named the fast wheel without ever touching the plugboard. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Clock (cryptography), including the worked example]
- **The calendar that made it matter.** In the early 1930s the clock's answer was worth little, because the Germans used the same rotor order for three months at a time — determine it once, use it for a quarter. On 1 February 1936 the order began changing monthly; on 1 November 1936 it began changing daily. Each quickening raised the price of the grill method's brute trying, and raised the value of a test that named the fast wheel cheaply. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Clock (cryptography)]
- **The death — 15 September 1938.** The clock lived on the doubled indicator, and the doubled indicator died on a single day: 15 September 1938, when the Germans switched to per-message keys. The same change killed the cyclometer overnight — this catalogue's Rejewski entry records it. The clock did not fail; its food was withdrawn. No doubled key, no recovered message keys, no pairs that start the same — and the method that had named the fast wheel since the mid-1930s had nothing left to read. [CORROBORATED — the 15 September 1938 procedure change as filed in this catalogue's Rejewski entry; the clock's dependence on the doubled indicator per the Wikipedia method description]
- **The afterlife — Banburismus.** Różycki's clock was later elaborated by Alan Turing at Bletchley Park into Banburismus, the statistical weighing machine this catalogue filed earlier today; the British improved the method further, and it let them use their limited number of bombes more effectively against five to eight rotors. The clock is the root of the Bletchley shelf: the Polish test that read a wheel off its turnover, grown by Turing into a machine that read the whole day off its statistics. With it filed, the shelf is seven deep — one Polish root, six Bletchley branches. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Clock (cryptography); VERIFIED — the seven-entry shelf as filed in this catalogue]
- **Decoder-design note (Clock Method → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Read what the settings cannot hide.** The grill method fought the plugboard; the clock walked around it, testing only what the plugboard could not change. A Gauntlet probe should aim at the same class of fact: the property of the specimen that survives every configuration the specimen can choose — its turnover letter, not its plugboard. (2) **The intersection is the answer.** One window left three rotors; two windows left one. Probes should be designed to intersect, not merely to accumulate: each answer should cut the candidate set, and the register should record the cut, not just the observation. (3) **Record what a method eats.** The clock did not fail in 1938 — its input was withdrawn, and the method starved the same day. Every Gauntlet instrument is filed with its input dependency named, so that when a probe goes silent the register can say whether the specimen changed or the food ran out. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]

## Zygalski Sheets — the perforated net, or: the holes that only lined up once

- **The problem it solved.** On 15 September 1938 the Germans switched to per-message keys, and the cyclometer and the clock method died the same day — both had fed on the fixed daily ground setting, and the ground setting was now chosen fresh for every message. The doubled message key still went out over the air: six letters, the second three a repeat encipherment of the first three — and Henryk Zygalski, about October 1938, built a machine out of paper that could still read it. Where Rejewski's characteristics had needed sixty messages on one setting, Zygalski's sheets needed only a handful of messages that carried a particular accident. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Zygalski sheets; the 15 September 1938 change as filed in this catalogue's Rejewski entry]
- **The flaw it exploited — the female.** Take the six-letter indicator. If its first and fourth letters are the same, the product permutation AD has a fixed point — a 1-cycle — at the place where the message key's first letter was enciphered twice, three rotor steps apart. The same holds for the second and fifth letters (permutation BE) and the third and sixth (CF). The Poles called such a coincidence a "female": a rare, visible accident that only certain rotor positions can produce. A female does not name the setting — it vetoes most of them. [CORROBORATED — the female as a 1-cycle in AD/BE/CF, Borowska et al., "The Cryptanalysis of the Enigma Cipher," Advances in Computer Science Research vol. 10 (2013)]
- **The method — superposition.** For each of the six possible rotor orders, Zygalski made 26 perforated sheets, one for each starting position of the left (slowest) rotor. Each sheet carried a 26 × 26 matrix — the 676 possible starting positions of the middle and right rotors, duplicated horizontally and vertically (a–z, a–y) — with holes punched wherever a female could occur. The cryptanalyst took the sheets for the day's females, superposed them, and slid them against each other in a strictly defined program, each shift set by the intercepted messages' ground settings. With each added sheet the visible apertures thinned; with enough data a single aperture remained. Rejewski, who operated the device: "When the sheets were superposed and moved in the proper sequence and the proper manner with respect to each other, in accordance with a strictly defined program, the number of visible apertures gradually decreased. And, if a sufficient quantity of data was available, there finally remained a single aperture, probably corresponding to the right case, that is, to the solution. From the position of the aperture one could calculate the order of the rotors, the setting of their rings, and, by comparing the letters of the cipher keys with the letters in the machine, likewise permutation S; in other words, the entire cipher key." Like the cyclometer's card catalog, the whole procedure was independent of the number of plugboard connections — the plugboard could not touch it. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Zygalski sheets, including the Rejewski quotation; CORROBORATED — the working sets were made in triplicate, 3 × 26 sheets per rotor order, one set for each product AD, BE, CF, each sheet a 51 × 51 field square, Borowska et al.]
- **The manufacture — razor blades and a tenfold bill.** For security the sheets were made by hand, by the mathematician-cryptologists themselves, cutting the holes with razor blades. By 15 December 1938 only a third of the job was finished — and on that day the Germans introduced rotors IV and V. Six rotor orders became sixty, and the labor of making the sheets grew tenfold overnight. Poland could not out-build the re-arm race: the sheets were priced beyond the Bureau's budget, and the same arithmetic priced out the bombas. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Zygalski sheets]
- **The afterlife — Netz at Bletchley.** The sheets were part of what Poland handed over at Pyry on 25 July 1939, five weeks before the invasion. The British, at Bletchley Park, undertook two complete sets, made with perforators by a section headed by John R. F. Jeffreys. At Bletchley the sheets were known as Netz, from Netzverfahren, the "net method" — Welchman later remembered them as "Jeffreys sheets," though that name properly belonged to another catalog Jeffreys' section produced. The first set was finished in late December 1939; part of the second set reached the Polish cryptologists at PC Bruno outside Paris on 28 December; the rest was completed on 7 January 1940 and couriered to France by Alan Turing shortly after. "With their help," Rejewski wrote, "we continued solving Enigma daily keys" — and the sheets served the first wartime decryption of an Enigma message, on 17 January 1940. With the sheets filed, the Enigma-methods shelf in this catalogue stands eight deep — two Polish roots, six Bletchley branches. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Zygalski sheets]
- **The death — May 1940.** In May 1940 the Germans changed the message-key enciphering procedure completely (one Norwegian network excepted) and stopped the double encipherment. The sheets went dead overnight — the same death the clock method had died in 1938, and the same lesson: the method was never beaten, its food was withdrawn. The Herivel tip, filed earlier in this catalogue, could still be used, and carried Hut 6 until the bombes arrived. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Zygalski sheets; the 1 May 1940 change as filed in this catalogue's Herivelismus entry]
- **Decoder-design note (Zygalski → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **A hole is a veto, not a vote.** No single sheet names the answer; each sheet says where the answer is not, and the finding is the aperture that survives every veto. Design Gauntlet probes the same way: outputs that rule out are sturdier than outputs that claim — let the surviving aperture be the finding, and let positive claims come from a different instrument. (2) **Precompute the catalogue; spend the day on the stack.** The sheets cost months of razor-blade labor; using them cost minutes of sliding paper. The costly work is building the probe library and the twin baselines once; a sitting should be cheap — slide the sheets, count the apertures. (3) **A method dies when its food changes, not when it is beaten.** The sheets were never outsmarted; the doubled key was withdrawn and they starved the same day. Every instrument names its input dependency, so that when a probe goes silent the register can say whether the specimen changed or the food ran out. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]

*[Grade: VERIFIED — Zygalski's authorship and the about-October-1938 dating, the 26 sheets per rotor order and six orders, the left-rotor-per-sheet construction, the 26 × 26 matrix of middle/right positions duplicated a–z/a–y, the holes as female positions, the Rejewski superposition quotation and what the surviving aperture yields (rotor order, ring settings, permutation S — the entire key), the plugboard independence, the hand manufacture with razor blades by the cryptologists themselves, the one-third completion by 15 December 1938, the rotors IV/V tenfold labor jump (6 → 60 orders), the Pyry disclosure, the two British sets under Jeffreys with perforators, the Netz/Netzverfahren name and the Welchman "Jeffreys sheets" misnomer, the late-December-1939 first set, the 28 December delivery to PC Bruno, the 7 January 1940 completion and Turing courier run, the "we continued solving Enigma daily keys" record, the first wartime decryption on 17 January 1940, and the May 1940 procedure change killing the sheets while the Herivel tip survived; CORROBORATED — the female as a 1-cycle in the AD/BE/CF products and the 3 × 26 triplicate sheet sets on 51 × 51 fields, Borowska et al. 2013; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## The Cyclometer — Rejewski's card catalog, or: the fingerprint that survived the plugboard

- **The problem it solved.** Rejewski's grill method could already recover the day's characteristic from the doubled key, but at a price: the grill was tedious, it leaned on sloppy clerk habits, and after it the Poles still faced a laborious search — a *Q*-catalog of 4,056 entries (26 × 26 × 6) eased part of it, but finding the ring settings could still require trying 17,576 possibilities. The grill worked well until 1 October 1936, the day the Germans stopped using six plugboard connections (*steckers*) and started using five to eight — more steckers could frustrate the grill outright. Marian Rejewski, "probably in 1934 or 1935," built a machine to replace the grill's toil with a lookup: the cyclometer, which catalogued the cycle structure of Enigma permutations. Two rotor banks at the top (one with its lid open), a rheostat at the left below, and an array of lamps and switches labelled with the letters at the right. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cyclometer]
- **The flaw it exploited — the doubled key.** The Germans doubled the message key instead of sending the encrypted key twice: ABL became ABLABL and was enciphered as the six-letter indicator PKPJXI. Rejewski read the machine as six sequential permutations, A B C D E F, one per letter position — and because the first and fourth letters were the same plaintext letter, the second and fifth the same, the third and sixth the same, the composed permutations AD, BE and CF could be pieced together from the day's traffic. With enough messages — about sixty on the same daily key — the whole characteristic fell out in Cauchy cycle notation, for example AD = (pjxroquctwzsy)(kvgledmanhfib), BE = (kxtcoigweh)(zvfbsylrnp)(ujd)(mqa), CF = (yvxqtdhpim)(skgrjbcolw)(un)(fa)(e)(z). [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cyclometer, including the worked 1930-manual example: wheel order II, I, III; ringstellung 24, 18, 22 (XMV); reflector A; plugboard A-M, F-I, N-V, P-S, T-U, W-Z; ground setting FOL; message key ABL → PKPJXI]
- **The insight — cycle lengths survive the plugboard.** Instead of indexing the catalog by the actual cycles, the Poles hit upon indexing it by the *length* of the cycles. The plugboard changed the identity of the letters in a permutation, but it did not change the lengths of the cycles — a stecker swaps two letters, and a swap conjugates the permutation, which preserves cycle structure. There are 101 possible patterns for the cycle lengths of one indicator permutation, and with three permutations in the characteristic about a million possible combinations (101³ = 1,030,301) — so the cycle lengths could serve as a hash into a table of the 105,456 possible settings. The odds were good that only one card — or a few — carried a given fingerprint. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cyclometer]
- **The method — a fingerprint lookup.** From the day's traffic the cryptanalyst recovered the characteristic, calculated its cycle lengths — in the worked example, AD: 13; BE: 10 3; CF: 10 2 1 — and looked them up in the card catalog. The card named the wheel order (II, I, III) and the initial position of each wheel, without much work, and the method worked however many steckers the Germans were using. The catalog did not include the actual characteristic: the cyclometer indicated only membership in a cycle, not the order of letters within it — the fingerprint, never the face. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cyclometer]
- **The recovery — the plugboard from the comparison.** The catalog did not disclose the plugboard settings, and for six plugs there are about 100 billion possible arrangements — trying them all was infeasible. Instead the cryptanalyst set an Enigma to the catalog's wheel order and positions, mapped out the unsteckered permutations A\* B\* C\* D\* E\* F\* by pressing each key and holding it while reading the lamp (holding the first key down keeps the machine from advancing the rotors), and compared the unsteckered characteristic against the day's real one. The differences read off the steckers directly: in the worked example, the plugboard cycles (un)(fa) of CF had to transpose with the unsteckered (vt)(mi); the singleton cycles showed "e" unsteckered while "w" and "z" were steckered together — and the comparison resolved to P-S, T-U, W-Z, N-V, A-M, F-I, exactly the day's plugboard. The only remaining secret was the ring positions (*Ringstellung*). [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cyclometer, including the key-hold mapping procedure and the recovered stecker list]
- **The build — a year of labor, fifteen minutes a day.** The cyclometer prepared a catalog of the cycle lengths and numbers for all 17,576 rotor positions for a given rotor sequence, and with six possible sequences the card catalog comprised 6 × 17,576 = 105,456 entries. Preparation of the catalog, writes Rejewski, "was laborious and took over a year, but when it was ready... daily keys [could be obtained] within about fifteen minutes." The utility of the catalog was independent of the number of plug connections the Germans used — and of the reconstruction of message keys. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cyclometer, including the Rejewski quotation]
- **The death — 15 September 1938, and the rebuild it survived once.** On 1 November 1937 the Germans changed the reversing drum, the reflector — and the Cipher Bureau had to start anew with a fresh card catalog, "a task," writes Rejewski, "which consumed, on account of our greater experience, probably somewhat less than a year's time." The cyclometer survived that death once. It did not survive the second: on 15 September 1938 the Germans changed entirely the procedure for enciphering message keys, and the card-catalog method became completely useless. The same change killed the clock method the same day — this catalogue's Clock Method entry records it — and it spurred the invention of Rejewski's cryptologic bomb and Zygalski's perforated sheets. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cyclometer]
- **The afterlife — a working machine, rebuilt in 2019.** Using drawings made by Rejewski, Hal Evans and Tim Flack at the Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge, constructed a working version of the cyclometer in 2019. And with Rejewski's later cryptologic bomb, the cyclometer can be viewed as a predecessor to the Bombe that helped break Enigma later in the war at Bletchley Park. With it filed, the Enigma-methods shelf in this catalogue stands nine deep — three Polish roots, six Bletchley branches. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cyclometer]
- **Decoder-design note (Cyclometer → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Index by the invariant, not the identity.** The plugboard could rename every letter in the characteristic, and the cyclometer never fought it — it indexed by cycle lengths, the one thing the adversary's renaming could not change. A Gauntlet probe should hunt the same class of property: the invariant of the specimen that survives every relabelling the specimen can perform — its cycle-length fingerprint, not its letter names. (2) **Precompute once; spend minutes per sitting.** The catalog cost over a year of labor and paid it back at fifteen minutes a day. The costly work is building the probe library and the twin baselines once; a sitting should be cheap — look up the fingerprint, read the card. (3) **A fingerprint is not a face.** The catalog named the wheel order and positions but never the characteristic itself, and never the plugboard — those still had to be recovered by comparison. A probe that returns a fingerprint has not returned the specimen: the register records what the instrument actually names, and the comparison step that turns the fingerprint into a reading is a separate instrument, filed separately. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]

*[Grade: VERIFIED — Rejewski's authorship and the "probably in 1934 or 1935" dating, the two-rotor-bank / rheostat / lamp-and-switch construction, the grill method's tedium and the Q-catalog's 4,056 entries, the 17,576 ring-setting tries, the 1 October 1936 six-to-five-to-eight stecker change frustrating the grill, the doubled-key flaw (ABL → ABLABL → PKPJXI) and the A–F / AD, BE, CF characteristic construction, the worked example's wheel order, ringstellung, reflector, plugboard, ground setting and message key, the 101 cycle-length patterns and the 101³ = 1,030,301 combinations, the 105,456-entry catalog (6 × 17,576), the plugboard-invariance of cycle lengths, the AD: 13 / BE: 10 3 / CF: 10 2 1 lookup, the catalog's membership-only character, the ~100-billion six-plug arrangements, the key-hold unsteckered mapping and the recovered P-S, T-U, W-Z, N-V, A-M, F-I stecker list, the "laborious... over a year" build and the "within about fifteen minutes" daily read, the 1 November 1937 reflector change and the sub-year rebuild, the 15 September 1938 procedure change killing the card-catalog method and spurring the bomb and the sheets, the 2019 Cambridge reconstruction by Evans and Flack from Rejewski's drawings, and the predecessor-to-the-Bombe lineage; the nine-deep shelf count as filed in this catalogue; CORROBORATED — the ~60-message characteristic recovery figure as filed in this catalogue's Clock Method entry; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## The Bomba Kryptologiczna — Rejewski's cryptologic bomb, or: the machine that ran all 17,576 settings at once

- **The problem it solved.** On 15 September 1938 the Germans changed entirely the procedure for enciphering message keys, and the cyclometer's card catalog became completely useless overnight — the same change killed the clock method the same day. The new procedure let each operator choose his own ground setting (*Grundstellung*) for every message and send it in the clear, then encipher the doubled message key from that setting. A catalog built for one daily ground setting had nothing to index on anymore. The Poles answered with two instruments at once: Zygalski's perforated sheets, filed in this catalogue, and Rejewski's cryptologic bomb — the *bomba kryptologiczna* — which stopped precomputing the search and mechanized it instead. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cyclometer (the 15 September 1938 procedure change killing the card-catalog method and spurring the bomb and the sheets); Wikipedia, Cryptanalysis of the Enigma (the bomb method, invented in the autumn of 1938); quadibloc (ground settings chosen at random by the operator, and sent in the clear with each message)]
- **The flaw it exploited — the females.** The doubled key survived the procedure change, and with it the coincidence it made possible: one letter of the message key, doubled to protect it against transmission errors, could be enciphered to the same character at the first and fourth positions, the second and fifth, or the third and sixth — groups like WAVWHA, where the first symbol came out as W on the first and the fourth position. The Poles called these doublings "females" — Rejewski wrote they had designated them thus "for lack of a better idea" — and the modern term is "fixpoint." A female means the same plaintext letter was enciphered twice under rotor states three key-presses apart, and three females at the three spacings are enough to pin the day's setting. [VERIFIED — Link 2009, Cryptologia (the WAVWHA example, the 1–4 / 2–5 / 3–6 positions); CORROBORATED — the "for lack of a better idea" attribution, via Link's reading of Rejewski]
- **The insight — run the machine instead of reading the table.** The cyclometer had spent over a year of labor to answer in fifteen minutes; the bomba spent electricity to answer in about two hours. It consisted of three pairs of Enigma rotor sets driven by an electric motor via a planetary gear — six rotor sets in all, an electrically powered aggregate of six Enigmas — and instead of looking the day's setting up in a table, it turned all 17,576 possible rotor positions past the coincidence test and stopped when the test fired. The sheets needed about ten females to work; the bomba needed only three. [VERIFIED — Link 2009 (three pairs of Enigma rotor sets, electric motor, planetary gear); Wikipedia, Cryptanalysis of the Enigma (six Enigmas aggregate; exhaustive analysis of the 17,576 possible message keys; three females instead of about ten for the sheet method)]
- **The method — a stop on coincidence.** The operator "programmed" the bomba with three messages whose indicators carried females at 1–4, 2–5 and 3–6 respectively — in Link's reconstruction, GKD WAVWHA, JOT IWABWN and MDO OTWYZW, the first three letters of each being the *Grundstellung* in clear and the last six the encrypted doubled message key. The first pair of Enigmas was set to the indicators that had produced the coincidence at the first and fourth position, GKD and GKD+3 = GKG — the offset of three reflecting that in a female the same letter recurs three key-presses later — and the machine ran. When all three pairs simultaneously produced the same output letter, the bomba stopped: that rotor position was the day's setting. The cipher message transmitted the *Grundstellung* in the clear, so a match revealed the rotor order, the rotor positions, and the ring settings. [VERIFIED — Link 2009 (Figure 2 setup, GKD/GKG offset of three); Wikipedia, Cryptanalysis of the Enigma (the match revealing rotor order, positions and ring settings)]
- **The recovery — everything but the plugboard.** The match left exactly one secret standing: the plugboard permutation. Like the cyclometer before it, the bomba never named the steckers — they were recovered by comparison afterwards, setting an Enigma to the bomba's wheel order and positions and reading the plugboard off the differences between the unsteckered and the real characteristic, the procedure this catalogue's Cyclometer entry records in full. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cryptanalysis of the Enigma (the only remaining secret was the plugboard permutation); the comparison procedure as filed in this catalogue's Cyclometer entry]
- **The build — six machines, one per wheel order.** Six *bomby* were quickly built by the AVA Radio Manufacturing Company (*Wytwornia Radiotechniczna AVA*) in Warsaw in November 1938, one for each of the then-possible wheel orders. A run took around two hours to determine the positions of the rotors. [VERIFIED — Link 2009 (six bomby, AVA, November 1938, one per wheel order); BCS / McCarthy (around two hours per run)]
- **The death — priced out in a month.** The bomba was useful only as long as three conditions were met: the indicator had to include the repetition of the message key; the number of rotors available had to be limited to three, giving six different wheel orders; and the number of plugboard leads had to remain relatively small, so that the majority of letters were unsteckered. Barely a month after delivery the Germans introduced two additional rotors for loading into the Enigma scrambler, increasing the number of wheel orders by a factor of ten — six became sixty, and building another 54 *bomby* was beyond the Poles' resources. On 1 January 1939 the number of plugboard leads was increased to ten. The Poles therefore had to return to manual methods, the Zygalski sheets. The bomba's working life was barely a month. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Bombe (the three conditions, the November 1938 delivery, the December rotor increase, the 54-machine price, the 1 January 1939 plugboard increase, the return to the sheets)]
- **The afterlife — the British Bombe, and a 2019 rebuild.** Alan Turing designed the British bombe on a more general principle — the crib, a stretch of predictable plaintext — and Gordon Welchman's diagonal board made it practical; the first, *Victory*, was installed at Bletchley Park on 18 March 1940, and a run through all 17,576 positions for one rotor order took about twenty minutes. The British machine was developed from the Polish bomba, and the lineage is the point: the bomba proved that six Enigmas wired together and spun through every position could find a day's key, and Turing's machine generalized the coincidence it hunted. No original *bomby* survive; Rejewski's papers of 1967 and 1979 carry the sketch and the description of how the machine worked, and in 2019 Jeremy McCarthy, a volunteer at the National Museum of Computing, recreated a working bomba in a mixture of hardware and software. With it filed, the Enigma-methods shelf in this catalogue stands ten deep — four Polish roots, six Bletchley branches. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Bombe (Turing 1939 design from the Polish bomba; Victory, 18 March 1940; ~20 minutes per rotor order); BCS (no originals survive; Rejewski's 1967/1979 papers; McCarthy's 2019 reconstruction)]
- **Decoder-design note (Bomba → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Brute force is a design, not a defeat.** When the table died, the Poles did not build a better table — they built a machine that re-ran the search live, at two hours a sitting. A Gauntlet probe that exhausts all 17,576 positions is a probe, not a failure of imagination: the register records the cost, and the cost is part of the finding. (2) **Three coincidences beat ten.** The bomba needed only three females where the sheets needed about ten — a sharper instrument needs less luck. Probe design should count the coincidences it needs: fewer, sharper, cheaper is a design goal, not a boast. (3) **A machine's life is its conditions.** The bomba lived exactly as long as its three conditions held and died the month the fourth and fifth rotors arrived. Every instrument carries its conditions on its face, and a reading from an instrument whose conditions have expired is a dead reading — version the instrument with the procedure it attacks, and retire it the day the procedure changes. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the 15 September 1938 procedure change killing the card-catalog method and spurring the bomb and the sheets, the per-message ground setting sent in the clear, the females at positions 1–4, 2–5 and 3–6 (WAVWHA), the three pairs of Enigma rotor sets driven by an electric motor via a planetary gear, the electrically powered aggregate of six Enigmas, the exhaustive analysis of the 17,576 possible message keys, three females against the sheets' ten, the GKD WAVWHA / JOT IWABWN / MDO OTWYZW setup and the GKD+3 = GKG offset, the match revealing rotor order, rotor positions and ring settings with the plugboard permutation the only remaining secret, the six bomby built by AVA in Warsaw in November 1938, one per wheel order, the around-two-hour run, the three conditions of usefulness, the December 1938 introduction of rotors IV and V taking wheel orders from six to sixty, the 54 further bomby beyond Polish resources, the 1 January 1939 plugboard increase to ten leads, the return to the Zygalski sheets, the British Bombe's descent from the Polish bomba, Turing's 1939 design and Welchman's diagonal board, Victory installed 18 March 1940, the ~20-minute British run per rotor order, no original bomby surviving, Rejewski's 1967 and 1979 papers carrying the sketch and description, and the 2019 McCarthy reconstruction; the ten-deep shelf count as filed in this catalogue; CORROBORATED — the "females" name as "for lack of a better idea" (via Link's reading of Rejewski) and the third usefulness condition (plugboard leads few, majority unsteckered), which the Bombe article itself flags "dubious – discuss"; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## HPKE — Hybrid Public Key Encryption (RFC 9180), or: the one hybrid that replaced a zoo of them

- **The problem it solved.** Before HPKE there was no single interoperable hybrid: a zoo of non-interoperable ECIES variants — ANSI X9.63, IEEE 1363a, ISO/IEC 18033-2, SEC 1 — each with its own problems, relying on outdated primitives, lacking proofs of IND-CCA2 security, or failing to provide test vectors. HPKE, published February 2022 as an IRTF informational RFC from the Crypto Forum Research Group after twelve drafts, defines one construction with sufficient clarity to be interoperably implemented, and proves it IND-CCA2-secure under classical assumptions about the underlying primitives. [VERIFIED — RFC 9180 §1 (the ECIES zoo, the missing proofs and test vectors, the IND-CCA2 claim, the CFRG provenance); the twelve-draft count via Lipp]
- **The shape — three parts, one tuple.** A ciphersuite is a triple (KEM, KDF, AEAD), each chosen by a two-byte identifier from an IANA registry. The KEMs are all Diffie-Hellman: DHKEM(P-256, HKDF-SHA256) 0x0010, DHKEM(P-384, HKDF-SHA384) 0x0011, DHKEM(P-521, HKDF-SHA512) 0x0012, DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256) 0x0020, DHKEM(X448, HKDF-SHA512) 0x0021. The KDFs are HKDF-SHA256 0x0001, HKDF-SHA384 0x0002, HKDF-SHA512 0x0003. The AEADs are AES-128-GCM 0x0001, AES-256-GCM 0x0002, ChaCha20Poly1305 0x0003 — plus 0xFFFF, Export-only, reserved for applications that use only the Export interface and never encrypt. [VERIFIED — RFC 9180 §7, Tables 2–5]
- **The move — encapsulate, don't encrypt the key.** The traditional hybrid encrypts the symmetric key with the public key. HPKE inverts the phrasing: generate the symmetric key and its encapsulation with the public key. `Encap(pkR)` returns a fixed-length KEM shared secret and a fixed-length encapsulation of it; for DHKEM the encapsulation *is* the sender's ephemeral public key, so Npk equals Nenc — 32 bytes for X25519, 65 for P-256. The wire carries a public value, never the key itself. [VERIFIED — RFC 9180 §1 (the generate-and-encapsulate phrasing), §4 (Encap/Decap, Npk = Nenc for DHKEM)]
- **The four modes — one receiver key, three optional authentications.** Base (mode 0) encrypts to the holder of the recipient key and nothing more — anonymous sender, the usual hybrid. PSK (mode 1) mixes in a pre-shared key and its identifier, so the recipient learns the sender belonged to the PSK group. Auth (mode 2) adds the sender's static key pair through `AuthEncap`/`AuthDecap`, so the recipient is assured the secret came from the holder of that key. AuthPSK (mode 3) layers both. Every mode still takes the same `info` parameter — folded into key generation, e.g. identity information — and per-message `aad`. [VERIFIED — RFC 9180 §5.1, Table 1 (the four modes); the mode table via Lipp]
- **The context — one setup, many messages, and a second door.** Setup builds an encryption context holding a key, a base nonce, and an exporter secret; `Seal`/`Open` carry a sequence number, so nonces are derived per message and the context can encrypt a sequence. Single-shot `Seal`/`Open` cover one message. And `Export` derives almost-arbitrarily-long shared secrets from the exporter secret under an `exporter_context` — the second door, for when a fixed-size KEM secret is not enough: HPKE as a key-agreement machine, not just an encryption machine. [VERIFIED — RFC 9180 §5, §5.3, §6 (context, sequence numbers, Export); Lipp on Export]
- **The labels — domain separation is the design.** Every KDF call goes through `LabeledExtract`/`LabeledExpand`, which prefix the inputs with the version label "HPKE-v1" and a `suite_id` naming the ciphersuite ("HPKE" + the whole triple inside HPKE, "KEM" + the KEM inside DHKEM). The version is stamped into every derived key, so a future HPKE-v2 cannot cross-talk with v1 outputs — the labels are the boundary between versions, suites, and applications. [VERIFIED — RFC 9180 §4, §5.1 (LabeledExtract/LabeledExpand, suite_id, "HPKE-v1")]
- **The honest weakness — KCI in the auth modes, and the validation the RFC insists on.** The DHKEM `AuthEncap`/`AuthDecap` assurance is vulnerable to key-compromise impersonation: if the recipient private key `skR` is compromised, the assurance that the secret was generated by the holder of the sender key `skS` does not hold. Separately, senders and recipients MUST validate KEM inputs and outputs — P-256/384/521 points checked on-curve and not at infinity, X25519/X448 Diffie-Hellman outputs checked against the all-zero value, with failure aborting the operation. The authentication in Auth mode is real, but conditional on the recipient key staying secret. [VERIFIED — RFC 9180 §4.1 (the KCI caveat), §7.1.4 (validation requirements)]
- **Where it lives.** MLS (RFC 9420) — this catalogue's own MLS entry runs on HPKE throughout, and HPKE was named in the RFC's own introduction as built for MLS and TLS Encrypted ClientHello. Oblivious HTTP (RFC 9458) encrypts its requests with HPKE. COSE-HPKE (draft-ietf-cose-hpke-17, October 2025) carries it into the CBOR world this catalogue's COSE entry covers, supporting Base and PSK modes. The authors are Richard L. Barnes (Cisco), Karthik Bhargavan (Inria), Benjamin Lipp (Inria), and Christopher A. Wood (Cloudflare). [VERIFIED — RFC 9180 §1 (MLS and ECH as the named applications), authorship; CORROBORATED — OHTTP (RFC 9458) and the October 2025 COSE-HPKE draft status]
- **The post-quantum note.** Every KEM in RFC 9180 is classical Diffie-Hellman; the framework is deliberately KEM-agnostic, and §7.1.5 reserves the "Future KEMs" slot with security requirements for anything new. Post-quantum hybrids — ML-KEM layered into HPKE — are in draft work, not in the RFC. Until a PQ KEM is registered, HPKE is IND-CCA2 under classical assumptions only, and the catalogue's ML-KEM entry is the one that names the quantum horizon. [VERIFIED — RFC 9180 §7.1.5 (Future KEMs, security requirements); CORROBORATED — PQ hybrids in progress, not yet standardized]
- **Decoder-design note (HPKE → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Name the triple, not the product.** A ciphersuite is three independent choices — KEM, KDF, AEAD — and the Gauntlet's intake should record the same decomposition for any specimen, because a break in one primitive is not a break in the whole; a specimen graded as one blob hides which leg failed. (2) **Encapsulate, don't transport.** The wire carries an encapsulation — a public value — and never the key itself; a specimen whose wire carries its own key material has already confessed, whatever its cipher claims. (3) **Labels are the boundary.** "HPKE-v1" inside every KDF call is the version stamped into the key schedule; a specimen with no domain separation lets one context's keys bleed into another's. Test the boundary: replay one context's output into another's and watch whether the specimen notices. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]

## age — the file encryption format with one cipher and no config options, or: the envelope that wraps its own key

- **The problem it solved.** GPG is a key-management system with an encryption tool attached: keyservers, trust models, algorithm menus, decades of options. age — designed by Filippo Valsorda and Ben Cartwright-Cox, specified at age-encryption.org/v1 under the C2SP umbrella — is the opposite bet: one AEAD (ChaCha20-Poly1305), one native public-key algorithm (X25519), one native password algorithm (scrypt), no config options, small explicit keys, UNIX-style composability. The reference implementation is Go (FiloSottile/age, BSD-3-Clause, repository opened May 2019); interoperable implementations exist in Rust (rage) and TypeScript (Typage). [VERIFIED — the age README (designers, spec link, "no config options", implementations); the C2SP age specification (the v1 format); the repository creation date]
- **The shape — two parts, one fresh key.** An age file is a textual header that carries the file key, plus a binary payload encrypted with it. Each file gets a fresh 128-bit file key — 16 bytes of CSPRNG output, never reused across files — and the whole file must be treated as binary and is not malleable without knowledge of the file key. The header is human-readable by design: a version line, one or more recipient stanzas, and a MAC. [VERIFIED — C2SP age specification, "Encrypted file format" and "File key"]
- **The header — every recipient gets its own wrapping.** The version line reads `age-encryption.org/v1`. Each recipient stanza starts with `->`, names its type and arguments, and carries a base64 body wrapped at 64 columns; every stanza wraps the same file key independently, so a file encrypted to ten recipients carries ten independent wrappings and any one identity unwraps it. The header ends with a `---` line carrying a base64 HMAC-SHA-256 over the whole header up to and including the `---` mark, keyed by HKDF-SHA-256(ikm = file key, salt = empty, info = "header") — so a tampered header is caught before any payload byte is read. Unknown stanza types MUST be ignored (grease tolerance), and non-native recipient types SHOULD use fully-qualified names such as `example.com/enigma`. [VERIFIED — C2SP age specification, "Header", "Recipient stanza", "Header MAC"]
- **The X25519 recipient — an ephemeral share per stanza.** An identity is 32 bytes of CSPRNG output, encoded as Bech32 with the human-readable part `AGE-SECRET-KEY-`; the recipient is X25519(identity, basepoint), encoded as Bech32 with HRP `age` (the familiar `age1...` string). Each stanza carries a fresh ephemeral share; the wrap key is HKDF-SHA-256(ikm = X25519(ephemeral secret, recipient), salt = ephemeral share || recipient, info = "age-encryption.org/v1/X25519"), and the stanza body is the file key sealed with ChaCha20-Poly1305 under an all-zero nonce. An all-zero shared secret aborts the unwrap. [VERIFIED — C2SP age specification, "The X25519 recipient type"]
- **The scrypt recipient — the passphrase door, and it stands alone.** A passphrase stanza carries a 16-byte salt and a decimal logN: the wrap key is scrypt(N = 2^logN, r = 8, p = 1, dkLen = 32, salt = "age-encryption.org/v1/scrypt" || salt, passphrase), and the body is the file key sealed the same way. The spec's worked stanza uses logN 18. The hard rule: an scrypt stanza, if present, MUST be the only stanza in the header — no mixing with other scrypt stanzas or any other type, because password-based encryption carries an implicit expectation of authentication that mixing would break, and implementations MUST reject mixed headers. [VERIFIED — C2SP age specification, "The scrypt recipient type"]
- **The payload — a STREAM you can seek.** The payload opens with a fresh 16-byte nonce; the payload key is HKDF-SHA-256(ikm = file key, salt = nonce, info = "payload"). The body is split into 64 KiB chunks, each encrypted with ChaCha20-Poly1305 under a 12-byte nonce built from an 11-byte big-endian chunk counter and a final-chunk flag byte (0x01 for the last chunk, 0x00 before it). This is the STREAM construction (ePrint 2015/189): streaming decryption must signal an error if the end of file arrives without a valid final chunk, the payload can be seeked by jumping in chunk increments, and the payload must never be modified without re-encrypting as a new file with a fresh nonce. [VERIFIED — C2SP age specification, "Payload"]
- **The plugin door — SSH keys, hardware tokens, post-quantum.** The two native types are the whole core spec; everything else is a plugin or an extension. The reference tool also encrypts to `ssh-rsa` and `ssh-ed25519` SSH public keys (decrypting with the private key file; ssh-agent not supported), and to GitHub users' listed SSH keys via `-R`. Hardware PIV tokens such as YubiKeys work through the age-plugin-yubikey plugin. Post-quantum hybrid keys (ML-KEM-768 × X25519) are built into age v1.3.0 and later: generate with `age-keygen -pq`, identities start `AGE-SECRET-KEY-PQ-1...`, recipients `age1pq1...` and run to roughly 2,000 characters. `age-inspect` reads a file's metadata — recipient types, post-quantum use, payload size — without decrypting it. [VERIFIED — the age README (SSH keys, plugins, post-quantum keys, age-inspect); CORROBORATED — the ML-KEM-768 × X25519 hybrid naming via the age-inspect example and independent implementation docs]
- **The honest weakness — encryption is not authentication of the sender.** age encrypts to a recipient; anyone holding the recipient's public key can produce a file that decrypts cleanly, so a decrypted file proves nothing about who wrote it — there is no sender signature in the format, and a recipient who needs provenance must add it outside age. Two more honest edges: the header is not encrypted, so the stanza types (and, for SSH recipients, an embedded public-key tag) are visible to anyone holding the file — the README warns SSH support makes it possible to track files encrypted to a specific public key — and ASCII armor is malleable unless the reader uses a strict PEM parser and enforces canonical base64, which the spec tells implementations to do. [VERIFIED — the C2SP age specification (header plaintext, armor malleability note); the age README (SSH tracking warning); CORROBORATED — the no-sender-authentication reading, standard for public-key file encryption]
- **Decoder-design note (age → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **One algorithm is a fingerprint.** A specimen that offers no algorithm menu — one AEAD, one KEM, one KDF — has removed the downgrade surface by construction; the Gauntlet's intake records the menu size alongside the algorithms, because a specimen with a menu is a specimen with a downgrade attack to test, and a specimen without one is not. (2) **The header is the interrogation surface.** age puts its recipient structure in readable text before a single payload byte: stanza types, counts, and (for SSH) identity tags are all visible without the key. A specimen whose envelope is readable is interrogable before it is decryptable — the Gauntlet reads the envelope first, counts the wrappings, and asks what each wrapping costs before it asks what the payload says. (3) **Grease is a doctrine, not a tolerance.** Unknown stanzas MUST be ignored — the format plans for recipients it has never met. A specimen that chokes on an unknown field has confessed its parser is brittle; the Gauntlet's first probe of any envelope is an unknown field, and the specimen that errors on it is graded on the error. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's own doctrine, never run.]

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the one-cipher/one-KEM/one-password design, the designers, the spec location, the reference and alternate implementations, the file-key rules, the header shape and MAC construction, the X25519 stanza construction and Bech32 encodings, the scrypt stanza construction and its no-mixing rule, the STREAM payload construction and its seek/error rules, the ASCII-armor construction, the SSH and plugin support, the post-quantum hybrid in v1.3.0+ with its key prefixes, and the SSH tracking warning; CORROBORATED — the ML-KEM-768 × X25519 hybrid naming and the no-sender-authentication reading; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's own doctrine, never run.]*

## Morse code (1837–1844) — the code with no secrecy in time, or: the set's named-but-unwritten second member

- **The gap this entry closes.** The Semaphore design note (2026-11-01) lists the catalogue's "no secrecy" control set as four channels — "Braille is touch, Morse is sound-in-time, semaphore is sight-in-space" — and the Chappe note closes the set as its fourth member. Morse, the set's second member, was named in that note and never written: grep-verified this pass, the catalogue carries 11 mentions of "Morse" and no entry — one-word references in the MVUEH, Bankrbot, ADFGVX, and Lorenz entries, a "Morse's wager" aside in the Huffman note, and the Semaphore note's own naming. This entry writes it. [VERIFIED — the Semaphore note's list; the grep]

- **The invention — Morse's numbers, Vail's alphabet.** Samuel F. B. Morse, a portrait painter turned inventor, conceived the electric telegraph in the 1830s on Joseph Henry's electromagnet work; his first code was numbers-only, a codebook of numbered words. Alfred Vail, who joined in 1837 and whose family financed the work, rebuilt it as the dot-and-dash alphabet the world actually used: each letter its own pattern of short and long pulses, the shortest codes given to the most frequent English letters (E a single dot, T a single dash) — frequency analysis baked into the code itself. Morse submitted the patent in 1837 ("The American Recording Electro-Magnetic Telegraph"). [VERIFIED — Library of Congress, Morse Papers; U.S. House history; CORROBORATED — the Vail frequency-weighting attribution, standard histories]

- **The first message — 24 May 1844.** Congress appropriated $30,000 in 1843 for an experimental line; Morse and Vail completed the roughly 38-mile Washington–Baltimore line in May 1844. On 24 May 1844 Morse, seated in the Supreme Court Chamber of the U.S. Capitol, tapped "WHAT HATH GOD WROUGHT" to Vail at the Mount Clare railroad depot in Baltimore — Numbers 23:23, chosen by Annie Ellsworth, daughter of Patent Commissioner Henry Leavitt Ellsworth. The paper tape survives in the Library of Congress. The first official signal had run three weeks earlier, 1 May: the Whig nomination of Henry Clay, sent from Annapolis Junction. [VERIFIED — Library of Congress; U.S. House history]

- **The shape — time is the alphabet.** International Morse (ITU-R M.1677-1) is a timing language, not a mark language: a dit is one unit, a dah three; the gap inside a letter is one unit, between letters three, between words seven. The symbol set is two marks and three silences — the silences carry as much of the message as the marks, and a reader who cannot time cannot read. Gerke's 1848 simplification (one dash length, uniform spacing) displaced American Morse's variable dashes and intra-character gaps; the German-Austrian telegraph network adopted it in 1851 and the Paris conference standardized it internationally in 1865. SOS — three dots, three dashes, three dots — was adopted at Berlin in 1906, in force 1908, and made famous by Titanic in 1912. [VERIFIED — ITU-R M.1677-1 timing; Library of Congress and House history for 1844; CORROBORATED — the Gerke 1848 / 1851 / Paris 1865 sequence, SOS 1906/1908, and Titanic 1912, standard histories]

- **The long afterlife — the code that refused to die.** Commercial maritime Morse ended 1 February 1999, when GMDSS replaced it for distress traffic — 155 years after the first message. It survives where the channel is cheapest: aviation navaids (VOR and NDB stations still broadcast their identifiers in Morse) and amateur radio, where operators still hold conversations in it by ear. A code with no secrecy is still in live service while every secret cipher in this catalogue's first section is a museum piece — because its channel, a beep and a silence, is the cheapest channel ever built. [CORROBORATED — the 1999 GMDSS retirement; the aviation-navaid and amateur-radio afterlife, standard references]

- **Decoder-design note (Morse → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Time is a symbol.** Morse's alphabet is durations and gaps; the marks alone decode nothing. A specimen that speaks in timing — packet gaps, blink rates, retry cadences, beacon intervals — is speaking Morse whether or not it knows the name, and the Gauntlet's first question of any timed channel is "what are the units" before it asks "what are the marks." (2) **The code leaks its own statistics.** Vail weighted code lengths by letter frequency, so the length table IS the frequency profile: the commonest letters are the shortest marks. A specimen whose encoding is visibly optimized for some distribution has confessed the distribution it expects — the interrogator reads the code's own economy as the plaintext's profile, and a specimen whose length table matches no natural distribution is either lying about its traffic or speaking a language the table was not built for. (3) **No secrecy means the attack surface is the channel.** Morse hides nothing, so its failures are all channel failures: a jammed wire, a spoofed sender, a mis-timed gap that turns one letter into two. A specimen whose channel is public must be graded on authentication, never on confidentiality — and the Gauntlet's first probe of any open channel is a forged correction in the channel's own tongue, because the correction signal is the thing to forge. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's own doctrine, never run.]

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the Morse/Vail/Henry roles, the numbers-only first code, the 1837 patent, the $30,000 appropriation, the 24 May 1844 first message and its wording, sender, receiver, and venue, the Annie Ellsworth / Numbers 23:23 provenance, the surviving Library of Congress tape, the 1 May Clay signal, and the ITU timing units; CORROBORATED — the Vail frequency-weighting attribution, the Gerke 1848 / 1851 / Paris 1865 sequence, SOS 1906/1908, Titanic 1912, the 1 February 1999 GMDSS retirement, and the aviation/amateur afterlife; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run.]*

## The Borg cipher (1600s) — the Vatican medical manuscript in 34 signs, or: the book that waited four hundred years

- **The gap this entry closes.** The Borg cipher is the catalogue's most-cited unwritten cipher: the DESCRYPT note (2026-11-05 research loop) leans on it as the worked example of a machine-read historical cipher — 408 pages, Borg.lat.898, 34 symbols, a 500-symbol extract decoded in just over 29 minutes — but the cipher itself has no entry of its own. This entry writes it, and it also flags a date conflict the DESCRYPT note carried: that note said the Borg was "solved in 2014 by Megyesi's own team," while the sources read this pass put the decipherment in 2016 (Nada Aldarrab, Kevin Knight, Beata Megyesi). Adjudicated 2026-11-07 by the research loop — 2016 stands, the note is corrected. The 2016 date is filed here; the 2014 claim was handed to the research loop and adjudicated 2026-11-07 — no source supports 2014 (Wikipedia, citing Stockholm University and the ICDAR 2019 paper, and the BBC date the decipherment to 2016; the ACL 2021 paper cites Aldarrab's first automatic crack as 2017), so 2016 stands as settled and the DESCRYPT note's 2014 is corrected to 2016 in both files. [VERIFIED — the DESCRYPT note's reliance on the Borg as its example; the grep (no Borg entry before this one)]

- **The manuscript — 408 pages of medicine nobody could read.** The Borg cipher is an encrypted manuscript, probably from the 1600s, held at the Vatican Library as MSS-Borg.lat.898: 408 handwritten pages, the only unencrypted parts the first page in Arabic, some fragments and headings in Latin, and the last two pages in Italian. The contents, once read, are medical recipes for treating symptoms and diseases — hundreds of them, for dysentery, fever, and the rest, including the much-quoted "meat and broth of ravens for fluxes from the bowels." Scholars place its making in Northern Germany or Scandinavia in the 17th century. The inside cover carries the title "Itineris de septentrionales fructus" — "the fruit of a journey to the North" — and the manuscript is read as a copy of Montpellier H.505, a handwritten manuscript of Johannes van Heeck, one of the founders of the Accademia dei Lincei (1603). [VERIFIED — Vatican shelfmark, page count, languages, and medical contents via Wikipedia (Stockholm University and BBC as cited sources); CORROBORATED — the Northern Germany/Scandinavia origin and the ravens-broth recipe via BBC/AzerNEWS, June 2026; CLAIMED — the van Heeck / Montpellier H.505 attribution, Nick Pelling's reading on Cipher Mysteries, 2016, not independently verified this pass]

- **The cipher — 34 signs, and the word lengths given away.** The cipher uses 34 different characters: graphic signs (astrological and alchemical-looking marks among them) plus Roman letters with diacritics. There was no known key. One mercy for the attacker: the encipherer did not bother to disguise word lengths — word boundaries survive in the ciphertext, what the American Cryptogram Association calls an aristocrat cryptogram rather than a patristocrat — so the shape of the plaintext leaks through the symbols. An early hand attempt (Pelling, 2016) transcribed folios and ran them through a solver, and the solver said no: not Latin, not Italian, not Dutch — the failure was not the tool but the plaintext, 17th-century Latin used very differently from Caesar's, which the same tool decrypted with ease. The alphabet was recoverable almost in full by hand once the patterns were seen; the hard part was never the substitution, it was the language underneath it. [VERIFIED — the 34-character count and the graphic-signs-plus-diacritics composition via Wikipedia; CORROBORATED — the undisguised word lengths and the solver's failure on 17th-century Latin via Pelling's first-party account; CLAIMED — the exact "almost all of the alphabet by hand" extent, Pelling's own report]

- **The break — 2016, by machine translation, not by a key.** The Borg was decoded in 2016 by Nada Aldarrab, Kevin Knight, and Beata Megyesi, applying statistics-based translation techniques — the same machinery that had cracked the Copiale cipher — to the manuscript's symbols. No key was ever found; the cipher fell to language modelling over the symbol stream, the way a translation system learns a language it has never seen written in that script. The decoded text turned out to be the medical compendium described above: thousands of 17th-century treatments, of little medical value today and considerable historical value — a window into what late-medieval and early-modern medicine actually prescribed. The 2026 news is not a new break: the DESCRYPT chatbot re-decoded a 500-symbol extract of the already-solved Borg in just over 29 minutes, against weeks of manual work, and the honest reading (filed in the DESCRYPT note) is tool speed on known-plaintext ground truth — the tool earns its keep only when it produces a first reading of something still unread. [CORROBORATED — the 2016 decipherment, the three decoders, and the translation-technique method via Wikipedia (Stockholm University / ICDAR 2019 as cited sources) and the BBC, May–June 2026; the DESCRYPT 29-minute figure per the filed DESCRYPT note]

- **Decoder-design note (Borg → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The key is not the only way in.** The Borg fell with no key ever found — the attack was a language model over the symbol stream, not a key recovery. A specimen whose key is unrecoverable is not therefore unbreakable: the Gauntlet asks what the plaintext's language looks like before it asks where the key is hidden, and a specimen whose symbol stream carries a natural language's statistics is already half-open. (2) **Word lengths are a confession.** The encipherer left word boundaries visible, and every boundary is a free constraint on the plaintext — the solver's search space collapses by the shape of the words alone. A specimen that preserves any structural metadata — lengths, gaps, punctuation, timing — has handed the interrogator a skeleton to fit the flesh to, and the Gauntlet's first read of any ciphertext is its shape, before a single symbol is attacked. (3) **The solver can be right about the cipher and wrong about the language.** Pelling's tool failed on the Borg not because the cipher was strong but because its model of Latin was two thousand years out of date — 17th-century Latin is not Caesar's. A specimen's plaintext is a language with a date on it, and an interrogator who brings the wrong century's model will fail on a trivial cipher and blame the cipher. The Gauntlet grades its own language models alongside the specimen: a failed break is reported with the model that failed, not as a verdict on the cipher. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's own doctrine, never run.]

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the Vatican shelfmark MSS-Borg.lat.898, the 408-page count, the Arabic first page / Latin fragments / Italian last pages, the medical-recipe contents, and the 34-character graphic-signs-plus-diacritics composition; CORROBORATED — the 2016 decipherment by Aldarrab, Knight, and Megyesi, the translation-technique method, the Northern Germany/Scandinavia origin, the ravens-broth recipe, the undisguised word lengths, and the solver's failure on 17th-century Latin; CLAIMED — the van Heeck / Montpellier H.505 attribution and the hand-recovery extent; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run. ## Rongorongo (Rapa Nui) — the script that may be writing's fifth invention, or: the island that forgot how to read

- **The gap this entry closes.** Rongorongo is the catalogue's named-but-unwritten undeciphered script: the last two runs' "Next:" lines name it first among the remaining gaps, the UNDECIPHERED watch-list carries it only as a one-line table row ("Unsolved") and a passing mention in the Byblos entry, and grep-verified this pass the catalogue carries zero mentions of "Rongorongo" anywhere — no entry, no footnote, no aside. Phaistos Disc shares the gap and stays named for the next run. This entry writes Rongorongo. [VERIFIED — the grep; the "Next:" lines in the research log]

- **The corpus — two dozen wooden objects, none left on the island.** Twenty-six commonly accepted texts survive — the 2024 radiocarbon paper counts twenty-seven inscribed objects, and the count varies by scholar, 25 to 27. Most are flat tablets of irregular wood, sometimes driftwood, plus the Santiago Staff — a 126-cm chieftain's baton, the longest single text in the corpus — a bird-man statuette, and two reimiro chest ornaments. They are scattered in museums and private collections — Rome, London, Paris, Berlin, Washington, Santiago — and none remain on Easter Island. Only half are in good condition and authentic beyond doubt. The name is Rapanui roŋoroŋo — "to recite," "to chant out." The script was first noticed by outsiders in 1864, when the missionary Eugène Eyraud reported the tablets; writing had already ceased, and most tablets were lost or destroyed in the 1860s — the slave raids that carried off the island's learned men, then the missionary salvage that carried the survivors abroad. [VERIFIED — the 26-text count, the object types, the 1864 first notice, the 1860s loss; CORROBORATED — the 27-object count, the museum scatter, the "only half in good condition," the Eyraud attribution, the slave-raid cause]

- **The shape — reverse boustrophedon, and a sign list nobody agrees on.** Rongorongo is read bottom-to-top, left-to-right, rotating the tablet 180 degrees at the end of every line — reverse boustrophedon, the reader turning the wood like an ox turning at the field's edge. In a third of the tablets the lines sit in shallow fluting carved into the wood. The glyphs are outlines of human, animal, plant, artifact, and geometric forms, often joined into compounds. The sign inventory itself is disputed, which is the first problem any decipherer faces: Barthel's 1958 catalogue lists 632 sign shapes, which he parsed to about 120 basic glyphs; Pozdniakov reduced the inventory to 52 base glyphs covering 99.7% of tokens; Horley (2021) proposes 130 basic shapes. The classic corpus runs to roughly 15,000 glyphs — 14,906 across tablets A–S by the 2026 preprint count. [VERIFIED — the reading direction, the fluting, Barthel's 632 shapes and ~120 parse; CORROBORATED — the Pozdniakov 52, the Horley 130, the corpus size]

- **The two things that are known — a calendar and a genealogy.** Two passages have survived every challenge. In the mid-1950s Butinov and Knorozov, reading the small Santiago tablet, noticed triadic groups — every block of three glyphs beginning with the same sign, then a name, then a patronymic with a regular tail-like suffix — the shape of a genealogy. And Barthel spotted that two and a half lines of Tablet C, the Mamari tablet, read as a lunar calendar — a list of the nights of the moon; Guy (1990) developed it as an intercalation tool, a way to calculate when extra nights must be added to the month, and Valério (2024) calls the list an "artificial bilingual," the closest thing the corpus has to a Rosetta Stone. Nothing else is read: no continuous sentence of rongorongo has ever won general agreement, and whether the signs encode spoken Rapanui at all — full writing, or a mnemonic that cues a recitation learned by heart — is still open. [CORROBORATED — the genealogy pattern and the Mamari calendar; VERIFIED — no accepted continuous reading]

- **The 2024 date — wood older than contact.** Ferrara and colleagues, *Scientific Reports* 2024 (DOI 10.1038/s41598-024-53063-7), radiocarbon-dated four tablets held in Rome. Tablet D, the Échancrée, is wood of 1493–1509 CE — more than two centuries before Europeans reached the island in 1722; the other three are nineteenth-century wood (Tahua is European ash). The date is on the wood, not the carving — a fifteenth-century board can carry a nineteenth-century inscription — but it moves the invention question: the script could predate outside influence, which would make Rapa Nui one of only a handful of independent inventions of writing in human history, beside Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, and Mesoamerica. [CORROBORATED — the peer-reviewed dates and the wood identifications; the medium-vs-message caveat is this entry's own filing]

- **The claims that did not stick — and the 2026 preprint flood.** Steven Roger Fischer (1997) proposed the Santiago Staff records a creation chant in triadic procreation formulas; Guy and Pozdniakov showed the statistical patterns he identified arise from the script's structure rather than any specific content, and the field did not accept it. Davletshin (2012, 2022) proposed syllabic readings for individual glyphs by logogram substitution; no consensus followed. The 2026 preprint flood claims more: ALBA (March 2026) proposes 48 phonetic signs covering 93.6% of the classic corpus, and "Reading Rongorongo" (March 2026) an 89-entry dictionary covering 96.9% of tokens — both self-published, self-classified exploratory, neither peer-reviewed, and as of October 2026 no widely accepted continuous reading exists. A preprint proposing a solution is not a replicated decipherment. [CLAIMED — the Fischer, Davletshin, and 2026 preprint claims as claims; CORROBORATED — their non-acceptance, per the October 2026 survey]

- **Decoder-design note (Rongorongo → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The inventory is the first cipher.** Before any reading, the interrogator must decide what counts as a sign — Barthel's 120 against Pozdniakov's 52 against Horley's 130 is a two-and-a-half-fold disagreement on the alphabet itself. A specimen whose symbol inventory is disputed is graded on inventory discipline first: every claimed reading must name its sign list, and a reading that changes its inventory mid-attack is three readings, not one. (2) **One bilingual is worth a thousand statistics.** The Mamari calendar is the corpus's only anchor — a passage whose function is known before its reading. The Gauntlet's rule for undeciphered corpora: find the anchor first and grade every claimed reading against it before anything else; a reading that cannot reproduce the calendar is not a reading of the corpus, and a reading that reproduces only the calendar has proved one passage, not the script. (3) **Date the medium, not the message.** The 2024 radiocarbon dates date the wood, not the carving. A specimen's age claim must name what was dated — medium, ink, carving — and what it bounds; a date on the wrong layer is a false antiquity, and the Gauntlet treats any claim that slides from "the wood is old" to "the writing is old" as an undeclared inference, graded as one. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's own doctrine, never run.]
