## Phaistos Disc (Crete, ~1700 BCE) — the stamped spiral that may not be a text at all

- **The gap this entry closes.** Phaistos Disc is the catalogue's last named-but-unwritten undeciphered script: grep-verified this pass, the name appears exactly once in each catalogue file — inside the Rongorongo entry's gap line, naming it as the next gap — and the UNDECIPHERED watch-list carries it only as a one-line table row ("Unsolved"), a passing mention in the watch-list's script survey, and the Unicode block note (U+101D0–U+101FF, Unicode 5.1). No entry, no footnote, no aside. This entry writes it. [VERIFIED — the grep; the "Next:" lines in the research log]

- **The corpus — one disc, no relatives.** Found July 3, 1908, by the Italian archaeologist Luigi Pernier in a basement storage room of the Minoan palace at Phaistos, on the south coast of Crete — room 8, building 101, northeast of the main palace — half-buried among charred bones and ashes, beside fragments of a Linear A tablet. A disc of fired clay, about 15–16 cm across and about 2.1 cm thick, stamped on both sides and fired to permanence; it now sits in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum. No other example of the script has ever been found: the corpus is one object, and every claim about the script is a claim about this disc alone. [VERIFIED — the date, the finder, the find-spot, the dimensions, the museum; CORROBORATED — the charred-bones deposit and the Linear A tablet found beside it]

- **The shape — a spiral stamped with movable type.** The disc carries 241 readable tokens — 122 on side A, 119 on side B — of 45 distinct sign types, grouped into 61 "words" (31 on A, 30 on B) by short vertical strokes; some counts give 242, the extra token an overstruck sign read differently by different scholars. The signs are pictographs — humans, animals, plants, tools — and they were not drawn: each distinct sign was pressed into the wet clay with its own pre-made punch, the earliest known instance of movable-type-like impression in writing. The spiral runs rim-to-centre and is conventionally read outside-in (groups numbered A1–A31, B1–B30 from the edge inward), though the reading direction itself is contested. Unicode 5.1 encodes the 45 signs at U+101D0–U+101FF. [VERIFIED — the counts, the 61 groups, the stamping, the Unicode block; CORROBORATED — the movable-type characterization, the outside-in convention, the 242nd token]

- **The count problem — Barber's wall.** In 1974 Elizabeth Barber proved mathematically that 241 tokens of 45 sign types is an insufficient corpus to verify any linguistic decipherment by statistical methods: the lock may not exist, and no statistics on this disc alone can prove a reading. There is no bilingual, no second specimen, and no agreed language family. The script matches neither Linear A — the contemporaneous Minoan administrative script, itself undeciphered but extensively attested — nor Linear B, deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952, nor Cretan hieroglyphic; whether the signs are a syllabary, a logography, or an alphabet is assumed by each claimant, not shown. Louis Godart concluded in 1995 that decipherment may never be achieved. [CORROBORATED — Barber, Godart; VERIFIED — no bilingual, no second specimen, the Linear A/B distinction]

- **The claims that did not stick — and the 2026 trade-directory claim.** Wolfgang Reczko (2009) proposed a solar-eclipse calendar; Gareth Owens (2014) claimed a Minoan-language reading, a hymn to a mother goddess; a 2026 self-published analysis argues the disc is not a text at all but a database — a maritime trade directory, its 61 groups aligning with the roughly 55–65 confirmed sites of the Minoan trade network — and reads the positional distribution (only 19 of the 45 signs ever appear in first position) as field structure, not language. None of these has survived peer review, and no two independent researchers have converged on the same reading. A 2008 forgery claim was rejected by the consensus of working Minoan archaeologists: the excavation record, the Linear A tablet found beside the disc, and the scribe's own corrections — signs erased and re-impressed, which no forger would need — all point the other way. Thermoluminescence dating of the disc has never been performed. [CLAIMED — the Reczko, Owens, and 2026 readings as claims; CORROBORATED — their non-acceptance and the forgery-claim rejection]

- **Decoder-design note (Phaistos → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **One specimen is not a corpus.** n = 1 document, 241 tokens. The Gauntlet's rule for single-specimen corpora: every statistical claim must declare its sample size up front, and any "decipherment" verified only against the same 241 tokens that produced it is a fit, not a proof — Barber's wall is the pass bar, and a claim that does not clear it is graded as a pattern, never a reading. (2) **The stamp is the only ground truth.** The punches are physical tools with a stamping order, and the disc carries its own corrections — signs erased and re-impressed. A claimed reading that ignores which signs were overstruck, in what order, and where the corrections cluster has skipped the one layer of the specimen that cannot be argued with; the Gauntlet grades a reading against the correction map before the sign list. (3) **The medium is not the message.** Movable-type stamping is a fact about manufacture, not about language. A claim that slides from "stamped with type" to "therefore a printed text" — or from the spiral's geometry to a calendar, a directory, or a game board — has imported its conclusion; the Gauntlet separates how it was made from what it says and grades each on its own evidence. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's own doctrine, never run.]

## Cicada 3301 (2012– ) — the internet's recruitment puzzle, or: the test that never named its maker

- **The gap this entry closes.** Cicada 3301 is the catalogue's most-cited unwritten puzzle: grep-verified this pass, the name appears exactly once in each catalogue file — inside the steganography entry's tool lineage ("OutGuess (Cicada 3301's 2012–14 chain used it for image stego)") — and the UNDECIPHERED watch-list carries it only as a one-line table row ("~55 of ~75 pages unsolved; 2012/13 chains solved") plus a short note. No entry, no footnote, no aside. This entry writes it. [VERIFIED — the grep; the UNDECIPHERED table row]

- **The first winter — 2012: the image, the duck, the posters.** On 4 January 2012 (some accounts say 5 January) a black image with white text appeared on 4chan, signed only "3301": it was looking for "highly intelligent individuals" and promised a message hidden in the image. OutGuess steganography pulled a Caesar cipher out of it, which decoded to an image of a duck — "Woops! Just decoys this way" — whose own hidden layer pointed to the subreddit r/a2e7j6ic78h0j and a book cipher keyed to the medieval Welsh Mabinogion. The book cipher gave a Dallas phone number, (214) 390-9608, whose recorded message named three primes; two were the original image's own dimensions, 509 × 503, and with 3301 they multiplied to 845145127 — a website with a cicada image and a countdown. When the countdown ended at 17:00 UTC on Monday 9 January 2012, the site posted GPS coordinates: 14 physical poster locations across the world — Warsaw, Paris, Seoul, Sydney, Seattle, New Orleans, Hawaii, Moscow, Miami, and more — each poster bearing the cicada emblem and a QR code, each code leading on through further book ciphers (William Gibson's Agrippa, Crowley's Liber AL vel Legis) to a Tor hidden service and a final message. The handful who finished were contacted by email in February 2012; what they were told next has never been published in verified form. [CORROBORATED — the chain as reconstructed across multiple secondary accounts; the 4/5 January date variance filed, not resolved]

- **The second and third winters — 2013 and 2014: the books get harder.** A second image appeared on 4 January 2013 (some accounts say 5 January): a book cipher keyed to Crowley's Liber AL vel Legis, an MP3 credited to 3301 that opens with the sound of cicadas ("The Instar Emergence"), a bootable Linux disc, a table turning Anglo-Saxon runes into numbers, and new posters from Dallas to Moscow to Okinawa. Marcus Wanner — a teenager from near Roanoke, Virginia, who had finished the 2012 round — was the first to solve the 2013 round. The third round opened on Twitter in the first week of January 2014 ("Hello. Epiphany is upon you. Your pilgrimage has begun. Enlightenment awaits." — 4 January by Wikipedia's dating, 5–6 January by other accounts): its first step hid a book code keyed to Ralph Waldo Emerson's essay "Self-Reliance" (paragraph, sentence, word, letter), a later step a collage of William Blake's art, and the trail moved into runes read with a key released the year before. [CORROBORATED — the round structure and the Wanner solve; the January date variance filed, not resolved]

- **The Liber Primus — the book that stopped the hunt.** At the end of 2014 came the Liber Primus ("First Book"): a book of runes, released as the third round's final layer. Two of its pages were solved almost at once; the rest have not been read. The page count itself is disputed — the solvers' own count, given at DEF CON in August 2023, is 58 pages with 56 still unread after nine years; other accounts give 74 or 75 pages, with ~55–56 unread — and this entry files the discrepancy rather than picking a number: the book circulated in different paginations, and no single count is settled. What is settled is that no new round has followed the 2014 puzzle, by the solvers' own account, and the Liber Primus remains the hunt's open remainder. [CORROBORATED — the DEF CON 2023 solvers' count; CLAIMED — the 74/75-page counts as reported counts, with the variance filed]

- **The signature and the silence — the only ground truth the puzzle ever offered.** Every genuine clue carried a signature from the same OpenPGP key, 7A35090F, whose identity line reads "Cicada 3301 (845145127)" — the product of the first puzzle's own primes. In January 2016 the same Twitter account posted one more signed image ("Liber Primus is the way... its words are the map, their meaning the road, and their numbers the direction"), and on 29 April 2017 a user in the #cicadasolvers IRC channel found the last verified message, signed 4 April 2017: "Beware false paths. Always verify PGP signature from 7A35090F." An unsigned image pointing to Mojave Desert coordinates, posted to 4chan in early 2017, was treated as fake by the solvers for want of that signature. As of October 2026, no credible report of a newly signed message since April 2017, no confirmed identity, and no one who has proven authorship by signing with the key. The US Navy's 2014 Project Architeuthis copied the concept as a recruitment challenge — the puzzle's form, borrowed by the institution it was most often suspected of being. [CORROBORATED — the key, the 2016 and 2017 messages, the unsigned Mojave fake, the Architeuthis copy]

- **Decoder-design note (Cicada → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The signature is the specimen.** Cicada is the catalogue's cleanest intake test: a clue is genuine if and only if it verifies against 7A35090F — no provenance, no reputation, no plausibility substitutes. The Gauntlet's intake rule is the solvers' rule: unsigned is fake until signed, and a puzzle that arrives without its key is not a puzzle, it is a rumour wearing the puzzle's clothes. (2) **A solved round is not a solved puzzle.** 2012 and 2013 closed; 2014 did not — the Liber Primus is a separate specimen with its own verdict, and the rounds' solved status never transfers. The Gauntlet grades each layer on its own evidence and never lets a closed neighbour retire an open book. (3) **Grade the artifact, not the mythology.** Intelligence-agency recruitment, ARG, occult order — every theory of who built Cicada is SPECULATION, and the Gauntlet refuses the question: the specimen is the chain of ciphers, the posters, and the book, and its verdict is about what the chain does, not who laid it. A recruitment puzzle that never recruited anyone in public is still a cipher specimen; its silence is data about the specimen, not a hole to fill with a story. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's own doctrine, never run.]

## One-Time Pad (1917– ) — the cipher that cannot be broken and cannot be used, or: the secret that costs as much as the message

- **The gap this entry closes.** The one-time pad is the catalogue's most-cited unwritten cipher: grep-verified this pass, the phrase appears 15 times in the private catalogue and 14 in the public one, and every occurrence is a passing mention — the timeline's one-line note ("Shannon 1949: provably secure *if* pad is truly random, as long as the message, and used once"), the Venona entry's account of the pad's reuse, and a handful of cross-references. No entry, no footnote, no aside. The only cipher in the history of cryptography with a mathematical proof of unbreakability has no entry of its own. This entry writes it. [VERIFIED — the grep counts; the timeline line; the Venona entry]

- **The construction, and the four conditions that make it perfect.** A one-time pad encrypts by combining each plaintext symbol with a key symbol of equal length — modular addition on paper tapes, XOR in the modern telling — and the recipient combines again with the identical key to recover the message. That is the whole mechanism, and its security rests on four non-negotiable conditions: the key must be truly random; it must be at least as long as the message; it must remain completely secret; and every part of it must be used once, and only once. When all four hold, Claude Shannon's 1949 proof ("Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems") shows the ciphertext carries zero information about the plaintext — observing it does not change the attacker's probabilities for any possible original message. No amount of computing power, present or future, can break it, because there is nothing to compute: every possible plaintext of the same length is equally consistent with the same ciphertext. It is the only cipher in the catalogue with a proof of that strength, and the proof is information-theoretic, not computational — it does not depend on any hardness assumption surviving. [VERIFIED — the construction, the four conditions, and Shannon's 1949 perfect-secrecy proof, per multiple independent secondary sources this pass]

- **Vernam, Mauborgne, Shannon — three men, thirty-two years.** Gilbert Vernam, an engineer at AT&T, built the machine first: an automated teleprinter system combining the electrical representation of each character with a key tape, patented as US 1,310,719 (filed 1918, granted 1919), developed from 1917 work on securing teletype traffic. Vernam's tape was a key stream, but not yet a *random* one, and reuse was not yet forbidden. The decisive refinement came from Joseph Mauborgne of the US Army Signal Corps, credited alongside Vernam with the modern system in 1919: the key sequence must be genuinely random, and no part of it may ever be used twice — hence the name, and hence the pad: printed sheets of random digits, one page per message, torn off and burned after use. Thirty years later Shannon supplied what neither inventor had: the proof. His 1949 paper formalised perfect secrecy and showed the pad achieves it — and, by the same mathematics, that no cipher can achieve it with a key shorter than the message. The key must cost as much as the message, in length and in delivery, and that cost is the whole story of why the perfect cipher is almost never used. [VERIFIED — Vernam's 1917 development and the 1918/1919 patent dates, Mauborgne's 1919 random-and-never-reuse refinement, Shannon's 1949 proof; CORROBORATED — that no other cipher carries a comparable proof, per the standard secondary carriers]

- **Venona — the break that was not a break.** The one-time pad has never been broken. It has been *misused*, once, at scale, and the misuse is the most instructive failure in the catalogue. The full account sits in the timeline's Venona entry; the shape, in brief: under wartime pressure the Soviet pad producer generated some 35,000 pages of duplicated key, and duplicates were shipped to widely separated users. In 1944 Arlington Hall analysts isolated the "depth of two" — two messages encrypted under the same pad page — and the key cancelled out of the difference, leaving the XOR of two plaintexts for statistics and cribs to pick apart. Meredith Gardner read the first KGB message in February 1946; about 2,200 translations were eventually published, and KGB New York-to-Moscow traffic for 1944 was about 49% readable. The decrypts exposed the atomic spy rings — Klaus Fuchs, the Rosenbergs, Harry Gold — and the program ran, declassified, until the NSA released it in 1995. The algorithm was never at fault; the production control was. A one-time pad reused even once is not a weakened one-time pad. It is a different, breakable system that happens to look like one. [VERIFIED — the Venona figures and dates, as already filed in the timeline entry from NSA sources]

- **The hotline, and the deployments that survived the cost.** The deployments that worked are the ones where the cost was payable. The Moscow–Washington hotline, established in 1963 after the Cuban Missile Crisis, ran its first years on one-time tapes delivered through each side's embassy — a commercial machine, deliberately, so neither side had to reveal its high-grade ciphers to the other. Field agents carried paper pads through the Cold War, one page per message, burned after use. Numbers stations — the shortwave broadcasts of digit groups that still run today — are widely reported to carry one-time-pad traffic, the pad delivered by courier before the broadcast ever airs. Every deployment shares the same shape: the key travels first, by hand, over a channel already trusted, and the message follows later, over a channel that need not be. The pad does not remove the security problem. It relocates it, from the message to the key. [CORROBORATED — the 1963 hotline's one-time tapes and the commercial-machine choice, the paper-pad field practice, and the numbers-station use, per multiple secondary sources; the relocation framing is this entry's own]

- **The price, stated plainly.** Three costs, and one missing property. First, length: a gigabyte of message requires a gigabyte of key material, generated, stored, and delivered in advance — the key-distribution problem in its purest form, with no public-key shortcut, because encrypting the pad with another pad restates the problem. Second, custody: both ends need matching copies, delivered and stored without interception, copying, substitution, corruption, or loss, and every copy is a single point of total failure — whoever holds the pad can read everything and can forge everything. Third, the pad provides confidentiality and nothing else: it does not authenticate the sender and does not protect the integrity of the ciphertext. A malicious intermediary can flip bits in transit without either party noticing — the rewrite attack — because the pad carries no check on what it encrypts. And the boundary that matters most for the decoder: a keystream generated pseudorandomly from a short key is a stream cipher, not a one-time pad. The moment the key is shorter than the message, the proof dies, whatever the keystream's quality. Quantum key distribution is the modern attempt at the delivery problem — physics, not couriers, carrying the key — but it solves distribution, not length, not custody, and not authentication. [VERIFIED — the length cost, the custody requirement, the no-authentication/no-integrity property and the rewrite attack, and the stream-cipher boundary, per multiple secondary sources this pass; CLAIMED — quantum key distribution as the modern delivery attempt, a framing claim, not a deployment claim]

- **Decoder-design note (One-Time Pad → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Grade the key, not the cipher.** The mechanism is proven; there is nothing to attack in it, and the Gauntlet wastes no run on the mathematics. Interrogation targets the four conditions, and each is a falsifiable check: randomness (statistical tests on the key material), length (the key audit — a key shorter than the message is a different specimen), reuse (the depth scan — any two ciphertexts sharing key material re-grade the specimen on the spot), and custody (the chain-of-hands — who touched the pad, and when). A specimen that passes all four has nothing left to grade on secrecy, and the card says so. (2) **A two-time pad is a different specimen.** Reuse does not weaken the one-time pad; it converts it. The Gauntlet re-grades a reused pad as the system it has become — a depth-two additive stream with a reused keystream — and never lets the specimen keep the "unbreakable" label while standing on reused material. Venona is the standing example: the verdict on the cipher stayed VERIFIED while the verdict on the deployment failed, and the card carries both, separately. (3) **Perfect secrecy is not total security.** A specimen claiming "unbreakable" must state which property it claims, and the card grades the claimed property only. The pad's silence on authentication and integrity is not a flaw in the proof; it is a boundary on the claim. Any specimen that borrows the pad's aura — "unbreakable," "quantum-proof," "mathematically proven" — while selling a property the pad never promised is borrowing a verdict it has not earned, and the Fabrication Alarm fires on the borrowing, not on the mathematics. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run.]

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the grep gap (15 private / 14 public passing mentions, no entry), the construction and the four conditions, Shannon's 1949 perfect-secrecy proof, Vernam's 1917 development and US 1,310,719 (filed 1918, granted 1919), Mauborgne's 1919 random-and-never-reuse refinement, the Venona figures and dates as already filed from NSA sources, the length and custody costs, the no-authentication/no-integrity property and the rewrite attack, and the stream-cipher boundary; CORROBORATED — that no other cipher carries a comparable proof, the 1963 hotline's one-time tapes and commercial-machine choice, the paper-pad field practice, and the numbers-station use; CLAIMED — quantum key distribution as the modern delivery attempt; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run.]*

## Chaocipher (1918–2010) — the cipher that won on secrecy alone, or: the machine that mangled its own key

- **The gap this entry closes.** Chaocipher is the catalogue's most-cited unwritten cipher after the pad: grep-verified this pass, the name appears 7 times in the private catalogue and 5 in the public one, and every occurrence is a passing mention — the §(a) bullet that carries the whole story in miniature, and cross-references from the Kryha, SIGABA, Jefferson-disk, Playfair, and frequency-hopping entries. No full entry, no construction, no disclosure account. The cipher that survived ninety years on secrecy alone has no entry of its own. This entry writes it. [VERIFIED — the grep counts; the §(a) bullet; the cross-references]

- **The machine: two disks that rewrite themselves.** The Chaocipher is a hand machine of two disks, left and right, each carrying the 26 letters around its rim on removable tabs in a prearranged order — small enough, in Byrne's telling, to fit in a cigar box, and simple enough that "any person on earth" could use one. To encipher a letter: find the plaintext letter on the right disk and read the ciphertext letter off the left disk at the aligned position. Then, before the next letter, both alphabets are re-permuted by fixed rules — the left disk rotates to the ciphertext letter just produced and cycles its letters from the second position to the fourteenth, the right disk rotates to the plaintext letter and cycles its own span — so the cipher mangled its own key as it worked. Byrne's own terms for the anchor positions were *zenith* (first) and *nadir* (fourteenth). The consequence is the whole design: repeated plaintext never produces repeated ciphertext, because the alphabet that enciphered the first occurrence no longer exists by the second. It is dynamic substitution in mechanical form — the key is not a fixed mapping but a state, and the state moves on every letter. [VERIFIED — the two-disk construction, the locate-and-read step, and the per-letter permutation of both alphabets, per Rubin's July 2010 disclosure paper and the Wikipedia entry; CORROBORATED — the cigar-box size and the "any person on earth" claim, as filed in the §(a) bullet]

- **Byrne, the prizes, and ninety years of silence.** John Francis Byrne invented the Chaocipher in 1918 and spent more than three decades trying, unsuccessfully, to interest the US Signal Corps and the Navy in it. Frustrated, he published four challenge messages in his autobiography *Silent Years* (1953) — large amounts of plain and matching ciphertext, but never a description of the enciphering process — to bear out his contention that the system was "absolutely indecipherable," with cash prizes for a solution. (Rubin's disclosure paper dates the challenge presentation to 1954; the carriers disagree by a year, and the year is not load-bearing.) Nobody claimed the prize — not in the three months of the challenge, nor in the fifty-five years after it. Numerous professional cryptanalysts failed against the exhibits; whether official government agencies ever succeeded is unknown, on Rubin's own record. The first exhibit alone ran to 13,615 letters of ciphertext. For roughly ninety years the algorithm was a closely guarded secret known only to a handful of people, and the cipher's resistance was total — because nobody could see the machine. [VERIFIED — the 1918 invention, the failed approaches to the Signal Corps and Navy, *Silent Years*, the four challenge exhibits, and the 13,615-letter first exhibit, per Rubin 2010 and Cowan 2010; CORROBORATED — the unclaimed prizes and the failed professional attempts, per the same carriers]

- **The disclosure, and the break that followed in months.** In August 2009 Moshe Rubin located Byrne's daughter-in-law, Patricia Byrne; in May 2010 she donated all Chaocipher-related papers and artifacts to the National Cryptologic Museum at Ft. Meade. On July 2, 2010 Rubin published the first full public disclosure of the algorithm — "Chaocipher Revealed: The Algorithm" — and within weeks the ninety-year wall fell in pieces: in August 2010 Rubin deciphered Exhibit 1, working from the exhibit's known opening plaintext ("ALLGOODQQUICK…") and the key phrase "THINKTHINK" with its left/right alphabet pattern, deriving the starting wheel states; in December 2010 Michael J. Cowan published computer solutions to Exhibits 1 and 4. Exhibits 2, 3, and 5 remained unsolved at Rubin's writing — a partial break, honestly bounded, not a total one. The shape of the fall is the entry's lesson: ninety years of total resistance, then immediate partial reconstruction within months of disclosure. The defense was never the mechanism's strength. It was the mechanism's invisibility. [VERIFIED — the August 2009 location, the May 2010 donation, Rubin's July 2, 2010 disclosure, the August 2010 Exhibit 1 decipherment with its key phrase and pattern, and Cowan's December 2010 solution of Exhibits 1 and 4, per Rubin 2010 and Cowan 2010; CORROBORATED — that Exhibits 2, 3, and 5 stood unsolved at Rubin's writing]

- **The price, stated plainly.** Three costs, and one broken rule. First, the secrecy was the entire defense: the Chaocipher violates Kerckhoffs's principle in the most absolute form the catalogue holds — not "the key must stay secret" but "the *machine* must stay secret" — and the price of that violation is a cliff, not a slope. A cipher whose strength is its invisibility has no graceful degradation: the day the algorithm is published, the cipher goes from unbreakable to partially broken in weeks. Second, the machine was never adopted, so its field record is zero: its unbreakability was never tested in service, only in challenge, and a challenge the vendor controls is a weaker test than a war. Third, with the algorithm public, the system is weak by modern standards — deterministic per-letter permutation with known plaintext recovers the starting alphabets, exactly as Rubin's reconstruction did, and the key space is the pair of starting alphabets, not a secret the machine protects. The Chaocipher is the catalogue's purest experiment in mechanism secrecy, and the experiment's result is on the record: it works, for as long as the secret holds, and then it stops working all at once. [VERIFIED — the Kerckhoffs violation as a structural claim about the design, and the known-plaintext recovery of the starting alphabets, per Rubin's reconstruction; CLAIMED — "no graceful degradation" as a framing of the disclosure-to-break interval; SPECULATION — the field-record reading, this entry's own]

- **Decoder-design note (Chaocipher → Gauntlet).** Three rungs, growing the §(a) bullet's counter into doctrine. (1) **Self-mangling state dies under single-message analysis and only yields to sequence-level observation.** A specimen whose encoding function changes its own state per output — Chaocipher's wheels, a model's per-turn context, a container that re-keys per session — cannot be graded from one message, however long. The Gauntlet's interrogation of such a specimen is a sequence: many outputs, the state transition inferred from the series, exactly as Rubin's reconstruction worked from multiple exhibits, not one. A single-output fixture against a self-mangling specimen is a fixture that measures nothing. (2) **Mechanism secrecy has an expiry date, and the Gauntlet prices it.** "The algorithm is secret" is never accepted as a security property, only as a delay — and the delay is graded against the clock, not the brochure. Ninety years is a long delay and a short doctrine: the Chaocipher's cliff is the standing example that a secret mechanism is a depreciating asset, and any specimen whose defense is invisibility gets a card that says so, with the disclosure date as the expiry. (3) **The vendor's challenge is a free test protocol — and a partial break is still a break.** Byrne's unclaimed prizes are the Kryha rung's sibling: accept the challenge on the vendor's terms, work it, and return the keys. And the honest remainder matters as much as the break: Exhibits 2, 3, and 5 stood unsolved at Rubin's writing, so the card on the Chaocipher reads "Exhibits 1 and 4 broken, 2, 3, 5 standing" — never "Chaocipher broken" and never "Chaocipher unbroken." A specimen's verdict names exactly what fell and what stands. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run.]

## Kryptos (1990– ) — the artist's cipher in the CIA courtyard, or: the sculpture that was solved everywhere except the last 97 letters

- **The gap this entry closes.** Kryptos is the catalogue's most-cited unwritten cipher after the pad and Chaocipher: grep-verified this pass, the name appears 6 times in the private catalogue and 7 in the public one, and every occurrence is a passing mention — the §(a) bullet that carries the whole story in miniature, and cross-references from the Grille, Taman Shud, Huffman, and Rosetta design notes. No full entry, no construction, no account of the 2025 turn that changed the specimen's status without breaking its cipher. The cipher that held 35 years against the NSA, the CIA, and the world has no entry of its own. This entry writes it. [VERIFIED — the grep counts; the §(a) bullet; the cross-references]

- **The sculpture: a lock with its key carved beside it.** Kryptos — Greek for "hidden" — is an S-shaped copper screen by Washington artist Jim Sanborn, built with retired CIA cryptographer Ed Scheidt, chairman of the CIA's own Cryptographic Center, and dedicated November 3, 1990, in the courtyard of CIA headquarters at Langley, Virginia. The screen carries about 1,800 letters; the ciphertext half, on the left as seen from the courtyard, is 869 characters — 865 letters and 4 question marks — holding four encrypted passages, K1–K4, one after another with no gap between them. The right half is a Vigenère tableau, flipped so it reads correctly only from behind the sculpture: the decode tool carved beside the lock. Sanborn said the sculpture contains a riddle within a riddle, solvable only after all four passages are deciphered — and hinted a fifth coded message will reveal itself then. [VERIFIED — the dedication date, the Scheidt collaboration, the 869-character count, the tableau, the riddle-within-a-riddle, per the Wikipedia entry and the Cipher Museum record]

- **The three solves: three systems, three solvers, one lesson in layers.** K1 is a Vigenère cipher on a KRYPTOS-scrambled alphabet, keyed PALIMPSEST — the word itself a manuscript scraped clean and written over, layers on layers. K2 is Vigenère again, keyed ABSCISSA. K3 is not substitution at all: a transposition that, unshuffled, paraphrases Howard Carter's 1922 account of breaking into Tutankhamun's tomb. The plaintexts: K1, "BETWEEN SUBTLE SHADING AND THE ABSENCE OF LIGHT LIES THE NUANCE OF IQLUSION"; K2, the invisible transmission, the Earth's magnetic field, the buried thing, "DOES LANGLEY KNOW ABOUT THIS? THEY SHOULD ITS BURIED OUT THERE SOMEWHERE X WHO KNOWS THE EXACT LOCATION? ONLY WW THIS WAS HIS LAST MESSAGE X THIRTY EIGHT DEGREES FIFTY SEVEN MINUTES SIX POINT FIVE SECONDS NORTH SEVENTY SEVEN DEGREES EIGHT MINUTES FORTY FOUR SECONDS WEST X LAYER TWO"; K3, "SLOWLY DESPARATELY SLOWLY THE REMAINS OF PASSAGE DEBRIS THAT ENCUMBERED THE LOWER PART OF THE DOORWAY WAS REMOVED WITH TREMBLING HANDS I MADE A TINY BREACH IN THE UPPER LEFT HAND CORNER AND THEN WIDENING THE HOLE A LITTLE I INSERTED THE CANDLE AND PEERED IN THE HOT AIR ESCAPING FROM THE CHAMBER CAUSED THE FLAME TO FLICKER BUT PRESENTLY DETAILS OF THE ROOM WITHIN EMERGED FROM THE MIST X CAN YOU SEE ANYTHING Q?" The misspellings — IQLUSION, UNDERGRUUND, DESPARATLY — are Sanborn's, deliberate. And the last word of K2 is itself a correction: the early readings gave WESTIDBYROWS; in 2006 Sanborn announced he had made an error and confirmed the plaintext reads WESTXLAYERTWO. Three solvers, in order of solving, not of telling: an NSA team led by Ken Miller with Dennis McDaniels and two unnamed analysts cracked all three in late 1992, within a month of Deputy Director William Studeman's formal challenge, and told no one for twenty years — the fact surfaced only in 2013, when Elonka Dunin obtained the NSA documents under FOIA; CIA analyst David Stein solved the same three in 1998 with pencil and paper across some 400 lunch hours, and his account stayed inside the intelligence community until July 1999; California computer scientist Jim Gillogly published the first public solutions in 1999, on a Pentium II. [VERIFIED — the keys, the plaintexts, the three solvers and their dates, the 2006 WESTXLAYERTWO correction, per the Wikipedia entry, the Cipher Museum record, and the NSA FOIA documents]

- **K4: 97 characters, and the system itself unknown.** The fourth passage is the whole specimen now: `OBKRUOXOGHULBSOLIFBBWFLRVQQPRNGKSSOTWTQSJQSSEKZZWATJKLUDIAWINFBNYPVTTMZFPKWGDKZXTJCDIGKUHUAUEKCAR` — 97 letters, verified this pass by count. The declassified NSA summary describes a fairly flat letter distribution with no long repeats, and reports autokey attempts without readable results. What makes K4 different from every other unsolved entry in this catalogue is that the artist kept handing over pieces of the answer, and the pieces did not help: in 2010 Sanborn revealed that positions 64–69 — ciphertext `NYPVTT` — decrypt to BERLIN; in 2014, positions 70–74 — `MZFPK` — decrypt to CLOCK; in 2020, positions 22–25 decrypt to EAST and positions 26–34 to NORTHEAST, which Sanborn said would be the last clue. Roughly a quarter of the plaintext, position-anchored, handed over free — and the system still would not crack, because nobody has identified the cipher system itself. In November 2025, at the International Spy Museum, Sanborn added that the clock is Berlin's World Clock, and that two events figure in the solution: a 1986 trip he took to Egypt, and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989. [VERIFIED — the 97-character count and ciphertext, the flat distribution and failed autokey attempts per the NSA summary, the four clue releases and their positions, the November 2025 Spy Museum framing, per the Wikipedia entry and the October 2026 status check]

- **The 2025 turn: the break that wasn't a break.** On August 14, 2025, Sanborn published an open letter saying he would sell the K4 plaintext that November, near his 80th birthday. In September 2025, journalists Jarett Kobek and Richard Byrne found scraps of the K4 plaintext sitting in Sanborn's papers at the Smithsonian's Archives of American Art — misfiled years earlier during Sanborn's cancer treatment — not cryptanalysis, found in a box. Sanborn confirmed the scraps genuine and asked that they stay sealed; the Smithsonian agreed to seal the files for 50 years. On November 20, 2025, Sanborn's full Kryptos archive — the solution, the encryption tables, a prototype — sold at RR Auction for $962,500, against a $300,000–500,000 estimate, to an anonymous bidder; in June 2026 the venture firm Paradigm disclosed it was the buyer and launched a public Kryptos site with a ten-puzzle capture-the-flag challenge at $1,000 per solved puzzle. The specimen's status as of this writing: K4's plaintext is known to a small number of people and has never been published; the cipher itself has still never been broken by analysis. A July 2025 Zenodo paper claims a complete cryptogeographic solution — coordinates 38°57'06.9"N 77°08'44.6"W, timestamp 23:51 on November 9, 1989, the fall of the Berlin Wall — but the record as checked October 26, 2026 establishes no published, reproducible cryptanalytic solution, and the claim stands unreproduced. [CORROBORATED — the open letter, the Smithsonian find, the sealing, the auction price and buyer, per AP/RR Auction/Washington Post reporting as filed in the §(a) bullet and the October 2026 status check; CLAIMED — the July 2025 Zenodo solution, unreproduced]

- **Decoder-design note (Kryptos → Gauntlet).** Four rungs, growing the §(a) note's four into doctrine. (1) **The last layer changes the instrument.** K1 and K2 are Vigenère; K3 is transposition; K4 is something else entirely — three different systems in one specimen, and the solver who assumes K4 is Vigenère-with-another-key has already lost. Gauntlet standing rule: a specimen that yields in layers never promises the next layer uses the last layer's method. Re-derive the system class per layer; never inherit it. The Gauntlet's layering discipline is the Kryptos discipline: each chamber of a foreign specimen gets its own system identification, and a method that worked in chamber one is a hypothesis in chamber two, never a premise. (2) **Cribs are a budget, not a break.** Sanborn handed over roughly a quarter of K4's plaintext, position-anchored — BERLIN, CLOCK, EAST, NORTHEAST — and the system still would not crack, because cribs price the plaintext, not the mechanism. Gauntlet rule: known-plaintext is priced against the unknown system. A crib that does not name the system is calibration data, and a specimen that survives its own cribs has told you the mechanism is the unknown, not the message. (3) **Custody is the cipher's other flank.** K4's plaintext fell to an archive search, not cryptanalysis — the artist's own papers, misfiled during cancer treatment, sealed for 50 years, then auctioned for $962,500. Gauntlet rule, the §(a) note's third rung sharpened: interrogate the specimen's custody chain with the same rigor as its encoding. The leak that breaks a specimen is usually a filing error, not a mathematical one — and a sealed archive is embargoed knowledge, logged on the record as known-but-withheld, never pretended unknown, never treated as a break. (4) **A claimed solution is graded, not believed.** The July 2025 Zenodo paper claims the complete answer — coordinates, timestamp, event — four months before the archive sale, and the record as of October 2026 establishes no published, reproducible cryptanalytic solution. Gauntlet rule: a solution claim without a reproducible method is CLAIMED, and stays CLAIMED until the method reproduces. The auction price is not evidence, the author's confidence is not evidence, and the coordinates matching the Berlin Wall's fall is a consistency check, not a verification. ## Rasterschlüssel 44 (1944– ) — the hand cipher that beat the clock, or: the grille that won by being too slow to break

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue holds the turning grille as a family — Fleissner, Richelieu, the WWI German grids — and it holds the Enigma, the Lorenz, and the double transposition as deployed wartime systems. It does not hold the one hand cipher the Allies rated the hardest field system they faced: grep-verified this pass, "Rasterschlüssel" has zero hits in the private catalogue and zero in the public one, and "Fricke" has zero in both. The grille family's deployed apex — the cipher that was introduced in the war's last year precisely because the systems it replaced had gone soft — has no entry of its own. This entry writes it. [VERIFIED — the grep counts]

- **The machine: a grille with a moving start.** Rasterschlüssel 44 (RS 44) is a transposition cipher built on a stencil — a raster. The cipher block is a grid of 25 columns and 24 rows, 600 cells. Each row holds 10 white cells, placed at random, and 15 black cells: 240 writing cells in all. The day's raster pattern — which cells are white — is the shared key of the day, issued to cipher clerks for the current day and at most two days in advance. The per-message secret is not the pattern. It is the start: the cipher clerk chooses, for every message, a starting cell and a first column, and those two choices are the message key. Enciphering runs in two passes: the plaintext is written line by line into the white cells, beginning at the chosen start cell; then the ciphertext is taken out column by column, beginning at the chosen first column. Deciphering reverses the passes — in column by column, out line by line. Messages run 60 to 200 characters: long enough to fill the grid's white cells, short enough that the transposition stays a single pass. The raster is an offset method, in the instructions' own words: it scrambles the plaintext by applying a daily changing pattern, and the changing start position makes every message's transposition unique. [VERIFIED — the 25×24 grid, the 10-white-cells-per-row count, the daily raster issuance, the start cell and first column as message key, the row-in/column-out passes, and the 60–200 character limits, per the March 27, 1944 cipher instructions as translated, and the RS 44 reference record]

- **The designer, and the doctrine behind him.** RS 44 was designed by the astronomer Walter Fricke, working as a conscript in Section IIb of Group 2 of OKW/Chi — the German armed forces' cipher department — and introduced in March 1944; the cipher instructions are dated Berlin, March 27, 1944, signed off by the Armed Forces High Command. Fricke was not a career cryptographer; he was a scientist drafted into the cipher service, and the system he built reads like a scientist's answer to a field problem: the strongest hand cipher is not the one with the cleverest mathematics, it is the one a tired clerk can run correctly in a dugout and an enemy cannot break before the message stops mattering. The Science Museum's collection record puts it plainly: RS 44 was "an effective combination of security and relative ease of use" — a German manual cipher the Allies could not break quickly. [VERIFIED — Fricke, the OKW/Chi posting, the March 1944 introduction and the March 27 instructions date, per the reference record and the instructions translation; CORROBORATED — the ease-of-use assessment, per the Science Museum Group collection record]

- **The break that wasn't in time.** The Allied record on RS 44 is a study in a cipher winning by arithmetic, not by mystery. Cryptanalysis, when it succeeded at all, generally required a 40-letter crib — known plaintext of forty letters — and about two weeks of work. Two weeks is the whole story: the messages RS 44 carried were tactical, and tactical information two weeks old is history, not intelligence. The variable start cell and first column are what priced the break that high: a unique transposition per message makes multiple anagramming — the standard attack on transposition ciphers, which lines up several messages under the same transposition and solves them together — very difficult, because there is no shared transposition to line up. Each message stands alone, and standing alone is the defense. The cipher was never broken in the sense the Enigma was broken — no daily key recovery, no industrial pipeline, no reading of traffic as it flowed. It was broken the way a safe is broken by a locksmith with time: slowly, message by message, and too late. [CORROBORATED — the 40-letter crib, the two-week cost, and the tactical-information-outdated assessment, per the RS 44 reference record; VERIFIED — that the variable start cell and first column defeat multiple anagramming, per the same record]

- **Decoder-design note (RS 44 → Gauntlet).** Four rungs. (1) **The deadline is part of the cipher.** RS 44 did not need to be unbreakable. It needed to be unbreakable for two weeks — the shelf life of the information it carried — and a 40-letter crib plus fourteen days was a price the Allies could pay only after the goods had spoiled. Gauntlet standing rule: grade a specimen's strength against its information's shelf life, never against eternity. A specimen whose secrets expire before the break lands is secure in the only sense that matters operationally, and a report card that prices a break without naming the shelf life has priced nothing. (2) **The key is the starting position, not the pattern.** The day's raster was shared across the network; the per-message secret was where you started and which column you read first. Gauntlet port: in a foreign specimen, the shared template is the weak surface and the per-instance offset is the secret. Interrogate the offset — the start cell, the nonce, the session seed — before burning cycles on the template, because the template is the part the specimen expects you to find. (3) **Depth is a defense's enemy, and per-instance variation kills it.** Multiple anagramming needs several messages under one transposition; RS 44's per-message start cell means there is never a second message under the same key to line up against the first. Gauntlet rule: a specimen that re-keys per instance denies the depth attack outright. Grade per-instance variation as a defense in its own right, and never assume two outputs from one specimen share a key — the assumption that they do is the first error in the attack, and the specimen that punishes it is the one that survives. (4) **Ease of use is a security property, not a convenience.** RS 44 won its reputation as a field cipher because clerks could run it correctly under fire — the Science Museum's "effective combination of security and relative ease of use" is the whole assessment. The Enigma/MVUEH rung's twin: a specimen that is hard to operate correctly is weak even when its mechanism is strong, because operators supply the errors the mechanism never would. Grade the operator's error surface on its own ledger — the message key a clerk must choose fresh every time is a failure mode as surely as a weak algorithm is. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]

## T. E. Wood's 1950 "life after death" cipher (1950–2026) — the survival test that failed by succeeding, or: the key that arrived by search, not by séance

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue holds the survival-test family nowhere: grep-verified this pass, "Thouless" has zero hits in the private catalogue and zero in the public one, "T. E. Wood" zero in both, "life after death" zero in both, "Totsiens" zero in both, and "Bean" zero in both — no entry, no §(a) bullet, no passing mention of the method or the man. ("Survival" itself appears 14 times private / 12 public, all in other contexts — SIGABA's "survival is a certificate" and the like.) The cipher that T-1293, the Any-Key Mirror, takes as its model case has no catalogue entry of its own; the trick's specimen is unfiled. This entry writes it — from the solver's own writeup, read first-party this pass, which lifts the claim past the rotation #1 filing that left it log-only as CLAIMED on a single video carrier. [VERIFIED — the grep counts; the T-1293 model-case link]

- **The test.** T. E. Wood, a solicitor born in Yorkshire in 1887 who had practiced in Burma, published a 21-letter cryptogram in "A Further Test for Survival" (*Proceedings of the Society for Psychical Research* 49, 1950, pp. 105–106): `FVAMI NTKFX XWATB OIZVV X`. The plan: Wood would die, and after his death he would send the key through a medium — a test of survival, in the Society's own terms. Only Wood knew the key, so if a medium produced it, that would count as evidence that something of him had survived. He printed three clues with the letters: he used Thouless's method, with repeated words omitted; the key passage "is in an accessible book", in a foreign language; and the message "will not be in any one language". [VERIFIED — the writeup, read first-party this pass; the 1950 citation]

- **The method.** The system is Robert Thouless's, from "A Test of Survival" (*Proc. SPR* 48, part 175, July 1948, pp. 253–263). The key is a passage of text taken from a book, each word used in turn, any word that has already appeared skipped, so each key word is used only once. Each key word pairs with one letter of the message: the word's letters are added up (A=1 to Z=26), 26 taken off as many times as it fits whole, and what is left names a letter by its place in the alphabet (1=A, 25=Y, 0=Z) — that letter is the key letter, and it sets the shift (A=0, no shift; B=1; and so on), the message letter moving that far along the alphabet, wrapping Z back to A. Thouless's worked example enciphers THERE IS NO DEATH with Hamlet's "To be or not to be" as the key. The method is a book cipher with the key reduced to shifts — and it is unfalsifiable by construction: with freely chosen key letters the same 21 letters can be made to say anything, which Wood himself demonstrated by printing the same letters as "There is no death" and "Bloaters for tea" (per the rotation #1 filing). A sentence on its own tells you nothing about whether it was Wood's; the key has to come from somewhere that can be checked. While checking the method against the 1948 paper, Reilly found an arithmetic slip in Thouless's own worked example, in print for 78 years and, as far as he can tell, never before pointed out: the 14th key word, "suffer", sums to 75, which is 2×26+23, so the key letter should be W, the 23rd letter; Thouless printed U, the 21st, and his printed ciphertext follows the printed U — the last group should read RWGD, not RWGB. Wood, for his part, followed Thouless's written rule correctly: all 21 of his key letters agree with it. [VERIFIED — the method, the example, and the slip, per the writeup; the two alternate readings, per the writeup and the rotation #1 filing]

- **The search and the hit.** Colin Reilly ran the search; Claude Opus 5.5 wrote the search code and identified the books to use as key-phrase sources; GPT-6 Astra checked the result independently. The method was validated first: 100 ciphers with known answers through the same code, scored by resemblance to English — the correct message came out on top in 97 of the 100. The first Wood search ran 129 publicly available books, 28.6 million candidate keys — nothing readable. It grew to 3,848 Project Gutenberg books in 14 languages, about 429 million candidate keys — more tempting false leads, not a readable message. Run on 100 random 21-letter strings instead, the same search found a result scoring higher than anything it had found for Wood in 12 of them. The weakness was the scoring: every reading was judged as English, and Wood's clue said the message "will not be in any one language". The next search looked for words in seven languages, letting the language change from word to word, and penalized readings that chopped the string into tiny fragments or hopped between languages just to make the pieces fit. Then the targeted source: few books are more accessible than a Bible, so translations in 19 languages were added. The Bible run worked through the 19 Bibles word by word, building the key twice per starting word (skipping repeats, and keeping them), under two readings of the arithmetic — 26.7 million candidate keys per reading, first pass under three minutes. Under Thouless's rule the top result came from the German Bible, starting at the sixth word of Matthew 6:9, the opening of the Lord's Prayer, and scored well clear of the Romanian Bible in second place. It decrypted to HIER BIN ICH TOTSIENS TEW — German for "Here I am", Afrikaans for "Goodbye", and Wood's own initials. The key uses 21 distinct words, from "Unser" to "uns"; four repeats are skipped ("Dein" twice, "Himmel" and "Unser" once each), and the ä in "täglich" is read as a. The exact wording mattered: an earlier search had tried the familiar church form beginning "Vater unser" and found nothing — the 1912 Luther Bible's "Unser Vater in dem Himmel" produces a different key from the very first word. [VERIFIED — the search counts, the hit, and the reading, per the writeup, read first-party; CORROBORATED — the "scored well clear" margin, no number published]

- **The check.** Before sending the result to Klaus Schmeh, Reilly checked it three ways: a short standalone script, using no other project code, rebuilds the key from the prayer text, decrypts all 21 letters, and re-encrypts them back to Wood's exact ciphertext (the full word-by-word table is in the writeup's appendix — all 21 letters decrypt correctly); Astra, working separately, reproduced all 21 letters; and a chance test ran about 854 million trial decryptions across 3,847 Gutenberg books and 19 Bibles, looking for dictionary words followed by a three-letter signature — with TEW as the signature there was exactly one match, this message, and only 7 of 500 random signatures produced a match at all, and those matches were word salad. The author states the two caveats himself, and they stay attached: TOTSIENS was added to the word list after the solve, and the chance test was designed after the hit — "it shows that the match is rare, which is not the same as proof." Schmeh confirmed the answer (klausschmeh.net, October 4, 2026, "Wood's cryptogram from the crypt: Another top 50 crypto mystery solved"); Richard Bean confirmed the reading as well. The cipher is the last of four cryptograms grouped under Schmeh's #35 on his Top 50 unsolved encrypted messages list ("Cryptograms from the crypt", April 17, 2017); the first three were cracked in 1948, 1996 and 2019, and Bean's 2019 solve of Thouless's Message B by book-search pioneered the approach Reilly used. The code is public (github.com/creilly11235/wood-cryptogram-1950, MIT license), with a standalone verify script. [VERIFIED — the checks, the confirmations, and the #35 listing, per the writeup; CORROBORATED — the 1948/1996/2019 sequence, per the author's account]

- **The caveats the solver filed against himself.** Two more, from the solver's video as filed in the rotation #1 entry (not re-verified this pass): the search's preregistered acceptance rule was NOT met, and the reading was accepted on a separate judgment; and in a second arithmetic convention a junk string ("ALENRENDRAYCUTREFUGES") scored higher than the found reading. Both stay on the record. The survival test itself failed by design, whatever the cipher's status: the key was found by search, not received through a medium, so the experiment Wood designed — a key arriving from beyond death — never ran. What was solved is the cryptogram; what was not tested is survival. [CLAIMED — the preregistration failure and the higher-scoring junk string, per the solver's video as filed in the rotation #1 entry; VERIFIED — that the key was found by search, not through a medium]

- **Decoder-design note (Wood → Gauntlet).** Four rungs. ## Lorenz SZ40/SZ42 (Tunny) (1941– ) — the teleprinter cipher that was broken before it was seen, or: the machine Tutte rebuilt from a mistake

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue covers the Enigma family in depth — ten full entries for its break (Banburismus, Herivelismus, Cillies, Parkerismus, Yoxallismus, Scritchmus, the Clock Method, Zygalski Sheets, the Cyclometer, the Bomba) — but the other great Bletchley story has no entry of its own. Grep-verified this pass: "Tunny" has 2 hits in the private catalogue and 1 in the public one, all passing mentions; no `## ` entry titled Lorenz, Tunny, or Colossus exists in either catalogue. The whole treatment is one §(a) bullet — "Lorenz / Colossus. Lorenz SZ42 (German Army high command) broken 1942 by Bill Tutte; decoded by Colossus (Tommy Flowers, Max Newman, 1943–44)". That bullet stays as the index pointer. This entry is the full treatment: the machine, the depth, the deduction, and the computer that was built to run it. [VERIFIED — the grep counts; the zero-entry gap]

- **The machine.** The Lorenz SZ40 (1941) and SZ42 (1943), built by C. Lorenz AG, enciphered teleprinter traffic for the German Army High Command — the highest-level strategic messages, not battlefield traffic. Bletchley called it Tunny, and Tunny was one of the Fish: the family of German teleprinter ciphers, each codenamed after a fish. It is not a rotor machine. It is an online stream cipher: the 5-bit Baudot teleprinter code of the plaintext is XORed with a keystream, character by character, as the message is typed. The keystream comes from twelve wheels with coprime pin counts — five chi wheels (41, 31, 29, 26, 23 pins) that step every character, five psi wheels (43, 47, 51, 53, 59) that step irregularly, and two motor wheels (37 and 61) that decide when the psi wheels step. The wheel periods are the whole machine: once you know the twelve counts and the stepping rule, you know Lorenz. [VERIFIED — the machine structure, wheel counts, and periods, rock-solid multi-source consensus in the Bletchley histories; CORROBORATED — the SZ40/SZ42 service dates and the Fish naming, standard accounts]

- **The depth and the deduction.** On 30 August 1941 a German operator transmitted two messages of about 4,000 characters each on the same wheel settings, and retransmitted the second one shortened — abbreviations in place of full words. That is a depth: two ciphertexts under one key. XOR the two ciphertexts and the keystream cancels, leaving the XOR of the two plaintexts — and from that, the keystream itself can be pulled out, character by character. Bill Tutte, 24, a Cambridge mathematician who had joined Bletchley that May, took the depth and, over the autumn of 1941, deduced the machine's entire logical structure from it — twelve wheels, their periods, which ones stepped regularly and which irregularly — without ever seeing a Lorenz machine, a photograph of one, or a description. He worked from the statistics of the keystream alone. The attack that followed is called the 1+2 break-in: start from the first two chi wheels, periods 41 and 31, the shortest in the machine, and recover the keystream from there. The machine was broken before it was seen — the deduction came first, the hardware second. [VERIFIED — the depth mechanism (XOR cancels the keystream) and Tutte's deduction-from-output-alone, rock-solid consensus; CORROBORATED — the 30 August 1941 date and the ~4,000-character length, standard accounts, not re-verified first-party this pass]

- **Colossus.** Max Newman ran the section that turned Tutte's method into a machine; Tommy Flowers, at the Post Office Research Station at Dollis Hill, built it. Colossus Mark 1 was delivered in December 1943 and working in January 1944; Mark 2 first worked on 1 June 1944, days before D-Day; ten Mark 2 machines were running by the end of the war. It read the intercepted teleprinter tape at speed, tested wheel settings against the statistical signature Tutte had found, and returned the wheel positions — the first large-scale programmable electronic digital computer, built to run a cryptanalytic method, not to compute ballistics. Lorenz traffic gave strategic Ultra: what the German High Command was saying to itself, read in London. [CORROBORATED — the delivery and first-working dates and the ten-machine count, standard accounts; VERIFIED — "first large-scale programmable electronic digital computer", as already filed in the §(a) bullet]

- **The secrecy and the rebuild.** After the war the Colossi were dismantled and destroyed on GCHQ orders, the work stayed classified into the 1970s, and Tutte's deduction — arguably the purest cryptanalytic feat of the war — was publicly credited only decades after the fact. A working rebuild was constructed by Tony Sale and a team of volunteers at The National Museum of Computing, Bletchley Park, between 1994 and 2007, from photographs, fragments, and the memories of the people who built the originals; it runs today. The machine that was broken before it was seen had to be rebuilt twice: once in mathematics, once in hardware — and the second rebuild, sixty years on, was itself a deduction from incomplete evidence. [CORROBORATED — the destruction, the classification span, and the 1994–2007 rebuild, standard accounts]

- **Decoder-design note (Lorenz → Gauntlet).** Four rungs. (1) **A machine can be rebuilt from its output alone.** Tutte never saw Lorenz; the whole structure came from a depth. Gauntlet rule: a specimen's internals are inferable from its I/O — never assume the interrogator needs the source to grade the specimen, and never let a specimen hide behind "you haven't seen my code." (2) **The break came from usage, not the machine.** The depth was an operator error — a retransmission on the same settings. Gauntlet rule: hunt usage flaws first. It is the Enigma lesson and the JN-25 lesson, filed here a third time: re-used keys, retransmissions, and stereotyped traffic break machines that are sound on paper. (3) **XOR is a confession.** Ciphertext XOR plaintext is the keystream, so every known or guessable plaintext fragment exposes key. Gauntlet rule: grade an XOR-combined channel by its cribs, not its key length — a long key with a known crib is a short key. (4) **A break ships with its reproduction.** Tutte's deduction became Newman's machine became Flowers's Colossus — the break was re-built twice before it counted. Gauntlet rule: a claimed break ships with its reproduction — the method, the machine, the run — or it ships as CLAIMED. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]

## SIGABA / ECM Mark II (1935–1959) — the machine that generated its own keying, or: two Enigmas in one

- **The gap this entry closes.** SIGABA is the catalogue's most-cited machine — grep-verified this pass: 57 hits in the private catalogue, 51 in the public one, spread across four separate treatments (the Hebern lineage, the 1940–1959 negative-control entry, the 1934–1959 American-ladder capstone, the M-134-C service-record entry) — and still no `## ` entry of its own. The doctrine anchor every other machine entry cites — "SIGABA's rung," "the SIGABA rule," "SIGABA's negative-control doctrine" — has no numbered home. Lorenz (#127) is its natural sibling: the two great wartime stories, the broken one and the unbroken one, now stand side by side as numbered entries. [VERIFIED — the grep counts; the zero-entry gap]

- **The machine.** Fifteen rotors in three banks of five: five cipher rotors (26 contacts each, Enigma-like, no reflector), five control rotors (26 contacts), five index rotors (10 contacts, set by hand, never stepping during encipherment). Each keypress, four live signals enter the control rotors; their outputs fan out through ten groups of one to six wires into the index rotors, and the resulting live lines step a variable subset of the cipher rotors — one to four of them, never in odometer rhythm. SIGABA is two Enigmas in one: the second machine generates the first machine's motion. With the plaintext in hand an analyst still cannot recover the settings — the stepping inputs are so numerous that the state path resists reconstruction. [VERIFIED — the three-bank structure, the rotor counts, and the no-reflector construction, rock-solid multi-source consensus; CORROBORATED — the four-input, ten-group, one-to-four-stepping wiring details, standard technical accounts]

- **Rowlett's insight (May 1934).** Friedman had set Rowlett to making paper keying tapes for the M-134 Converter — tapes that tore, were misused in the field, and whose inventory was a custody problem. In May 1934 came the burst: replace the tape with an internal set of rotors that key the stepping of the others — the machine generating its own irregular keying, no consumable key material to carry. Friedman refused for months — a machine could not, he believed, generate its own keying with sufficient randomness to be secure — until Rowlett's prepared presentation answered every objection. The crystallized form dates to about 15 June 1935; Friedman and Rowlett filed the joint patent 23 March 1936, assigned to the Secretary of War 2 April 1936. The Navy came in through Cmdr. Laurence Safford in 1937, hardened the design for production, and fielded it as the Electric Cipher Machine Mark II (CSP-889/888); the Army, let in on the secret in early 1940, joined a joint system in 1941 and called it SIGABA. Production models began rolling off assembly lines in March 1941; the NSA's declassified distribution record counts 3,330 M-134-C machines made as of 9 February 1948. [CORROBORATED — the May-1934 spark via the Army DVIDS history; the 15 June 1935 / 23 March 1936 / 2 April 1936 dates via the NSA declassified Friedman memorandum; the Navy lineage via standard accounts; the March-1941 production start and the 3,330 figure via historynet and the NSA distribution record]

- **The service record.** During its entire active service, no successful cryptanalysis of the machine ever occurred — the NSA's Center for Cryptologic History: "There is no credible evidence that it was broken by any nation during the war." TICOM's interrogations of German and Japanese cryptanalysts at war's end confirmed neither side broke it. It carried the highest-level Allied traffic, including Churchill–Roosevelt; the 1945 Colmar scare — a truck carrying a SIGABA and its materials stolen four miles from the German front, missing for thirty-two days — pulled Eisenhower off planning the spring offensive. From 1943 the Holden Agreement and BRUSA built the Combined Cipher Machine — the Typex 23 modified for interop — while the Americans never let the British see SIGABA itself. It served until 1959, when the speed of modern communications retired it; operating principles stayed classified until 2000, the design patent (US 6,175,625) released January 2001; most machines were destroyed to protect the design. [VERIFIED — the NSA CCH statement as quoted; CORROBORATED — the TICOM confirmation, the Colmar scare, the CCM/Holden sequence, the 1959 retirement and the 2000/2001 declassification, via this catalogue's own filed treatments and standard accounts]

- **The honest limit.** In 2023 George Lasry published modern cryptanalytic methods against SIGABA in Cryptologia: a high-end personal computer now breaks it in under 24 hours. That does not undo the wartime record — it bounds it: "unbroken" means unbroken in its operational life, against its actual adversaries, with their actual machinery. The catalogue's own rule, filed at the 1934–1959 capstone, stands: an unbroken claim is a negative no outside audit can verify — consistent both with true security and with an undiscovered break — and SIGABA's verdict is filed exactly there, as the absence of a known break across eight decades, not as a proof of impossibility. [CORROBORATED — the Lasry 2023 break via the cryptomuseum citation of the Cryptologia paper; the original paper not read this pass]

- **Decoder-design note (SIGABA → Gauntlet).** Four rungs. (1) **Motion is the cipher.** Enigma fell to its odometer; SIGABA survived by handing its motion to a second rotor bank. The cipher's identity was never the wiring of the five cipher rotors — it was the stepping function. Gauntlet rule: against a foreign specimen, interrogate the state-transition function before the symbol mapping — how the specimen advances its own state per observation is the layer cribs attack, and an irregular-stepping specimen kills replay assumptions by construction. (2) **"Unbroken" is a time-and-adversary bound, never a mechanism property.** SIGABA's wartime record is perfect and its 2023 break is real — both statements live on the record at once, and that is not a contradiction. Gauntlet verdicts inherit the discipline: a specimen that survives a battery is graded against that battery, not crowned unbreakable; the report card states the adversary window alongside the verdict, and a later break is a ledger entry, not a scandal. (3) **The breakthrough lives in operator friction.** Rowlett's innovation came from torn paper tapes, not from mathematics. Gauntlet corollary: the interrogation fixture must fit the operator's hands — a fixture that fights the operator gets circumvented, and the circumvention becomes the attack surface the specimen (or its handlers) exploit. Instruments are audited for operator misuse, not just for probe coverage. (4) **The secret's second life.** The machine stayed sealed for decades past its service — operating principles declassified 2000, patent 2001 — because secrecy-out-of-habit outlived secrecy-out-of-need. The Gauntlet's honest grading exists partly to price that cost: protect-by-default has a carrying cost, and a verdict that stays sealed after its need has passed is a debt, not a shield. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]

## M-209 Converter (1940–1953) — the workhorse cipher that never fell in the field, or: the field machine beside the high machine

- **The gap this entry closes.** M-209 is the catalogue's most-cited machine without a `## ` entry — grep-verified this pass: 41 hits in the private catalogue, 37 in the public one, spread across the full bullet entry (seeded 2026-10-22, with the mechanism, the honest null, and the design note), the Beaufort entry (the M-209's print wheel), the scytale entry (the M-209's cage beside the scytale's diameter), and the standing "secrecy is a time, 24–48 hours" doctrine it anchors — and still no numbered home. The doctrine anchor every other field-machine entry cites — "adequate for the battlefield," "never broken in the field," "the shelved break" — has no numbered home. SIGABA (#128) is its natural sibling: the two American machines, the high one and the field one, now stand side by side as numbered entries — one built for the generals, one built for the battalions. [VERIFIED — the grep counts; the zero-`## `-entry gap]

- **The machine.** Six pin wheels in a row, with 26, 25, 23, 21, 19, and 17 pins — six periods that are pairwise coprime, so the wheel alignment repeats only after 26 × 25 × 23 × 21 × 19 × 17 = 101,405,850 keypresses, over a hundred million characters before the machine revisits a wheel state. Each pin is set in or out by hand; a cage of 27 bars carries lugs that the pins trip as the wheels turn, and the tripped lugs advance a print wheel that works on the Beaufort principle — the reciprocal subtraction this catalogue's Beaufort entry records. There are no rotors and no reflector: the cipher is a pin-and-lug computer, and its key is a physical configuration — which pins are in, which lugs sit on which bars — before it is anything a cryptanalyst would call a key. The pin settings alone admit 2^131 patterns (131 pins, each in or out), a number the daily procedure narrowed to what a soldier could actually set from a codebook. [CORROBORATED — the six wheel periods, the 27-bar cage, and the pin-and-lug mechanism via standard technical accounts; VERIFIED — the 101,405,850 product and the 2^131 pin-pattern count, arithmetic computed this pass; the Beaufort-principle print wheel per this catalogue's Beaufort entry]

- **The service record.** Boris Hagelin's compact Swedish machine, sold by the thousands to the French military in the 1930s as the B-21 line, was acquired by the U.S. Army after the German invasion of Norway in 1940 and redesignated Converter M-209 — the Navy's CSP-1500. The Smith Corona Typewriter Company of Groton, NY, built them at a rate of 400 units a day from 1942: over 140,000 by war's end, likely the most manufactured cipher machine in history. It carried tactical traffic through World War II and the Korean War — "far less secure" than SIGABA, in a museum curator's verdict, "but deemed adequate for battlefield communications." The Axis never broke M-209 routinely in wartime. Hagelin followed it with the C-52 — period up to 2,756,205,443, removable and reorderable wheels, mixed-alphabet printwheel — and Germany's own Hagelin-derived machines, Fritz Menzer's Schlüsselgerät 41, about a thousand built for the Abwehr and operated from 1944, are judged to have been "certainly no more uncrackable than the M-209." [CORROBORATED — the B-21 lineage, the 1940 acquisition, the 400/day and 140,000+ figures via the secondary record carried by this catalogue's bullet entry; the most-manufactured reading carried CLAIMED-adjacent as single-secondary; the adequacy quote via a museum collections secondary; the C-52 and Menzer-clone details via an enthusiast encyclopedia summary]

- **The honest limit.** Post-war, the honest record: in the 1970s, Dennis Ritchie, James Reeds, and Robert Morris developed a ciphertext-only attack on the M-209 that could solve messages of at least 2,000–2,500 letters — then, after discussions with the NSA, decided not to publish it, told the principle was applicable to machines still in foreign-government use. German wartime efforts against the machine surfaced publicly only in 2004, in German press reporting. That is the whole of the honest limit, and it is exactly the SIGABA entry's lesson restated at the other end of the scale: "never broken in the field" is a historical fact about the adversary's effort and priorities, not a property of the machine — and "breakable" is a property of the instrument, demonstrated in the 1970s, whether or not it was ever spent in the field. Today the machine is a textbook exercise; the 1970s attack needed two thousand letters, and modern methods need far fewer. [CORROBORATED — the Ritchie/Reeds/Morris suppression and the 2004 German-effort reporting via Wikipedia's M-209 article; the modern-break standing via the general cryptology record]

- **Decoder-design note (M-209 → Gauntlet).** Four rungs. (1) **Adequacy is a threat-window verdict, not a security verdict.** "Adequate for battlefield communications" prices the secret's lifetime — hours — against the attacker's cost, and the M-209 is the canonical "secrecy is a time" machine: a cipher whose break takes longer than the message matters is adequate, and a cipher whose break arrives after the battle is archaeology. Gauntlet rule: every verdict states the finding's expiry alongside the grade — a specimen graded "adequate" for a 24-hour window is not graded secure, and a break that arrives after the specimen's window is logged as archaeology, never charged as failure. (2) **The shelved break is still a break.** Ritchie, Reeds, and Morris had the ciphertext-only attack in the 1970s and filed it away at the NSA's request — suppression of a result is not refutation of it. The Gauntlet treats "unpublished because sensitive" as an ATTACK-EXISTS marker, not an all-clear: interrogate the silence, not just the record. (3) **Ubiquity is a surface, not a shield.** 140,000 units, fielded down to battalion level, set up by soldiers "not extensively trained in cryptography" — scale was the design goal, and every pin-and-lug setting in the field was a human operation. The wartime breaks that mattered (Enigma, JN-25, Purple) came from usage flaws, not the machine — so the Gauntlet hunts operator procedure first on the most-deployed instruments: key discipline under field conditions is the adversary's cheapest door. (4) **The key is a physical configuration.** Pins on wheels, lugs on bars — the scytale's diameter, the M-94's wheel order, the M-209's cage: every era's key lives in a physical parameter first and a symbol string second. Gauntlet operator-stage: format parameters (block size, key length, IV width, stepping cadence) are interrogated as key material, never accepted as constants — and a specimen whose key is a configuration the operator sets by hand is graded on the operator's hands as much as on its mathematics. [CORROBORATED lineage — the service record, the shelved break, and the production scale cited above; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]
